reviews.text:
Read the review by Doc Opp; I think he covers it quite nicely. He explains how Tolkien was the forefather of fantasy writing, and why that makes his books important. He also shares his opinion that the historical importance sort of causes people to overlook that Tolkien couldn't write worth beans.

Opp posits that perhaps it has something to do with the concept of heroism being different in Tolkien's days than it is now. I'm not sure I agree with that. I mean I agree that his characters are a study in perserverance without being able to really fight or do anything but perservere, I just don't know that I buy that it's a sign of the times. I think Tolkien was just boring.

I don't disagree, also, that the Shannara series is essentially the same storyline with a better writer at the helm.

My venom towards Tolkien is greater than Opp's perhaps because we read for different reasons. I have very little patience with writers who have great ideas or imaginations when it comes to the physical world, but can't get inside the head of a person to save their lives and thus can't tell a story. This sort of writer is often found in sci-fi/fantasy, because the genre is geared to reward the most innovative and plausible inventing of a future or past timescape.

If guys like Opp were always doing the commentating I might not hate Tolkien with such a passion, but unfortunately the world is filled with people who don't read sci-fi but who recalled their lit teacher spoke Tolkien's name once and probably said something about how he was the father of modern fantasy, and those people went on to shout Tolkien's name from the rooftops to the extent that a movie even got made out of it. Now the movie I could actually stomach (a little) because Hollywood realized they couldn't completely bore the pants off of people and still make money. But I digress.

I cannot conceive of any reason one would read these novels unless they were forced e.g. for a class. And even then, it'd better be a history class and not a writing class, unless the objective was to teach how not to write. There's no pace, no character development, the focus shifts between groups of characters ala Robert Jordan without any of Jordan's redeeming qualities (although Jordan certainly has faults as well).

The most compelling reason to read these novels is so that you can rip someone a new one when they bring up Tolkien by making a point by point case where you describe all the things he does wrong.

Let me put it this way, I have read some of the most God-awful books in my time. I mean when I was younger I would read a phone book if it was handy. But I could not finish the Fellowship of the Rings.

Comparing Tolkien to Asimov is just...I mean that's like comparing me to Asimov. I have an imagination and so does Asimov, comparison ended. Asimov came up with a plausible future that was interesting, and then he wrote characters within that adventure that were compelling. Caves of Steel is brilliant because whatshisface the detective is sort of an everyman and Asimov deals with things such as embarrassment because your Dad's job doesn't rate you high enough to eat at the right hydroponics diner. I'm mangling things, but you get the point. Asimov may have been the best ever at having really cool ideas and not wasting them by forgetting to write about people.

I hate Tolkien, I blame him for his vacuous and enraging fan base, I blame him for every author that followed him that spent 5 hours describing a blade of grass, I hate him for taking a genre that I like and making me want to vomit on it, even if he was the first. It makes me want to burn my entire fantasy bookshelf down to the ground.

That's my review.
I don't understand the phenomenon around this series. I find it slow, long and boring. It's not for me.

Ancient non-governmental organization conspires to commit perhaps the ultimate act of terrorism in world literature by setting up a crack cosmopolitan team to destroy the primary resource of the predominant sovereignty in the setting, which team includes four barefoot ragamuffins with a taste for the sweet leaf, four worthless aristocratic sons placed therein as nepotistic favors, and a pious greybeard who gets ganked in his first fight.

OK...NO ONE can say that I didn't give Lord of the Rings a good try.

I read The Hobbit (it was ok), watched the first Hobbit movie (again ok), tried to watch the first Lord of the Rings movie 3x but fell asleep each time and just read Fellowship of the Ring. It's just not my thing...and even though it's ok for it to not be my thing it's one of those things where if you don't like it people are all up in arms saying, "what do you mean? it's a classic! If you don't like this you don't like true literature/fantasy/ect, don't you know a good film when you see it?" and similar pretentiousness.

Not that my friends would say this but just know I TRIED and I TRIED DAMN HARD, but I'm not going to be a sheeple and I'm not going to lie. : /

Why didn't I like the book specifically, for the same reason I didn't like the movie, it drags so very much! I found everything to too detailed, and wasn't terribly interested in the events or characters. For the record I do not hate the characters, it's just that nothing draws me to them and it doesn't help that I don't really care what they're doing (or care for how long it is taking).

I do respect Tolkien for his contribution to the fantasy genre and literature, but that respect does not necessarily lead to any enjoyment.

I give up. I fuckin' give up.

After four weeks of struggling through this book, I've decided life is too short.

How it ever became a beloved classic is beyond me.

I tried so hard: I trudge, trudged, and trudged through the pages, laden with Tolkien's flowery prose and bogged down in descriptions and details. It was painful. Very painful.

I did watch the movies years ago and loved them much.

I enjoyed reading the Hobbit... it was smooth sailing.

Perhaps, I'd try the audio book (I'm I not merciful?)

I HATE THIS BOOK!
i got it 3 years ago but never got around to reading it because it seemed so boring
but since everyone loves it so much i decided to read it
THIS WAS AWFUL! The whole book could have been 250 pages shorter if the author had removed the stupid history references which are of no use and if he had just written "they walked till they reached so and so place" the characters kept walking and camping for 95% of the book >:( walk walk walk walk walk walk walk walk walk eat, sleep, walk walk walk walk walk walk walk walk walk battle then walk walk walk walk walk walk walk
AWFUL! hated it~!

Every few years I let a different well-meaning friend talk me into picking this up again, and every time I let my sense of sport trump my better judgement, I end up reaching the same conclusion I did when I was twelve: this book is unreadable. By me. I am evidently a tiny and aberrant minority.

First off, I should admit that I am hobbit-intolerant. I can't stand those little suckers, their gross feet, and their obnoxiously idyllic Shire. They are romanticized, hairy footed little people, best described as simple-minded reactionary caricatures. The elves are not much better, with their magical magicalness and aloof aloofness, but at least they don't have gross feet. They're just bigots. An interesting trade-off, no? Then there are all those epic mandudes doing long-winded yet epic mandude things at an excruciating pace, which Tolkien obviously mistook for a mythic feel and epic scale, a mistake that instills in me the raging and irrational desire to resurrect the author for the sole purpose of beating him back into the grave with his magnum opus.

I am not going to talk about Gandalf. Gandalf is better in the movies, because Sir Ian.

So, the half star (just half; Goodreads is lying to you about this rating) is for the entertainment value I derive out of raging about this book. We all get our kicks where we can.

This book is among the most tedious books I have ever had the misfortune to read. The only way I see that people can enjoy this is that people saw the hollywood blockbuster by Peter Jackson. When people see Elijah Wood and Orlando Bloom, they feel as if they must read the book in order to fully understand the boring intricacies in order to be wise. If you are planning on reading this book, do not waste your time. There are long areas of exposition that you will glaze over, and the rest of the series relies on your assumed knowledge of these chapters.

The Fellowship of the Ring

Never again will I read another J.R.R. Tolkien book. This was the second worst book I've ever read - surpassed only by The Scarlet Letter!

Fuck Tom Bombadil and the horse he rode in on. Here's a plot hole for you: I have this wicked ring that does some wicked stuff to everyone...we need to destroy it! It's way hard to do this and it's going to rock the ring-bearer's shit if he does this. OOOOORRRRR we can give it to Tom Fucking Bombadil and let him destroy it as it has no effect on his stupid ADHD-having moronic brain. But no. We'll choose to create an epic story despite this.

Horrible!

Did I enjoy it? No.

Would I recommend it? Only to an enemy.

I really, really did not like this. I feel like I need to give it some credit for being one of the first, so for that I will give it 1.5/5.

This was really slow. I have heard a lot of people say that before, but I really had no idea how slow. I was at it for days before Frodo even left the shire. He spent so long just talking to Gandalf and deciding what to do. Before anything even happened. And then when they got to the elves they were there so long talking and making more decisions. And there was so much freaking singing!

And through all this I feel like I never really learned who Sauron was or what the ring did. I reread the parts that discussed and it still seemed so vague. The world building was poor. I heard so much about Tolkien's amazing world and now I am wondering where it is. Do you have to read all the extra content and history books in order to make sense of the first book in the series? That should definitely not be the case. And what I saw of the world, Middle Earth, wasn't that great. I have read high fantasy with way more interesting worlds and more diverse species. This is where is gets a little credit for being one of the first, but I guess that just means it hasn't aged that well when you compared it to all the great fantasy that have come out since.

This is my second attempt at reading this book. I tried reading it about 15 years ago but only got about 100 pages in before I was bored to death. So I decided to try again, and managed to finish it this time, but it really did not improve my opinion of it at all. In fact, it made it worse. I will not be continuing this series.

Lạy hồn, quyển này:
80%: đi bộ trong rừng, ngâm thơ và ca hát, cảnh thiên nhiên, đi bộ tiếp

Mà khúc 20% đó so với truyện fantasy bây giờ thì cũng quá bình thường rồi, không có gì đột phá cả. Nhưng phải công tâm xét việc quyển này đi đầu cho fantasy nên ok có thể hiểu được, dù sao đọc cũng hay, có ý nghĩa.
Mình biết là mình không nên kỳ vọng nhiều màn hành động hay gì, nên từ từ chill tận hưởng hành trình này nọ. Ok cái đó mình hoàn toàn hiểu, nhưng 80% lận đó... chỉ có đi bộ trong rừng...
Mình sẽ thử đọc tiếp tập 2,3 do mình coi phim rồi nên biết những phần sau sẽ có nhiều chuyện xảy ra hơn.
Còn quyển 1 thấy tốt nhất nên xem phim. Lol không ngờ có ngày mình recommend phim chuyển thể hơn là sách.
I'm so glad this is over. The end.

1.0 The following rant is from an email that I wrote in January 2002, where I made some pretty blasphemous confessions about a Fantasy classic. I have recently given the genre another try with the "Game of Thrones" books, and have been so impressed, that it may change my perception of the genre entirely. So perhaps I will revisit this subject. But this is how I felt at the time:

I am 'Bored of the Rings', and I've had it with the Hobbits!!

With the movies and all, I finally decided to read one of the Lord of the Rings books. I am 150 or so pages into the first book of the trilogy, "Fellowship of the Ring", and am bored to tears. I did something that I never do, I skipped ahead to about page 250 to see if things would pick up and found passages that seem almost identical to page 150.

Does anything ever HAPPEN in this book? The Hobbits are described walking across the land on their mysterious journey, singing songs, and engaging in idle Hobbit chit-chat. Every now and then, they run into someone, and you anticipate that something might actually HAPPEN. But instead they just engage in more uneventfull chatter (in their quaint, annoying Hobbit-speak, or in their equally quaint but equally annoying Elf-speak or Dwarf-speak, depending on who is doing the talking), discussing dangers that they think MIGHT befall them on their journey. This gets your hopes up, but in the end, they just say their goodbyes, and start walking again. 100 (and I suspect 200) pages later they are doing the same thing.

So then I began thinking that maybe the attraction of the book is not so much the plot as the prose and character development. That would be ok with me. I can appreciate fine literature on occasion. Maybe this should be judged as a true literary work, more along the lines of Toni Morrison than John Grishom...

WRONG!! Not only are the Hobbits boring, they are boring and one-dimensional.

I don't get it. This is supposed to be a classic. People rave about how they have read it a dozen times. It affirms my general belief that sci-fi/fantasy readers have low expectations in general where novels are concerned. They are more impressed with gimmicks, and the trappings of whatever new universe is being described than the normal mechanics of good writing or even just good storytelling. It allows mediocre writers to thrive. Its true to a lesser degree with Horror writers when they are writing Non-Earthbound stories. Outside of Stephen King and possibly Clive Barker (WeaveWorld), I have yet to read a Non-Earthbound story that I felt represented truly good writing. The authors all rely way too much on the crutch of whatever Gimmick they are offering. This is why my favorite Stephen King books are those that are more reality-based.

Well, so much for my "Rings" exasperation (I had a similar first impression of Dune, but haven't really given that one a fair chance yet).

Am I way off-base here?
I guess there's always the movie..

Look, I tried to read this book. I really did. But halfway through it (long past the place when I really should have stopped), I just can’t go on. It’s just not good. I have never in my life read something so incredibly boring. I don’t care about any of the characters because all of the book is dedicated to histories and tales that happened long before the characters lived, and very little is dedicated to developing the characters inter- or intra-personally. Honestly, reading this book was a miserable, torturous experience for me. I found Bilbo somewhat interesting and nothing since then was really enjoyable.
i fucking hate hobbits and i also fucking hate gandalf. they walk and walk and walk some more and nothing happens.

In brief, this is the story of physically and mentally weak half-humans who have willingly submitted themselves to the tyranny of societal obligation. The story begins with capitalist hero Bilbo Baggins planning a lavish birthday party for himself and his freeloading nephew Frodo. Every half-human in the village is invited to behold the greatness of Bilbo's wealth, and Bilbo calls in all his markers, even securing the services of a wizard, to ensure that the lazy villagers are suitably impressed. At the party our hero hands out extravagant gifts to all his guests, which on the surface may seem an altruistic misstep, but in actuality is a brilliant way for Bilbo to impress upon his inferiors just how much better he is than they. He then proceeds to give a speech in which he cleverly insults everyone, then disappears, thereby ensuring that he gets the last laugh. At this point of the novel I am still a fan of Bilbo; he is a rich half-man who has learned how to live his life for himself and use his vast wealth to get what he wants when he wants it. The other mediocre half-humans envy his power and importance, and like all Takers try to elevate the value of their mediocrity so as to devalue Bilbo's greatness. But Bilbo has stood strong against their vile attempts to tear him down for sixty-odd years, laughing in their pitiful faces all that time. I have only one small worry; Bilbo's soft spot for his do-nothing nephew.

After the party we discover that Bilbo plans to leave the village forever, and to bequeath his vast personal fortune to Frodo, who has done nothing to earn it. All he plans to keep is one small ring. While packing Bilbo is confronted by the wizard Gandalf, who forces him to leave the ring to Frodo. All my respect for Bilbo is now gone. Not only has he given everything he owns to his lazy nephew, but he has also allowed himself to be dominated by someone else's will. On the other hand I feel that Gandalf has potential; the way he used his great personal power to break Bilbo's will impressed me. Sadly this impression would not last.

Bilbo is now gone from the story, and it is at this point that we begin our journey with the pathetic Frodo. To be brief about it Frodo discovers that the ring his uncle left him is in fact extraordinarily powerful, and instead of taking that power for himself he decides to travel with his friends, Sam, Merry, and Perry, to the collectivist enclave of Riverdell, where the fate of the ring, Frodo's personal property, will be decided by people who have no ownership claim to it. Along the way they run into trouble and have to be saved by the powerful hippie Thomas Bombadil. Bombadil refuses to journey with the half-humans, presumably because he needs to tend to his marijuana plants, and thankfully we never see him again. Before the group reaches Riverdell we are introduced to two more characters of note; Aragorn, a failure constantly whining about about his family's lost glory rather than making something of himself, and Glorfindel, an incredibly powerful elf. Once at Riverdell Frodo bows to the demands of a council of bureaucrats, who decide that the ring of power should be destroyed. Why this should be done is never clearly explained; all we are given is some leftist jibber-jabber about the corrosive nature of power. A group of disparate persons, the titular fellowship, is chosen to take the ring to a volcano and throw it in. Startlingly Glorfindel is not chosen to be in this group, though the much less powerful elf Legoland is. Only one person from amongst this fellowship is in any way intriguing. Boromir is the prince of some place or other, and he wants to use the ring to destroy his enemies. Of course the pantywaists who comprise the rest of the fellowship shout him down. They would rather see the ring destroyed than allow Boromir, or anyone else, to achieve personal power and distinguish themselves from the pedestrian masses.

What follows in an insipid and uninspired story of weak-willed people constantly sacrificing themselves on the alter of the Greater Good. Only one character, the ostensible antagonist Sauron, acts in his own rational self-interest, while we the readers are treated to several hundred pages of disturbingly short-sighted protagonists and their naïvely altruistic philosophies. One can only hope that as this story continues into the next two novels, which I will not read, Frodo will finally wake up and utilize the ring for his own personal profit, or failing that, Sauron will regain the ring, which belonged to him originally, and destroy those who oppose him. Likely though the story will not end that way. How exactly it will end I do not know, or care to know. What I do know however is this: if Bilbo had left the ring to the Sackville-Bagginses instead of his worthless nephew Frodo none of us would have had to suffer through this travesty.

Por fin! Después De una eternidad pude terminar este libro. Me siento triste porque definitivamente odie cada parte de el y de verdad creí que sería un 5 estrellas.

Entiendo su importancia en la fantasía moderna (justo por eso lo quería leer) y entiendo la construcción del mundo pero me quedó muchísimo a deber, tenía esperanza que el final levantara el evento pero nope. Para mi es el primer libro que 100% la película es mucho mejor.

Mis problemas con el libro:

- Este es un gusto personal pero la narración de Tolkien definitivamente no es mi estilo, me transporta a otro lugar pero no al libro literalmente leía una frase y me ponía a pensar en otras cosas en lo que fuese menos en lo que estaba leyendo ,creí que no estaba en el mood de leer pero creo que los 20 días que tarde en terminarlo definitivamente hubo tiempo suficiente para entrar en el mood lector.

- Es tremendamente descriptivo, le deberían dar un premio por poder describir senderos y prados de mil maneras diferentes y la verdad es que no era necesario, se entiende que en su viaje a tierras lejanas de la comarca pasarían por partes con praderas y laderas. Si se editaran las partes que están de más son pedos sería mínimo la mitad del libro.

- Es tremendamente aburrido! Al ser tan descriptivo le quita el ritmo a la historia pero, aunque ese sea el estilo de narración del autor, también la historia en sí es lenta por ejemplo cuando Frodo se entera que debe de sacar el anillo de la comarca en la película en la misma escena se va de ella pero en el libro pasan 9 años antes de que suceda. Y esta bien puedo leer libros que exploren más a los personajes y que no haya tanta acción, pero esto no le añadía nada a la historia y es fantasía por eso creo que absolutamente no funcionó para mi. Y quiero decir que si lo intenté, traté de leerlo en físico y digital y como no me concentraba al mismo tiempo escuchaba el audiolibro y aún así no funcionó 🙌🏻

- Los hobbits son muy aburridos (son palabras de los elfos, no mías). Creo que mi problema es que no los tomaba en serio, son súper caricaturescos y aunque si explica un poco más el libro porque un hobbit es el ideal para ser el portador del anillo, no hacen nada más que meterse en problemas y alguien más tiene que rescatarles! Es el peor héroe de la historia, siempre he tenido un issue con Harry Potter porque me parecía que no era tan buen personaje principal pero Frodo definitivamente lo destronó. Las partes que más disfrute fueron las de Gandalf aunque también lo exageran creo que tiene mucha más coherencia.

- Las problemáticas son repetitivas y se resuelven fácilmente, hubo partes donde parecía un episodio de Dora la exploradora y que se resolvían con Frodo diciéndoles zorro no te lo lleves a los jinetes de Sauron (juro que si hay una escena donde pasa) y aunque después hay una mini explicación de porque sucede, dude es doloroso leer una escena así de estupida.

- Me hizo darme cuenta de un pet peeve que nunca había notado, odio con todo mi ser que los libros incluyan canciones, esto en la película me pareció increíble sobre todo las de los elfos, pero aquí la mayoría no agregaron nada a la trama y además hay una fucking canción casi en cada página.

- Aunque un libro sea parte de una saga debe de ser auto conclusivo, entiendo que el plot principal no se resuelva pero el primer libro termina súper anti climático (no está la pelea final de la película, supongo que se desarrolla en el siguiente libro) y simplemente sucede lo que me hace pensar que literalmente los tres libros son una sola historia que está dividida en tres.

Resumiéndolo fue doloroso de leer, por primera vez pensé en darle dnf a un libro que llevaba más del 50% leído. Obviamente no me torturare con el resto de la saga y mejor solo veré las películas (solo he visto la primera pero creo que el guionista y el director merecen un premio por hacer un libro tan aburrido parezca que si tiene acción y tenga un buen ritmo)

Si tu amas la historia lamento no haberla disfrutado.
I forced myself to like this but I just couldn't.Definetely better than the last time I read it but still it doesn't make me want to read the next books.I feel so bad

AHHHHH!!! 97 DAYS!!! 97 freaking days to finish this book!!

It was mostly, agonizing.

It started like this: my students were appalled that within my reading repertoire, I had never read the Lord of the Rings trilogy. So, with much convincing I indulged them and approximately 7 of us began our voyage with Frodo and the Fellowship ... it was actually a little fellowship of our own, if you will. Needless to say, it took only until the end of the prologue for our "fellowship" to start disbanding. Students started dropping like flies, making claims that they just couldn't do it and they agreed that it was indeed, awful. Well that left me in quite a pickle as I never abandon a book (minus one that was so disgusting, I just couldn't take it anymore). So, it may have taken me 97 days, but I did indeed finish it.

Now, my remarks on the read itself -- it was:
LONG
There were so many locations and people to keep track of. I felt like I needed to build myself a character map to go with the world map that was included in the beginning of the book.
While I can appreciate what I assume J.R.R. Tolkien was attempting to do with the storyline falling on its own merits without the constant use and need for action, the length of the tale and the lack of action made me want to pull my eye balls out.

Really, I thank God that I am done and that I can now claim to have read it, but I will not be continuing on with Frodo and Sam Gamgee. I do, however, bid them good luck.
I think the story should have been about Bill the pony instead.

What a huge disappointment.
After reading any other Fantasy Adventure book, its a guarantee that in the comments you will see a huge group of people slating it. Because it simply does not compare to lord of the rings e.t.c.
Now for years I have let this go. But now I finally decided to give LOTR a go and all I can say is I am really glad all the other books are nothing like this!

To me it seems that people enjoy reading a load of prattle with no much plot, Let me explain every time Frodo heads anywhere we get at least twenty pages of text telling us every twist and turn they took and lets not forget the three pages at the end of each chapter explaining how they where hungry so had food and a bath.
and we are lucky if we actually get 2 pages of plot and oh my god everything is so easy I mean one minute there about to die then they call for help and suddenly there saved just like that!
For example in the old forest when all is lost our hero yells for help and it happens to come very quickly and everything is good again (well that was well worth a ten page build up right.)
Heck I would be so bold as saying you could skip the whole first book (213 pages) and within reading 4 pages of the 2nd book you will know everything that has happened beforehand . This is because once you skip all the amazing scenery descriptions and the characters he has created nothing actual happens. Then just in case the the reader can't keep up Tolkien retells us what just happened anyhow (YAWN) and if that is not bad enough he puts in bard style accounts in poems.

As for crediting him for creating this fantasy world god some people will believe anything if they want to! I am into old legends like King Arthur (with Merlin) and Beowulf so fortunately i know this is un-true as all the creatures existed in these book and as for the amazing middle earth battles well King Edward I of England was obsessed with the legend of Arthur and believed that he got power from relics so he set about recapturing these relics from Ireland, wales, Scotland and his own people in England.
Which is brilliantly explained in in The Insurrection Trilogy by Robyn Young So although it was not rings you can see where he got the idea . But most people don't realise Tolkien was a historian who edited history into a story and let others believe he created everything .

Fortunately now you do not have to be a historian to do this because this book exists ain't that right J. K. Rowling,Terry Brooks and Christopher Paolini?
I am well aware many people will hate me for slating this book but fortunately very few people read my reviews, so hopefully I can speak the truth about books without having a backlash of angry fans. (Famous last words?)
:-P

1.5 stars
SO. MUCH. DESCRIPTION.
I'm sad to have to say this but this is the single most boring thing I have ever read, and I've read Of Mice and Men 16 times. (fuck you to all my English teachers who made me sit through countless torture sessions *cough* I mean English lessons)
Admittedly I'm young, I only just turned 16 and there are definitely people out there who are far more experienced in the fantasy genre and who can give a genuine in depth review on the writing style, the set up and the pace of this book but I'm just going to go off how many dribble spots have smudged the ink on my copy of FOTR from when I fell asleep.
There are 12 if your wondering, although that may partly be due to the fact I dropped Nutella on chapter 6 and felt obliged to clean it up. With my tongue.
Jokes aside I really didn't enjoy this book, I actually did fall to sleep one or two times and I've probably gone half mad after reading 6 chapters of frodo describing a pebble (okay that didn't happen but things similar to that happened so shh)

I remember vividly the moment I picked up this book for the first time, the sky was blue and the birds where singing in harmony, the planets had aligned and for a short while everything was right in the world. Then I started reading and everything went to shit.
I assumed I'd read this and think it was gods greatest gift to the world (even above Nutella and kittens) I was fully prepared to stand atop a cliff, holding this book towards to sun singing '"ZAAAAAAAAAAAAAAHHHH SOWHENYAAAAAAA MAMAAABEATSEBABAAAAAHHH" As all the authors who have ever authored bowed before the supposedly greatest fantasy book ever written. I'm disappointed I didn't get to do that, I bought a grass skirt and all that body paint for nothing!
Remember that one blade of grass? Yeah the one that saved middle earth fro- oh that's right, the blade of grass didn't save everyone SO WHY THE FUCK DID WE GET BASICALLY A WHOLE BOOK ON HOW THE FUCKING BLADE OF GRASS DANCED IN THE WIND AND GLEAMED WITH THE MISTY MORNING DEW?

I understand people will be angry with me, you'll call me immature and say my brain is too simple to understand such complexity and In all honesty I'd have to agree.
I have such a short attention span and I struggle to comprehend how I manage to read at all but my attention span usually isn't an issue if I'm reading an amazing book.
I can sit and read a 600 page book in one sitting, I've only been reading since I was 12 and many of you will harshly judge my taste in books for this but how any one is able to sit and read 10 pages dedicated to how the sun casts shadows on each individual leaf on a tree is beyond me.
I applaud you for being able to tolerate so much world building and race development but me and my simple and immature brain are going to give the rest of the books a pass.
I'm not sure I can dedicate another 4 months (yes it took me 4 whole months to finish this bloody book) to something I, for the most part, didn't enjoy.

******************
Okay. So I finished this vapid stinker months ago but didn't even have enough interest in it to come back to its review. Now I will. It was awful.

I really, really tried, too! I know how important it supposedly is to the genre - which is my least favorite genre, but I thought if I tried the classics... - and to my in-laws and many friends, etc. But here's the rotten truth:

Tolkien can't write. He can't build character. He can't advance a plotline. Nothing in it was scary (the ring wraiths just *sniff*?? Are you kidding me?? That's downright silly.). Nothing in it was fun (especially not the damned rhymes and feasts. Bleh.). And there were plenty of socially offensive features in it, too, which I so didn't expect! Seriously - the ring wraiths in the book were just called "black men" - repeatedly(!) - not, like, supernatural scary ghosties who happen to wear dark black robes. Racist. But I guess if you were obsessed with Northern European history/culture and were a white man from S. Africa in that time period, as Tolkien was, you *would* think black men were scary. And there are *NO* women to actually speak of. Patriarchy. And sheesh with the Sam being Frodo's very *slave-like* manservant gardener - not an equal or friend!

UGGGHHH.

Thus I will take this time to praise Peter Jackson for making some really incredible movies out of *HOGWASH* source material! Wow! I never really liked those movies before I read The Hobbit and Fellowship, but now that I have, I totally appreciate his work! MAN! Gandalf was a badass *character* in those movies, and so was Aragorn. The hobbits still grate on my nerves no matter what, but at least they had real relationships with each other that didn't offend me. Arwen was totally rewritten for the film to actually have a role - and a badass one, at that. The action sequences were all really scary or cool-looking, at least. There is little to no DRAAAGGGGGGING of the plot, and some plot points are relocated in the plot sequence to better, more sensible or effective moments - like Boromir's temptation in the ice and snow, allowing the audience to anticipate what comes and also building his character *and* others' - instead of right at the end, when it just doesn't work. Etc. Etc. Etc. The movies really *ROCK* compared to these horrid books! Go Jackson!!

Some day I reckon I will read the next two, just for the accomplishment's sake, but I do *not* look forward thereto.

I just can't. I give up. There are not many books I just couldn't finish.
It's not like I think it's bad. It's just "boring". The plot is very stretched. It's too far stretched for me. I can take Stephen King or Robert Jordan with their weird writing style but that's probably the magical line for me.

I wish I could have finished the book because I seriously wanted to read and love the Lord of the Rings but I just kept nodding off, I couldn't focus on it.

It's sad. I anticipated this read so much and it was such a let down for me. I'm so mad at myself.











































But maybe it was just not the right time for me? Maybe I can read this book one day and enjoy it as much as most people do. I honestly hope it will happen but for now, I have to move on.

Creo que esta ha sido la decepción más grande que me he llevado con un libro en bastante tiempo. El señor de los anillos es prácticamente una religión en lo que a fantasía épica respecta, y yo quería dejar de ser el único que no lo había leído. Sabía que La comunidad era un libro cuesta arriba, con muchos diálogos y descripciones según a lo que me habían contado y lo que había leído en internet. Tengo tres problemas con este libro que me han impedido disfrutarlo; sobra decir que ni siquiera me ha gustado.

El lore

Yo a Tolkien no le puedo negar que su lore me llama la atención; cada que hablaba de la historia del Anillo, de Gollum o de Isildur quería saber más, pero siento que en este libro todo eso está desaprovechado. Son solo pequeñas pinceladas que supongo que se cuentan de forma seria en el Silmarillion. El problema está en cómo Tolkien decidió enfocar su lore; siento que le da un protagonismo excesivo a los hobbits, raza que a mi parecer, es la más irrelevante de todas las que habitan la Tierra Media. Pero por un motivo extraño, Tolkien escribe sobre ellos todo el tiempo; desde sus costumbres hasta cada mínimo detalle de sus vidas. De verdad que no sé a quién pueda interesarle lo que ocurra en la comarca más que a Tolkien.

Descripciones

El concepto del viaje que emprenden los héroes está presente en este libro hasta la última página; todo es una gran caminata que a mí se me ha hecho soporífera por ser amable. No entiendo por qué el escritor tiene que describir cada mínimo detalle de los bosques, las hojas y los animales; entiendo cuando se utiliza como una forma de decorar la narración con ciertos adjetivos que, aunque tengan un impacto nulo en la trama, pueden servir como una forma de representar lo que perciben los personajes. Aquí esto no pasa, las descripciones son largas y continuas, casi que son otro personaje. Pero 566 páginas después, si alguien me dice lo azul que está el cielo o lo verdes que son los árboles, no puedo garantizar que esa persona salga ilesa.

El bien y el mal

Mi mayor problema con el Señor de los Anillos es que está demasiado enfocado en el bien y el mal. Aquí no hay medias tintas, y siento que se pierde la emoción de la épica el saber que incluso con la corrupción que el anillo ejerce, los buenos están condenados a derrotar al Señor Oscuro, en la Tierra de Mordor donde se extienden las sombras. El dualismo no tiene porque ser un aspecto negativo per se; la dimensión de la obra también influye, ya que aunque no haya leído el libro hasta ahora, me he tragado todos los spoilers posibles a lo largo de los años incluso sin ver las películas. Y la forma en la que está escrita la historia, como el plot armor del tamaño de un edificio que no solo tiene Frodo, sino todos los hobbits, lo hace todavía más evidente. Lastimosamente, siento que emprender el viaje a través de esta saga no resultó tan idílico como me hubiera gustado.

PD: Hay libros que he calificado con dos estrellas que me parecen mucho peores que este; no se pueden calificar a todos los libros con el mismo criterio y desde luego las estrellas no son un recurso suficiente para definir la calidad de una obra literaria. La comunidad me parece malo, que no terrible. Su nota es más que nada por los motivos que ya expuse.

Continuing the story from his light-hearted children's tale, The Hobbit; Tolkien expands the story into a serious, dry and detailed epic. I'm just not sure why.

The problems I had with this book are numerous, despite my fondness for it's fore bearer. The whole book comes off as over-detailed and makes poor choices of what to detail. Despite it being an epic, it doesn't focus on the action and drama, as a Dumas story might; or the effects of society on it's people, and a people on their society, as Tolstoy or Allende would. It seems to focus mostly on the land. Where this river heads, what color the leaves are here. The details chosen to focus on are mostly pointless, boring.

Meanwhile, the characters are hardly fleshed out if at all, almost completely one-dimensional, and still, some of them (Gandalf especially) come off as inconsistent.

Despite the mature, historical tone, there are odd bits of whimsy thrown in; chiefly, the garden-gnome/nature god Tom Bombadil. Who mostly, just really likes singing about himself.

The book also features many 'songs', long, graceless poems, that are usually tangentially related to the story, at best.

Foreshadowing is under-used, and when used, is extremely heavy-handed.

There are a couple of really interesting parts, mostly focused around 'the eye', but mostly, this story reads like it was hammered out on a typewriter, and edited only for proof. I am puzzled at it's following and will not be joining in further adventures.

reviews.text:
No matter how many times I try Tolkien, I just get bored. My mind wanders. My eyes get heavy. I start wondering how many hairs I have on my head. I thought that consistently falling asleep during the Hobbit was deployment exhaustion. But no, The Fellowship of the Ring is worse. He has random poetry and passages that do not make sense in the context given. The plot is disjointed. The conversations are hollow.

I think Tolkien built a fantastic world (the world building was magnificent) and could spin beautiful one liners, but foremost he was a linguist and a scholar not a novelist. It is disappointing to me. I wanted to really love Tolkien. He inspired novelists, gamers, movie arbiters....but to me his plot has no linear consistency and is like talking to a dementia patient on the final legs of the disease- random, confusing, and heart wrenching.

I wanted to be a Tolkien fan. Fantasy novels are amongst my favorite genres. I tried, and it saddens me greatly to have failed in loving his books. However, I just couldn't help but get lost in his maze of imagery and contextually misplaced conversations and poetry.

I'm not going to spend anytime reviewing this here. Instead, I'll just copy paste my rant on Twitter.

"I am incredibly disappoint. Maybe I shouldn't have started reading this at all."

"< /rant>"

However, I'm going to try my best to finish the trilogy and keep and open mind. Maybe I'll end up actually liking it at the end.

Also, before anyone says it, I'll say it myself.

"Haters gonna hate".

After reading “The Hobbit,” I was very excited to jump into the Lord of the Rings trilogy, but I was taken down a very sad road. After reading the first couple of chapters it becomes very obvious Tolkien just wanted to stretch the success of “The Hobbit” over 1000 more pages. The lack of imagination and purpose of this novel makes it clear Tolkien couldn't repeat the genius and creativity of “The Hobbit,” so this book simply drains the reader with its repetitiveness; walk, eat lembas, sing, sleep and repeat. I can't understand why this book has such die-hard fans; I was bored to tears! As much as I wanted to throw this trilogy in the garbage, I held strong and I suffered through it just so I could read “Bored of the Rings,” (one of the best parody novels I’ve ever read). If it wasn't for the comedic genius of Henry Beard, I would have quit this trash and moved onto something worth my time!

Good points: 

* He finished writing the series - certain modern fantasy authors could really benefit from following that example.

* I like the place names Rivendell and Lorien.


Bad points: 

* Worldbuilding - I know this is where Tolkien is meant to excel, but the setting is not that interesting. It's basically just the English countryside. He didn't even bother to disguise it, e.g. the hobbits live in the Shire, and there are boroughs of England called the Shires. The lore is stolen from classic myths and traditional tales, the idea of the rings is taken from an old German saga, etc. etc. He also spends an inordinate amount of time on things like listing family lineages and mentioning historical heroic deeds. It isn't storytelling; it's notes for an RPG. And I cannot forgive the place name Mount Doom. Tolkien was a professional linguist and that's what he came up with?

* Tolkien clearly didn't understand the myths he was ripping off. He interprets everything in an ultra Christian, dualistic way, stripping out everything that gives the old stories meaning and makes them interesting.

* Characterisation - it's not just like notes for an RPG; it's like the players didn't bother filling in their character sheets. The hobbits are interchangeable. The elves are interchangeable. Everyone exists as a mouthpiece for Tolkien’s summaries of things that have no bearing on the story (such as it is). In 400 pages, not a single character talks about anything personal. We have no sense of who they are, what they want to achieve in life, what they’re afraid of, how they grew up, etc. Instead, we are told that someone is tall, or they're fat. Sooooo many characters are called fat, with no further comment.

* Description - fans say Tolkien is a master of description, while others say he includes too much description. In fact, he isn't really describing; he just lists unnecessary details in an utterly undistinctive voice. There are no unique observations, no interesting turns of phrase, no feeling. Instead, we get lines like: ‘Sam thought they were a kind of crow of large size.’

* The hobbits are unbelievably stupid. Frodo asks a lot of idiotic questions, purely to enable Gandalf to tell us things. Tell tell tell, that's all this book is. There's a rule in writing - show, don't tell. Tolkien didn't understand this at all. There is zero intensity. There are no real stakes.

* There's no plot - most of the book is just summaries of things we’re not experiencing with the characters. If there’s any action (very rare), Frodo usually sleeps through it and gets told about it afterwards, in a few paragraphs. They got attacked by snakes in the second half, and the peril was over in literally three paragraphs. At one point, someone actually says, ‘This is a serious journey, not a hobbit walking-party.’ No, Tolkien, that is precisely what this book is - a hobbit walking-party. Absolutely nothing happens until the last chapter.

* There are no heroes and there's no rationale. The characters show no development, there are no lessons they need to learn, there are no meaningful challenges, etc. When Gandolf tells Frodo about the ring at the beginning, the exchange pretty much boils down to, ‘There’s this ring and it needs destroying’ - ‘How do we do that?’ - ‘Someone has to put it in this fiery pit, and they’ll probably die’ - ‘Oh, cool, sign me up!’ Why, Frodo? Why are you doing this? Then he tells his friends about his plan and they say they already worked it out (how?) and they’re going with him anyway, even if they die (why?). Then, when the elves tell them the details further on, the hobbits whine about it a lot, even though they signed up to it at the start. And if Gandalf, Legolas and co are with them, doing literally all the work and giving all the explanations, why are the hobbits even on this journey? Answer - to carry the ring and do the deadly work at the end. The hobbits are just sacrificial virgins being taken to the volcano god, while the nobility sit at home and feast.

* The ring is underpowered for too, too long. Until the very last chapter, I was thinking this is The Ring, the One to rule them all, and all it does is make you invisible. Yes, it then sucks you away through addiction, but there wasn’t enough power in this thing to cause that addiction in the first place. I could see no reason why whole armies should be after it, just for that power, especially when there are wizards in the mix. Lady Galadriel's mirror demonstrates far more power. The ring only becomes interesting in the final chapter. By that point, it was too little too late. The whole book needs to be culled by about 350 pages, if it wants to be a story instead of someone's notebook of disparate ideas.

* People claim this story is the foundation of all modern fantasy and mythmaking - this just isn't true and demonstrates extremely narrow reading, not to mention an incredibly white, Brit-centric view of the world. Fantasy is a HUGE genre, spanning the globe. Other cultures have their own fantasy traditions going back millennia. Think of manga in Japan, The Epic of Gilgamesh in the Middle East, The Ramayana or the Mahabharata in India, etc., all of which are far, far older and more imaginative - and they have substantial characters who grow as people.

If you just look at traditions in Britain, the fairy stories we have today have been passed down to us as orally transmitted folk tales or via writers like Shakespeare, e.g. The Tempest and A Midsummer Night’s Dream. There are dozens and dozens of anthologies of stories going back centuries. There are sagas passed to us from the Vikings, the Anglo-Saxons, the Normans, etc. Fantasy as a genre takes its inspiration from all sorts of sources. Robin Hobb cites The Three Musketeers as her big inspiration - which could be said to have had a huge influence on western high fantasy overall, being a trilogy (so long that the third book was broken into a sub-trilogy), with a complex story full of political scheming, assassinations, romance, scandal, religion, war, subterfuge, you name it. Of course, it in turn was inspired by real historical events, also a huge influence on the fantasy genre to this day. On another note, Rick Riordan looked to Greek myths for his inspiration. Cassandra Clare looks at the folklore of fairies, vampires and werewolves. I could go on. 

Even when someone writes about elves today, this does not automatically mean they were inspired by Tolkien. The mere suggestion effectively erases Celtic tradition and hands the credit to a white, middle class Englishman - and, frankly, if you look at how the English have historically treated the Irish, we don’t need any more of this. If someone writes a quest story, that's not automatically LOTR either - it hails from things like King Arthur and the Holy Grail. If someone writes about a fellowship, my first thought is again King Arthur and his knights of the Round Table, and Robin Hood and his merry men. Joseph Campbell and Carl Jung had already laid out their theories about archetypes and the hero's journey before LOTR was published. LOTR didn't invent these things - it slotted into well established storytelling traditions that go back as far as humans.

* It’s sexist - Tolkien’s ‘astounding worldbuilding’ almost completely excludes women. I don’t understand how any of the elves, hobbits, etc. even exist when there are so few females. When they make their rare appearance, they generally don't speak. There were a few hobbit wives in the beginning (summarised, not shown), there was Farmer Maggot’s wife (honestly, the names), and there’s Arwen the elf who appeared for about a paragraph and then quickly left the story so the men could talk. The irritating-beyond-measure songs littered through the book are almost exclusively about male heroes from times past. About 80% into the book, Lady Gadriel finally turns up, but she feels as substantial as anyone else in the book - she's perfect and beautiful and ethereal and has some magic, and that's about all you need to know. Then she's gone after about 10 pages, and it's all men again.

* It’s xenophobic and racist - the whole premise hinges on ‘good’ races (actually described as ‘white’ or ‘of the light’) on a mission to keep other races (called ‘evil’ and ‘the black’) from coming into their land. Remember Tolkien wrote this story over many years, throughout WW2 and during a time when the British Empire was collapsing and immigration first became a thing - for instance, the Windrush arrived in Britain in 1948, and the Caribbean migrants were definitely not accepted by most of the locals. The whole book reads like the author is mourning the end of colonialism. Fear of the Other is stamped into every sentence. And there is no distinction among the races. The hobbits are all the same, the elves are interchangeable, the dwarves, the orcs. Everyone within their respective races has the same ideas, the same temperament, the same everything. I’ve never read anything as black and white in my life.

When Gandalf tells the story of how Saruman turned to the side of the black, he says he used to wear a white robe and then one day he wore a robe of many colours. Gandalf literally tells him he preferred him white. The orcs are presented like a colonialist’s depiction of 'tribal savages’, dark, with eyes glowing in the night, beating drums and so forth. When the Fellowship talk to other elves about the dwarf in their company, they are met with prejudice against the whole dwarf race and then justify his presence by essentially saying, ‘But he's one of the good ones.’ It's just gross, from top to bottom.

* It's classist and it romanticises the ‘common folk’. This story was obviously influenced by fears of industrialisation at the time. It's also clear that the hobbits are the working class - literally ‘the little people’, lorded over by ‘the big people’. They are uneducated and ignorant, and the big people smile and laugh at them for it, like isn't it charming how they know absolutely nothing of history or science or the modern world. Gandalf (blatantly the character Tolkien related to) pops in now and again, as a sort of anthropological scholar who explains every damn thing to the little people, but the elves (blatantly noblemen / the upper middle class) keep out to such a degree that the hobbits are over-awed by them when they meet. Gollum is the working classman who dares to aspire to something more and gets punished for it.

Reading this, I kept thinking of Tolstoy. (Tolstoy, Tolkien…spooky.) They both romanticise their country bumpkins to a sickeningly patronising degree. (Honestly, the way Gandalf talks to those hobbits - even when they're running in peril the, like, one time there was any, he was still patronising and insulting them.) Everything about the hobbits and the Shire is so damn twee, it hurts. They are perfect, precious innocents whom the elves and Gandalf must protect at any cost. Why? We’re never told. It’s just imperative that their way of life be protected, even though these other races never spend any time with the hobbits, because the classes are clearly kept separate.

Tolstoy owned hundreds of serfs (effectively slaves) and yet he endlessly wrote about how the peasant class was the salvation of Russia and rural living was the way to holiness (see Anna Karenina, for example). He would dress up in peasant clothes and do a bit of farming with them, for a laugh, rape some of the women from time to time, and then when he’d finished his day of cosplaying at real people’s lives, he’d get back into his silk suit and go to a ball at a friend’s fancy estate. Gandalf’s part in LOTR feels just like this. The whole thing feels like it’s written by someone who has a fantasy about the magical working class and is idealising them without any real idea of how they live or who any of them are. And let's face it, Tolkien was a white, middle class man, privately educated, employed by Oxford University, honoured by the royal family, and best friends with C. S. Lewis (which is damning in itself, if you read to the end of The Chronicles of Narnia and see how out of touch and judgmental HE was).

* The writing itself - can we just circle back to the fact that this book is so. blandly. written. There is nothing outstanding about it at all. There is no attention given to the language (ironic for a linguist), there are no insights, there’s nothing that makes your heart pound. The end of this book, even…I cannot believe how anticlimactic it is, and all due to the way it's written. I have zero interest in reading the sequels. I just don't care.

* The constant poems - make them stop! I say this as someone who loves poetry and loves medieval ballads. Tolkien clearly thought if you stick some lines in verse and make them rhyme, that’s enough. It's not.

* In conclusion - I think people read these books because they think they have to. That’s certainly the only reason I picked them up. But that doesn’t automatically mean they’re good. It means they have good PR. And if you think LOTR is the blueprint for all fantasy ever since, it's just not true. It’s only the blueprint for LOTR ripoffs - and most of the fantasy genre does not fall in this category.

At this point I’ve kind of just accepted that I will probably never finish reading LOTR, let alone The Fellowship of the Ring. Because every time I put this book down, I honestly have little interest in picking it up again.

I think it was the info-dumps. They were so pointlessly long that they lost me. Which really is a sad thing. I wanted to love this. I wanted to embrace my inner Stephen Colbert and geek out over this story, these characters, this world.

But I couldn’t. No matter how hard I tried.

I was told that I should push through until I met Strider. And if I was still bored then, I probably wouldn’t enjoy the rest of the story.

Well, I made it past Strider. And all the way to Rivendell. Over halfway through the book. Almost to 300 pages. And it just wasn’t worth it to me anymore.

I’ll probably give it another go some other time. But at the moment, there’s just 1,000 other books I’d like to read, that I know I’ll enjoy. So even though I know this is, like, a literary masterpiece, what’s the point in reading it if I’m spending the entire time wishing I were reading something else??

Let me make it very clear that I don’t hate Tolkien. I’m well aware the man was a genius. But I couldn’t do this. I’m really, really sorry.

Please forgive me.

Overall: My friends hyped it a lot, and I finally caved to read the cult classic. However, expectations were too high for any book to realistically be able to deliver on. Much as I want to give it more stars, this read-through was unfortunately disappointing.

Pacing: If I had known ahead of time that the trilogy was one story published in three volumes (versus three novels), I would have had better expectations for the pacing. Because I didn’t know this, I expected climactic action when really the whole book is exposition.

Characters: The Company disbands at the end, and I was only sad about leaving one or two of them - which tells me that the character development was lacking, since I didn’t emotionally connect with them.

Also, in a continuation of the style of The Hobbit, each species/race basically has one “character” which all members of that species inhabits. I couldn’t tell you the difference between one Wood Elf and another, for example. Perhaps this is too modern of a take for the publish date of the book, but I prefer more character trait nuance between the various members of a species/race. “All elves are good, all trolls are bad” (which is admittedly an oversimplification of Tolkien’s portrayal) contributes to a deeply unhelpful worldview.

Genre: This narrative read so much like a history book at times that I was distracted and annoyed. “Will these characters/places be plot-relevant later?” was answered in the negative more often than I liked (read: nearly always). I had the included map out next to me while reading and was constantly referencing it. This made it feel more like research or homework than pleasure reading.

I’m also unused to reading epics, with such large casts of characters, and so many side characters who appear for an episode then minimally, if ever, again. I got attached to characters who never showed up again (though now I wouldn’t be able to tell you their names, because of the aforementioned large cast of characters).

Redeeming qualities: There were a handful of quotes that spoke beautifully to deeply human, relatable traits like friendship or courage.
The artwork included in the edition I read, done by the author, beautifully illustrates (pun intended) both the world and the author’s breadth of artistic talent.

From where do I begin? I had a lot of issues with this book. So for those who love this book I’m incredibly sorry for what I’m about to say.

Let’s begin, shall we?

But first to say that Tolkien is an awful writer would be a huge disgrace due to his massive contribution to literature for only an astounding and amazing writer can achieve what Tolkien’s achieved. He is an amazing author but his books are not my cup of tea.

I had issues with The Hobbit at first but I thought to myself that maybe I should give Lord of the Ring a chance... oh how I wish I hadn’t done that.

The Fellowship of the Ring started out as a promising tale, I was truly intrigued. I wanted to know what’s going to happen but 150 pages later monotony took over. The exact same issues that I had in The Hobbit I met in this book.

1. The characters were very bland. There was no character development. Everything was black and white. There was no complexities within the characters. I realise that for the first book that’s a lot of demands but, it’s not a lot when the book is 500 pages long!!!

2. There was a lot of details!! I do know that details enhance and enrich the book but that wasn’t our case. I found myself skimming and skipping parts and parts of the book then going back to read them. I just couldn’t understand what’s happening or what he was describing which was a bummer for the book is built entirely on details!!

3. It was too big of a book for a simple plot. It could’ve been a really good book with 300 pages but alas that wasn’t the case.

He is what a twelve-year-old imagines a smart person to be. Almost all characters are unbelievable, pretentious and flat.

The only character that is interesting and has any kind of depth to him is Gollum. He is neither good or evil, but a conflicted and twisted being. Any encounter and interaction with him is interesting. Ironically he's the most human and relatable character in the whole story.

The writing is extremely tedious and descriptive. The events are too unbelievable. The characters are too unbelievable. Reading 30 pages about how nothing happened for 12 days is not entertaining for me, and I found myself skimming long parts of the book trying to find some action. Second, I felt too lost with all the names and the references to mythologies with which I was unfamiliar. I'm not sure if I should have read the mythology ahead of time, but given that this book was published before that one, I was expecting to not be confused while reading it. Instead, there are a million allusions to a million people with unique and unpronounceable names and to events that happened 'before' but with an extremely difficult to discern timelines. I feel like this is a book for study; you have to sit with a notepad and make notes so you can build the timeline of Middle Earth as you go along. I do admire the skill it takes to create an entire mythology and language, and the meticulous patience with which the book was written, so as to not leave any details out. It is just not for me.

The Fellowship of the Ring is the first book in The Lord of the Rings trilogy from JRR Tolkien. This is perhaps one of the most well-known books that I have read so far; being one of the most sold books in the world and also having highly successful film adaptations. I had loved the films as a teenager and wanted to get to reading the books someday. So, in this review, I would evaluate if it was worth reading the book.

The story happens in the world built by the earth, Middle-Earth, inhabited by various different species – being the hobbits, elves, men, dwarves, orcs, etc. The story begins with Bilbo Baggins celebrating his birthday in The Shire (the village of the hobbits) and leaves his possessions to his beloved nephew Frodo, including a ring with special powers. Frodo is visited by Gandalf the wizard, and is told of the evil powers of the ring; previously possessed by Sauron, the ruler of the land of Mordor. Frodo is joined in this mission by his gardener and close friend, Samwise, along with two other friends from the Shire, Merry and Pippin. The rest of the story is about their adventure and their path towards destroying this evil ring or as they say in the book, the one ring to rule them all.

This was a book that I wanted to like, a book that I had been meaning to read for a long time, it was a film that I enjoyed as a teenager, enjoyed the games that were from the universe, etc. However, the key word phrase here is that I wanted to like but I could not bring myself to like this book despite my best efforts. To start with, the narration was drab and often flat, providing no nuance to the characters and the manner in which they expressed themselves at various points. This was a standard young adult novel where each character had a clear identification of who was good or who was evil and there were hardly any layers to the personality of any of the characters.

There were aspects that could have made the book interesting, such as the distrust between the dwarves and the elves, and how they make do with that, but then, the ‘Fellowship’ is closely knit (something unusual for a group created on the spot by an elven lord, with only notable exception being the character of Boromoir who had shown some levels of dissent).

One could praise the writer for the detailed world that he has built and how this has inspired several other fantasy novel writers, whom I have personally enjoyed, but with that said, this book was a travelogue in a world that I was not interested in. There was nothing more to it than a bunch of people walking together, complaining about the weather, describing the surroundings, and moving from a point to another point. What was expressed in this particular book could have been expressed in a third of its size without losing the essential content of it.

While this book contains the features of a standard young adult novel, unfortunately, it is not a very easy read for a teenager either. Thus, I am unsure of whom it appeals to (no wonder this often features in the list of books people ‘pretend to have read’).

To summarise this book, I would say that it is a boring travelogue featuring drab characters happening in a world that I am not interested in. On that note, I award the book a rating of one on five.

I was so excited to read this series as an avid fan of LOTR movies. But my God is it a struggle to go through. I don't even know where to start honestly.

I'll try by talking about the pacing first. It was horrible. For the entirety of Book One and half of Book Two is just descriptions of walking and walking and walking. I understand it's meant to portray a long journey, but if you really enjoyed reading various tellings of the same action for pages and pages, I applaud you. Also the entire Tom Bombadil stuff just has to go. HE HAS NO PURPOSE TO BE THERE, I can maybe say he'd saved the hobbits but it helps to make his character appear rather than working on developing the story of the hobbits. And it's not just an arc that appears in a short time but he takes like half of the Book One... Not to mention he's a walking plot hole, which the story tries to tackle on, telling that he'd lose the ring or something. A very weak attempt to save it honestly.

And if it's not walking, it's BACKSTORY handed what many I assume considers "worldbuilding". Now, I understand that the book shows its time and should be regarded thus but it's just really puts before your eyes why these things don't work--why you hear many authors warn against writing like this. I just find it a bit ironic that this one is considered a classic. As many others have mentioned, this book feels like early Samsung phones as it is bloated with unnecessary things that only hinder your experience. What you usually hear is that Tolkien was a genius at worldbuilding, and I can see that but it's really not executed well at all! I don't think on the nose in-canon-mythology references to the characters are very impressive, nor is reading a full poem in another language in between that's been put there for no reason other than Tolkien wanting to showcase his linguistic skills I guess??
That I have no problem with, I'm impressed by all that, all the history he'd built for his world, but I think those things should be fed to the reader slowly and naturally rather than just inserting an entire Wikipedia entry on the history of where each species came from.

Show don't tell? No, this book understood it as "tell don't show". For example, the entire Saruman corruption arc is told from Gandalf in a table discussion and at that point I was so disappointed I couldn't even show any emotion reading it.

It picks up barely after a bit more than the half of the entire book, and there are a lot of saving graces it has, but I honestly think the movies solved a lot of the pacing issues. (ex. Frodo takes MONTHS to get out of Hobbiton, and even then he has no purpose, and doesn't even know where to go. In the movies he's got a clear purpose. HE'S SUPPOSED TO BE THE MAIN CHARACTER.)

I will try to read the rest of the series (bc Eowyn!! Rohan!!) but reading this first installment felt more like a CHORE so I don't know if I'm ready for it. Maybe reading fantasy is not for me?

Yritin, NIIN yritin. Tein kaikkeni. Tuntuu kuin olisin lukenut paksua, kuivaa ja vanhaa kirjaa koulua varten. En vain pystynyt nauttimaan tämän lukemisesta. En ole nähnyt Taru Sormusten Herrasta -elokuvia, ja olisin halunnut lukea nämä ennen kuin näen elokuvat. En siis tiedä tästä maailmasta mitään ja olisin voinut kokea kaiken ensin kirjoista. Sitä toivoin ja ajatus kiehtoi, mutta en vain pysty enää.

Ymmärsin, että kirja paranee toisella puoliskolla, ja tämän tiedon voimalla jatkoin… ja jatkoin… askelsin, suunnistin, samoilin, kuuntelin lauluja ja seurasin yksityiskohtaisen tarkkoja kuvauksia nousevasta ja laskevasta auringosta, juurakoista ja poluista, ilmansuunnista ja no, ilmansuunnista. Ja vaikka vihdoin pääsin kohtaan, jossa alkoi tapahtua, en tuntenut mitään sen kummempaa. Ehkä 300-sivuinen alku vain turrutti niin, etten enää kykene kiinnostumaan. Jäin sivulle 364.

Pidin kirjan alusta: juhlista ja sormuskeskustelusta. Pidin myös esimerkiksi Tom Bombadilista. Tai siis, jotkut lauseet olivat hauskoja, mutta yleisesti lukukokemukseni ei muuttunut paremmaksi, vaikka kirjassa kuinka kuvailtiin polkua myöten pomppivaa hattua ja laulettiin Bombadilin veikeää nöpölaulua. Hobittikin oli vaikea lukea, mutta Bilbo oli kiinnostavampi päähenkilö kuin Frodo ainakaan tähän mennessä, ja Hobitissa oli paljon enemmän veikeyttä ja huumoria ja sellaista muumimaisen hauskaa meininkiä. Siksi se sai yhden tähden enemmän.

Tämän kirjan kohdalla valkeni entistä kirkkaammin se, että pystyn kyllä näkemään visuaalisia mielikuvia, mutta vaihtelevan heikosti. Jos teksti tuntuu kuivalta, kuvittelu on entistä vaikeampaa ja häilyvämpää. Piirsin kuviakin, jotta ymmärtäisin ja pääsisin osaksi tätä maailmaa. Aina, kun olin tehnyt valtavasti työtä kuvitellessani senhetkisen miljöön, tulikin taas uusi ja sitten taas uusi edellisenkaltainen, mutta silti kai erilainen maisema. Polku eteni, muttei vienyt minnekään. Huomasin myös, että koska kirjassa ei ollut sellaista modernia juonirakennetta, johon nykyään on totuttu, huomion keskittäminen ja tärkeän ja ei-tärkeän erottaminen oli itselleni vaikeaa. Tiedän, että tämä on vanha kirja ja tiedän, että Tolkien pohjusti koko modernin fantasian kentän ja niin edelleen, mutta kokemukseni ei hetkahda suuntaan tai toiseen, vaikka kuinka tiedostan nämä asiat.

Kirja vastasi ennakko-oletuksiani, joiden toivoin rikkoutuvan: paksu historiankirjantuntuinen teos täynnä ihmeellisiä vanhoja sanoja ja nimiä, jotka tipahtelevat mielestä. Olen huono muistamaan sanoja ja nimiä, en pidä historiasta enkä historiankirjojen kaltaisesta tekstistä… Tämä kirja vain ei ollut minua varten, ainakaan nyt.

Harmittaa!! Niin toivoin uutta kiinnostavaa maailmaa, johon uppoutua ja jota lukea uudelleen ja uudelleen. Ehkä palaan tähän joskus. Taidan ensin katsoa elokuvat ja tuumata sitten uudelleen. Lukemalla en enää etene tässä suuntaan tai toiseen.

1/10 Bored me to the death. The first half of the book is mostly filler, you could probably tell what happens in 40 pages, and yet the book takes over 280… There’s endless descriptions of terrain and plants… and yet almost no description of faces, clothes or shapes of most characters. Hobbits move from point A to point B, find peril and are rescued by someone else, and repeat. This dynamic turns very irritating very fast. I also have to question the entire existence of Tom Bombadil to be honest.

As for the second half of the book, there's a deliberate choice to tell of a meeting between characters, where they tell stories of what happened to them in the past... these stories could have made great content, told as they were happening instead of the filler from the first half… so more negative points here.

Passing the 80% mark the boredom was overwhelming, and I was exhausted, and that’s not even considering the songs. Up to this point the book was salvageable, but then it ground to a halt with unbearable slow motion, it was like being stuck in a black hole event horizon. The last 100 pages would not move ffs.

The Hobbit is a million times better than this. AFAIK Tolkien's publisher requested a sequel after the Hobbit, and Tolkien offered the Silmarillion, but the publisher said no. So Tolkien had to write this. Not being his first choice, it could somewhat explain why there is so much filler and why it’s so distant from the Hobbit I guess… that’s the only defense I can come up with, and yet that’s useless upon the waste of time suffered. Oooooh boy! When I hear the name Tolkien, I immediately think of an amazing author who was able to create one of the best fantasy series in the 20th century. So, going into this, I was very excited and was holding high expectations for this book. My hopes of this, though, were immediately crushed. I'm sorry, but what the hell! The first 20 pages of this book could have immediately been skipped, and you wouldn't even have noticed. Most people say for fantasy, get through the first 100 pages, and you'll be fine. That 100 pages felt like 1,000! It seemed to take FOREVER for them to get out of the Shire! And then, once they hit the road, Tolkien, with his masterful writing, comes in. He describes them eating, walking, eating, walking, and describing some random mountains, eating, and walking. And it goes on and on and on and on throughout the whole book. The only shining light from this book were some of Tolkeins descriptions, like when they got to Lothlorien and he describes the scenery, it was beautiful. The way the Nazgul are described is terrifying, much better than the way the movies portrayed them. My one last gripe, though, is the way the party reacted to Gandalfs death. I mean, come on, all they say is that they miss him...I'm sorry, but Frodo has known this wizard for all his life, and he doesn't shed a single tear. And that's kind of how the rest of the party acts, it's like nothing happened. In conclusion, if you like walking tutorials, this book is great for you. And if you want to learn about some mountains that won't pop up at all, later in the book, go right for it! All in all, I'm disappointed.

So, I'm writing a retrospective review that does not cover the whole book. I was like 14 when I tried to read this, and I was very disappointed. Hitherto picking this up I had constructed an identity for myself as a "nerd" or "geek". Liking things like Lord of the Rings and Star Trek were central to the subculture, so I naturally picked up a familiarity with them. I convinced myself that I liked them, despite having never engaged with the source material.

I began reading this not too long after I read Game of Thrones (ASOIAF #1). I was sure I'd love it. I was already a massive fan of fantasy. I already knew bits of the Elvish language. I had a "The One Ring" that I sometimes wore around my neck on a string.

I bought the book from Barnes & Noble, and I finally cracked it open to give it a go. And I think that was probably the last time I made any real progress. Reading the Prologue and the First chapter I very quickly realized that Tolkien is not a very good writer by modern standards. It would be absurd for me to sit here and pretend I don't recognize how amazing and intricate his worldbuilding his, but worldbuilding is *not* all there is!!

Tolkien writes pages and pages of Lore-Dumping. You'd be embarrassed to write something like that today. He spends far too much time describing stuff and referencing stuff. It's a slog to read.

Now maybe I was missing out on great macro-level storytelling, but I'm skeptical of this because next I tried to binge the film trilogy, and even that was boring for me.

Needless to say, I was in an existential crisis over my identity as a nerd/geek.

I honestly just read this book out of curiosity -to see what the OG fantasy was like. That being said, I definitely did have a certain level of expectations. The first hundred pages or so were pretty promising. I was looking forward to see where the story of the ring would take me. I guess I shouldn’t have been expecting Harry Potter level of adventure, twists and emotional rollercoasters. I was practically setting myself up for disappointment.

It took me 350 pages to realise that this was just a really boring book and it wasn’t about to get any better. It’s the kind of book where you can skip 10 pages and still not miss anything significant. The main characters are 40 year old hobbits with no personality whatsoever. For a fantasy book, it has a surprising lack of suspense or tension. For 80% of the book, it feels as if the characters are just walking -almost like a Dora the Explorer scenario where they have to get to multiple different destinations before reaching the end of the map. Except nothing intense or interesting enough happens either during the walking or at any of the destinations. I may or may not be guilty of skipping 2 or 3 chapters.

I really tried to keep an open mind, and hold space for respect for J. R. R. Tolkien for being a pioneer in his field, but I just found that so difficult to do when I wasn’t enjoying his work. The 1.5 stars is for the basic premise (I did really like the idea of the ring and how it can hold power over its wielder and the idea that it must be destroyed) and the scenes with Gollum in it.

HOW is this part of popular culture? I am a picky reader when it comes to books I love, but it takes a lot for me to dislike a novel - this one has made it to that very short list. I am convinced that many who says they love LOTR have never ventured to read it.
When, in the final hundred pages, I began to realise that the sequel isn't a sequel at all but very much still part of this same story, I became so annoyed that I resolved to diagonal reading for the final 100 pages - that's when it became legible. I feel like the goal of the book was crafted language which exudes the air of history and fantasy, but it was gobbledygook to me. So much irrelevant information in running paragraphs, rehashing of the plot, and endlessly droning on everything. The start of book 2 where they met the elves nearly took me out.
I am annoyed and feel misled about the fact I would need to read another one of these books (and I'd expect also the last one) for the plot to be resolved. There's zero resolution at the end of this one and I don't think I can mentally do another one of these books. It was a true test of my perseverance.
I always hear people talk about the world building and that was the key reason I wanted to read it, but even that felt poorly executed. Would love for someone who does like these books to explain to me why because if I would've read this without knowing its role in popular culture, I would've expected this to be that book at the back of the library shelf that no one ever takes home and of which part 2 never got published.
