I could not stand this book at all. I was listening to the audiobook version from Andy Serkis, and he did a great job narrating the characters, but the story was SO dry.

Tolkien describes a scene very vividly, but that's all he does. Throughout the book, many of his story telling went, "The sun rose, Froto and his crew ate food, the sun set." He would describe the clouds, the lighting, the characters, etc, but there was very little emotion for me to feel with the characters.

In highly stressful scenes, all Tolkien gave me was, "Froto was scared! Sam and xyz shook nervously with fear." I couldn't feel the intensity of their emotions because all of it was described from a third party perspective. I wish the author let me imagine how they felt rather than bluntly telling me, "Bilbo was happy!"

It took me months to finish this story because I was so bored when listening. The audiobook was 20 hours long, and I hoped things would become more interesting as the story progressed, but by hour 10, I only committed to finishing because I already invested so much time into it.

I do truly believe that Tolkien is a phenomenal world builder, and I thought maybe this book would be better than The Hobbit, but I just can't listen to a story that doesn't let me experience the events.

Let me just say this...in my entire lifetime, I have NEVER left a book incomplete. Once I start a book, even if it doesn't capture all of my attention, I always finish it (we'll call it my OCD streak). its worse when the book belongs to a series because....you guessed it -- I have to finish the series (again...the OCD streak).

Then I came across LOTR. I started with The Hobbit. Didn't particularly enjoy it too much but because it was a part of a series, I went on to this book...and Oh My God...I just CAN'T!

I've been trying to read through this for two months and I haven't made it past page 339. For the past two weeks, I pull out the book to read on the bus and end up staring out the window after reading a couple of pages. I just cant bring myself to finish the remaining pages!

I understand that this is considered a classic and all but it didn't do it for me at all. The pace of the story is too slow...I don't particularly enjoy reading about a company walking through woods and forests for pages and pages! No matter how much a situation builds up, I can assume that there's always going to be an escape...someone or some beast is going to come to the rescue of Frodo and his friends. Its like reading the Hobbit all over again...not to mention all the new names of characters and places to keep track of!

After dedicating about 3 hours a day for two months to this, I've decided to call it quits. Perhaps a part of the reason is that my life is hectic at the moment and when I open a book, I'm looking to unwind and have a break. Reading the Fellowship is like taking a course and adding more work to my pile.

Maybe I'll appreciate the writing and the story more when I'm older or when life isn't so hectic but for now, this book remains the only book and this series remains the only one that I've abandoned mid-way.

My apologies for LOTR fans and whoever gets offended by this review but I think its only fair that I get to express my dislike for the book the same way you get to express your love for it. :)

Started it when I was 12, finished it when I was 13. No, my birthday wasn't the day after I began reading it.

I've realized that while I love stories, I don't necessarily enjoy reading. I have liked books, but I'd tried reading LOTR some time ago and only got through the first chapter before I fell off and couldn't keep going with it. Understanding all of this, I decided to give this one more shot by listening to an audiobook version while I settled for the night with drawing or mindless video-gaming. I knew the language of the book was pretty dry, so having it spoken to me while I doodled definitely worked out better.

However, after getting through half of whatever chapter followed Khazad-dum, I'm shelving it. I've seen the movies, so already knowing the story certainly puts the book at a disadvantage in that regard, but there are also enough differences and things that are book-exclusive that it could still have been interesting.

Unfortunately, there is nothing interesting about any of it.

Folks seem to love the story (as do I) and the world-building (I do not), but the reason I'm not bothering to continue with it is that the characters are all so dull and shallow. There is no reason for me to care about them or their journey, and that's what will keep me or take me out of a story. The movies, for their flaws, succeed in this regard immensely -- they made the characters enjoyable and gave them all a depth that is just completely absent in the book. Maybe that changes later on, but given that Tolkien was primarily interested in creating his own world and languages, I doubt it. As it is, even by this point in the story that I reached, the movie's interpretation excelled in just about every regard. Sure, the movies did Pippin a little dirty in that the book version of him isn't so dopey, but then again, that makes his payoffs down the line in the later movies that much better. There are also quick and simple changes that are better in the movie, such as giving Frodo the opportunity to realize the Dwarf door was a riddle, as opposed to the book version of Gandalf just figuring it out after a short wait, but in the end it's not these simple alterations that leave the book a failure by comparison... it's everything.

Yes, the (amazingly) frequent songs are something I skipped through every time, but I actually didn't find Tolkien's descriptions of the world and such too offensively extensive. These seem to be common complaints about this book, but it wasn't the ultimate detriment. The characters, in the end, are all just entirely flat, with no emotional depth to pull me in or engage me with who they are, and they're basically all interchangeable -- they all speak the same and have the same habit of randomly telling each other about histories or locations as if they are video game NPCs. They all come across so stiff and detached that the closest bond seemed to be between Sam and Bill. I genuinely felt his sorrow over that pony (it comes up a couple of times, too), and it was the only bit of feeling I experienced in the whole of my reading. Even after what happens at Khazad-dum... the book casually mentions their weeping, as if quickly brushed through in obligation, but then it's done and over. Aragon cries out (paraphrased) "Farewell! I warned you about going through here, and now we're without hope!" and then says they need to all move on, and they do. Maybe they reference Gandalf later on, I'll never know, but it's all so strangely cold and, I can't do without repeating the word, stiff. Sure, I think Gandalf is a lousy and unpleasant character, made otherwise by a performance in the movies of warmth and friendliness, but then after the bridge and some weeping, the book characters are right back to describing the land around them and walking on so all is well. I felt no weight, no gravity.

So, I'm moving on.

Structurally, the book is odd as well. There is a great danger about, and then eventually Frodo and friends are out on a dangerous quest to rid themselves of this ring that the great doom master is hunting for (so, you know, he can conquer the earth with evil), but they're absurdly slow and chill about it taking care of it all. There's rarely any sense of urgency, and I've read plenty of retorts that "this isn't supposed to be an action movie story," which is fine -- but this world has defined its own terms, and it starts to feel silly in how easy-going everyone is in their endeavor.

I have an awfull relationship with Bored of the Rings. I have never been able to connect with either the books or the movies the way we are supposed to.

The biggest problem is the annoyingly evil fandom. I often find discussions around The Lord of the Rings turning into endless comparisons where fans try to diminish the legacy of Harry Potter or A Song of Ice and Fire, even though both of those series offer far more engaging characters, more complex conflicts, amazing storry telling and stronger emotional connections.

When it comes to George R. R. Martin, I have my own frustrations with his writing style, especially the enormous amount of description that sometimes slows the story down. That is one of the reasons I never continued further with the books. However, I cannot deny that A Song of Ice and Fire is an exceptional story, with morally complex characters, unpredictable twists, and a level of realism that makes it stand out. The show on the other hand is pure perfection minus the last season.

Unfortunately, I do not feel the same way about Tolkien's so called writing. My biggest issue is the way the story is structured. Well written books are those that establish a clear goal early on, giving the reader a strong sense of direction from the very beginning. Once that objective is in place, I want the story to build momentum through exciting events, meaningful conflicts, and steady character development.

Bored of the Rings never gave me that feeling. Instead, I felt like I was wandering through pages of descriptions, lore, and constant introductions to new characters without a strong narrative drive. Rather than pulling me deeper into the story, it often left me wondering where it was all leading. That style of storytelling simply doesn't work.

I also find it frustrating how selectively people choose which creators to criticize or defend. Some authors are heavily criticized for their personal opinions, while others are often treated with far more forgiveness despite having expressed strong negative views about other works and creators.

The Fellowship of the Ring (The Lord of the Rings - Book 1) – Review:

My Rating: 1/5*
Method of Engagement: Audible | 22.5 hrs | Narrated by Andy Serkis

My Thoughts:
I have been quite reluctant to leave my review of this book. I feel I must preface my thoughts by saying that I have never read Tolkien's series before, and was introduced to it via the films. I adore the LotR movies and because of this, have come to love the world inspired by the works of Tolkien. So having recently read The Hobbit, I wished to try LotR too.

With that in mind, I did expect differences between the LotR book and its related film, but I didn't anticipate just how much variation there would be between them. So much so, that I honestly felt disappointed. The more I continued with the story, the more frustrated I got...it was so disheartening.

One of the biggest issues I had was with the character Tom Bombadil (a character I have heard referenced but am unfamiliar with entirely). The story was especially challenging to follow whenever they were present. It was as if his section of the book was disjointed from the rest, due to how much it deviated from the progression of the plot. Aside from that, the dialogue was exhausting to listen to and the character development felt bland. It honestly was a struggle to become invested at all.

Ultimately, it took me months to get through the audiobook. I listened to it in small sittings, because I didn’t know if I could get through it. The only saving grace (from my experience) was Andy Serkis’ performance. He was committed to making this story and these characters come alive and his energy and enthusiasm should be commended [5 stars for performance].

However, this book was not "it" for me. I sincerely wish I had the same experience I had with The Hobbit, but sadly, I did not. At a later date, I may try to continue with the book series, but if I never get there, I remain content with watching the films.

AHHHHH!!! 97 DAYS!!! 97 freaking days to finish this book!!

It was mostly, agonizing.

It started like this: my students were appalled that within my reading repertoire, I had never read the Lord of the Rings trilogy. So, with much convincing I indulged them and approximately 7 of us began our voyage with Frodo and the Fellowship ... it was actually a little fellowship of our own, if you will. Needless to say, it took only until the end of the prologue for our "fellowship" to start disbanding. Students started dropping like flies, making claims that they just couldn't do it and they agreed that it was indeed, awful. Well that left me in quite a pickle as I never abandon a book (minus one that was so disgusting, I just couldn't take it anymore). So, it may have taken me 97 days, but I did indeed finish it.

Now, my remarks on the read itself -- it was:
LONG
There were so many locations and people to keep track of. I felt like I needed to build myself a character map to go with the world map that was included in the beginning of the book.
While I can appreciate what I assume J.R.R. Tolkien was attempting to do with the storyline falling on its own merits without the constant use and need for action, the length of the tale and the lack of action made me want to pull my eye balls out.

Really, I thank God that I am done and that I can now claim to have read it, but I will not be continuing on with Frodo and Sam Gamgee. I do, however, bid them good luck.

I know a lot of people think this book and this series are amazing, but I personally don't see the appeal at all. The book moves along pretty slowly, and on the whole, there is very little that actually happens. That in and of itself is not a problem for me, as there are many books that are slow-moving and generally low-action that I enjoy(like the GOT series). The difference with this book is that it felt like a lot of the events in the book have no real explanation or logic behind them, and they just kind of happen.

It also felt like there were no stakes. That might sound weird considering the fate of the world is at stake(apparently), but it was hard for me to really BELIEVE that because every time a character talked about how the Ring would end the world, all I could think about is how a simple invisibility ring could hold that much power. Another point was that at many points when the characters' lives were in danger, they got saved last second by some random person or thing happening/appearing out of nowhere to save them. That was less of a problem later on in the book, but those early events made the later ones a lot less intense because instead of wondering what would happen to the characters, I was just wondering about what random inexplicable thing would save their lives that time.

Take this review with a grain of salt, because I know this franchise has a huge following so I likely just don't get it, or this book doesn't suit my personal tastes. Because of its popularity, I still think it's worth a read, but personally, it's not for me.

the start of this book was more promising than the hobbit - there was more action & more intriguing elements. but it quickly went back into the same sort of style (not exactly sure what i was expecting though, maybe that's on me). i think if i was a 60 year old man i would enjoy reading this more in the sense that unfortunately i'm a young person who's grown up reading one era of fantasy books that place a large focus on personalities, relationships, character development, & internal thoughts - all of which the FOTR doesn't do very much.

i'm an active supporter of always reading the book before watching the movie, but after my experience with reading the hobbit, i watched the movie first. i can see how they extrapolated the book characters' actions into entire personalities e.g. pippin's goofiness. i also hate saying i like a movie more than the book, but i think because so much of tolkein's writing is descriptions of the setting, it's nice to just see all of the settings on screen & watch the action happen.

in saying all of this though, it would be foolish to ignore the incredible concepts. everything from the 'dark lord' to the 'chosen one' to the 'one powerful, damning object' - these are all things we see over & over in our modern fantasy. tolkien ran so all our current favourite authors could walk.

i know how loved this series is & it is for good reason. overall, the story itself has great substance, but the writing style & pacing 0f events make the book less of an enjoyable read for me personally.

I’m a dick, I’m an asshole, I suck, I’m no fun, I know. And I hated every moment of reading this. This is the first certifiable classic of literature that I couldn’t stand. I hate the fucking songs. I hate Tom fucking Bombadil. I hate the hobbits. I hate the elves and all their fun flowery sing-song paradises and cosmically beautiful women and everybody falling in love with them and having a wonderful time. I hate Tolkien’s writing style. I hate the slow fucking drag that it's paced. I never wanna hear the fucking word “slopes” ever again. And I hate all the pointless goddamn lore that does nothing for the story that I will never derive anything from or think about in the real world. I don’t read books to collect a bunch of fucking fictional facts about a world I have no reason to care about. Nor do I care about all the characters getting along jovially and having a great time and getting saved from all peril by happy coincidence. I don’t want fictional characters to be fucking happy. I want misery, I want chaos and blood and death, I want PERSONAL STAKES. This dynamic between author and reader is fundamentally incompatible.

I haven’t hated any other classics I’ve read because none of them felt like they were wasting my time every page. Moby Dick was a real test of patience, but this is so far beyond that, because at least Moby Dick made up for its slog with some occasionally great moments and lines. Every sentence of all 458 pages of this was abysmal. My primary motive to finish this book was getting to the other two books—but I can tell I’m not in for much better.

I really struggled with this one. There’s a lot of walking, describing landscapes, and long passages that didn’t move the story forward for me. I get that world-building is important, but it felt like it took forever to actually get going. I didn’t feel fully invested in Frodo Baggins or the journey.

Reading Tolkein is doing many good things for me. It's helping me participate more intelligently in discussions about medievalism. I'm learning about some of Rowling's inspiration. It's giving me better success watching _Jeopardy!_ (of course, _South Park_ did that for me, too) and enabling me to make clever remarks about one's "precioussss." Thanks to Middle Earth, I could understand the irony when I literally could not pass a car whose license plate read "GANDA1F." I concede that I appreciate Tolkein's significance.

I even liked a couple of things about this book. The songs intrigue me, as narrative devices (though they annoy me excessively). I liked the passive aggression in Bilbo's dispersion of personal effects, and I find Sam's devotion endearing.

All around, though, I am not entertained. In fact, listening to these books while I drive is probably a safety hazard, as I am so bored I might fall asleep at the wheel. I feel the same at the conclusion of this book as I have at the conclusion of each installment in the _Twilight_ saga (yes, I said it): I can't believe I have to read MORE of them.

I will give the others a chance, but I foresee the same problems. The characters and setting aren't going to change, I assume, and those are my problems. I rarely enjoy fantasy, and I even more rarely enjoy this kind of self-conscious, deeply nostalgic medievalism.

I had really high expectations for this book, and I honestly wanted to like it. Fantasy is my favorite genre, but I couldn't wait for this one to end. It took forever to finish because I only ever read it before bed to put me to sleep.

The vast majority of the story describes their treks through forests and mountains, and nothing really happens. There are parts that are extremely interesting, but there's just so much of nothing in between. And I still don't understand the point of all the songs. Why isn't normal dialogue enough to convey this information? Or is the song form meant to indicate information that is completely irrelevant?

This book is full of characters, there are so many I could hardly keep track of them all, and yet there are only four women. One is obnoxious and disliked, another is a complete moron, the third doesn't have a single line of dialogue, and the fourth is valued primarily for her physical beauty. All of the women are described in terms of their beauty, which would be fine if the same importance was accorded to the men's beauty, but it isn't. That alone would be enough to make me dislike this book, even if I had found the story interesting.

I hate to leave a series unfinished, but I'm not sure I'll ever have the patience for the rest.

I cannot say that I cared much for this one, the writing wasn’t particularly good and the whole thing lingered too much at times. At times it felt like Tolkien was just stuck or lost and just stumbling around a bit The songs, languages etc. all seemed like needless fluff to me & no I wasn’t impressed with all the pointless gibberish that they were for me. . That is not even mentioning the fact that this reminded me a touch too much of Wagner’s “Der Ring des Nibelungen” (or one of the saga’s that inspired it, I haven’t read those). I prefer greatly the movies which were at least streamlined, didn’t suffer from the writing and were visual eye candy. I do not get what people see in this book, the movie was fun to see once as popcorn entertainment but this one not so much.

Usually when confronted with fans of this novel, after expressing the fact that I didn’t care at all for it, I get blank stares in disbelieve from them. Afterwards they generally come to the conclusion that I just do not like literature or that I do not understand it. It is possible & quite likely that I do not understand literature but I do like reading. I befuddling as it might seem to other people, I simply didn’t think that the writing was good and it all seemed like a drag to me. Oeps, sorry.

Proprio non mi sembra vero poterlo dire dopo la bellezza di / quattro / anni, ma sono finalmente riuscita a completare perlomeno questo primo capitolo dell'immensa saga de Il Signore Degli Anelli. E dopo L'Eroe Perduto, per il quale ho impiegato più o meno lo stesso tempo - sebbene, ovviamente, abbia fatto pause immense tra un capitolo e l'altro - mi sento potente come mai. Spero che questa determinazione duri ancora un bel po', perché sono veramente stanca di trascinarmi dietro libri per secoli e secoli.
La Compagnia Dell'Anello non è stata una lettura facile, per me. Quattro anni fa ero sicuramente molto più immatura di quanto sia ora, e soprattutto non avevo né un buon metodo di lettura - non sempre, perlomeno - né una "coscienza" di ciò che leggevo. Aggiungete al tutto il fatto che a me il fantasy non faccia impazzire, che lo stile di Tolkien è quello che è... Un disastro, insomma.
Ma sono veramente felice di aver dato a questa saga una seconda possibilità, e devo ammettere che a 'sto giro è riuscita sicuramente a conquistarmi di più. Cercherò di far passare quanto meno tempo possibile prima di iniziare Le Due Torri, nella speranza che sia ancora tanto presa da non doverci mettere altri quattro anni per finirlo * LMFAO *.

I know… giving lotr two stars seems crazy. Everyone loves lotr and literally anything Tolkien has written, as well as the movies.

But I genuinely do not understand the need for this amount of world building. I appreciate it, to a point. I do not however need to have descriptions of every tree they pass or every rock they kick. I swear all I was reading was world building to an extremely unnecessary extent.

The lack of dialogue was also astounding. I found myself peaking ahead to the next few pages to see if anything would be said. Dialogue was either few and far between, or extremely lengthy for example when they’re talking to walking trees. I find it very difficult to read book told through mostly descriptions, recollections or thoughts when characters are not actually talking aloud often. I would read several,several pages in a row with zero dialogue.

Another problem I had with this was the lack of action for a good 80% of the book. For that 80% that was lacking in anything engaging they were walking, walking in the hopes of getting something somewhere in enemy territory. But quite literally endlessly walking.

The only reason I finished this book is that I was buddy reading it.

Debo empezar diciendo que quizá el libro no merezca una estrella pero la decepción tan grande que me he llevado hace que le ponga la nota más baja posible.
He crecido escuchando que tanto las película como los libros del Señor de los Anillos son obras maestras y los cimientos de la fantasía actual pero lo único que he sentido al leerlo es que estaba leyendo una guía de TripAdvisor.
Es increíble la cantidad de descripciones que da sobre los caminos que recorren cuando en su mayoría son totalmente irrelevantes (no me importa que el camino tuerza al sur durante 50 millas y después continúe durante 20 millas al oeste o que las hojas de este bosque sean ligeramente más verdes que las que crecen en un jardín de la comarca) y solo ha conseguido sacarme de la historia porque no podía parar de pensar "aquí viene otra guía de viaje".
Para terminar los hobbits también representan un problema para mí, entiendo que no son los típicos héroes pero sinceramente son unos personajes muy aburridos que solo son rescatados por otros personajes.

Tried to figure out how to review a book that is so widely loved and that I hated, and I think I figured it out:
It bored me to tears.
I hated the writing style, I hated that there was multiple pages describing what a fucking forest looks like, the dialogue didn't grab me at all, I couldn't keep track of the characters in all the goddamn backstories to everything, and even if I could keep track, honestly, I didn't care what happened to them.
It was like reading the Bible, but with less adventure and more songs.
I truly do not understand why people love it so much. And for the people who have told me that you suffer through this one, because the next one is so good, I don't understand why you would bother to even read the next one.
This book made me understand why so many of my friends hate reading, because if thats the experience they have with books, I get not wanting to pick up another one.
I seriously don't get it. Sorry.

Typisch voorbeeld van een boek dat op handen wordt gedragen door mensen die zich voordoen als de intellectueel betere lezer. Ik heb de boeken nu al meerdere keren gelezen tijdens mijn leven en de conclusie blijft hetzelfde: de personages zijn zo plat als een pannenkoek, de verhaalstijl is saai en de plotlijnen zitten vol inconsequenties. Een voorbeeld van dat laatste: Frodo komt te weten dat hij de Ene Ring bezit en wat doet hij? Vooral niet wat logisch is: zich uit de voeten maken zonder een spoor achter te laten. Nee, eerst wacht hij nog een jaartje en bovendien zorgt hij er voor dat de hele wereld weet dat hij gaat vertrekken uit zijn huis. Mét duidelijke aanwijzingen in welke richting hij vertrekt. Bovendien is het boek al één vierde ver vooraleer het zo ver komt. *zucht*.
En zo kan je wel even doorgaan met het opsommen van negatieve punten. Tolkien was belangrijk voor de ontwikkeling van een genre, maar een hedendaagse lezer kan zich toch maar beter houden bij de films...

I started reading this book because some coworkers and others started doing the Lord Of The Rings conqueror challenge. I would give this book 3.5 out of 5 just because nothing really happens in it.

Edit, thinking back to this book I really only wanted to like it but honestly nothing happened and it was extremely boring. 1 out of 5.

It has been more than half a year since I started on this book but I cannot, for the life of me, finish it. I rarely give up on books, but with all the other ones I plan to read and am actually excited about, I have to accept defeat and just let this one go.

I tried my hardest to like LotR, what with all the praises I've heard from its fans. I even read The Hobbit, gave that 4 stars, but The Fellowship of the Ring, the actual first book of the "epic" series, I just cannot finish.

Fantasy, I love, and LotR is a world of fantasy! But I just tend to get so bored and instead of being thrilled with the adventure, I find myself dozing off or putting my Kindle down!

Is it me? Maybe. Is it the way it was written that didn't appeal to me? Most likely. Sorry, J.R.R. Tolkien, but it seems your works are just not for me.

I doubt if I've ever been more morose about shooting down a book. But I tried. I really really tried. 12 times I tried. It's been roughly 6 years since I've attempted and left and then attempted and then left the book again. I mean, Come on! I refused to watch the movies and they're on TV every week. That's the level of Book Snob value I've given to these series.

I'm sure Tolkien is a genius with creating a world of fantastical creatures and a dark kingdom but I DROWNED in all the description of the woods and trees. 700 pages on and Bombadil stil seems useless. The plot is still meandering woefully. And what is with the POEMS!. This was a fantasy drama and not a musical.

I finally admit defeat.

this is fantasy by a technical writer - an interesting story made boring. plus it's a boys club with no guy on guy action - the only thing that makes these kinds of patriarchial stories worth the read. in my version of the story, aragorn is getting it on with the pretty legolas who wears braids and a miniskirt. the dwarf has to be jealous because you know something is going on between him and the elf. frodo and sam are in this totally codependent relationship - sam carries frodo up the mountain after he's taken no end of abuse from frodo throughout the third book.

my friends urged me to read these books with the encouragement that each book was better than the last. so i slogged through until book three, at which point i finally realized that i really just hated the writing.

I just barely read this one... I know, years behind... When the movie came out, I went to it and was so confused I fell asleep... and frankly didn't care enough to try to watch it again. A decade or so later I decided I should at least give it a chance and read the series and I'll probably enjoy it and the movies. However I must say that I have never been a huge 'fantasy' fan, and after reading this - I'm still not. It was ok, didn't feel that it really explained things well and jumped a lot. I honestly have no idea what all the fuss was about. I'll finish the series for one reason only - to say that I have read them and have my own opinion about them. If you are into fantasy you might like it.

Żałuję, że nie zdążyłem przeczytać książki przed obejrzeniem filmu. A już na nią polowałem, już prawie miałem ją w rękach, dowiedziawszy się jak wielkim klejnotem literatury fantasy jest Władca Pierścieni.
Niestety ekranizacja w reżyserii Jacksona powaliła słowo pisane. Spodziewałem się wybuchających w wyobraźni obrazów podpalanych przez epickie opisy, sceny i akcje. Tymczasem przyszło mi przedzierać się przez dłużyzny, opisy rzeczy, które mnie zupełnie nie interesowały, a wszystko, co miałem nadzieję spotkać przeszło jakoś bokiem, pominięte, napomknięte ledwo co.
Być może trzeba by mi to przeczytać w ojczystym języku autora, potraktować jak dawne, specyficzne legendy i cieszyć się z niuchania starego papieru.

Lord of the Rings is the embodiment of my rating metric: "Not my cup of tea, but if you like Earl Grey, drink up." It is very descriptive of every plant species and creature the crew comes across. There is tons of lore and songs meant to make the world feel real and lived in, and there are just so many characters and backstories. None of this is what I look for in books, and in fact, I find that to be incredibly dense and boring. If you read that description and think, "hell yeah, I love when books are like that," then this is your type of book. I know a lot of people who absolutely love this book and see Tolkien as a master of his craft. It's just not for me.

This book gets 0.5 stars for having poor pacing, not being interesting, and Tolkien's real-world racism and anti-semitism.

this book would definitely be well deserving of a five star review from me, but I’m prohibited from doing so purely because of the presence of this useless little hog….frodo…count your days…

I just could not get into this or ANY of Tolkeins books. I think it's the excruciating attention to detail to every bit of minutiae of every moment.
I have LOVED every screen adapation I have seen of the books, and this is in part owing to the very reason I couldn't stand reading the books. I just couldn't read through all that detail myself, despite the fact that the genius of it all is so very clear throughout.

Pssst! C'mere! Lean closer... I want to tell you a secret, one that few other people will: Tolkien sucked! Horrible dialogue, two-dimensional characters and a plot that, moving at a snail's pace, lasted at least one book longer than it should have; all this and more makes the Lord of the Rings trilogy one of the most overrated pieces of claptrap in the 20th century. Should have stopped at The Hobbit, which only sucked slightly less and thank the literary gods, was only one book long.

reviews.text:
Never have I been so sad to give a low rating to such a revered book. I'm so sorry. I can't tell you how sorry I am.

Again, I'm so sorry, but I found this book unbelievably dull. I really am so, so sorry. I'm desperately sad about this. This series has been such a foundation for modern-day fantasy that I'm incredibly disappointed in myself for not liking this. I have always wanted to be a Tolkien fangirl. I've always wanted to learn Elvish and get completely offended à la Stephen Colbert but I can't. I just can't.

I want so desperately to love Tolkien, but it just ain't happening.

I've been trying this book for 17 years. Tolkien and I have a sad history. I've always been a book lover, when I was young, I would persist through any book, no matter how trying. The Hobbit was the first book that made me fall asleep. It's memorable to me because that's the first time, and only the second time it's ever happened. The other book that made me fall asleep? You guessed it.

The Fellowship of the Ring.

I tried The Fellowship in 10th grade. I couldn't get past Bilbo's birthday party.

I tried it again almost 10 years ago when I was stuck in bed for several days due to, oh, a giant surgical wound in my neck. My doctor said I had to stay in bed for a few days. So, I reasoned, what better way than to resume my attempt at reading one of the greatest literary classics of all time than whole having no other option?

Audiobook it was! I didn't last past Tom Bombadil before I decided, fuck this, I'm going to head to the gym with a bloody bandage on my neck. True story. I got a lot of really weird looks. My doctor gave me a prescription for Vicodin because he was concerned the pain would be too much to bear. Apparently, I didn't even need the Vicodin because that pedophile Tom Bombadil put me right to sleep.

Seriously, were it not for the fact that it is written by Tolkien, I would have hated this book. It was so unbelievably dull. There were parts, that to a Tolkien amateur like me, didn't have a whit of relevance or anything interesting to add to the plot (namely, say, the first 700 pages of the book). Seriously, what the fuck is up with the farmer and Tom Bombadil?

The plot was all sorts of disjointed. Some parts just didn't make any sense. Tolkien is a linguist at heart, and it shows, because all the famous quotes we know from him are just sound bytes. In context, sometimes they don't really make any sense. All the poems and songs are in there to sound pretty, and frankly, they bored the fuck out of me.

For instance, in the middle of a serious dinner party where the company is just trying to decide what to do about the ring (surely a simple task), all of a sudden little Frodo stands up and solemnly announces.
All that is gold does not glitter,
Not all those who wander are lost;
The old that is strong does not wither,
Deep roots are not reached by the frost.
From the ashes a fire shall be woken,

A light from the shadows shall spring;
Renewed shall be blade that was broken,
The crownless again shall be king
I was like what the fuck, man?! Where did that come from? It makes absolutely no sense in the context of the scene. Oh, sure, it's an inside thing on how Aragorn was the secret king, but nobody knew that! Everyone, elf, hobbit, dwarf, (and me) would have thought he was completely high on some elven grass.

Let me make this clear: I do not, for an instance, doubt Tolkien's literary value. I think he has been an inspiration to generations of writers, artists, hell, gamers. My beloved World of Warcraft game featured elves, pretty much every fantasy book we have these days have been inspired in one way or another by Tolkien. Again, he was an amazing linguist, his work developing the Elvish tongue, among others, as well as his efforts in developing the rich, fantastic history of the world within his books is not to be disregarded by any means.

But again, he is a linguist. He is a scholar. He may be the most brilliant one of those in the world, an inspiration to generations, but for me, personally, his writing is not to my tastes.

But damn, the movies were amazing!

Potentially the most controversial review I've ever done... I really wanted to enjoy this, I really did, but I didn't enjoy the first instalment of The Lord of the Rings at all. Though Tolkien's world creation is clearly exceptional, it is a pretty dull read. Each character's dialogue is identically crafted, to the point where the names of the Fellowship are essentially interchangeable (bar Gandalf and, perhaps, Strider), and the 'journey' narrative has such little life breathed into it. It seems unnecessarily strung out and there are a lot of irrelevant details with no interesting descriptive techniques employed to justify them This series has always been on my to-read list, but I don't think I'll bother with the next two.

(p.s. I did enjoy The Hobbit much more!)

You know how they say


That's


The Fellowship of the Ring is proof of that! It takes the rule of show-don't-tell and flushes it down the toilet, because who would rather experience all the kick-ass action scenes themselves when they could just hear someone discussing them over dinner tables like they were discussing rice vs. potatoes? Pffft, no one ofc....

Right?

I mean, who likes action anyway. Why don't we just drop all the action in general and add pages of pages of scenery descriptions instead?

Hearing about the gorgeous colors of the trees is so much more gripping than hearing about how PEOPLE ALMOST GET KILLED BY HORRIBLE CREATURES OF EVIL TRYING TO DESTROY THE WORLD AND RUIN ALL THINGS GOOD!

I'd say go watch the movie.

I should have known this wasn’t going to be for me. It’s not that the writing was bad… it is quite an old books so I was ready for the old style. But there is no way to put it other than this: I found this book to be incredibly boring. Everything that unfolded happened in a very slow and steady way. No where in the book did the pacing pick up or get too suspenseful.

I also found it to be utterly predictable. It was a journeying book, as they are travelling through the majority of it. Me and travelling or road trip books often struggle, so partly this is personal. But every time they journeyed on and faced an obstacle, it was so obvious that they would defeat the creature or solve the problem. There was no excitement behind it. Some obstacles were even incredibly drab in what they were – pages were spent on Gandalf trying to open a locked door using a spell, for example.

I also didn’t really connect to any of the characters, which was another reason why it didn’t work for me. Sure, Frodo is nice enough. But I didn’t really care that much about him, or any of his travel companions.

Honestly, the most entertaining thing about this book was learning about hobbit culture in the beginning and feeling slightly amused at how much they value food and eating. (Same.)

Update: About a year after reading this, I picked up The Two Towers on impulse and started reading it. I went on to read The Return of the King, and found both books much more fun to read than the first book in the series.
A note about The Return of the King: a good chunk of the end is just appendices; most of them are pretty boring and you can skip them without feeling too guilty.

I know, I know...but hear me out. I generally struggle with classic fantasy and sci-fi. It's just really not my thing, but I try to give it a chance every now and again.

Unfortunately, I didn't have a lot of success with TLOTR. I totally appreciate how much work Tolkien put into this book--he had some insane world-building skills--but the plot was just so slow, and the descriptions were so long, that I really struggled to stay interested.

I imagine that my friends and followers are divided into two camps right now.

Group 1. Those who have relished every sarcastic update and laughed at every gif. Thank you. You are the audience this frustrated stand-up comedian lives for. *blows kiss*

Group 2. Tolkienite purists who are breathing a sigh of relief that I am no longer desecrating LOTR with my irreverent sense of humor. Ehhh . . . I don't reaaaallly understand why you love this book so much? but I still really like you and hope we can remain friends! <3

Ammendment: All of my Tolkienite friends have been exceedingly gracious about my updates and exhibited the most wonderful sense of humor. I am grateful for you for putting up with my silliness. :P Making all of you a laugh with my comedy routine brings me joy.

Suffice it to say that I walked into this book ALMOST as torn as Frodo Baggins as he debates on whether to go to Mordor or Minas Tirith.

Being a fairly broad-minded person with very wide tastes in reading, I was prepared to like this book and being converted from my previous opinions.

On the other hand, I am also naturally suspicious of anything that is widely popular, with a strong instinct to run in the opposite direction of the herd. And, being a person that loves to fly in the face of convention, I must confess a certain glow of rebellious contentment that I have walked through these pages and not been pulled in by the planet-wide, mass adoration of Tolkien and his works. The Ring does not corrupt or tempt ALL, my friends! #KIDDING


Can I see strong writing skills or a (very few) good points to the story? The answer, my Fellowship, is yes! But, this book, like the Ring, is a tricky and burdensome thing to a no-nonsense dwarfess, such as myself.

However, I shall refrain from further comment because I have not yet read the entire trilogy. To express a full opinion now would be akin to judging A New Hope without having seen the entire Star Wars trilogy. This is merely the first chapter.

Whether or not I turn the next page to The Two Towers or not is still, as yet, undecided. Consider me cloistered in a inner council similar to one of the endless "should we, or shouldn't we?" debates that grace the pages of The Fellowship of the Rings.

So, for now, you may consider your beloved Middle-Earth safe as I pack up my cheeky sense of humor and leave your Shire in peace. That troublesome and peculiar Baggins is leaving the Shire with a great to-do and a bang. Consider the "professional disturbance" gone from your midst . . . for the moment.

After all, a wizardess cannot resist poking her nose into trouble anymore than she can resist fireworks - even if she might burn her fingers in the process.

I’ve never been the biggest fan of the Lord of the Rings movies. I like a lot of the characters, but I found the movies to be so slow that I had never watched any of the movies from start to finish until earlier this year. Because of this, I knew that I would most likely struggle with the pacing of the books and that I’d most likely not be super fond of the books. My assumptions were correct as I found this book to be so slow and boring that I nearly fell asleep at multiple points in the book. I won’t even get into the prologue here because that was a mess and a half that readers can just skim read, but most of the slowness for the main story was because this book was at least 50% of just setting descriptions. I understand a little bit of setting here and there, but those long passages were extremely uncessary and they pulled away from the main plot of the story. There was some fun action ocassionally throughout the story that helped break up these descriptions, but the action was few and far between.

There were four changes made in the movie that I think made it better than the book.

1. Arwen is more of an important character. This series lacks strong female representation (as most people probably know). There were only four female characters in this first book. All four are constantly with a man in the story and Arwen in particular is just there to look majestic. Arwen is more of a powerful, independent woman in the first movie though. I think changing Arwen for the movie was a great idea since the books are filled with mainly just cis, straight, white men.
2. Merry and Pippin were made to be comic relief in the movies. Merry and Pippin were always my favorite characters in the movies, so it was a shock to me that they were like stale bread in the book. If I hadn’t seen the movies before reading this book, I wouldn’t have remembered who they were since they are bland and unimportant in this first book.
3. The movies cut out most of the poems/songs. I wanted to rip my hair out from all the pointless songs in this book. Why was any of it necessary? I’ll never know. Tolkien seems to just have a random interest in songs, and this interest annoyed me to no end.
4. The ending was entirely different. Sam’s speech at the end of the movie was one of the most impactful movie scenes ever. The book had a different, less meaningful version. There was also no death or kidnapping at the end of the book. I felt that the way they ended the movie was a solid cliffhanger, but it’s literally no where in this book? I’m guessing it’ll be at the start of book two but the kidnapping and death works better as the ending for The Fellowship of the Ring as opposed to the start of the sequel.

Now this book wasn’t all bad. I definitely liked Sam, Legolas, Aragorn, and Gimli as characters. I just think that it would’ve been exponentially better if it had been thoroughly revised. Maybe keep the same general plot in tact, but add more diversity and cut out both the excessive descriptions and songs.

I will eventually finish reading this series. I feel like I have to since I own the other two books and I feel like all hardcore fantasy fans need to read this classic series at some point. I don’t think I’ll enjoy the sequels though - I much prefer The Hobbit and the Lord of the Rings movies to this book.

Thank you, Tolkien, for inspiring so many writers, however, I’m sad I didn’t enjoy this as much as others did. I feel disappointed, but this wasn’t my cup of tea.

It was dense, and my mind would wander so many times that I wouldn’t know what I listened too. I don’t know if there was a moment after picking it up that I would remember what I previously read.

Ormai so che non entrerò mai in sintonia con lo stile di Tolkien, con la sua storia e la magia che circonda il fandom stesso. Da un punto di vista tecnico, ci sono tanti problemi: l’autore ignora il principio dello “show, don’t tell” rendendo le descrizioni (già lunghe) pesanti e la narrazione una sorta di riassunto delle vicende della compagnia; i personaggi, ahimé, sono piatti all’inverosimile. Mi risulta già un grande risultato ricordarne i nomi, perché oltre a quello non saprei fornirvi molti altri dettagli.
Se però vi piacciono i racconti, le storie scritte a mo di favola, allora capisco il perché dell’apprezzamento. Io purtroppo con una scrittura così ricca di problematiche non riesco a venirci a patti.
Il mondo di Tolkien è ricco, ed è questo il merito che riesco a conferirgli. Di sicuro c’è stato un grande lavoro in tal senso, e non mi aspetto niente di meno da uno studioso come lui. Però, però. Neanche questo è riuscito a convincermi, perché con questa scrittura (non ce la faccio, riesco solo a vederne gli errori) e uno stile così pesante per i miei gusti non sono riuscita ad apprezzarne i dettagli, le peculiarità. Un peccato.
Sono affascinata da questa serie per la rilevanza che ha avuto sul genere fantasy, ma devo dire che se non fosse per questo (insieme alla mia ostinazione e curiosità per la conclusione della saga) avrei trovato ben poco di salvabile.
Mi dispiace un sacco, Tolkien. Avrei voluto amarti.

There's no doubt that Tolkien was incredibly talented, having created a vivid landscape, developed the Elvish tongue, and creating a whole history for this world. It's just that his descriptions were so lengthy that I found myself skimming over them. The plot unfolded at a snail's pace to the point where the action (what little there was) felt underwhelming. I had to keep reminding myself that I was reading what many people considered a masterpiece. I tried to keep an open mind and immerse myself in their world. But I couldn't. If I'm 250 pages in and a book still hasn't gripped me, the writing isn't working.

There's no disregarding that Tolkien has gone on to inspire hundreds of writers and is an incredible linguist. His writing style just isn't for everyone. I have the other two books sat staring at me as I write this, but I don't think I'll be picking them up anytime soon. Sorry!

Que mi puntuación no desmerite en lo más mínimo la obra. Reconozco su ambición y su importancia con la misma claridad de declarar que los tiempos de lectura no son siempre los correctos. Hace diez años, por lo menos, me habría impresionado La Comunidad del Anillo, descrestándome su historia y envolviéndome en sus múltiples episodios. Creo pagar con esta lectura una deuda frente al yo-adolescente, cuyas lecturas demandaban acción y eventos y un relato superior al lenguaje en él empleado. Ahora es distinto, de ahí que por fuera de lo entretenido no consiguiese conectar con la obra.

Paso a explicarme, brevemente. El lenguaje en esta primera entrega de El señor de los anillos es plano, básico, llenísimo de lugares comunes. Las cosas oscuras son "negras como la noche", las cosas que brillan lo hacen "como el oro" o "como el amanecer", la belleza es enunciada como "belleza", la fealdad es "fealdad". Por eso se lee en un soplo lo contenido, por eso el despliegue de imaginación, el increíble mundo extenso propuesto, no hacía sino parecerme un terreno ya conocido.

No me aburrió la lectura, ni un solo momento. Pero tampoco consiguió ese punto extra de obligarme a cerrar el libro para reconocer en voz alta el poder de la literatura. Insisto, quizás haya algo de anacrónismo en mi experiencia, quizás no fuese el momento adecuado, o quizás la literatura fantástica de carácter épico no encuentre en mi vida un puente para lograr conmoverme. Hubo demasiados puntos de fricción entre la novela y yo. Los diálogos, por ejemplo, me parecían de una impostura redundante, puestos allí para que los personajes expresaran en voz alta, por ejemplo, que estaban tristes (en lugar de narrar esa tristeza, de hacerla imagen, de hacerla otro lenguaje).

No sé. Disfruté explorando los mapas, disfruté con los mitos (las canciones incluidas me parecen de una riqueza creativa poderosa), disfruté con la secuencia de aventuras. Pero no dejé de sentir nunca el artificio, y eso, cuando no es deliberado, no es lo mejor que puede pasar al leer.

Me tomaré un tiempo antes de seguir con Las dos torres, y es seguro que compartiré este libro con mis primos más jóvenes. Quizás leyéndolo junto a ellos, a la luz de su entusiasmo, disfrute mucho más una relectura.

"Many that live deserve death. And some that die deserve life. Can you give it to them? Then do not be too eager to deal out death in judgement. For even the very wise cannot see all ends."

If you noticed the number of stars I gave this book, then you already know I did not like it. However, and before starting to explain my reasons, I want to make something completly clear, so we are all in the same page. I do not doubt, not even for a second, the literary value of Tolkien. He is the reason so many Fantasy books exist nowadays. Elves, wizards, dwarves, trolls, orcs. It was Tolkien the one responsible for making them so famous, something so many writers nowadays enjoy to write about. The world he created is unique, magnificently detailed, well-built and simply beautiful, and no writer till now was ever capable of creating a world that can ever be compared to Tolkien's. He was a literary genius, a man with an extraordinary imagination and unmatched talent for descriptions and world building. That is not at stake, that is not something any reader can disagree on. J. R. R. Tolkien was a literary genius and the greatest inspiration for all the fantasy related things we have nowadays and like so much.

However, he is also a writer from a different generation, from a time when descriptions were far more important than the plot development. They were appreciated, a necessity even. And nowadays that is not necessarily true anymore. They are still appreciated but there are really few readers still capable of reading (and enjoy) a whole page of description. At least, I can not. And they are so long and sometimes unnecessary that most of the time I skipped them and ended up unable to imagine the places at all. But worst than that was when he mixed the descriptions with the action, thoroughly describing every move the characters did down to the last detail, completly destroying all the action and any interest the scene may have sparked.

Not to say that no matter how much I may have liked the world, with all its details and creatures that make it so, so special and unique, I can never say that the plot is anything I have liked or that I could classify as interesting. They have a task, a mission they need to complete. And to do that they have a terribly dangerous journey ahead. Sounds insteresting, right? But it isn't when all they do is walk, eat, walk, sleep, walk, reach some new place, walk, meet a few new characters, walk, fight, walk, walk, fight and walk. I mean sure, they have to reach a place far away. But they do not need to spend the whole book walking. And definitely not when the book has 400 pages. Especially because walking is not necessarily an action full of drama and danger to keep you interested in the story and wanting to keep reading. In fact, it's the complete opposite. It made the story so dull I usually couldn't read more than one page or two before giving up.

And the fact that I couldn't read those long descriptions Tolkien wrote made it impossible for me to connect with any of the characters, because after all we learn a lot about them in the descriptions, even if sometimes we think we don't. It's the descriptions that more than their words tell us how they react, how they act, what they do. And what they are like. Because how can you connect with someone you cannot imagine? And the dialogues between characters did not help. The way they talked was so weird, so different from our way to talk nowadays that I simply couldn't wrap my head around the idea that anyone could really talk like that.

Therefore, I cannot say it was a reading I enjoyed because it wasn't. It was boring, difficult and most of the time all I wanted was to throw the book against a wall and never pick it up again. In fact, the only thing I could appreciate was the world, with all its creatures and details that made it sound so real. But I cannot deny that everyone has different opinions and yours may not be mine. And that's why I say that you should try to read this book if you haven't yet. Because while reading I had a lot of time to understand that if only I was a reader to appreciate long descriptions, there was an high chance I would have loved this one. And considering its (and its writer) historical importance, I believe that everyone should give it at least a chance.

I am about to come at you with an unpopular opinion. I haven’t read Lord of the Rings, I watched the films but was completely lost and hated them so much. I’ve tried to watch them so many times and simply gave up.

This is a series that I want to love so so so bad. I have multiple copies of the books but I am afraid to read them because I hated the movies so much and feared I would find the books boring.

Having discovered audiobooks recently, I thought this would be a good time to try my hand at reading this classic series especially with this fantastic narrator. After all, Tolkien is like the inventor of the modern fantasy genre so it’s basically required reading in my opinion!

Ok so let me just say that the narrator was fantastic. He read with such enthusiasm and heart that I feel the need to commend him. Plus it was nice to have someone else pronounce the odd names and places rather than me making things up in my head as I go along. However, the one thing I have noticed with audiobooks is that I don’t know that I fully pay attention or absorb the story in the same way I would if I was reading. Especially a story like this where locations and maps are important. I think I needed to physically read this one rather than listen to it.

That said, I found the story so boring. It basically seemed like one long walk where nothing really seems to happen except that we meet other random characters and keep right on walking and debating about what to do with the evil ring. I all honesty, I fell asleep so many times listening to this book and I had to go back and read the Sparks Notes summaries as I went along so that I made sure I knew what was going on. I don’t know how much of that was narration/listening versus physically needing to read the book—-but either way I found myself happy that it was over.

However much I found this book boring—-I want to love it so bad still. Tolkien is an incredible writer with beautiful descriptions and prose. His influence is easily recognizable in a number of modern fantasy like the Game of Thrones books and Harry Potter. I spent a lot of time reflecting on why I didn’t like the book as much as I had hoped. What it came down to for me was it was quest driven rather than character driven.

So much of the story seems to be about the ring itself and the journey—what to do with the ring and how to destroy it. Where as books like Game of Thrones (I know I am comparing apples to oranges here but just go with it). focus so much on the characters and their flaws and strengths and how they respond to conflict and the ‘call to action’. In this book, I don’t seem the same level of development (at least at this point in the series) and I found the journey simply boring. I felt like I needed much more in the way of character evolution and development.

But even if I struggled to like this one, I soldiered on and kept listening and trying to pick out areas of the story that I found interesting. I feel the need to keep reading the series but this time rather than listening to an audiobook, I am going to physically read the second book and see if that helps me to become invested in the charters and world more or not.

I am also going to give the movies another go. I just simply want to love this series so much because so many others do and I hate that I am not gushing over this book. Please tell me the story picks up!

- I like the world. It's a creative and really interesting world, to be honest. Magic, mythical creatures, dangerous places in a dangerous world... It has everything to be good!

~ Gandalf. A wizard that helps the Fellowship.
~ Boromir. An elf Prince. Member of the Fellowship.
~ Sam. Frodo's friend. Member of the Fellowship.

Ben bu kitabı severim sanmıştım ya. Hobbit de biraz sıkmıştı ama genelinde keyifli bir kitaptı fakat *nervous laughter*, not this motherfucker, no.

İyimser olursam %60'ı çöptü. Atlayarak okuduğum yerlerden bahsediyorum, bir insan bunu başka nasıl bitirebilir bilmiyorum zaten. Yolculukların saati saatine, dinlenmelerden kahvaltılara, çay saatinden yemeğe, geçilen yerlerin aşırı gereksiz coğrafik detaylarına inen betimlemelerine kadar anlatılması beni tek kelimeyle sinirlendirdi. "Üç günlük zorlu bir yolculuktu," de geç... Bir süre sonra karakterlerin söylediği şiirleri, şarkıları falan da okumayı bıraktım çünkü içeriğindeki pek çok şey gibi umurumda değildi.

Benim elimden bir editten geçse bu kitap muhtemelen yarısı kalırdı. Daha da yerebilirim ama sevdiğim şeylerden bahsedesim var biraz da: Bilbo'nun doğum günü, Aragorn, Moria'da olanlar ve aşkım balrog, Galadriel ve Boromir'in Frodo'yla yaptığı son konuşma.

Gandalf'ı zaten severdim fakat Aragorn'u hep soğuk bir karakter olarak düşündüğümden bu kadar ısınacağımı düşünmemiştim. Legolas biraz hayal kırıklığıydı çünkü favorim olur sanmıştım. Hobbitler sinirimi bozuyor bu arada, sevdiğim tek hobbit Bilbo şu an. Diğerlerinin salaklıkları beni benden aldı.

Tanrı Peter Jackson'ı kutsasın, bu kitapların özünü çıkarıp mükemmel filmler çektiği için. Tom Bombadil'i iplemediği ve Arwen'e nehirdeki sahneyi bağışlayıp Hobbit'e Tauriel'i eklediği için. Hala Bechdel testinden geçemez filmler belki ama en azından Testosteron Yoldaşlığı'nı izlerken birkaç kadın karakter görmek beni mutlu ediyor.

İki Kule'yi alıp okumaya başlamam uzun bir zaman ve biraz da cesaret alacak gibi. Direkt açıp filmini izleme ihtimalimi düşünmezsek tabii.

Bu arada Game of Thrones karakterlerindeki griliği düşününce LoTR'daki "iyi-kötüye-karşı-burada-her-şey-siyah-beyaz" kafası da pek hoşuma gitmiyor doğrusu. Kötülükten ibaret düşmanlardan nefret etmek çok kolay...

Söyleyecek söz kalmadı. Tolkien efendiye laf atmaya meraklı değildim aslında ama buradayız işte. Kitabı ikinci okuma çabamdı ve ilk seferki kadar sıkıcıydı. Bitirebildiğim için kendimi tebrik edesim var. En sevdiğim sahne balrog sahnesi bu arada, filmde de öyleydi. Çok havalı bir sahne.

He bir de kültürler açısından bakılınca kitaptaki dünya inşası harika elbette, filmlerde de en sevdiğim şeylerden biri elflerin veya cücelerin saraylarıydı. Ayrıca sürekli aralarında geçen ırkçı laflardan sonra Legolas ve Gimli'nin kanka olması güzel bir mesaj bence. Aklıma bir şey gelirse editlerim burayı artık, lütfen beni öldürmeyin.

Not: Filmin müziğiyle okumak keyifli oluyor.

Jag började läsa denna bok med mycket höga förväntningar. Liksom hallå, det är ju sagan om ringen! Den mest lästa, älskade och välkända fantasy boken någonsin! Det måste ju vara en helt fantastisk bok, eller hur? Nej.

Detta var en oerhört långsam bok, varje sida var seg och långtråkig. Även när det hände spännande saker, som tex strider, kändes det som om jag kämpade mig fram genom en seg gegga. Jag var så urless på denna bok redan 50 sidor in och det enda som fick mig att fortsätta läsa den var det faktum att det var "Sagan om ringen".

Det enda som händer i hela boken är att dom är ute och reser, möter monster och faror men klarar sig sen iallafall. Ibland stannar dom till i en stad och pratar med lite personer, men fortsätter sin resa en viss tid senare.

En annan sak jag fann frustrerande var alla dessa namn!! Herregud, vad namn det fanns! I vanliga fall har jag inga problem med att hålla koll på karaktärer och platser (läste "Sagan om eld och is" utan problem!)med detta var en riktigt utmaning! Speciellt platserna och personerna med snarlika namn var extra krångliga för mig att greppa. Och av någon irriterande anledning fanns endast ytterst få av platserna utmärkta på kartan! Jag tycker mycket om att studera kartorna i böcker och följa karaktärernas resa, men i denna bok hade jag sällan någon aning om vad "brödraskapet" befann sig!

I sista halvan av boken talade dom ofta om "Minas Tirith". Jag hade inte en susning om vad Minas Tirith var. En plats visste jag, men var det en stad, ett slott, ett berg eller en ås? Ingen aning! Jag var tvungen att googla och för mig är det ett ganska starkt tecken på att boken var 1) ointressant 2) svårförstådd om man måste googla saker för att förstå. Det är i och för sig mycket möjligt att jag bara missade beskrivningen av Minas Tirith men jag borde ändå kunnat lista ut vad det var när jag fortsatte läsa. Guess not.


En sak som gjorde boken mer uthärdlig var karaktärerna. Vissa var helt underbara. Jag älskade Sam Gamgi över allt annat, hans godhjärtade och lojala natur lyste upp hela romanen.

Så för att sammanfatta;
Sagan om ringen är välkänd och älskad över hela världen men jag förstår inte varför, eftersom jag endast uppfattade den som långsam och onödigt komplicerad.

I understand that Tolkien is considered the father of fantasy as we know it and that this book is prolific for this reason. There are several salient components that people note when crediting this book for such: its depiction of sentient inhuman races and mythical creatures (including his linguistic redoing of the pluralized word for elf); its extensive metahistory and mythmaking; its linguistic grandeur. What troubles me—even if it doesn’t surprise me—however, is the lack of discussion about Tolkien ushering in the genre’s enduring determinism and binary logic, of which is largely inextricable from unabashed racism.

It’s rather frustrating that Tolkien had the ability to construct an entirely new world, with laws of both governance and physics that so deeply oppose our own reality, but nonetheless steeped it in the same tenets of white supremacy. In a storyworld that is otherwise so vast and complex, Tolkien recapitulates—and simultaneously damns the genre that he has spearheaded toward this predilection—the not only offensive, but deeply boring connotations of whiteness as goodness and blackness/darkness as evil; the primary Big Bads of the books are called Black Riders for crying out loud, with the antagonists flippantly being referred to as “black men” and “black fellows” throughout the book. The differing sentient groups in this book are referred to as different races entirely, with the orcs and Black Riders and their other explicitly darkly complected ilk depicted as a beings that are inherently evil, completely irredeemable, and deserving of nothing other than destruction.

There are other reasons this wasn’t for me: the prose is too purple, the pacing is too slow (it’s not until past the halfway point that we even meet Aragorn!), and the plot too hollow. I appreciate the depth of the storyworld’s lore, but it was simply not enough for me to remain engaged, especially when its phrenological underpinnings are so profound.

Just completely and utterly not for me. What a shame.

Tenía mucha ilusión de leer a Tolkien, pero realmente no es para mí.

So.

Coming from the place of being a huge fan of Peter Jackson's movie adaptations of this trilogy, and having just come off listening to The Hobbit, or There and Back Again, also narrated by Andy Serkis, I am mightily disappointed that I just did not get more out of this book.

Such a beloved and timeless book — classic high fantasy that sets the tone and stage for most other fantasy novels to come. And yet, sigh. Tolkien uses all the words. All of them. I was unhappy with the pacing ("By all means move at a glacial pace. You know how that thrills me."), the lack of dialogue that wasn't stilted, and most especially the incredibly unbelievable amount of singing.

Why? Why all the singing?!

On top of all the singing, what set the pacing so wrong was partly because Tolkien insists on using five paragraphs to describe something when five sentences would easily suffice. Not to mention all the stopping and starting in this journey, along with the endless songs and recitations. Did I mention how much singing there was here? With the movie so familiar to me, I had a good many key moments as mile-markers and it felt like we went around the world and back again in between the points of the story I know so well. I found the style to be actually surprisingly reminiscent of mid-century science fiction — which I also don't particularly like — the tone in the narration was closed off and distant, stale.

Ultimately, I had to revisit this in stops and starts, it was a tedious visit each time. I much prefer The Hobbit, but I'm actually jealous of people who have read this trilogy more than once! I wanted nothing more than to love it so. I know how much big Tolkien fans adore this trilogy — I really hoped to join the ranks — but I must bow out.

Audiobook, as narrated by Andy Serkis: Serkis was the only thing holding me up. His performance is practically perfect in every way. I will absolutely check out another book narrated by him — it just won't be the remaining two of this trilogy.

I have an interesting history with The Fellowship of the Ring as this was my fourth attempt to actually read it, in the past I was either too young to actually pay attention to what was going on or other things in my life got in the way and I never finished it. Being in a lot of literary and geek circles this is a series that gets referenced and brought up quite a lot, and usually whenever I would mention that I hadn't read the novels I would get shrieks and gasps followed by people asking why.

I fully acknowledge everything that these books have done for the fantasy genre, Mr. Tolkien is largely responsible for the way that epic fantasy is formatted and written in this day and the level of sophistication in Mr. Tolkien's world has made everyone's world building better. I did find, however, that it was largely the excellent world building that caused the rest of the novel's downfalls, I'll explain.

When my mentor and I taught a creative writing enrichment class at my High School we had a set path we would take when teaching young writers how to craft a piece of fiction. We would use a snow globe as an analogy for their novel and it would start by asking them to build the snow globe. What kind of place is it? Where is it? What is its history? They would write everything that was neccesary about the place(s) where their book was to take place.

Once they had the first step finished it came to the population of the snow globe. Who are the people in there? What is their story? Where are they from? What do they want? Once the students had finished that step we then asked them a single question, and once that question was asked they would begin writing.

What happens when you shake the snow globe?

If books are to represent slices of experience and history from places that never existed then the author has the difficult job of not only crafting a world but making the world real and filling it with people that we can relate to, laugh with, cry with, and struggle through the situation alongside. Now there is of course an exception to this rule, history books, these bound materials are not prose but rather information copied down for the purpose of knowledge.

The fundamental flaw of Mr. Tolkien's first novel is that, at least to me, he seems trapped. He has built a history, cultures, languages, and put more work into creating a universe than anyone else probably has. Mr. Tolkien is trapped because he needs to somehow make that information digestible while still telling an important story with well crafted characters, and in that struggle the novel somehow ends up flat on its face.

There are two fundamental problems with this book, the characters and the prose. Each character that we are introduced to has little to no actual characterization, anytime we learn something about them its typically two other characters describing the first. Most dialogue that doesn't follow the above formula is typically history or explanations of strategy and geography which leaves very little left over for meaningful talks between characters about emotions and what makes them who they are.

The second major issue concerns how this book was written, I dont understand the obsession with songs that Mr. Tolkien seems to have but there are so many breaks for musical numbers which, once again, tell history and tales of heroes in the same way of epic poems in eras gone by. Secondly I dont understand some of the choices he made when it comes to describing the environments, after Mr. Tolkien spends half a page describing the tree leaves he then goes into long digressions on the history of the area and just how special it is. These more lengthily descriptions made me lose focus on what I was reading and there is so little actual dialogue for most of the book that it just gets boring at moments.

For all of its flaws the novel is still very impressive, the history and extensive world building does indeed make it feel like a real place but it isn't communicated well. There are also moments of real genius in the novel, such as the council of Elrond, the conversations between Galadriel and the Fellowship, and when Boromir attempts to convince Frodo that he could use the ring for good. Unfortunately the novel has so much filler crammed in that getting to the moments of genius can be really taxing, and its for that reason that it took so long for me to finish this book.

I think that Mr. Tolkien has one of the most fascinating worlds that is just short of being real on his hands, but it would work so much better in the style of a history book because it would give him the freedom to talk about the history of Middle Earth from the view point of a researcher rather than attempting to intertwine it with a story. I will continue to follow the journey to Mount Doom but how much better these can get I know not.
