Before I start, I want to emphasize that I do know the cultural and literary significance of these works, and I'm not making any kind of judgement on it in that sense. I am reviewing this book solely as a reader in 2011 who enjoys fantasy, and my review is just to help people decide if they may or may not enjoy the book. It's not supposed to be a judgement of whether or not the book is "good" or "bad", just whether or not you will enjoy it or not if you read things the way I read them.

That being said, I really struggled to get through this book. It felt way longer than its 400-something pages would lead you to believe. A good 2/3 of the book consists of a group of travelers plodding along silently, looking in each direction and describing in detail what they see -- only to move on two minutes later. So you'll have 3 paragraphs about the specific curvature of the path ahead, and the way the bank slopes up, and how half of the bank has tall grass and the rest has short grass... and how if you look to the south you will see the beginnings of the mountains, past a rolling hillside that is three different colors... and then if you look southeast you see a wide path that curves north then east, getting narrower and then slightly overgrown... you get the idea. It's incredibly exhausting to try to picture everything and then realize that it was pointless, because nothing happens and they just move on, and this dry description starts over again. It would be interesting, maybe, if this fantasy setting and world was something pointedly unique, but it's really not. It's hills and grass and mountains and trees and... basically, it's just like we're following people walking through a forest or hills in Europe except that there happen to be hobbits.

The characters, too, are incredibly flat and unchanging. They have their (somewhat) unique characteristics, but no one's character does or says anything more involved than "I believe we should take this path," or "We must hurry... I feel the orcs might be about." We only get the most shallow of introspection from Frodo, and nothing from anyone else. We get surface conversation, characters that don't change, and not much else. I'm huge into character so this bores the hell out of me.

So if it's not about character it should be about the adventure right? Wrong. Like I said before, most of the book consists of topography lessons and lots of things that "almost" happen. So it doesn't have much of a plot, the description is dry and tedious, and it has no character development. No matter how significant this work is in the overall picture of fantasy history, I cannot say I enjoyed it. In fact, I'm not even sure I can finish the series. At least right now I'm not -- I'm going to start Game of Thrones instead. Tolkien has lost me for now.

A student told me she would report me to the Librarian Council Authority if I didn’t read this book, so I read it while I was in England. I read Hobbit in high school and remember liking it. When I first tried reading Fellowship of the Rings (after being inspired by re-watching the movie version), I could not get past the tediously detailed Introduction which is like some kind of Encylopedia of the World of Middle Earth. I whinged to my student how it was soooooooooooo boring and could I skip a bunch of chapters and get to the part where they’re already on the quest and they meet Strider aka Aragorn aka Hello, Handsome! ? Student and I worked out some kind of deal, which I ended up forgetting because after skipping the whole Intro and starting the actual book, it was actually OK. The beginning Hobbit bits are really well done in a slightly dry humorous small village in England kind of way. Like, our narrator is kind of mapping out the whole Hobbit social scene and describing the foibles of the different villagers and you can totally imagine Tolkien getting even with actual people he grew up with from his village. While I enjoyed that and was happy when the quest got off the ground, I still found Tolkien’s style very tedious and over-descriptive. I did a lot of skimming throughout the book. I will now sum up my main reactions to the book as a whole:
-Like I said, I really enjoyed all the observational humor that had to do with the Hobbits, throughout the book
-Gandalf is rad. I would have to think hard about a Gandalf v Dumbledore face-off.
-The descriptions of the environment and the history of elves etc were horribly tedious. The whole book could have been trimmed by a ⅓
-I thought the way Tolkien set things up with the elves being a superior race (with blond hair, pale skin and tall) and all the other races having a hierarchy that is reflected in their perceived levels of beauty as compared to a western European ideal to be very creepy and gross.
-A lot of the “high fantasy” language was cheesy and hard to take - you know, the inverted semi-Biblical sentence structure.
-Gandalf is actually totally mean and snotty to some of the Hobbits - it’s bitchy and fun but kind of mean! I can’t decide if I like it.
-When there is an actual sustained action sequence it is very entertaining.
-Was I allowed to skip the Tom Bombadil parts or not? Because I totally skipped it. It seemed boring and pointless.
-I prefer the movie to the book by a large margin. I think the movie edited out a lot of the pointless plot things as well as the descriptions and got to the good stuff.

I didn’t read all of Fellowship; I only read up to the end of Book 1 (since Fellowship is divided technically into two “books.”) I found that I was not enjoying the book.

So what didn’t I like?

1-The writing: Now, don’t get me wrong; Tolkien's prose is pretty dang excellent from an objective standpoint. However, there is something about the writing of LOTR that just puts me to sleep. I loved Tolkien's style in The Hobbit, though; it struck me as a great deal more fun and easy to read.

2-Too much physical description: Tolkien's world is fantastic, but I just can’t handle a book where over half of the words seem to be describing plains, valleys, and the daily weather. It works well in the movies, though, because a picture can paint a thousand words.

3-Underdeveloped characters: Please don’t lynch me for this statement. But I sensed virtually no personality from Frodo, Merry, or Pippin. It got to the point where I wouldn’t even really have cared if they died. Sam is amazing, though. Nobody can possibly dislike Sam! And I really liked Maggot in his brief scene. Simply, I felt like the movie characters (while still fairly one dimensional) were sharper, easier to differentiate between, and far more lovable.

4-Lack of female representation: Now I don’t consider myself a feminist or anything—but I still feel like there could have been a few females that could have played more prominent roles. It seemed like all the characters really involved in Frodo’s mission and the battle of good versus evil were male. As a Christian, I believe that everyone has a role to play there.

5-Gratingly slow pacing: All the characters seemed to be doing was wandering through dense forests and avoiding Black Riders.

6-A lack of emotion: The LOTR movies simply drench the viewer with the feels. But I personally feel like Tolkein does a very poor job at conjuring genuine emotion within the reader. The potential for an emotional roller coaster is present in the books (as we see from the movies), but Tolkein does not capitalize on this potential.

So, what did I like, then? Well, I do love Tolkien's complex and multi-faceted world. I adored Sam and his fascination with elves. And I do know that the plot eventually gets pretty epic because I do adore the movies. (To be honest, I could watch those film endlessly.) But, alas, I just couldn’t get into the books. Perhaps I’ll try to give them another chance some other time. Or maybe I won't.

Evil Jewelry

The pure of heart must save a magical world threatened by evil jewelry. This is the history book about it, translated by one Tolkien, fluent in the tongues of Middle Earth. Good for him.

Honestly, this was a surprise read in many ways. I didn’t expect, for one thing, to gain a newfound appreciation of the beautifully made and boring Peter Jackson movies. They actually achieve a grandeur Tolkien’s smothering prose constantly undermines. At least it better conveys the superficial attractiveness of the fantasy.

Another surprise was how underwhelming the worldbuilding is, as this series has a reputation for its vast and meticulous lore. The worldbuilding so far is strictly mytho-poetic side, a careful mimicry of the poetic epics of yore without any of their zaniness (save for Tom Bombadil, which did feel more like a trickster god). The languages are well done, as you’d expect from a linguist. Tolkien’s own character building is at kindergarten levels. Gandalf falls to his death and the Fellowship barely blinks, lamenting only that he can’t be here to tell them where they’re going. No doubt they had a consoling talk by their creator assuring them that he will return, so courage, friends! I had more pity when Sam had to leave Bill the Pony behind.

Tolkien’s prose is readable, if awkward and inelegant. There are some early modern cadences in the dialogue I appreciated (Tolkien knew his Shakespeare, obviously) but they are completely drained of all possible vitality, all hint of suggestion of fresh-and-blood people. His verse is pure trot verse save for the “All that is gold does not glitter” and as songtext they are scarcely tolerable.

There’s a very good reason why I did not pick up the tome before, and I have unfortunately been vindicated. The Fellowship et al. is good, Sauron et al. is bad, and never shall the twain meet or reside in one breast except when the narrative calls for it. I really am too old for this.

Tolkien is very clearly the father of worldbuilding with some of the most solid and believable work in the entire genre. He's the author fantasy writers aspire to. But for all the brains that went into LoTR, it's missing its soul-- that is, character development. In the films (I'm actually comparing a book to its movie! Scandalous!), we got to feel out the characters. Sam was the friend everybody wanted, Pip and Merry were goofballs, and Legolas and Gimli's friendship was quirky and beautiful. We get none of that in the book. It reads like a textbook of Middle Earth, and there's nothing wrong with that, per se, but the heart of any story is its characters. You don't read fiction to be lectured; you read fiction to harbor a connection with exciting, believable, and relatable characters-- perhaps in a setting like our everyday lives, perhaps in a world with magic and dragons. Whatever strikes your fancy. As much as it pains me to say it, I couldn't like any of the characters from reading the book. Aragorn and Legolas both I love from the movie trilogy, and that was the love I had to bring to the table to finish reading the book. As interesting as it was to read about Middle Earth, it couldn't keep my attention; there was only so much I could read about my favorite Elf and Ranger without them doing anything of note. There were so many missed opportunities to give insights into the characters' minds that Tolkien just let pass by!

I’ve been reading seriously again for about three years now. It’s been wonderful to sink my teeth into things that I missed when I was in college (or getting my feet under me teaching) and reading things that didn’t catch my eye as a kid. This past year I’ve felt like I’ve finally started to see how my reading tastes have grown over time, and I decided it was time to return to Lord of the Rings. I’d read it as a kid and remember being vaguely unimpressed, but it was a long time ago and I’m a very different reader now.

Normally I’d start with a plot blurb, but I won’t bother here. A short version of my thoughts is that I felt like Fellowship was underwhelming and had some fairly serious issues, but that there were enough of interest that I’ll reread book 2 someday, though I likely wouldn’t for pretty much any other series I felt this way about. I’ll try to keep my review organized, but I have a gut feeling that this one will meander a bit. When it comes to Lord of the Rings though, it’s all about the journey.

The Good: I think Fellowship is at its best in the beginning and ending of the book. I truly loved the bits in and around Bilbo’s birthday party. Tolkien had some subtle humor that was quite enjoyable - a memorable moment about hungover hobbits has stuck with me - and I think the prose was at its best here. The pastoral reputation of Lord of the Rings (or at least, of book 1) lives or dies by the bits here in The Shire, and I think it really works. It felt like a cosy small town, with all the squabbling that comes with it. Had there been more meth, I’d have said it felt like home.

I also thought taking the time in The Shire was essential to set up the idea of the journey being a primarily sad one. Yes there’s adventure, but the bits that hit home in the second half (and which came more often near the end of the book, which make me hesitantly optimistic for sequels) was the longing for the simple life left behind. And you need to spend some time in that simple life for those moments to feel powerful. It’s clear to see the influence of Tolkien serving in World War I here, and in the general melancholy of the journey instead of the indulgent violence we see in so much fantasy (I do love an epic fight scene though).

I also thought the ending sequence, beginning for Boromir’s attempt to get the ring from Frodo, was extremely engaging, possibly in part because I felt like it was one of the few times since the shire where I thought Tolkien did a good job of creating emotion in a scene. There was tension, and this was the first time that I really felt the weight of the ring and its corrupting power in a more visceral way.

My Issues with It
There were quite a few, and they were especially disappointing considering how well written the beginning bit was. However, as soon as Frodo left home and the journey began, I felt like things went downhill for me rather quickly.

Fundamentally I think it’s an issue of bloat, or perhaps of a strange set of choices around focus that Tolkien made. I’ve got no problem with slow pacing in books. The Rook and Rose series probably could have been written in half the pages, but took its time for some reasons that I think paid off extraordinarily (and the series going to come up a few more times as a comparison point in various ways). Slow pacing can work really well when the author is developing characters, a world, or a theme. However, I don’t think Tolkien particularly succeeds in any of those areas, and I found myself frequently feeling like entire sections could have been cut without affecting any sort of characterization or thematic heft Fellowship had.

Yes, I did just say that I didn’t think Tolkien succeeded in worldbuilding. More specifically, I don’t think the ways he chose to include his worldbuilding to be interesting or engaging. It is undisputed that Middle Earth has a long, detailed, and chronicled history. Pretty much everything has a past, and Tolkien is more than willing to tell you about that past. That can work really well. I’ll turn to Rook & Rose again: significant time is spent building a complex network of political and cultural forces of a single city, and ensuring that the various players in the books are put into the context of the history of the world, along with reveling in clothes the way Tolkien reveled in songs. Tolkien’s books, however, seem interested in sharing history totally unrelated to the narrative. I remember thinking soon after Frodo left his home that more time was spent describing a location and its past than the characters spent interacting with it or within it. For some, I’m sure these details are a big plus. However, I don’t see these historical details as enhancing the story in meaningful ways, instead drawing out scenes for little reason.

It didn’t help that I found it frustrating that these info dumps were given space not just in narration, but dialogue as well. Every character seemed to be a history textbook, and the prose of their explanations felt scant different in dialogue than in narration directly to the reader. And while I certainly know quite a bit of casual history that a reader from another world would need to know if my life were a story, I don’t often spout it off while I’m traveling from one place to another.

Even putting aside that the characters became a mouthpiece for historical tangents, I didn’t find most of the Fellowship terribly interesting or different from each other. Gandalf’s vacillating temper stands out, as does Sam’s singleminded determination to serve Frodo (even if its a bit odd), but many of the characters blended together for me, to the point where it felt like many pieces of dialogue could have been given a different speaker tag without it feeling out of place in the slightest. There was just so much telling me what a character was like (and telling can work when done well. A Hundred Years of Solitude is a masterpiece that is almost wholly telling), but I could only deal with so many times of being told how wonderful Frodo was when he rarely did much. Even in camp interactions he felt more like a blank slate for others to act upon, yet I’m told he’s a charismatic lodestone which the group revolves around even putting aside the ring.

And for all that I feel like I’ve heard that Lord of the Rings has gorgeous prose, I just didn’t feel it. There were moments of brilliance, certainly. Many of the oft-quoted lines show that Tolkien can pull some incredible writing off. However, those moments tended to live in isolation, surrounded by drudgery of writing that felt utterly bereft of emotion. The scenes of mourning after the group loses Gandalf come to mind as a moment I haven’t mentioned before which was gorgeously written, filled with sadness, regret, and yearning (and was one of the more successful of the songs, many of which felt out of place). However, so often I found that Tolkien was so intent of describing a physical detail that he lost the spirit and emotion of what was being described. Literature is filled with beautiful writing about nature. For how much of this book was devoted to geography however, it didn’t stand up to that history. The underground journey through the mountains should have filled with tension, the scene of Gollum on a log one of shock and revulsion and fear, the elven domains filled with wonder. But so often I felt bored more than anything, only to be yanked out by a tidbit that seemed genuinely wonderful to read before drifting back into endless drudgery.

Does the Lord of the Rings have pacing issues? Perhaps, but not because it took its time with things. I actually think that a slower pace was necessary for the type of story that Tolkien was going for: one not defined by its epic battles, but by the more human moments of how this unrequested adventure wears on its participants. But when Tolkien set plot by the wayside, I needed something else to compensate for it. The answer was, I think, supposed to be the history of the world. But in the end I felt like I’d learned a lot of random facts that didn’t matter to the heart of the story being told.

Assorted Musings
Tolkien used the word Queer a lot. I’m not particularly interested in claiming that Tolkien was a raging homophobe like some (and also, I am highly uninterested and unimpressed by the claim that he was ignorant of the harmful use of it towards the LGBTQ+ community. That definition had been at use in Britain at least since Tolkien was a toddler). He’s very clearly using the word queer to mean strange. However, it’s obvious that the word was one of his crutches in his writing, because for all people like to complain about quirking eyebrows or tugging braids in fantasy, there were a whole lot of ‘queer’ things in this book. I think this might have something to do with my dislike of these books as a kid, when I wasn’t able to separate the two uses quite as much. There was a lot of ‘smear the queer’ games going on in my hometown. Now, I just saw it as one of Tolkien’s cliche terms, which almost all authors have.

I won’t go deep into the race essentialism hole, as there are large arguments on this subreddit alone that you can find which probably dive far deeper than I have. I did find myself extraordinarily uncomfortable when the only person to stand up and defend Gimli from the extraordinarily blunt elvish racism was Aragorn. Everyone else seemed totally fine with it. And while I don’t need every character to act in a morally upbeat way, it really shaded my view of how Tolkien was using races/species in his world.

On the Legacy of Tolkien
I’ve never subscribed to the view that Tolkien is the father of fantasy. One of them certainly, but not the sole one. A common complaint is that later authors ripped the trappings of Tolkien while missing the spirit of him. And while I do wish that fantasy had kept a larger branch that acknowledged the pain and sadness of these types of journeys instead of focusing on epic fights (though the genre absolutely should have epic fights too), I find myself thankful that so much of Tolkien’s style was not emulated, just the superficial details of world and epic journeys.

I also find myself thankful that we are pretty much fully out of Tolkien’s shadow as a genre now. Not only do I find monotony boring in a genre (other than perhaps romance, where the predictability and repetition is a feature, not a bug). However, I can’t help but imagine a world where the fantasy genre was influenced by a Lord of the Rings that had a female member of the fellowship, or that spent the entire time following Frodo in his misadventures as Bilbo’s heir. And I find myself wishing that fantasy had chosen to pick an author like George MacDonald as the one to emulate (or, at last one of Tolkien’s books that drew more inspiration from MacDonald’s style). For I found that my sense of wonder and magic was higher with him than I ever felt while reading Fellowship.

There was enough good here that I’ll take a stab at rereading book 2 at some point, but I’m going to enjoy my diversions into other books for now, and perhaps try to stake out some time for Sword and Sorcery, to see where that falls on my spectrum of enjoyment of early fantasy writing.

Confession time: I hated The Fellowship of the Ring. I loved the movie, so when I first tried reading it when it first came out back in the early 2000s, before I had any kids, I quickly gave up the task and moved on to other things.

Fast forward 18 or so years, and now we're in the throes of Coronavirus. I have a high risk kid. So, I pull out all my kids from school and we're homeschooling. I find this excellent literature-based homeschool curriculum for my three kids that I adore. My 9th grader is assigned to read all of The Lord of the Rings.

Gulp.

So, I decide this is the time to finally cross this off my bucket list. Millions of people adore the novels! Maybe I just didn't give it enough time? I heard the first 100 pages were the hardest, and then it gets great!

So, I tried it again. Like a soldier, I trudged through it every day, highlighting as I went, to help my 9th grader with the literature questions that are assigned with the daily reading. Each day we're reading around 30-40 pages. That's not too bad, we can do this! Read all of LOTR in 6 weeks! I even got some friends on board to read along with us as a support network.

My kid must have the same issues with the book as I do. Because I'm doing my best going through it, and they're loathing literature time every day. I don't blame them. The book is such a slog. This kid is a huge lover of literature, too- in 7th grade, they won (with 3 of their friends) the Battle of the Books competition for their entire school district. Seriously, reading is not a problem for this kid. But this book? It caused actual tears. They finished The Fellowship of the Ring, and got about 1/3 of the way through Two Towers when I finally said, "OK, we can read something else." We'd had enough. Kid is happy. I'm happy.

Will I finish the other two books? I'm going to try. I'm still working on it. But, when I read, I read the words but can't comprehend what's happening. It took me a while to figure out why this was happening.

I love reading. I read a wide variety of books and enjoy so many different types of books. But there are a few books that I've tried reading and just can't get into. It's usually the characters. It's like I need to invest in characters of a book on an emotional level. In those cases, reading just feels like a chore, and when it feels like a chore, my brain turns off. I'm reading the words, but nothing makes sense. I can't visualize or see myself there. In LOTR, there's so many characters, and you just get the surface of each character. Nothing deep. They're just so flat. And I think that's why when I read it, I get nothing.

So, I'll continue reading the other books in LOTR, and maybe it will start to come alive for me. But if it doesn't, that's okay. It's just not my cup of tea.

I rated this book two stars instead of one because of the huge cultural impact it has had. I love fantasy novels and appreciate that it has inspired so many others. I'm just not one of them. I'll still watch and enjoy the movies. The books, though, they're not for me.

There is that clichéd saying that you should never meet your heroes in real life, because they can never live up to the ideals you have built around them. Well, few things could be more fitting than this when it comes to The Lord of the Rings.

To this day, I can easily watch the full extended version of the trilogy without getting bored or zoning out, but this novel is an entirely different experience. The first fifty pages start off very atmospherically, but then it becomes endlessly monotonous and boring. Action appears here and there for a few pages. Opening a gate takes one or two pages. The Balrog gets one page. The characters feel empty: they just keep moving forward, but they never truly interact with each other or with the world deeply enough for their personalities to unfold.

The hobbits are filler characters with zero personality and significance. They function purely as placeholders, as ring-transporting devices. Gimli and Legolas receive almost no introduction at all, and honestly, they feel as if they are barely even there. I only remembered they existed when their names were mentioned during one or two brief lines of dialogue. Boromir seems to be present solely to increase the physical headcount, and nothing more. As for Aragorn, we learn practically nothing about him, despite the fact that he is a central and important character. It is not that his past is mysterious; it simply does not exist. Gandalf is the only one who has some kind of background and actual significance, but he is far from enough to carry this novel on his shoulders.

The first half of the book is not only forgettable, but it offers absolutely nothing to either the story or the atmosphere — apart from, of course, the first, let’s say, fifty introductory pages. The constant singing and the detailed descriptions that lead nowhere did not just drain my desire to read; at times, they drained my desire for life itself.

The stops along the journey feel almost entirely insignificant. They are introduced as if they were meaningful, important milestones, but in reality, very little changes — if anything changes at all — after each new checkpoint is reached.

Something does happen at the very end of the volume, but for me, it is nowhere near enough. The second and third books will remain on my shelf, because by God, I am not finishing this as long as I live.

Supplemental – The Fellowship of the Ring
Part 1 was probably the weakest entry to the book series. The plot does not move anywhere for a good half of the book. Once it starts trudging along, we start to delve into elven society.

The Lord of the Rings
Lord of the Rings has built up a formidable reputation among fantasy readers, who consider this book the ultimate expression of the fantasy genre. They often consider Tolkien to be the father of fantasy. Does Tolkien deserve such praise or not? I slogged my way through these three books, and the short answer is I did not like them. Here is why.

I approached these books after reading the Hobbit and Watching Peter Jackson’s six films. I have a great deal of respect for Jackson’s first three films, and I wanted to see what the source material did differently. Though my poor experience of the book, The Hobbit has already tainted my opinion, I wanted to discover which way my opinion would go. What bothered me the most was that I did not feel like I was a proper fantasy reader until I had read The Lord of the Rings. My reading of these books was inevitable.

Tolkien presents us with his own fully realised world built from the ground up. He uses some familiar concepts, both in fiction and reality, melding them all together and giving them a Tolkien twist to present us and himself Middle Earth.

The way he takes this vast world in transferring it to the page is a different matter. His descriptions are highly detailed and incredibly informative of the lands and societies of Middle Earth. We can learn a lot about Tolkien’s world, to the point where his books can read like history books. If they were history books, I would find them interesting – after all, I find our planet’s history endlessly entertaining – and as a bonus, I get an education. I do not feel the same way about Middle Earth. Tolkien’s world is not a real history. The Red Book was not a part of some forgotten mythology or legend, though I thought it a nice touch for Tolkien to imply such a thing. I do not think Middle Earth is as important as our reality and I do not share the same passion of its fans to learn every single intricate detail in this world. I do not find it entertaining to read twenty-odd pages describing a simple river or forest or mountain for the millionth time.

What is worse, Tolkien makes for an unreliable voice. He gives us a lot of arbitrations on a matter, often vague descriptions on some matters sometimes describing something as no more and no less than good or evil. What am I supposed to imagine when I see “good” in someone, or imagine a man as “kingly?” These descriptors tell us nothing to discern, describe or flesh out the characters, the story, or the world. Describing someone as Kingly does not tell me anything about the character, even if they were to show it or if they were a King. I could not find any imagery in the phrase. I feel like such expressions of this and in characters’ metaphorical hights are simply expressions of Tolkien’s backwards beliefs in feudalism.

Continuing from that, Tolkien really did not like the colour black. I expect it has something to do with Christian purities, but it was annoying just how often that word came up. The orcs were black, the riders were black, a blackness came over characters when they were the slightest bit ill – it was excruciatingly painful to read that word time after time. This blackness was so repetitive, so non-descriptive when there were different descriptors, which happened to be just as vague in their description as blackness, I had to stop myself from putting the book down and never returning to it again.

Furthermore, descriptions where they were not so vague were often telling and far too exact. There were points where Tolkien would describe the exact order that the characters appeared in a line as they marched on to Mount Doom, or wherever. I did not need such specific information. It made an already slow book even more enduring.

I did not enjoy the overall pacing of the whole story of The Lord of the Rings, but especially in “The Fellowship of the Ring.” I have already stated my opinions on all the unnecessary details and descriptions, but there were entire chapters sometime that seemed to exist merely to fluff up the book. Hardly anything in all of Tolkien’s books had a significant bearing on the plot, the characters, or the world. There was so much unnecessary fluff, and virtually no flow to the story, whatsoever.

One of the qualities I really do not like about Tolkien as a person, he was a stout and stubborn supporter of the feudal system. He once claimed in an interview ‘Power should belong in the hands of those who were born to it,’ this coming from a man of high-class decent. We see this side of him come out when it comes to his representation of the hobbit families and their power dynamics through family names, in the puritan, angelic, Aryan nature of the elves, and in Aragorn’s contrasts to lesser people who are either docile and happy to serve, or black and crude. As examples, Samwise held up his submissive attitude towards Frodo right the way through these books and was “good,” but compare him to the foetus-like, toothless Gollum, or the squirming, black-clothed Wormtongue – it is a joke!

It frustrates me to think about the implication of such class-based stereotypes. Tolkien attributed character behaviours based on their class. The higher their social standing, the better fighters they were, the brighter and whiter their clothes, the less floors they had. Tolkien treated each character like a tool used to express his archaic views through these books.

I will cut Tolkien some slack. He did a brilliant job in realising Middle Earth, building on it simply as a hobby. He spent years studying language and mythology which he used supposedly as his primary influences for the world.

I will say though that every trope present in these books contained existing fantasy tropes before The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings. What Tolkien did, he collected those tropes, included a few such tropes from science-fiction, another genre on the rise at the time, and collected them all in a handful of books.

That is not enough to give him his legendary status, but he partially deserves the legendary status that so many give him for publishing these books. I give key credit to those early fantasy fans who picked up this book, and books like it and read them. They were the people who made the fantasy genre so popular simply by consuming, and they were the people who got more authors and publishers interested in writing and publishing fantasy. While Tolkien was not inventing new tropes, he helped coin them all, bringing them to the attention of future authors, who borrowed so heavily from his work.

Simply put, I doubt fantasy would have been nearly as popular if Tolkien’s work had not been successful, and we would not recognise the fantasy genre today if he had not collected all those tropes and done all his research. I am just in awe that he wrote these books primarily as a hobby, and now his “hobby” is the most recognisable fantasy book around.

I am so sad. I wanted to love this book so much. Elves? Dwarfs? Hobbits? Humans? Dragons? Magic? Ticks every single one of my boxes! A long journey with some magical objects and an unknown evil enemy and betrayal? Sign me UP!!! And yet... I was so incredibly bored.

I enjoyed the prose at first, and the rich history was incredible. But by about page 200 I was looking ahead to figure out how long until the next chapter and I could feasibly take a break. The books became simply 'deep description of the surroundings while walking, lonnggggg conversation between characters discussing some deep history with 20 new people that you will never hear of again, SONG!'

I see how this translated well into a movie... there are no internal monologues that are at risk of being missed out, and much of what can be omitted are simply long histories and various names that only seem to serve to confuse the reader. Huge chunks can be skipped and nothing is lost of the story... if Tom Bombadil wasn't there there would be no change to the story... the Barrow-wight could also have been completely missed and there would be no difference.

I feel slightly guilty rating such an iconic fantasy classic two stars… but if I’m being honest, finishing The Fellowship of the Ring was a genuine struggle for me.

The world-building is undeniably incredible. Tolkien created something enormous, detailed, and hugely influential, and there are moments where the beauty and scale of Middle-earth really shine through. As a big fan of the films, it was fascinating to experience the original version of the story and see where so much fantasy inspiration comes from.

But unfortunately, I found the actual reading experience very difficult.

The pacing is extremely slow, there’s an overwhelming amount of detail, and the constant songs completely took me out of the story at times. Some of them are whimsical and atmospheric, but eventually it started to feel like every journey, meal, or mildly emotional moment required a full musical performance.

I also found it difficult to stay emotionally engaged for long stretches because the narrative often prioritises lore and atmosphere over momentum. While I can absolutely appreciate the craftsmanship behind it, I personally struggled to enjoy it consistently.

By the end, I felt more relieved to have finished it than excited by it - which is never the best sign.

I completely understand why this book is beloved and groundbreaking, but I think I’ve learned that this style of classic fantasy writing just may not be for me.

An impressive and iconic story… but one I found far more admirable than enjoyable.

I had read books recommended to me by my mother in the past, and decided to switch it up a bit and get a book from my sister. She doesn't read too many books, but told me that she loves Lord of the Rings. Realizing I hadn't actually seen the movies or read the books, I decided to start. I wanted to enjoy this book, but I couldn't.

The book follows Frodo Baggins, cousin of Bilbo Baggins, and begins on Bilbo's 111th birthday party. Decades prior, Bilbo had disappeared from home with a wizard named Gandalf, and went on an adventure. Bringing home many different treasures and stories, he was still the topic of many conversations. One of these treasures was a small gold ring, which made him invisible, which he used to make his secret exit from the party. Packing his things at his home, and begrudgingly leaving his gold ring behind, he sets off from home, leaving the home to Frodo. Blamed for the disappearance of Bilbo by the other hobbits, Gandalf departs as well, promising to visit Frodo at some point. Years later, Gandalf returns, telling Frodo the tales and danger of the ring he possesses. Frodo is given the task of destroying the ring before the Dark Lord Sauron can regain it and rule over middle-earth. Sam Gamgee, a friend of Frodo, overhears the conversation and is allowed to join in on the quest. Frodo's cousin, Pippin, also joins the two in the Fellowship of the Ring.

The journey itself is where I begin to have trouble, much of it blends together. Tolkien's writing requires a lot of patience, which I have very little of in place of high amounts of stress. Descriptions of landscapes can take up pages, and uninterrupted exposition can continue for even more pages. Like I said, it all required a lot of patience I currently have trouble getting. I hope that if I pick this book back up over the summer, when I won't have to stress out about school anymore, I'd be able to enjoy it like so many others do.

There were parts of the book I admit were good, however. The world itself feels extremely well thought out and detailed, with even a map of middle-earth in the first pages. Tolkien shows his passion for this world in each detail and character he adds, it's obvious he put a lot of care into it. I especially found Gandalf memorable, seeming wise and aged, yet showed authority and intimidation when necessary. The world of Lord of the Rings is very interesting, and will convince me to pick this book back up once I think I can handle it.

In fact, it seems mostly to be a book about the geography of Middle-earth and the genealogy of its peoples, with a tiny little plot that can be summarized in about 2 sentences. Which, great, if you're interested in this fictional world already. But I needed a reason to be interested, and didn't feel like I got one here. I'm a bit sad, to be honest, because I was hoping to like it, given all the hype. But I do appreciate becoming LOTR literate, as it were, even if the story isn't for me.

Rereading Martin's A Song of Ice And Fire--something written specifically as a counterpoint to Tolkien's work, and the various works in fantasy Tolkien inspired with it--has led me to realize just how off-the-rails HBO's famous (infamous?) television adaptation has gone. While earlier seasons stick closely to Martin's work (to great effect), latter seasons begin to depart, first in minor fashion, then in necessarily major strides as they surpass Martin's books and the weight of wrapping up the series falls on their heads alone. This has had the expected disastrous effect on the show's writing quality; a series once praised for its gray characters, complex machinations, and authentic fantasy world has devolved almost completely into a Marvel-inspired fantasy epic that consistently breaks its own rules and resorts to cheap faked-death cliffhangers where once it was renowned for playing seriously with its characters lives. The show is completely unrecognizable from its source material. Its appeal remains as genre pulp; fan-pleasing mental junkfood that's pretty to look at but no longer espouses the qualities that made it so revered.

Imagine my surprise, then, to learn that Peter Jackson's now world-famous Lord of the Rings film adaptations are actually quite adherent to their source material. I was in high school when the film series released and had not yet read Tolkien's legendary masterwork, yet I adored the films for the ethereal, otherworldly sets, make-up, and special effects they provided, bolstered further by the iconic score constructed by Howard Shore; one now so iconic to fantasy films that it rivals comparisons of Ennio Morricone's famous spaghetti western themes.

In stark contrast to the HBO adaptation of Ice and Fire falling far short of Martin's work, I honestly believe that Fellowship works far better as a film than it ever did as a novel, and that Jackson's rendition of Tolkien's work is about as perfect as you can hope for. I'll even go as far as saying I'm shocked that this isn't a more common opinion.

In novel form, perhaps the strongest aspect is Tolkien's grasp of language. Not the English language in specific, but of the history of language: its etymology. Tolkien's background as a linguist allows him to construct the foundation of this world not with long paragraphs of exposition (although he does frequently fall victim to this), but with words; the languages present, names of structures and lands, and even the songs the characters sing. A lot of Middle-Earth feels fantastical because it's built around these languages. It does a lot to impart a feeling of foreignness that so much modern fantasy lacks.

Most disappointing to me was the constant parroted opinion that the characters of the films are much simpler versions of their book counterparts. I can confidently say, at least in this first episode, that this isn't entirely true. Are the characters altered? Sure: Gimli is used a bit too much as comic relief in the films and his people and character lack development, but honestly, he doesn't get much development in this novel, either.

And that's my main problem with Fellowship. Where the film has its fantastic visuals to fall back on, the book has only descriptions. Which is fine, but I wanted something more. I yearned for something like Martin's brilliant, colorful cast of dozens of characters, or Abercrombie's biting sardonic wit to fill these pages. The bulk of Fellowship is filled with our characters moving from place to place, experiencing this wonderful world that Tolkien has created, but we learn very little of them and not enough depth of these locales we're witnessing is provided. Tolkien breezes past description of ruins, rivers, old settlements, etc, with very little time devoted to creating any depth or substance. Sure, those ruins sound great. I like ruins! But then we're onward once again.

Instead it felt too often that Tolkien caved to his indulgence, filling his pages with something like song, which is fine as a display of this world's culture, but I wanted something more substantial to dig into.

I am admittedly not a huge fan of fantasy. I've read quite a bit of it, but very little I've liked, and maybe it's just the fantasy formula in general that turns me off of Fellowship rather than Tolkien himself. After all, this is a beloved novel. But it just wasn't for me. Too much of it was pretty window-dressing; meandering through lovely lands without meaningful history. Contrary to what Tolkien fans espouse, the characters were paper-thin and failed to grow, and the world, though pretty to imagine, never inspired me with its history like Martin's does, even when he's at his most indulgent and taking us on seemingly pointless tours through Essos in A Dance With Dragons.

After finishing, I began to view Martin not so much as the aforementioned "counterpoint" to Tolkien, but rather an evolution of him, as I believe Martin features a lot of what makes Tolkien attractive--an old, interesting world and a compelling narrative with strong themes--but Martin constructs his world and his characters with more care and roots said construction more within reality than fantasy, and provides each with exponentially more depth, thus making them far more intriguing than Tolkien does his.

Yes, yes, I know: Burn the witch. Who doesn't like LOTR? But I can't help it: This is my second time reading Fellowship, and charming though he can be, Tolkien just doesn't work for me.

Tolkien’s influence in the fantasy genre is a sight to truly behold. So, as a lover of fantasy, I decided it would be worthwhile to delve in to Middle-Earth with Frodo and Company and see where it all began. I haven’t seen the movies so my review of The Fellowship of the Ring and the two other books will be free of movie bias.

Plot

The ring that Bilbo Baggins found in The Hobbit makes a return in The Fellowship of the Ring. It is up to his heir, Frodo Baggins, to bring the ring to Modor where it may be destroyed forever. The ring is dangerous, especially in the hands of the one who seeks it, Sauron.

The plot isn’t something I’d call very exciting. It’s really not. Destroy the ring by bringing it to the fires of Mordor. Simple enough plot. There are trial and tribulations along the way but the story is really simple. That doesn’t make it bad, mind you. There isn’t anything else I can really say about the plot because the majority of the book was descriptions and Tolkien dragging his feet.

Writing

Heavy is a word I’d use to describe the writing. Heavy, but unnecessarily so. I feel like this book could have been half its size and just as good. The thing about Tolkien’s writing is that I can appreciate it but I do not like it. It’s heavy and dull and drags on and on for no good reason. I spent nearly two weeks on The Fellowship of the Ring when I should have finished in within a week easily, all because of the writing.

This book was about ninety percent description. And even then, it wasn’t good. More description is supposed to add to the story but it did not in this book. Tolkien had a bad habit of over explaining and describing landscapes and such without actually giving the reader a clear picture of it. I could not for the life of me picture anything he described because he didn’t do it very well. It was also irritating how we pretty much got no descriptions of the characters.

I will give it up to Tolkien that when he wants to pick up the pace, he’s a good writer. Unfortunately it took him three-fourths of the book to think “Gee, maybe I should speed things up a bit”.

Characters

I didn’t care about the characters at all. Since most of the book was spent talking about the journey to Mordor, descriptions of nature, or Middle-Earth’s confusing history, very little time was spent on the characters. I couldn’t even connect with Frodo, our protagonist. He had no personality to speak of. I have no doubt that Tolkien gave him a wonderful personality in his own head, but he certainly didn’t put it down on paper. The only character I liked was Sam Gamgee. He was an adorable little hobbit who’s fiercely protective of Frodo and loyal to boot. Sam’s a sweet character and he’s the only one that has any semblance of a personality. Everybody else was just…there.

Things I Didn't Like

The pacing, descriptions, and history of Middle-Earth were three things I really didn’t like. I actually didn’t like a lot, but these are things that I especially didn’t enjoy. The pacing was very, very slow. I didn’t like it one bit. I was nearly a fourth of a way through the book before Frodo even made it out of the Shire! That’s not a good start to a fantasy-adventure book. Nearly the entire novel crawled at a snail’s pace. It only picked up in the last fourth of the novel.

The descriptions of things were terrible. I couldn’t imagine anything for the life of me. I haven’t seen the movies so all of these locations and details were completely lost on me. Tolkien is not very good at helping form an image in his readers’ minds (at least not mine). I had to actually look up images from the movie to try to understand what Tolkien was saying.

The history of Middle-Earth that is dumped on the reader was such a pain to read. It was like being dropped in the middle of an ancient Chinese history class and being expected to know what everybody’s talking about. People are always talking about Tolkien’s world building but I didn’t see any of it in The Fellowship of the Ring. He created a complex world, yes, but that doesn’t mean he built it well.

Diversity

Middle-Earth is very white. Some people are described as having brown skin but none of our main characters. There is one female character I can name, Galadriel, and she’s kinda neat? She doesn’t have all that much time in the book and doesn’t actually do much. As far as diversity goes, it’s obvious that Tolkien’s creativity stops here.

Overall

I’m sad but not surprised to say that I didn’t like The Fellowship of the Ring. I didn’t like The Hobbit so it’s no wonder I didn’t like this book either. I liked the fact that the hero wasn’t someone who was especially strong or smart or cunning. He was an ordinary little hobbit who was tasked to go on an extraordinary quest. I’m willing to stick out the other two books just because I want to see where a lot of present fantasy novels get their influence from. Tolkien’s influence is in a lot of places and if I didn’t read his works then some things would be lost to me in those other books.

Jeigu „Hobitui“ iš 5 daviau 2 už siužetą ir 4 už literatūrinį stilių (galutinis – 3), tai „Žiedo brolijai“ už siužetą galiu duot tik 1, gal 1.5, jau labai dosniai pažiūrėjęs gal ir 2, o už stilių ne daugiau 2.5, tad ir visumoj tik 2 iš 5.

Knyga gerokai prastesnė nei „Hobitas“, kuris pats buvo pakankamai vidutiniškas, nors ir vertas skaitymo dėl stiliaus. Tuo tarpu čia siužeto požiūriu viskas vyksta kur kas vangiau, nebėra to gyvumo, nuotykiškumo, visi nuotykiai susiskaito lyg stebėtum juos per kokį gaubtą vos įžiūrėdamas, mažai kas įeina atmintin, nėra tokių ryškių ir vaizdingų scenų kaip „Hobite“. Niekas iki tokio aiškumo neįsiminė iš „Žiedo brolijos“.

Literatūrine prasme stilius irgi labai smarkiai priblėsęs, nebėra to žaismingumo, nebeatskleidžia jis personažų konflikto tarp to, ko jie nori, ir to, ką turi daryt (kas buvo puikiai padaryta „Hobite“ su Bilbu), apskritai visas siužetas persikėlė į išorę, keliaujama po platų pasaulį sutinkant pačius įvairiausius jo gyventojus, vietoves, reiškinius, bet vidinis pasaulis ne tai, kad tuščias ir skurdus, o jo praktiškai išvis nėra. Stilius toks, kad dažnai tiesiog nuobodu skaityti, tenka laužtis nelyg einant per kokius brūzgynus, puslapiai nekabina versti dar vieno, po to dar vieno. Prisiverti skaityt veikiau iš nenoro užmest to, kas jau perskaityta, o ne iš noro perskaityt, kas toliau parašyta.

Nėra absoliučiai jokios personažų raidos, jokio vystymosi, jokių transformacijų, neskaitant epizodinių sutrikimų geidžiant žiedo, nėra jokių moralinių ar egzistencinių įtampų ir dilemų, viskas labai skaidriai sudėliota į lentynėles, kas čia geras, o kas blogas, nėra jokio santykių sudėtingumo, jokių įtampų tarp personažų, jokių dviprasmybių, sumišusių sentimentų, kankinančių neapsisprendimų, nėra jokios vidinės kančios, išskyrus pigius pasamprotavimus, ką čia dabar toliau daryti ir kaip sumažinti rizikas, beveik nėra jokių mįslių, slėpinių, nežinios, istorijos pasakojimas personažų pateikiamas pagret konkrečių veiksmų, tarsi jie patys nori įsikontekstinti istorijoje joje beveikdami, ir tai labai nenatūraliai susiskaito.

Gendalfo personažas apskritai veikia nelyg deus ex machina. Žinau, kad daug kas alpsta iš susižavėjimo juo, bet šis personažas man atrodo vienas rimčiausių trūkumų šiose knygose apskritai. Jis vos ne viską žino, pakursto kitus kažką daryti, juos palydi, o tada, žinodamas, kad jų laukia nelaimės, bet jie pajėgūs jas įveikt, pasišalina su savo reikalais, o kai tie pakliūva į bėdą, iš kurios nebežino, kaip išsivaduot, tada stebuklingai pasirodo ir visus išgelbėja. Jis tarsi pats Tolkienas savo kūriniuose, viską iš anksto žino, numato ir supranta, įsuka veiksmą ir pasišalina, kad tas iš savieigos ar inercijos toliau rutuliotųsi, o kai viskas įstringa, kai rašymas priveda prie aklavietės, tada jis nelyg Platono mitas ar deus ex machina viską išsprendžia, pažarsto savo išminties, pamotyvuoja personažus toliau judėti, ir tada vėl juos įsukęs iš naujo pasišalina iki atskiro įstrigimo.

Skirtingo tipo būtybės (elfai, orkos, goblinai, vargai, nykštukai, juodieji raiteliai ir pan.) visiškai neatskleistos savo skirtingumo požiūriu. Vieninteliai hobitai kiek ryškesni, o kitoms būtybėms nėra nei skirta daug vietos jų išvaizdos aprašymui, nei atskleisti jų charakterių savitumai ir skirtumai, išskyrus tai, kad sudėlioti jie į geriečius ir blogiečius.

O galiausiai ir tas pasaulio kūrimas (worldbuilding) nuvylė, nes mažai naujo čia pridėta lyginant su tuo, kas buvo „Hobite“, ir ta skirtingų būtybių įvairovė nėra paties Tolkieno išgalvota, goblinai ir elfai ateina iš įvairių kitų literatūrinių ir mitologinių šaltinių.

Tad nesuprantu visų tų kalbų, kad Tolkienas sukūrė Bibliją su visa mitologija, atskiru pasauliu ir sąveikomis jo viduje. Jau Biblija man atrodo pervertintas dalykas, bet „Žiedų valdovui“ iki Biblijos yra laaaaabai toli, ten pasaulis kur kas turtingesnis, įvairesnis ir sudėtingesnis tiek išorine, tiek vidine prasme, o pas Tolkieną vidinio pasaulio beveik nėra, o išorinio turtingumas atskleistas veikiau kiekybiškai nei kokybiškai, nes visko yra labai daug, bet niekam, išskyrus pačius hobitus, nėra tiek daug skirta kokybinio aprašymo ir atskleidimo.

Nesuprantu, kodėl knyga taip šlovinama ir vertinama. Ypač, kodėl tai galėtų patikti vaikams, nes man atrodo, kad kaip tik jiems turėtų būti išskirtinai nuobodu, nes knyga yra sunki ir brandi ta tokia labiau blogąja prasme, ją skaityti nėra visiškai lengva, neplaukia kalba sklandžiai ir knyga neįtraukia savo stilium ir vaizdingumu taip, kaip tą padaro „Hobitas“ ar kad ir „Haris Poteris“, kur net jei siužetas neįdomus, knygą įdomu ir malonu skaityt vien dėl stiliaus. „Žiedų valdovo“ pirmoj knygoj viso to nėra.

Turbūt nereikia ir sakyti, kad tai mano įspūdžiai. Gal aš nemokėjau perskaityti tos knygos, gal kažko nepastebėjau, nesupratau ar pan. Bet jei „Hobito“ atveju šitų problemų tokiu mastu nebuvo, tai esu linkęs manyt, kad reikšmingas negatyvus kokybinis pokytis nuo „Hobito“ čia yra.

While "Hobbit" got 2 from me for the story and 4 for literary style (overall – 3), "The Fellowship of the Ring" can get only 1 for the story, maybe 1.5 or even 2 if I would be very generous, but for the style it can't get more than 2.5, therefore overall only 2 out of 5.

The book is substantially worse than "Hobbit", which was quite mediocre, although worth reading for the writing style alone. Meanwhile here in terms of the story everything looks more sluggish, the vividness and adventurousness of the previous book are gone, all adventures and action seem like you would look at it unclearly through opaque bell jar, only few things stay in my memory, there are no more any distinct and graphic scenes like there were in the "Hobbit". Nothing stayed in my mind so clearly from "The Fellowship of the Ring".

From a literary point of view, style is a lot more jaded, the playfulness is gone, it no longer reveals a conflict between what a character wants and what he has to do (it was done really well in "Hobbit" with the character of Bilbo); the whole story settles in external world, there are trips around the wide world in which we meet a variety of its habitants, we face a lot of different locations, phenomena, but the inner world is not just empty and poor, it's rather nonexistant. The style often makes reading pretty boring, you have to go through pages as if you would have to work your way through bushes. You force yourself to read not because you want to know what happens next, but rather because you don't want to throw over what you have already read.

There are no character devolepment, no transformations, except a few confusions for craving after ring, there are no moral or existential tensions or dilemmas, everything looks crystal clear and everyone belongs to its own shelf about who is good and who is bad, there are none of complex relationships, no tensions between characters whatsoever, there are no ambiguities, confused sentiments, painful situations without being able to make a decision, there are no inner suffering, except cheap reasonings about what to do next and how to reduce occuring risks, there are almost no mysteries, no puzzles, no situations of not knowing things, the historic context is brought up by characters alongside what they are doing, as if they would want to contextualize themselves in what they do. All that reads so unnaturally.

The character of Gandalf acts as if he is some kind of deus ex machina. I know that a lot of people can't help themselves in admiring him, but this character seems like one of the most significant drawbacks in these books. He almost knows everything and incites others to do something, he escorts them and then disappears with his own business while knowing perfectly well that other characters will have to deal with lots of tribulations, and when they get in troubles which they can't overcome themselves, then Gandalf magically appears and saves everyone. It seems that he represents Tolkien himself in his writings, he knows everything in advance, foresees it and understands, starts all the action and retreats from the spotlight and lets everything continue by gravity, and when everything gets stuck, when writing brings you to a dead-end, then Gandalf as if he was a myth in Plato's writings or a deus ex machina suddenly solves everything, he throws some insights of his wisdom, motivates others to move forward, and after everything comes back to normal, he retreats and disappears once again until the next time things will get stuck.

Entities of different kinds (elves, orcs, goblins, wargs, dwarves, black riders, etc.) are completely undeveloped in terms of their differences. Only hobbits are more distinct, while other creatures are neither described enough in how they look nor features of their characters are revealed, except that you know which ones are good ones and which ones are bad ones.

And finally even the worldbuilding disappointed me, because there are not so much new since "Hobbit" and the variety of different creatures are not even entirely created by Tolkien, for goblins, elves and similar types of entities come from other literary or mythological sources.

That's why I can't understand all those talks that Tolkien have created a Bible with all mythology, wholly new world and interactions within it. Even Bible seems to me overrated, but it's not even close for "Hobbit" and "The Fellowship of the Ring" to be on the level of the Bible, where the world is way richer, more diverse and more complex both in terms of the external world and of the internal world, while there are close to none of the internal world in these books of Tolkien, and the richness of the external world is expressed rather in quantity than in quality, because there are lots of things, but most of them soon just fade away because there are no place enough for them to be given descriptions or revelations in high quality.

I don't understant why these books are so glorified and praised. Especially, why would children love it, because it seems to me that it should be exceptionally boring, because at least this book is heavy and mature in a bad sense, it's not that easy to read, the language doesn't flow that easily and the book doesn't pull you inside its world with its style and vividness, contrary to how "Hobbit" ar even "Harry Potter" does, where it is interesting and enjoyable to read for the style alone, even if the plot is not interesting. As far as I'm conerned, the first part of "The Lord of the Rings" doesn't have that at all.

Probably there is no need to say that this is my impresssion. Maybe I was not able to read it correctly, maybe I haven't noticed something or misunderstood. But if in the case of "Hobbit" these problems didn't occur on such scale, I tend to think that this significant negative change in quality since "Hobbit" really exists.

Due to its incredible fame, I admit I had high expectations for this novel. Alas, while it was a lively read at times, it could often be incredibly dull. Interestingly, I found those moments when the characters were stagnant in one place (i.e. the Shire, Rivendell) to be the most engaging, as characters were given the opportunity to meaningfully interact and a unique culture was displayed. On the flip-side, when the fellowship was actively journeying, the novel would degrade into a minute description of the topography of Middle-Earth. While I can certainly see the appeal for those wth a prior deep vested interest in Tolkien’s world-building, such a writing style simply wasn’t for me.

Est-ce que j’ai besoin de présenter, même brièvement, l’histoire de ce premier tome du Seigneur des Anneaux ? Je ne crois pas, et donc je ne le ferais pas(1).

Pour en revenir à cette lecture, c’est, je pense, la troisième fois que je relis le seigneur des anneaux. Donc, forcément, je connais un peu l’histoire maintenant. Et en plus, au moment où j’ai lu ce tome, je venais de voir le film moins de deux semaines avant. Donc naturellement, je vais autant m’intéresser au roman en lui-même qu’aux liens et différences avec le film.

Comme je le disais, c’est donc une re-re-lecture. Et, peut-être à cause de mon âge, peut-être aussi grâce à toutes mes lectures, peut- être enfin par contraste avec le film, j’ai enfin compris la subtilité du récit et, surtout, des personnages(2). La subtilité, disais-je.

C’est bien sûr, évidement même, celle d’Aragorn, qui est pour moi le personnage central de cette histoire, tellement principal que Tolkien ose à peine s’y attaquer. Dans une moindre mesure, Frodon, par son expérience(3) montre bien tout le poids de la charge de l’anneau. Bref, c’est bien.

Ce qui l’est moins, c’est que pour en arriver là, l’auteur se laisse embarquer dans une authentique avalanche de détails sans importance. Du coup, forcément, on est un peu noyé sous les chansons, les heures et les heures de marche à pied, la généalogie hobbite et, surtout, surtout, une sortie de la Lorien longue, mais longue. Le genre de passage où on se demande vraiment s’il ne faut pas sauter quelques pages. D’un autre côté, je me demande encore maintenant si, dans ce passage, Tolkien ne fait pas exprès de faire traîner cette ambiance hors du temps, pour qu’on comprenne bien que Galadriel est femme de pouvoir.

Vous l’aurez évidement compris, je suis très mitigé sur ce roman. En vérité, je me suis presque emmerdé en reprenant cette vieille lecture. Beaucoup plus en tout cas qu’en regardant le film qui, lui, est formidablement bien. Bien sûr, il manque dans ce film Tom Bombadil et les Galgals, mais est-ce vraiment essentiel ? Pas suffisement en tout cas pour donner à ce livre (et à ses suites) plus d’intérêt que proprement historique.

(1) Et en plus, j’ai suffisement d’autres avis en attente pour ne pas me soucier de ce genre de détails qu’un site comme la wikipedia vous indiquera bien mieux.
(2) Sauf bien sûr Merry et Pippin qui sont, par construction, des clowns.
(3) qui disparaît totallement dans le film pour n’en faire qu’une espèce de jeune ccouillon aux prises avec une drogue un peu particulière.

C'est la première fois que je lis ce roman et je n'ai jamais vu les films. Par contre je suis bien au courant de l'engouement de certains au sujet du Seigneur des Anneaux. Donc j'ai voulu, moi aussi, participer à ce monument culturel et partager l'enthousiasme avec tout le monde. Et laissez moi vous dire que ça me fait vraiment mal au cœur de mettre que 2.5/5 à ce roman que tant adorent. Mais je peux pas mettre plus.

Pour moi ça a été une lecture longue et difficile et ce parce que terriblement ennuyeuse. J'ai lu les premières 150 pages sur 3 mois. J'ai passé mon temps à lire 5 pages et me dire "mais pourquoi tu lis ça en fait?" et reposer mon bouquin. Le prendre quelques jours plus tard et répéter le même scenario. Lire quelques pages, ni voir aucun intérêt, n’être captivée par absolument rien du tout et reposer le bouquin.
Le pire pour moi c'est le début du roman qui est rempli de lore sur les Hobbits et la Terre du Milieu et l'auteur nous balance 50 noms de personnages "historiques" différents, de lieux, c'est à en devenir fou. Tout ces gens ne sont même pas concernés par l'histoire en cours, c’est tous des figures du passé dont on aurait pu ne pas connaitre l'existence ou qu'il aurait pu introduire plus loin plus doucement, voir les noms de tous les Hobbits du village. Et sérieusement en quoi ça me concerne ou ça m'aide dans l'histoire? A la place d’être excitée ou intriguée par mon livre, j'ai juste super mal à la tête et j'ai rien mais rien retenu de toute cette exposition historique.

Et puis il faut se l'avouer il se passe pas grand chose dans ce tome 1 du seigneur des anneaux, surtout pas dans les 400 premières pages. C'est juste beaucoup de 'hobbit qui marche' 'hobbit qui mange et dort' 'hobbit qui chante' et je m'ennuie tellement que j'ai qu'une envie c'est refermer ce livre. Et puis ils sont tellement naïfs ces hobbits (pour ne pas dire bêtes); surtout ne met pas l'anneau - Frodo met l'anneau, surtout ne t'éloigne pas du chemin - ils s’éloignent du chemin, surtout ne fais pas ça - il fait exactement ça. C'est comme si à chaque décision qu'il doivent prendre Frodo & cie optent pour la mauvaise option. (par exemple toute la partie dans la foret bizarre où Tom vient les sauver 2 fois. Ou quand Frodo est sous couverture dans une auberge et qu'il enfile l'anneau devant tout le monde, nice).

Cette lenteur, selon moi, a fortement contribué à mon peu d'investissement dans le roman, ce livre est en fait écrit en suivant un drôle de cycle vicieux qui m'a grandement ennuyé. C'est pleins de pages ou les personnages ne font que marcher, manger et dormir (et chanter). Et cela pendant plusieurs jours, tous montrés sur page, là où on aurait pu avoir une ellipse nous on est obligé de se farcir des pages et de pages de roadtrip inintéressant, merci beaucoup Mr Tolkien.
Puis on a un petit moment "d'action". Généralement c'est plus dans le style de beaucoup de personnages qui se parlent pour faire avancer l'histoire avec un peu d'action si on est veinard. Et ensuite on est reparti pour 50 pages où ils ne font que marcher etc... Et à la longue ça fatigue. J'ai plus que une envie, c'est qu'ils se passe quelque chose de plus excitant que de marcher au couvert de la nuit.
Et c'est ça pendant la plus grosse partie du roman. Mon exemplaire fait presque 800 pages et honnêtement je n'ai pris du plaisir dans ma lectures que pour les genre 300 dernières pages du livre. Et même là, je n'avais qu'une envie, que ça se finisse.

Sérieusement, c'est peut être moi qui suis bizarre, mais je me suis juste affreusement ennuyé pendant les 3/4 de ma lecture. Du coup, dans mon cœur j'avais l'espoir de m'attacher aux personnages, et au début de ma lecture je me suis dit que j'allais vouloir continuer le roman pour eux. Mais manque de bol, même les personnages me fatiguent.

Pour faire bref Sam et Aragorn sont les seuls personnages auxquels je me suis attachée. Sam est choupi, même s'il me fait un peu de la peine, on dirait le chien fidèle de Frodo, Je sais pas. Et Aragorn il est juste badass. Mais les autres sur une échelle de 1 à 'je les déteste' on est à 'je m'en contre fou d'eux'. Ils sont là pas là, moi ça change rien, ils n'ont aucune saveur, aucun charme, aucune présence. (J'ai menti; j'ai bien aimé Glorfindel et Galadriel, mais je parlais des personnages principaux ici).
Du coup je suis même pas motivée à continuer ma lecture par le cast principal du livre. Frodo est tellement 'meh' comme personnage principal dans ce premier tome que j'ai pas vraiment envie de suivre ses aventures. En plus comme je sais déjà qu'il va réussir, puisque dans le livre on me raconte son histoire (inception, wow), j'ai même pas de tension à ce niveau là. Je suis juste de nouveau en train de m'ennuyer. J'admire sa détermination à vouloir mener à bien sa quête mais émotionnellement parlant, y a rien de plus qui se passe pour moi.

Bref, l'histoire en soit on a dit que c'était long et mou, les personnages m'ont pas inspiré plus que ça. Qu'est ce qu'il reste pour sauver ce livre à mes yeux?
Le style, la plume de Tolkien?
Haha, non! Je comprends pas là non plus tout cet engouement autour de Tolkien et son écriture et blabla. Évidement qu'il écrit bien, c'est agréable à lire, il a une manière de rendre son monde crédible qui est incroyable, certes. Mais au final c'est un style d'écriture plutôt simpliste et qu'on dirait fait pour les enfants (c'est fait exprès d’après ce que j'ai compris?). Et moi c'est juste pas mon truc. Rien que dans les dialogues entre les personnages, on dirait que c'est écrit en faisant en sorte que même Jeanne, 10ans, puisse lire le livre avec facilité. Ce qui est très bien, c'est juste pas à mon gout.

Pour conclure ce gros pavé, j'avais de très grosses attentes avant de lire "La Communauté de l'Anneau". N'y connaissant rien au Seigneur des Anneaux, j'ai voulu enfin plonger dans cet univers que tant adorent. J'ai voulu juger par moi même et tomber amoureuse de cet univers comme tant d'autres l'ont fait avant moi. Malheureusement ça ne c'est pas passé comme ça.
Ce premier tome a été une énorme déception pour moi. Je m'attendais vraiment à lire l'un de livres les plus magiques de ma vie et en fait ça a juste été fatiguant. Pendant longtemps j'ai du me forcer à continuer ma lecture, j'ai mis 5 mois à finir ce livre, c'est hallucinant pour moi.
En fait c'est simple, je me suis rarement aussi ennuyé dans un livre qu'on m'avait vendu comme absolument merveilleux. C'est triste.

Je suis assez négative, parce que j'ai été très déçue, mais il y a bien des moments où j'ai apprécié ma lecture ou je n'aurais juste pas fini le livre. Comme je l'ai déjà mentionné les 350 dernières pages je les aie lues en un mois environ, donc j'ai progressé beaucoup plus vite vers la fin du livre que dans toute sa première partie. L'histoire de Gollum était fascinante, les personnages d'Aragorn, Galadriel et Glorfindel m'ont beaucoup intrigué, je suis curieuse de voir comment Frodo et Sam vont retrouver leurs amis et je sais qu'il sont censé rencontrer Gollum, ça promet.
Donc voilà il y a bien des choses que j'ai aimé dans le livre, mais dans l'ensemble pas assez pour me faire aimer ce tome 1. Mais je vais lire la suite, parce que je suis curieuse, parce que je suis obstinée et je dois comprendre pourquoi tout le monde aime mais surtout parce que j'ai l'espoir que moi aussi je vais adorer le tome 2.

First of all, no one in all my years of hearing about Lord of the Rings ever mentioned just how much singing I would have to sit through in this book. The only time I wish I was reading it instead of listening to it was putting up with so many songs. There were five-minute songs in there that were hard to skip on audio, not to mention all the random ones we needed in there about having baths, walking, general merriment, and who knows what else.

Tom Bombadil was also a nightmare to put up with, I was so relieved when his part ended I actually cried out in frustration when he came back. That is not to say the rest of the story was horrible. I actually enjoyed some parts, some parts were genuinely interesting and had that adventure tone to them, and then other times it was just boring.

I wanted to like this story, it started off so interesting and each time I found myself becoming uninterested I felt I was doing this story a disservice. I know people talk about Tolkien being big into description and long-winded things but that wasn't a real problem, I didn't mind the walking and the travelling for most of the book, but for some reason the walking towards the end was incredibly dull and hard to listen to and there are some scenes that I think were entirely unnecessary.

I did like the characters though, I liked Frodo and I liked Sam's loyalty. Merry and Pippin weren't as silly as I recall them being in the movie and I especially liked the complexity of Aragorn. There is a good story here woven between the oversharing and focusing on that instead is a great way to get through the boring bits. Tolkien came through though with a good and interesting ending, after a dull stretch it suddenly takes off and you are whisked into a great conclusion that makes you want to head straight into the next story.

I am not a huge fantasy reader but I don't hate the genre, and this is after all THE fantasy novel, the beloved classic, and I am a little surprised, I thought I would like it more than I did. You can certainly see the Tolkien genius, but my goodness you have to put up with a lot of nonsense to get there.

This review was published on my blog Lost in a Good Book

This book was painfully boring, I didn't care about anything that was happening or any of the characters. I don't understand why Frodo was special because was starting to get corrupted by the ring pretty early on too. I didn't understand why everyone loves him like Sam would die for him and I don't get the loyalty. I don't understand Sauron, the book keeps saying he scary but I really didn't see why. I guess it because he is like "an all-seeing eye" and I don't know if it boring because it been redone so many times or if it just boring. Also at the end, Frodo mentions how war has broken out everywhere already, how. How can he know because they were in a weird elf place completely untouched by war and there were no signs of anything wrong when he left the shire. The songs, all the fucking songs I hated all of them they added nothing to the story I couldn't take them. Also, why did everyone have to have so many names? Like one of two fine but almost every character had upwards of 3 names and it wouldn't have been so bad if the reader was introduced to so many new characters with 4 names and 10 titles. Game of Thrones had nothing on this level of ridiculous names. Also, Aragorn being called "Strider" for most of the book annoyed the shit out of me, Frodo refused to call him Aragorn.

One of the things that really annoyed me was that everything was so "magical" that nothing seemed special. They felt commonplace in this world but are still talked about like myth and legend, and I didn't like it.

I thought reading the book would make me want to watch movies, nope. I'm done with all thing Lord of the Ring forever.
