Well. It's been 4 FREAKING WEEKS, and I am proud to say I FINALLY finished. Halleujah.

Now it's not that I didn't like it, but this books was clearly written in another time, for another generation. For a teenage 21st century girl, who's used to getting any information she wants at the click of a button, the details of every meal and every landscape were agonizing.

Which is not to say the genius of this book didn't shine through; I saw elements of Harry Potter, of Eragon, of the Books of Pellinor and more (even Percy Jackson). You can see how this became the daddy of all fantasy books- albeit with ONE FEMALE CHARACTER. (Hey, that's one more than The Hobbit) Seeing as this is a classic, and I'm not really qualified to really review a classic, I've decided to feature this book mainly in my favorite quotes: (to it's credit, there were many good ones)

"Deserves it! I daresay he does. Many that live deserve death. And some that die deserve life. Can you give it to them? Then do not be too eager to deal out death in judgement. For even the very wise cannot see all ends."
"I will not give you council, saying do this, or do that. For not in doing or contriving, nor in choosing between this course and another, can I avail; but only in knowing what is and what was, and in part also what shall be. But this I will say to you: your Quest stands upon the edge of a knife. Stray but a little and it will fail, to the ruin of all. Yet hope remains while all the Company is true."
"But do not despise the lore that has come down from distant years; for oft it may chance that old wives keep in memory word of things that once were needful for the wise to know."
Torment in the dark was the danger that I feared, and it did not hold me back. But I would not have come, had I known the danger of light and joy."
So I made it through the big guns. In truth, I saw it's brilliance, but it wasn't for me. I plan to watch the movie and read the other two, but probably in a long time.

Η ιστορία ξεκινάει στο ειδυλλιακό Σάιρ, όπου ο νεαρός χόμπιτ Φρόντο κληρονομεί ένα μυστηριώδες δαχτυλίδι από τον θείο του, Μπίλμπο. Σύντομα αποκαλύπτεται ότι αυτό δεν είναι ένα απλό αντικείμενο, αλλά το Ένα Δαχτυλίδι της Δύναμης, δημιούργημα του Σκοτεινού Άρχοντα Σάουρον, το οποίο περιέχει μεγάλο μέρος της δύναμής του και με το οποίο μπορεί να κυριαρχήσει σε όλη τη Μέση Γη. Ο Φρόντο, συνειδητοποιώντας τον τεράστιο κίνδυνο, αναλαμβάνει το βαρύ φορτίο να μεταφέρει το δαχτυλίδι στο μοναδικό μέρος όπου μπορεί να καταστραφεί: στο Βουνό του Χαμού, στην καρδιά της εχθρικής γης της Μόρντορ. Για να τον βοηθήσουν στο επικίνδυνο αυτό ταξίδι, σχηματίζεται η Συντροφιά του Δαχτυλιδιού, μια ομάδα που αποτελείται από τους συντρόφους του χόμπιτ Σαμ, Μέρι και Πίπιν, τον μάγο Γκάνταλφ, τον ξωτικό Λέγκολας, τον νάνο Γκίμλι, τον άνθρωπο Άραγκορν και τον Μπόρομιρ από το Γκόντορ.
Ο Τόλκιν, μέσω του έργου του, τονίζει με έμφαση τη σημασία της φιλίας, της αφοσίωσης, του θάρρους και της προσωπικής θυσίας. Το βιβλίο υπογραμμίζει την ιδέα ότι ακόμα και τα πιο μικρά και ασήμαντα πλάσματα (όπως οι χόμπιτ) μπορούν να διαδραματίσουν καθοριστικό ρόλο στην έκβαση μεγάλων μαχών και να αντισταθούν στη διαφθορά της απόλυτης εξουσίας που αντιπροσωπεύει το δαχτυλίδι. Επίσης, ο συγγραφέας προβάλλει έντονα την αγάπη για τη φύση και τη σημασία της διατήρησης της ομορφιάς του φυσικού κόσμου απέναντι στην εκβιομηχάνιση και την καταστροφική δύναμη του κακού.
Ο συγγραφέας χρησιμοποιεί εκτενείς περιγραφές τοπίων, πολιτισμών και μαχών, αναδεικνύοντας τον ρόλο του ως φιλολόγου και γλωσσολόγου με τη δημιουργία ολόκληρων γλωσσών και μυθολογιών. Ο ρυθμός της αφήγησης μπορεί να είναι αργός σε ορισμένα σημεία, καθώς ο Τόλκιν χτίζει προσεκτικά τον κόσμο του, αλλά κλιμακώνεται σε στιγμές έντασης και δράσης.
Αργός ρυθμό της αφήγησης, ειδικά στα πρώτα κεφάλαια, εκτενείς περιγραφές που κουράζουν και η ενσωμάτωση ποιημάτων και τραγουδιών που διακόπτουν τη ροή της ιστορίας καταγράφονται στα μείον
Ίσως να είμαι και η μόνη που βρίσκω αυτό το βιβλίο απελπιστικά βαρετό.

I just can't do it. I think this was my 5th time in my life trying to read this book, and I made a promise to myself I would finish it no matter what this time through. I want to get one thing out of the way, I think Tolkien is the absolute gold standard for fantasy world building. I will always hold this book in a place of respect for what it has done for the genre, and just sadly accept that it's not for me. It's astounding that Tolkien was able to create an entire history of this world, but if you're not sucked into it, it just feels like a slog. I could feel my eyes start to glaze over, 3 pages into the description of the third name of a mountain, given to it because a king from a land that we never visit had progeny that once might have allied with someone's great grandfather, who went by another name, because of this battle he had fought, but that reminds me of this kingdom, which fell, as told in the next paragraph completely in Elvish, and anyway Frodo be on your way.

I'd pick up and drop this when it went straight to Elvish, only to come back to absolutely riveting passages that seemingly have nothing to do with the plot like, "Only once before have I seen them from afar in waking life, but I know them and their names, for under them lies Khazad-dûm, the Dwarrow delf, that is now called the Black Pit, Moria in the Elvish tongue. Yonder stands Barazinbar, the Redhorn, cruel Caradhras; and beyond him are Silvertine and Cloudyhead: Celebdil the White, and Fanuidhol the Grey, that we call Zirakzigil and Bundushathûr. There the Misty Mountains divide, and between their arms lies the deep-shadowed valley which we cannot forget: Azanulbizar, the Dimrill Dale, which the Elves call Nanduhirion." <- I literally just flipped the book to a random page and put my finger down. The chances of landing on something interesting in this book is so rare that I would have deleted this entire review if my finger landed on anything to do with the journey, the fellowship, or the ring.
400 pages of straight YAPPING

Ciężko subiektywnie podejść do powieści z tak gigantycznym kulturowym ładunkiem. Ciężko się stwierdza, że coś ci się nie podoba, kiedy tak wiele ludzie jest tym czymś zachwyconych. Tak więc do połowy książki czytałam z zapałem i nadzieją "w tym musi przecież coś być". Ale potem stwierdziłam, że nie, że generalnie to mi się wcale nie podoba. Przede wszystkim - bardzo dużo chodzenia. W tej książce jest tak strasznie dużo chodzenia, że czuję się zmęczona siedząc na kanapie i czytając. Druga rzecz, która mi przeszkadzała to bardzo dziwne tempo narracji - jeden dzień jest opisany na kilkunastu (kilkudziesięciu) stronach w najdrobniejszych szczegółach (od koloru kory na drzewach po dzwięki wiatru) po czym następuje fraza "trzy misiące później". Rozumiem, że nie do końca było co opisywać przez te trzy miesiące, ale sprawia to też, że jest w tym jakiś chaos i nieporządek. Po trzecie - mamy wspaniałych bohaterów, bardzo zróżnicowanych i kolorowych, z ogromnym potencjałem, ale z drugiej strony - żaden z nich właściwie się nie rozwija, a ich charakter możemy poznać tylko przez sposób, w jak prowadzą dialog z innymi. I mi osobiście jest trudno związać się czy polubić żadnego z nich. Wielu fanów uniwersum Tolkiena zapewne poprawiłoby mnie w tym momencie, i wyjaśniło wszystkie powody, dla których Władca Pierścieni jest czymś wyjątkowym i wspaniałym i niepowtarzalnym i prawdopodobnie przyznałabym im rację. Ale samej jest mi ciężko znaleźć w tej książce coś pociągającego.
BYĆ MOŻE mój brak zachwytu jest spowodowany tym, że widziałam film (który też nie podobał mi się jakoś specjalnie, ale oglądałam z przyjemnością), więc nic co się fabularnie zdarzyło specjalnie mnie nie zaskoczyło. Generalnie wiedziałam, co się zdarzy, więc samego biegu wydarzeń nie byłam ciekawa. Dam znać, jak będzie z drugą częścią - bo drugiego filmu już nie widziałam, więc może jak dodamy do tej mało ciekawej całości zaskoczenie fabułą to będzie już lepiej.

Okay. I tried. *sob* I TRIED! I tried so hard to like it. I pushed through it, even while every part of my mind was screaming at me to stop and do something more interesting, even while my eyelids were drooping in sleep. I wanted to like it! I would've given up. It would've been one of my few DNFs but people told me it's good! And not just people, half the world's population! That Tolkien is this genius, that Tolkien is this master, this forerunner, this creator of modern fantasy.

Believe me. Come into my office and believe me. I have three friends who are OBSESSED with Tolkien. One of them constantly memorizes his poems, and does them for school stuff. One of them has a huge map of middle earth hanging in his bedroom. All of us have played Lord of the Rings online! I LOVED Lord of the Rings Online. It's one of my favorite things to do to just spend a few hours here and there exploring that great world that Tolkien created and the game brought to life.

And I'll preface this by saying that yadda yadda yadda Tolkien's influence etc. Yeah. I LOVE fantasy. I'm writing a fantasy epic (or attempting to) and I LOVE fantasy. Yeah people are still using and changing his ideas. Yeah Middle Earth is the greatest world to ever exist (in terms of detail). Yeah Tolkien made languages and went farther than anyone else to create a world. OKAY! Now that we've got that out of the way, moving on.

Where to begin? Where to even begin? Okay so I think the problem lies in the reason Tolkien made this story. He made it because he wanted a world to use his languages. That is CLEAR. Like yes it's a fantastic world! But he never meant to create a story with characters who were truly extraordinary. He, like CS Lewis before him (who I would argue has more fleshed out characters), wrote using a largely Biblical scope (very clear from the Silmarillion). That being said, I'm not saying the plot is bad. It's cool, but its purpose is clearly to showcase the world, and the world is not meant to showcase the story, and there lies the problem for me.

Everything is just so slow. From spending nigh a fourth of the book in the Shire, I assumed that Tolkien had reasons for doing so. Turned out that was the most interesting part of the book. No I'm not joking: the Shire is the place where people have the most personality, and I liked the sense of ominous foreboding, like something's wrong everywhere but the Shire.

Once they set out, though, after that whole affair is done (which is also interesting) everything stopped. I really like Tom Bombadil, and the whole walk through the Barrow Downs etc. Then after Elrond something happens. Something just slumps into complete oblivion. Everything just...dies. Everything is so boring. Tolkien spends so much time immersing us in his world without giving a second thought to story and character.

I didn't feel ANYTHING when Gandalf died. Why? Because he was cardboard. I was just like "welp, that happened." Then there's no emotion from the party either, so why should I feel emotion if this great man died and they don't seem to care? Aragorn was cool and then...nothing was done with his character. And Frodo has the worst case of chosen one syndrome I've ever seen (that is, very uninteresting character surrounded by interesting characters, except in this case there are no other interesting characters).

Also, whenever these characters had dialogue, if you took out the names, there was never any way to tell them apart. I invite you to try it next time you read it. Have a broken down copy you don't mind destroying? Sharpy out all the "Frodo said" and "Aragorn said" etc. There's no difference. The dialogue is very tired and never gives any actual development to these characters as people. Also, there were so many times when there would be this massive block of text from Elrond or somebody laying down their path for them: and it was just a ton of names on a page! None of them meant anything to me, and it happened so often that I can't excuse it. Yes there's a handy map in the front, but having to go back to that every few pages to understand just where they're going, or anything that's going on? UGH! AAAAARRRRGH.

So all that being said, this was a complete slog. Like I'm sorry, all right? I just told one of my friends my problems with it and they like disowned me or something. Yeah I GET the influence. I get it. But you can't just let a book's definition as a "classic" make up for it. This book is aging. I'm sure when it first came out this was normal to have characters who really didn't have to have personalities.

But what made this worse for me was Harry Potter. I read this through for about 300 pages well over two months ago now and set it down. I was on the verge of burn-out from reading like 20 books in the span of a month. And that book was the worst to end on, because it just created more sense of burnout. So when I picked up Harry Potter and read the series all the way through over the past two weeks, I was really refreshed! Harry Potter has great character work, intricate plot, and a world that only imploded on itself in the final book (if you really want to go find my review of Deathly Hallows. It was a disappointment). But what made it really digestable was the easily read prose style. THEN, when I give Fellowship of the Ring another go? Pain. Nothing but pain, because I was so used to Harry Potter. And Harry Potter is newer, even though the two stories share a lot of features.

All that being said. I liked the ringwraiths. Those were cool, and they clearly inspired the Forsaken in the Wheel of Time book series. I also liked the whole expedition through the Barrow Downs and Old Forest. The last 15 pages, yes, the last 15 pages of the book, with Boromir and Frodo in conflict, actually made it slightly interesting. Beforehand there was no sense of conflict at all in the party. No sense of character AT ALL. And then it was finally there. I enjoyed 15 pages of this book.

OH! And the themes. The themes hit really hard: Tolkien captures that sense of regret of the Elves, the sense that the world is moving on, really well. And obviously, living as he did during the whole of the twentieth century, through 2 world wars, it's not real surprise, is it? That was really good and was the only emotion I felt throughout the book. The emotion of a world past its prime, of a good, natural world that will move on without the nature itself, the nature which made it so beautiful in the first place. That was well-executed.

All in all, this is just an aging goliath. The songs are really random. The prose are not exciting when action is happening, and when he's going through lengthy descriptions of the world it's even worse. Yes I love Tolkien because of what he did for fantasy. But that was painful.

Lastly, I'm sorry Tolkien fans. Just...it didn't go well. I feel like I just wasted about 16 hours of my life.

Lord of the Rings is a title know by most people because of the popularity of the movies. They were originally books written by J. R. R. Tolkien. I watched through all the Lord of the Rings movies in a week for the first time and became obsessed. I found a copy of the first book, The Fellowship of the Ring, in my brother’s room and began reading.
My first impression of the book is that is was very similar to the movie. Some of the dialogue was word for word. However as I kept reading there were minor differences that built up
and up into huge changes. There were several chapters from the book that weren’t in the movies or hinted at in the movies at all. Entire characters that were skipped over. I found it really interesting to see the already humungous Middle Earth expanding more.
There was a downside to the book however, it was the slowest book I ever read. There were large portions of small text crammed onto a single page. There was page after page of songs and poems. And there were chapters of details and events that added nothing to the plot and it got boring. Now I could see why the movie cut out so many scenes, because they weren’t important and could put the audience to sleep.
The scenes in the book that were also in the movie were fun to read though. They certainly weren’t as cinematic and were dramatized more for the movies but it was nice to know how they originally went. Another thing I really enjoyed was how well things were explained. There is so much to Lord of the Rings that when watching the movie there may be jokes you miss or a war the seems pointless because you’re confused, forgot something or simply don’t get it. But reading the books helps you understand why things happened.I would say that the movies are definitely more engaging and exciting, but the books would be great for anyone who wants to learn more and it very patient.

Υπερεκτιμημένο βιβλιο. Σίγουρα ο κόσμος που δημιούργησε ο Τόλκιν είναι καλοσχηματισμένος και πειστικός, αλλά μια πειστική μυθολογία δεν ανάγει αυτόματα ένα λογοτεχνικό έργο σε αριστούργημα. Τα προβλήματα που εντόπισα αφορούν καταρχήν τη διαχείριση του υλικού αυτής της μυθολογίας. Σε πολλά σημεία, δηλαδή, ένιωθα πως οι πληροφορίες που παρέχονταν στον αναγνώστη για αυτόν τον μαγικό κόσμο, είτε από τον τριτοπροσωπο αφηγητή είτε έμμεσα από τους ήρωες, περιειχαν βεβιασμένες λεπτομέρειες που δεν ενδιέφεραν πρακτικά τον αναγνώστη, αφού δεν είχαν καμία επίδραση στην ιστορία. Και εδώ ξεκινά το κύριο πρόβλημα του Τόλκιν, που είναι το κακό editing. Πολλοί λένε πως σε όσους δεν αρέσει ο Τόλκιν απλώς έχουν πρόβλημα με τα πιο δύσκολα και λεπτομερώς περιγραφικά βιβλία. Δεν είναι έτσι. Μπορώ να διαβάσω με τις ώρες τον λεπτολόγο Προυστ, αλλά όχι τον πολυλογα άνευ αιτίας Τόλκιν.
Σε σχέση τώρα με τους χαρακτήρες, αυτο που δεν μου άρεσε, ήταν αυτό το δίπολο "κακός-κάλος", το τόσο μανιχαϊστικό και εξωπραγματικό. Ναι μεν οι χαρακτήρες αντιμετωπίζουν συχνά πειρασμούς, αλλά και πάλι η αντιμετωπιση αυτών των προσκλήσεων απηχεί μια εκνευριστικη βιβλικοτητα , όπου το "καλό" και το "κακό" είναι δύο πόλοι ξεκαθαροι, κάτι που φυσικά δεν αντικατοπτρίζει την πολυπλοκότητα της ανθρώπινης φύσης.
Όσον αφορά το ύφος, οι περιγραφές είναι μονότονες και τα λογοτεχνικά μέσα που χρησιμοποιούνται τετριμμένα, ελαχιστες φορές κατάφεραν να με ταξιδεψουν.
Για αυτούς τους λόγους βρήκα το βιβλίο μέτριο και σε μερικά σημεία αχρειαστα κουραστικό. Τα σημεία που μου άρεσαν περισσότερο ήταν η αρχή και το τέλος του βιβλίου. Σίγουρα λοιπόν θα συνεχίσω κάποια στιγμή στα επόμενα βιβλία, που ίσως να με κάνουν να αλλάξω ελαφρώς γνώμη, μιας και ακόμα και θαυμαστές του Τόλκιν παραδέχονται πως το πρώτο βιβλίο δεν είναι το καλύτερο του.

Having now completed the trilogy, I find it difficult to write my review.

I fell in love with middle-earth when I was ten years old and saw Peter Jackson’s masterpiece. A few years ago, I read The Hobbit and was enthralled by Tolkien’s storytelling. Thus, I came to the conclusion that The Lord of the Rings epic would be a combination of Jackson’s story and Tolkien’s writing so I should get off my lazy arse and finally read it! I could not have been more wrong.

Tolkien’s storytelling does a complete 180 and feels totally different from the Hobbit. To put it simply, I was bored for 95% of the story. There is so much useless information provided and just seemed never ending. Why on Earth would I want to know what happened to the bloody ponies the hobbits rode for all of five minutes? The story is also amazingly slow paced. “We must be not waste time and destroy the Ring… but first let’s spend a couple of months hanging out with Elrond.”

Next: the characters. There is not one likable character no matter how hard you look. This is for the simple fact that no one has any personality – not even Gollum who has two. Everyone is just an empty shell of a different race and I couldn’t feel anything for any of them. This brings me to Tom Sodding Bombadil. Never, ever have I wanted so much for a character to real so that I could have the joy of killing them. He was so pointless, annoying and unbelievably creepy.

I could rant forever but I’ll end by saying that I did give this trilogy my best shot. I so desperately wanted to enjoy it but it, sadly, just wasn’t for me. I will definitely return to middle-earth but it will be by the big screen rather than the pages.

Never could finish the trilogy and feel I'm losing geek creds for it. Hoping this time I won't quit before I finish the first book.

I think I could compare my feeling towards this book to that of a six year old in front of a plate of brocoli. I know it's there, it'not going nowhere and the only way to a better book / dessert is to just go through it.

The first book though is probably my favourite of the bunch. Sure, it has it's flaws. The pacing is slooooow and much of the book is basically devoted to describing an elaborate walk through the woods.

The main reproach I have to the whole Lord of the Rings saga however is that it is impossible to enjoy this book casually. If you don't read about the whole mythos surrounding all these characters you're only getting half the bang for your buck. Characters like Glorfindel and Tom Bombadil who make glorified cameo apperances only come alive in the appendices.

it's also stunning to see how vague everything is. Quick quizz everyone: how tall are dwarves, really? Do elves have pointy ears? Does the Balrog have wings? In fact, what does the Balrog look like at all? If you find answers to any of these questions, please point me to a reference inthe book. The internet yields probably thousands of pages of nerds vociferously defending either position in these questions.

And can somebody explain to me why the Fellowship of the ring pretends to represent the "Free Folk" when, at best, they represent monarchies, a form of government not historically keen on freedom for the masses.

I first read a translated version of the series years ago, and I wanted to re-read it in its original language to see how much it would hold up.

Well... While I admit I still love the story and the quality of the writing style I didn't remember The Fellowship of the Ring to be this... Boring. I will be brave and say that I definitely prefer the movies. YES IT'S TRUE.

Like I said, the writing is great: we can easily visualize and feel the landscape, we learn a lot about the territories, the peoples, the cultures... However, too many details and explanations can kill the pacing of a book, which is the case here.

The story is indeed extremely slow: the characters spend chapters after chapters in the same environment/situation without this furthering the plot. Also, the abundance of unnecessary details made me yawn at times. For instance, the author will say that the characters are leaving a certain place one after the other, and in the next sentence he has to tell you in which order they're leaving. This is completely irrelevant. This is not what the reader wants to know.

Also the songs... I didn't mind them when I first read the book but this time... Yikes. As an adult, I hate songs in books, at least when they are too numerous. I've come to dislike stories about literal journeys too. I need more than protagonists going from place A to place B to place C... You know.

I was planning to re-read the whole trilogy but will instead re-watch the movies!

Original rating was 4/5.

I suppose I had to give it two stars, since I did listen to the whole book and enjoyed it also, in a way. In this world, white is good and black is evil, no more tones are needed (figuratively speaking - there is a ton load of silvery and golden things). Tolkien treats his readers well: chews and vomits everything onto the pages so as not to burden our minds too much. Listening to this audiobook was like listening to the rain, or some mindless radio program. It was my companion for cooking and cleaning and as such it worked well. I appreciate the humor value of its repetitiveness: when we marvel at yet another golden thing or when someone's eyes glimmer and sparkle for the millionth time (well, it IS a fantasy world so I suppose they could communicate with eye sparkles), when someone mentions the shadows growing and evil spreading, and another bad poem is thrown at us from nowhere (or maybe the poems just suffered in translation). I understand why people love this. And I understand why people hate it, too. Each to their own, right?

HOWEVER, the beginning, where Bilbo leaves and the reactions of the townspeople are described is pure genius. If the book was a short story about Bilbo leaving, I would probably give it five stars.

I know more or less what comes of the ring eventually from internet memes, although I've been spared from the movie so far. However, the guy who reads the Finnish edition of the audiobook has such an epic voice that I might listen the rest of the saga just because of him.

Era il lontano gennaio del 2012 ( lo so perché sono andata a sfogliare lo storico dei prestiti della biblioteca) quando presi in mano per la prima volta La Compagnia dell’Anello. Ebbene, dopo otto anni, e dopo averlo cominciato e abbandonato almeno tre volte, l’ho finalmente terminato.
Capisco che sia importante per la storia del fantasy, e da un punto di vista filologico tutto il lavoro immaginifico che ha fatto Tolkien è davvero notevole, tanto che mi sono letta tutta la pagina di Wikipedia dedicata alla storia della Terra di Mezzo.
Però è anche uno dei libri più noiosi che abbia mai letto. Lo stile narrativo si limita a una semplice cronaca, super dettagliata tra l’altro, di tutto ciò che i personaggi fanno, cioè camminare (e partecipate a picnic vari). Non abbiamo mai un sentimento, uno stato d’animo espresso da un personaggio, tanto che tutti i personaggi rimangono piuttosto vaghi e indistinguibili l’uno dall’altro se non per il nome, accompagnato sempre dal patronimico. Nessuno suscita una particolare simpatia, ma sicuramente quello più insopportabile è Sam (ma doveva essere proprio lui ad accompagnare Frodo?).
Inoltre, avendo già visto i film, la narrazione non mi ha riservato molte sorprese (se non per l’episodio di Tom Bombadil, che si può tranquillamente dimenticare), per cui non sono stata per niente motivata a proseguire con la lettura.
L’unico motivo di “divertimento” è la traduzione in un italiano piuttosto antiquato, che suscita un sorriso per l’utilizzo di espressioni e parole che oggi risultano desuete e quindi buffe.

I guess what kept it from having a higher rating from me was all the songs that after a while got a tad annoying and felt unimportant, sometimes there was too much detail, and just an overall feeling of "That's it?" Don't get me wrong. I did like it. I liked the characters, and felt like it was easy to sympathize with certain ones in different situations. So like I said. I liked it and I look forward to reading the others ones.

È un romanzo trabordante descrizioni; lo sforzo di creare mondi nuovi è -in teoria- ammirevole, ma si traduce soprattutto in fatica per il lettore: occorre riprodurre nella propria mente tale mondo nuovo, descritto nei dettagli, e ricordare nomi esotici e impronunciabili.
La narrazione è distante dai personaggi. Di ognuno di loro si vede solo un lato della medaglia: quello apparente; questo rende ciascuno di loro assolutamente privo di sorprese, non c'è sviluppo dei personaggi e le dinamiche sono prevedibilissime.
Se ne sente parlare come di un fantasy epico, ma trovo sia cattiva epica, in quanto l'epica non è necessariamente retorica stentorea e rigida divisione in buoni e cattivi.
È anche fascistoide, c'è poco da dire. Ad agire sono solo gli eletti. Se un poveraccio fa qualcosa di meritevole è perché è di discendenza reale, e la cosa prima o poi verrà fuori. Le donne sono figure di contorno: per lo più cantano, servono, fanno sublimi doni ai maschioni -premi per le vittorie militari o amuleti per proteggerli in battaglia- e niente altro.
Insomma, la prima edizione è del 1954, non del 1254, questo romanzo è invecchiato male, trovo.
Se questo è un capolavoro fantasy, Harry Potter, in tutta la sua sublime complessità, è un capolavoro della letteratura mondiale.
Ah già, in effetti Harry Potter È un capolavoro della letteratura mondiale :D

Seriously, I'm shocked I can only give this only 2 stars. I honestly wanted to love it. Because let's face it: Tolkien is a master at world-building, with a depth of detail and layers upon layers that are hardly found in other books. But as a novel, this just didn't do it for me.
First, the prose: it was so heavy and slow that it was a struggle to walk along with the Company. Now don't get me wrong: I love description, and there were some beautiful passages that left deeply-imprinted images in my mind; but to have to read over every detail of every surrounding landscape, down to the last stone or leaf, was simply distracting.
Second, the characters: they were two-dimensional at best. Yes, they have a lot of history to them. But that's it; there is no individual voice or trait that made them leap off the page. I just didn't feel they were real (which was quite heartbreaking, actually, especially in Aragorn's case).
So I guess my main problem is that the story didn't envelop me, and I didn't feel the characters at all. The pace was too slow, the narrative voice too bland, the details distracting rather than enhancing, and the characters stuck to the page. I can't believe I'm saying this but- actually, the movies were better.

Oh my gosh. I FINALLY finished this. When I first read the Hobbit I thought "Why does everyone say Tokien is hard to read? This is easy." THIS... Lord of the Rings is why. When people say he's an excellent world builder, what they mean is that he will describe every subtle nuance of a tree or patch of grass. And throw a million names at you that you only hear once or twice and that only serve to confuse you.
The story line itself was good, and I have a thing that compels me to finish a book once I've started (usually, unless it's REALLY bad) so I read to the end, and I will subject myself to the second and third books too.
To be fair, it was really only super laborious for the first half and then it picked up somewhat. But as much as I love the story, Tokien's actual writing frustrates me. It takes a 5 star epic down to a 3 star. I shouldn't have to feel like reading a book is chore. He could have done with less songs and poems too.
This book would definitely appeal to those who like super fleshed out backdrops but for me it detracts from the events at hand.

Hobitit ovat hurmaavia ja ihania olentoja. Tolkien on ihan omaa luokkaansa siinä, kuinka pitkälle hän on mennyt maailman luomisessa aina hobittien sukupuita myöden. Kirja tuntuu kuitenkin välillä historiankirjamaiselta ja hahmoja on liikaa. Liikaa on myös epäolennaisia mainintoja ja tarinoita hahmoista ja tapahtumista, jotka eivät ole mitenkään tärkeitä tarinan kannalta. Tarinan alkuasetelma on varsin hyvä ja jännittävä, mutta jostain syystä oma mielenkiintoni alkaa hiipua noin kirjan puolivälin jälkeen. On myös ihanaa, että hobitit laulelevat ja runoilevat paljon, mutta valitettavasti runot ovat uskomattoman tylsää luettavaa. Lukuunottamatta Bilbon runoa ”Tulen ääressä istun ja mietin nyt…” Kyseinen runo on uskomattoman kaunis ja on jäänyt lähtemättömästi mieleeni tästä kirjasta.

"Some who have read the book, or at any rate have reviewed it, have found it boring, absurd or contemptible, and I have no cause to complain since I have similar opinions of their works or the kinds of writing that they prefer." J.R.R. Tolkien from the forward to The Fellowship of the Ring.

Mr. Tolkien, I really, really, really wanted to enjoy your work, but alas, I fall into the category of those who found it "boring, absurd, or contemptible." Perhaps I will finally accept that fantasy novels are simply not my cup of tea. The plot in this the first of the Lord of the Rings trilogy was practically non-existent and can be summed up in one sentence: a little person has possession of ring that has magical powers which will lead to corruption, so the little person engages the help of others to try to rid himself of the ring.

There’s no place for J.R.R. Tolkien as a good ‘worldbuilder’ in the fantasy genre. Fantasy means storytelling, which means that worldbuilding is inevitably going to be tied to the story -- and should be judged accordingly.

It is well-known that Tolkien sought to create an impression of depth in his stories. This impression of depth enhances immersion, and thus the experience. So, a Tolkien defender might argue that while a detail may be uninteresting or narratively irrelevant, it’s not pointless because it supports the impression of depth. Fellow Goodreads reviewer J.G. Keely largely sidesteps this objection.

To better understand this, we must look at the nature of fictional worlds. Ideas are always embodied through objects, setting and character. It’s the same with character – emphasize how their expressions, the tone of their voice, and the peculiarities in their speech, reveal their fears, worries, ambitions, dreams, and so on, and your character will start to feel like a real person.

Mentioning how many shits your character took last Thursday doesn’t make the character feel more real – we don’t learn anything about his interiority. It’s a fictional fact isolated from the rest of the story. Imagine a similar wasteful fact were mentioned in The Matrix. Wouldn’t it pull you out of the story? Why is that?

It’s because we expect some sense of purpose from our fiction. A simple example is narrative focus – we don’t just jump to different characters, details, and places each scene. Fiction is communication, and communication is selection. Similarly, we don’t use language to express every single association in our mind, because that would make everything we say utterly incomprehensible. The reason why there is such a thing like narrative focus at all, is because it helps to communicate more clearly and deeply.

This is one of the expectations we have from fiction. Once this promise is broken, we tend to draw back and examine the artwork with a more critical eye. So, when an irrelevant detail gets mentioned, we try to remember it, because we expect that it will be returned to later – otherwise, why would it have been included in the first place? It’s the principle of Chekhov’s Gun.

So, when Tolkien starts listing one irrelevant detail after another, and keeps not returning to them, he breaks that promise, the expectation that was set at the beginning. The reader that expects meaning is confronted with random meaningless details. The reader is not awed by the depth of his world, but instead is confused and overwhelmed by large amounts of superfluous information – and perhaps even left wondering about the artificiality of this world.

But still, this is something that can be overcome. After all, we have to recognize that these details may in some sense reinforce the impression of depth -- especially for escapists, even though their attitude is unjustified and should not be accounted for, as I explore here.

However, to really pressure Tolkien we don’t even need to ask whether they reinforce the impression of depth, but whether they reinforce the impression of depth in a way that another more focused method cannot achieve.

Let’s examine a random fragment of The Fellowship of the Ring:


"Long ago Gorhendad Oldbuck, head of the Oldbuck family, one of the oldest in the Marish or indeed in the Shire, had crossed the river, which was the original boundary of the land eastwards. He built (and excavated) Brandy Hall, changed his name to Brandybuck, and settled down to become master of what was virtually a small independent country. His family grew and grew, and after his days continued to grow, until Brandy Hall occupied the whole of the low hill, and had three large front-doors, many side-doors, and about a hundred windows. The Brandybucks and their numerous dependants then began to burrow, and later to build, all round about. That was the origin of Buckland, a thickly inhabited strip between the river and the Old Forest, a sort of colony from the Shire. Its chief village was Bucklebury, clustering in the banks and slopes behind Brandy Hall.”

This is written very much like a history or mythology, both of these being concerned with facts. But replace the factual with the fictional, and not much of meaning is left.

Certainly, there are some themes present here – there always are -- but they are isolated, and only depicted. There are the themes of colonization, settlements, determination -- but they aren’t interrogated, and neither do they interact with each other in an interesting way. Thematic interaction is missing here.

For example, we don’t see any perspective on colonization, and neither are the effects of colonization seriously examined, nor is it interrogated. Tolkien also could have told us about some of the troubles Oldbuck faced, or perhaps how he wanted to be remembered, and how he was actually remembered. The themes of determination, colonization, settlement, expansion are yoked together without revealing anything interesting about themselves.

That’s why merely stating what happened is most of the time not the best way to get information across. That’s one of the reasons why the show vs. tell rule exists. Insight is often gained instead by examining how something happened. If our protagonist kills someone, it’s the context that gives meaning to his character – say it’s in self-defense, or for revenge, or maybe we see his expressions during the killing, &c.

Therefore, it doesn’t have much significance that Oldbuck colonized a place or built his own hall – it happens all the time --, it’s how he did it, or what kind of unique things took place during it, and how the people around him reacted, &c., that’s what makes it worth telling. Depth doesn’t come from accumulation of information, but from density of interaction.

Now, let’s examine a method that deliberately tries to be focused and thematically interactive. In Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell, in a footnote:


“Beneath the Virgin's feet were a lion and a dragon who curled around each other in a most puzzling manner and bit each other's necks. These creatures had been carved by someone who had never seen a lion or a dragon, but who had seen a great many dogs and sheep and something of the character of a dog and a sheep had got into his carving. Whenever some poor fellow was brought before the Virgin and Child to be examined the lion and the dragon would cease biting each other and look up like the Virgin's strange watchdogs and the lion would bark and the dragon bleat angrily.”

Institutional symbolism is interrogated in a very amusing manner. Certain ideas about art are also interrogated and ridiculed, namely inspiration and the notion that art is objective. Yet the world feels no less alive than Tolkien’s. We can lively imagine these events taking place.

Tolkien’s description, on the other hand, is abstract -- a mere summary of events. It is detached from the real-world experience those kinds of descriptions usually rely on. Susanna Clarke doesn’t shy away from naming places, people, and books, but she always integrates them into an interesting whole, like here. She allows for thematic interaction.

The themes of sculpturing and institutional symbolism are introduced in the first sentence. Then in the second, they are expanded upon by the themes of creative inspiration and artistic representation of reality, and linked by examining the effects of limited creative inspiration upon sculpturing, symbolism and representation. In the third sentence, these themes join together into something absurd and tangible. The humorous contrast between the noble and fearsome creatures that we imagine as lions and dragons and a dog and a sheep reinforces the present themes.

Thus, fictional details have effectively been shared while the way they were transferred is grounded in experience, and much more meaningful – the passage points towards the human experience, not away from it.

So, while Tolkien’s method remains attractive to the escapist -- who is allured by any drab that manages to consistently hold his attention -- it remains inferior to other methods of storytelling; it is less efficient, less insightful, less immersive, and ultimately less rewarding. A supposed master of worldbuilding ought to have a fine control over symbolism, tone, and internal logic. Yet, when we look closer at The Lord of the Rings it starts to fall apart rather quickly.

There are a number of examples of clashing tone, from the macro to the micro, as even in small scenes, Tolkien manages to create a confusing thematic landscape. For example, in the Shire, when Gandalf does his speech about the Ring of Power, it’s a bright, beautiful morning in the Shire, teapots stirring, birds chirping, &c.

This is clearly a tonal contrast. The themes of the scene are mainly fear, weight of responsibility, doom, urgency, shock, embodied by descriptions of ancient kings and battlefields. Yet, the themes suggested by a sunny morning in the Shire are comfort, nature, beauty, security, and prosperity.

The setting doesn’t enhance the scene; it dilutes it. The message doesn’t feel urgent or fearful. One might argue that he intentionally placed this contrast. I don’t have a problem with tonal contrasts – only if they aren’t explored. What’s the point of weakening your story if you are not getting anything else out of it?

There’s also the lack of internal consistency. When talking about the Ring, Gandalf expresses this about Bilbo:


“I could not take it from him without doing greater harm; and I had no right to do so anyway.”

The second justification is more problematic, because it asserts an ethical principle: Gandalf will not violate someone’s autonomy – like taking the Ring from Bilbo -- for the greater good. But Gandalf clearly does do that later on in the story. A few pages later in the same exposition we get this:


“I endured him as long as I could, but the truth was desperately important, and in the end I had to be harsh. I put the fear of fire on him, and wrung the true story out of him, bit by bit, together with much snivelling and snarling.”

Gandalf expresses his care and fondness for the hobbits multiple times, yet he often manages to make use of belittling and rather insulting adjectives. Here, four of the adjectives are “absurd,” “helpless,” “stupid,” and “ridiculous”:


“Ever since Bilbo left I have been deeply concerned about you, and about all these charming, absurd, helpless hobbits. It would be a grievous blow to the world, if the Dark Power overcame the Shire; if all your kind, jolly, stupid Bolgers, Hornblowers, Boffins, Bracegirdles, and the rest, not to mention the ridiculous Bagginses, became enslaved.”

It’s not “I love you because of who you are,” but “I love you despite what you are.” When I express the fondness of my cats, I don’t express the power asymmetry (‘helpless’, ‘stupid’) -- unless I am completely entranced and stupefied by their cuteness. It’s called infantilization.

Later, the elves are described as wise, yet they throw this insult to the hobbits:

“But we have no need of other company, and hobbits are so dull,” they laughed.

Then, only a second later, to invite them to their company, inquiring of the hobbits’ occupations with an intense curiosity.

Now, if the elves were described as whimsical -- which they aren’t -- this would make more sense. Again, the elves are described as wise and careful about giving advice, but when asked for important knowledge about the Nazgul who are chasing the hobbits, who are still ignorant of what they are exactly, they reply:

“Is it not enough to know that they are servants of the Enemy?’ answered Gildor. ‘Flee them! Speak no words to them! They are deadly. Ask no more of me! But my heart forbodes that, ere all is ended, you, Frodo son of Drogo, will know more of these fell things than Gildor Inglorion. May Elbereth protect you!”

They place their own feeling of security over that of the hobbits who are in immediate danger. Any knowledge about who's chasing them can be helpful -- in this case, ignorance can be quite deadly, after all, they're not just servants of the Enemy, but deemed extraordinarily dangerous. The elves know, the hobbits don't.

Then the elves make a promise to the hobbits and the audience:


“In the morning we shall have gone; but we will send our messages through the lands. The Wandering Companies shall know of your journey, and those that have power for good shall be on the watch. I name you Elf-friend; and may the stars shine upon the end of your road!”

But this promise is never fulfilled or returned to in narrative terms -- they never get help from anyone outside Gandalf’s circle. The promise is of no significant consequence, which hinders the impression of depth Tolkien is trying to achieve. This inertia highlights the artificiality; this doesn’t seem like a world that continues to think regardless of the protagonist’s path. This entire scene is quite pointless in fact, as all the themes set up here are set up later in Rivendell anyway.

In contrast, in The King of Elfland’s Daughter elves resemble multiple different things at once, and this ambiguity is never betrayed as it is in The Lord of the Rings. Instead it is controlled, precise, and sprawling.

Then we also have the symbolism of the Ringwraiths, who dominate the first half of The Fellowship of the Ring as the antagonists, and which turns out so univocal and simplistic that only well-developed protagonists and more interesting dynamics could have detracted from it.

Tolkien adopts a partially realist style but retains mythic and romantic material. He ends up closely following his characters, yet his characters taste like nothing but cardboard. They are archetypal and symbolic, but the realist style suggests they have dreams, hopes, fears, worries, mannerisms, little reactions, and so on. Why know of every little thing that happens during their travels if you’re never going to explore a character or dynamic deeper, or reveal something interesting about nature, history, or people? After all, that’s what great travelogues have done in the past. In contrast to a travel blogger like Samuel Johnson, Tolkien fails to elevate both the mundane and the unfamiliar.

Finally, there’s the absurd yet popular notion that The Lord of the Rings isn’t racist. Are you really going to tell me that the author had no choice but to make all the good guys white and from the West, and the bad guys dark-skinned and from the East and South? And no, having one of your main characters wonder whether “they’re really evil at heart” does not redeem it. One can easily imagine a slave owner or colonist having a similar thought. It doesn’t mean the character or the story is suddenly exempt from racism, which was—guess what—racist. After all, Tolkien could have easily had a leader or rebellion of the South fight against Sauron.

Sure, it may not have been Tolkien’s intention, but The Lord of the Rings is not a piece of private (intentional) meaning but expressed meaning, which accordingly deserves different criteria -- and which can obviously include things that do not agree with the intention of the author. This is proof of a prejudice creeping into his work, just like some of my prejudices about writing and criticism will inevitably enter this text.

In the end, one may wonder how a work like this could ever achieve this level of fame. Yet this is not a new phenomenon. Even someone like Abraham Cowley — hugely celebrated in his own time, canonical, quoted endlessly — is barely remembered today. The Lord of the Rings is just another one of those flukes.

2 STARS
DNF, so this rating/review pertains to the first 181 pages (roughly, first half).

I'm sad - so desperately sad that I have to give this rating. Before I go into my qualms with this book, I do acknowledge the vast and overwhelming influence that Tolkien has held over the genesis and evolution of fantasy as a genre, as well as literature in general. I'm aware that many of the novels I love today would not have been in existence, or would be vastly different, without Tolkien's works. As a fantasy lover, how could I not acknowledge this? I've always wanted to be a Tolkien fangirl, and as I love the films with all my heart, naturally I wanted to love this book as well, the book where it all started. I wanted to have the glorious relationship that I have with the A Song of Ice and Fire series, where I desperately love the books as well as the television series (in addition to all of the companion novels) and I'm able to just bask in my all-encompassing love for the world and its characters in so many different formats. But truthfully, as I think another reviewer has aptly put it, if this novel was written by anyone else but Tolkien then I would've hated it.

While I love the world and story that Tolkien spawned in this series (I love the films!), I just cannot get onboard with Tolkien's writing style - pages and pages of rambling, verbose and unnecessarily long exposition, random characters and scenes that could be cut entirely out of the story and legitimately would not change the course of the plot or character arcs at all. And I'm the kind of person that loves description! But Tolkien's descriptions aren't lyrical, nor do they seem to add much to the story - I really didn't need to hear a two page description of a hill. If it was a beautiful, poetic and concise description of a hill, I could vibe with it. And I understand the importance of world-building, but I have also seen some brilliant, masterful world-building in action that took far less pages and far less flat and tiresome exposition. Alas...

Another issue was that the characters are unbearably flat. We know next to nothing about each character's background or (and most importantly) about the conflicts of their heart, past and present - the four hobbits, while having small differences between them, largely seem the same, and even Gandalf loses the wit and charm that he had in the films. This is an issue, especially as (at least for me) it prevented me from forming any kind of attachment at all to these characters, as I still didn't feel like I knew them, or that they were really real.

I remember having these same issues with the Hobbit, although reading that was more bearable, I suppose, due to its shorter length. But I reached almost 200 pages in, and the four hobbits STILL haven't even reached the Prancing Pony. I'll give credit where it's due though - Tolkien did create a magnificent and enchanting world, and the turns that his plots take are famous, and rightly so. But for little events of significance (either to plot or character development) to happen within 200 pages, I think, is a sign of some dreadfully slow pace.

It's clear that Tolkien was a linguist, and his background as a scholar can be easily seen through the masterful integration of mythologies spanning different cultures. There are so many glorious quotes that can be taken and treasured from this book, but the issue is that altogether, when taking a step back, one cannot (and shouldn't) discount the problems in storytelling evident in this book. There seems to be little emotion behind a lot of the writing in this book, just meticulous, excruciating detail - which is difficult for me, because reading this does evoke the warm and fuzzies from me, although I'm not sure if that's genuinely from the writing or (more likely) from re-immersing myself in a world that I've grown up loving, albeit in a different format.

I feel guilty, almost, for not only not finishing this read, but also for giving it a poor rating. But I'm also trying to be honest here, so screw it. I love this world, and I think Tolkien is a genius for the plot that he devised, especially given that he lived in a world where fantasy was something of a new invention. But I'm a reader that takes heavy notice of writing style, perhaps most out of all aspects of a novel, and his just wasn't to my taste. It's likely that I'll pick this back up sometime in the future just so that I can have read the books, but I don't see it happening anytime soon. In the meantime, I'm excited to pick up a different book, since this book sent me into an awful spiral of dreading having to read.

I really want to rewatch those movies now, though. Damn, were they glorious.

Disclaimer: reading this as a 26-year-old adult.

This is for people who wish their fables were much longer and had more songs, for people who read Famous Five but wished it could be an all boy group, for the adults who miss Enid Blyton.

This is NOT for people who found Star Wars very paint-by-numbers, because this is similarly constructed, to the point that you can practically see the seams holding the story together. This is also not for those who read stories mainly about men and then can only marvel at how men’s closeness and friendships feel worlds apart from women’s in a bad way, which is what I felt here. If this is the bar for good friendships, we're so over. If it weren’t for the cultural impact, I wouldn’t be reading this series. Now that I've finished the whole thing, I can confidently say I haven't missed out on anything important by not reading this sooner.

I've tried reading this book multiple times before and barely been able to make it past the Introduction, so I just gave up and listened to the audiobook. When I TELL YOU how I felt when I saw the 23 hour time-stamp.....I almost collapsed. Is it ever that serious??? Now, if this was 23 hours of detailed characterization, I get it but this was mostly dialogue and then plot. The characters were giving Jungian archetypes and I say this in the most derogatory way possible. The damage psychoanalysis has done to the field of English literature is irreparable but that's a debate for another day.

Th first book is cute and basic, I guess. I can argue for a day and a half about how disciplinary boundaries are arbitrary and harmful but when I listen to an English/Linguistics major, I immediately take it back because of how they've been shaped as PEOPLE by their poor training. These people are my mortal enemies (after econ and psych) for their a-sociological (fashioned after ahistorical) understanding of the world. I understand that LOR is less a proper story than a nice big empty world; Tolkien just wanted to create language systems and padded it out with characters. But his very poor understanding of how social systems work, given how he splits up the ‘races’ and then characterizes them in white supremacist ways, is a gross oversimplification of how living beings actually live together.

His author’s note said he cares more for history than fantasy and a bit of that can be seen in how much of the story is sheer coincidence. Much of history is an arbitrary confluence of factors, true. But I think he cares most for Christianity because that belief system drives most of the choices in the story. The nations here are entirely good or bad, with the bad ones literally being described as 'slant-eyed' :) I love eating blatant racism in popular fiction that literally shapes our shared reality for breakfast. Also it is WILD to see a language professor calling any language harsh or guttural.

The South is characterized as a place that draws evil and attacks the west in. Directions are political choices and locating your villain in the south, like the world empires do, feels antagonistic.

Unlike Lucille Bluth, Tolkien doesn't even bother hiding he has a favorite child: the super-white super-blonde elves that represent everything good about personhood apparently. Every mention of these losers aggravated me for how cloying and saccharine it felt. Religious people are less moved in a great sanctuary than Tolkien describing the elves.

I don’t disagree that Tolkien pioneered much of what’s popular in fantasy today but I like work that isn’t just the first to do something. When I read something, I don’t want to just be reminding myself to appreciate the trend it set, but to be impressed because it contains profound insights on the human condition relevant decades/centuries later. I like works where I can just enjoy the writing and this ain't it.

I had a few snickers at Gandalf's deadpan responses and I felt protective of Boromir for the sole reason that Tolkien's narration seemed to have it out for him. But that was all the warmth the story got from me. I have very little to say about it because it passed through me without moving me, changing me or making me reflect. How can a story this long have so little to say? Tolkien scoffs at allegories but this felt like one because it felt equally derivative. Events happened one after another and that was that.

I don't dislike LOTR but it is one of those books that I found easier to digest in audiobook form. Even as an adult with a fairly well-developed attention span I sometimes find my eyes glazing over and my thoughts drifting elsewhere while slogging through Tolkien.

I am going to be frank: I do not understand the continued stranglehold Tolkien has on the genre. This is not to say I think LOTR is all bad. The good parts are REALLY good. It's just that you can count all the good parts on one hand. There are several memorable scenes scattered across the whole of LOTR but the are as nothing compared to the especially boring bits, which make up about 80% of the story.

Film adaptations of Tolkien tend to change his characters so much that they may as well be entirely different people. I do not fault the makers of these adaptations for this. The characters as Tolkien wrote them are incredibly boring and one-note, barring a couple of notable exceptions. Here I must contradict some of the 1-star reviews (that I otherwise agree with), many of which accuse Tolkien of being a piss-poor character writer. I agree that he often did not write engaging characters. This is not to say he was incapable of it. The most memorable parts of the story have to do with the Rohan and Gondor drama spread across TTT and ROTK. Unfortunately you need to slog through FOTR to get there. I reject the notion that Tolkien should be appreciated as the granddaddy of modern fantasy or w/e, simply because he began the trend of front-loading fantasy stories with the worst and most boring bits. Even his most ardent fans tend to gloss over the insipid Shire section of FOTR and most of it was (thankfully) excised from the Jackson films, as was much of the hobbits' pre-Aragorn wandering about. That is nearly half the book. Ironically LOTR as Tolkien wrote it was already pretty streamlined by modern fantasy standards. What that says about the genre is up to you, dear reader.

Anyway: I'm not sure I would recommend FOTR necessarily and I don't think what Tolkien laid out should have served as the groundwork for modern fantasy. As I said in my review of Naomi Novik's Uprooted, I think he has left a dark legacy on the genre. I wholeheartedly mean that. People mistake the way Middle-earth sparked their imaginations for Tolkien having written an engaging story, rather than that he only created a very interesting constructed world. The problem is LOTR is often the opposite of engaging. I know many people (especially Christian fans of fantasy) may be reluctant to delve into the epic fantasy subgenre because so much of it is trashy and there is so much violence (and misogyny) spread across it. But I note also that many people who say this tend to gloss over the fact that Tolkien's books are incredibly violent. They are full of war and murder and I would argue he did glorify violence, though many of his fans will claim he didn't, because sometimes the characters deliver sentiments about the loss of human life, etc. etc. This does not erase things like Gimli and Legolas's killing contest at Helm's Deep, or the triumphant and unambiguously heroic moment Eowyn kills the Witch-King of Angmar, or all of the other instances of gleeful orc-slaying. Just because there is no explicit sex does not mean his books are squeaky-clean, wholesome Christian romps. Stop fooling yourselves.

I can’t believe I am going to say this, especially about such a beloved book but—This book is going on my DNF shelf.

I’ve tried so many times over the years to read this book, but I’ve always found it so, well, dull. I’m sad that this was my reaction to this book but, alas, it is what it is. To paraphrase a previous review “I wanted so desperately to love Tolkien, but it just isn’t happening.”

I made it to where the hobbits were in the house of Tom Bombadil before I decided to pack it in, but there were sooo many times I felt like quitting before that.

First Grievance- the introduction or, ‘On the Nature of Hobbits.’ The whole thing really, but one thing sticks out in my mind. Yes, the hobbits enjoy smoking a pipe, but was there really, really, REALLY a need to be given a (very) long winded and rambling explanation on the in universe production of tobacco (or smoke weed as it’s called here)? Do we REALLY need to know this? Overall, the introduction, which some may consider great world building, was dull, meandering and pedantic. And this theme pops up a lot- everything is just so long winded. Did anyone see the ERB of George R.R. Martin and J.R.R. Tolkien? One of George’s lines comes to mind “We don’t need the history of every f*cking tree branch.”

Second Grievance- the singing. Oh God- the hobbits have a song for everything. Going for a walk? Here’s a song. Running through the woods? Here’s a song. Eating a meal? Here’s a song. Having a bath? Here’s a song. Going to bed? Here’s a song. Starting a big adventure? Here’s a song (which was a modified version of the Dwarves ‘Misty Mountain,’ and not near as good). Oh God, even by the second time a character broke out into song, it just started to feel like filler, and since it was filler, that just meant NOTHING WAS HAPPENING AND THE PLOT AND STORY WAS NOT PROGRESSING. Don’t even get me started on the nonsense Tom Bombadil was uttering as song. It wasn’t so much a facepalm as Face-Meet-Desk.

Third Grievance- I got the audiobook and I am seven hours in with over fifteen hours left (fifteen hours thirty nine minutes roughly). My third grievance is the pacing. Everything. Is. Just. So. Slow. And. Drawn. Out.

Fourth Grievance- related to the third in a way, as it can put down to pacing, but nothing seems to happen. Even when Frodo and his buddies finally set of on their adventure- it was so slow and drawn out that I found it boring. Being chased by Black Riders, meeting Elves, been attacked by living trees- there was so little drama and tension that I really didn’t care. The only part that was ‘exciting’ was Tom Bombadil, and that’s because of Andy Sirkis’ brilliant audio performance. But, that incident seemed like more of an overcorrection at first, and got dull and boring really quick.

Look, if you are still with me at this stage, I may not have read the whole book, but I’ve read enough. I can’t deny J.R.R. Tolkien’s contribution to the fantasy genre. He is the granddaddy of modern fantasy. But, like Ulysses by James Joyce, the writing style didn’t appeal to me. I am after coming off re-reading some works by George Orwell and John Steinbeck- what Tolkien or Joyce could take three pages to say, Orwell or Steinbeck could say in half a page.

Two and a half stars because I can recognize the importance of the work, but not my taste.

I know I’m gonna get hate for a two star LOTR review😂 I will start off by saying I DESPERATELY wanted to enjoy this novel. And I did. For like the first two hours of the audiobook.

Things I liked:
•the world building was whimsical
•the narrative of the first few chapters was nice, like a fairy tale
•the narrator for the audiobook was fantastic!!
• the ring as an object of power is really cool and created some good conflict that I would have liked expounded upon

But um yeah, that’s about it. Here are things I disliked:

Character Development:

Bro I had more character development in the month after my ex left me than any of the characters do in this book. Most of the characters are interchangeable and don’t really stick out from one another-none of their personalities shine through.

These are the character traits I gathered from each of the characters:

•Sam-codependent
•Gimli-hair fetish
•Strider-brooding but not in the hot way Geralt is
•Gandalf-angry powerful boomer who refuses to use his power for anything truly useful

There is also no chemistry between any of the characters. The most well-developed relationship was between Sam and the fucking horse.

Overall, I wasn’t connected to any of this characters and it honestly didn’t seem like they were even connected to each other. We are constantly told they are close friends, yet nothing occurs in the narrative to support this. I didn’t care when Gandalf died (disappeared?) and it didn’t make sense why the characters were distraught, especially since Gandalf truly wasn’t that useful until the eleventh hour.


Narrative Development/Pacing:

Overall, it doesn’t feel like any encounters past the hobbits leaving the Shire were super necessary. Encounters should create opportunities for relationships to grow, characters to develop, and for them to near the climax of the novel.

There really was no climax, no clear goal. They just seemed to wander from place to place and pick up more camp followers without any true rhyme or reason. The conflicts that arose were repetitive and didn’t allow for growth or change.

I understand that this was supposed to be a third of one original publication, so it may explain the lack of true structure. However, if that is the case, Tolkien would really need to work on his narrative pacing. There was so much in this book that truly added nothing to the story and caused me to zone out while listening to the audiobook-causing me to miss important plot points at times/needing to re-listen to the entire chapter.


The Songs:

GODDAMN THE SONGS

I get it. Tolkien is a linguist. Fun. Funky. Fresh. I liked some of the songs, some added some good world building, some were whimsical.

But the frequency and overall unnecessary nature of the songs started to really grind my gears.


Overall:
I truly wanted to like this better than I did. Much like Dune, I see some good solid world building bones and plot devices; however, I think it was not properly done. I understand too that this is something that was written nearly a hundred years ago and things change.

I can see why people like it-it provided whimsy and building blocks for modern fantasy. I will not be progressing with the novels; but I am excited to sit down with some popcorn and watch the trilogy for the first time.

I can't prove it, but I think anyone who admits to vehemently disliking this book must admit himself to reeducation camp. I hope I'm wrong about that. I didn't dislike the book so much as I slogged through it. I'm sorry to all my followers in this space. I suspect I shall lose many of you now. I don't mean to be offensive. Let me try to explain my difficulty, and perhaps you can at least have a modicum of pity intermingled with your personal disgust.

I'm not sure what it is, but I think it has to do with old age. I read this 30 years ago when I procured my first guide dog named Hobbit. People who found out his name instantly assumed I was somehow a rabid fan of the books. Never mind the fact that the guide dog school picked the name, and I had nothing to do with IT. So, I read all four of these books sometime in the mid ‘90s. And I have at least a vague memory of thoroughly enjoying them. Zipping ahead 30 years, I apparently am not the person I was when it comes to cognition. I hate to admit that. Especially in a setting like this where the review never dies and can't go away. Still, it's probably better to admit to one's weaknesses and strive to find compensation for them than to pretend they don't exist and prove yourself a fool to everyone who pays even remote attention to you. So, I freely admit, and rather publicly so, that I apparently haven't retained some of the cognition skills I had 30 years ago. How do I know that? Because all the names and characters and their bizarre genealogies in this book tossed me and threw me for all kinds of loops. I must have either ignored it 30 years ago or simply been able to embrace it and move on. I couldn't this time. It frankly confused the heck out of me in a lot of places. I thought the old tales of long-ago exploits were somewhat blase. The music was just stupid as far as I'm concerned. Sorry about that those of you who love the books. Before you send in hate-filled comments about my warped perspective, let me try to redeem myself just a bit.

I thought the plot moved nicely. And who doesn't love a story where the underdog triumphs. The courage shown by this little Hobbit who inherited the ring on or around his 33rd birthday is impressive by every measure.

This is the story of a cadre of brave beings. It's an interesting mixture of elf, dwarf, human, and Hobbit. I presume the ultimate purpose for the journey that Frodo Undertook was to ultimately destroy the ring so that it could not fall into the hands of a dark and evil hegemon. In this first book, he at least gets part way on his journey. He has a brief unrewarding encounter with the ring's previous owner. The ring is itself evil. The more the owner uses and wears it, the more it takes possession of that individual's free will. You lose the ability to exercise your moral agency. The ring ultimately takes control if it can. There’s some battle action here, and the plot moves at a nice pace. I can't help but wish that it had been a little shorter perhaps, and that there had been a great deal fewer names and genealogies. It saddens me that I am so completely uninterested in genealogy. But that's grist for another mill.
