Lord of the Rings is a special series to me, because it marks the point as a kid where my dad stopped reading books to me and I instead started reading them myself. The final book my dad read to me was "The Hobbit", and I think this happened sometime in grade 4. I don't remember exactly what happened during "The Hobbit" to cause this transition, but my guess is that I found the plot interesting enough that I grew impatient waiting around for my dad to have time to read to me and must have started reading ahead myself. Whatever happened, somehow I decided I was capable of reading the sequel trilogy on my own, which I did, and then my dad never read to me again.

Rereading these books again as an adult, I find myself puzzled that they are so widely loved. The books come across as almost unbearably preachy, with a primary focus on black and white morality and virtues with the depth and nuance that I would expect of an eight year old (which is maybe why I liked the books so much at that age). This was especially noticeable in the way the character of Boromir (the one who tries to take the ring from Frodo) is depicted. Pretty much every time Boromir speaks, it goes something like this:

Boromir: "Here are some words that demonstrate my inferior morality and lack of virtue."
Aragorn/Gandalf/Elrond: "Silence" or "Here are some words which explain why what you just said demonstrates your inferior morality and lack of virtue".

When Tolkien isn't shitting on Boromir, most of the rest of the book is spent describing in excruciating detail the logistical details of travel. A typical passage might read something like this:

Aragorn: "Well, Legolas and I have returned from scouting, and we've found the trail that goes around the falls a couple of miles from here. We're going to need to carry the boats and all our supplies to the trail, and then down to the bottom of the falls before we can continue on our way."
Boromir: "That sounds like it will be difficult."
Aragorn: "Here is why what you just said demonstrates your moral failings."

** ten page description of the logistical details involved in portaging the boats through the forest to the trail, then down the trail to the bottom of the waterfall, and then getting the boats back into the river at the bottom of the falls and continuing to travel**.

I was originally going to reread the whole trilogy in Taiwanese Mandarin, but this series has not aged well and I'm not sure if I can stand any more of it.

Stories remain an essential part of our lives. Without stories, we lose focus on the greater picture &, arguably, we lose the essence of who we are. Few stories amongst the thousand published yearly have made their way into the conscious state of the masses. Without needing to have consumed the original manuscript or sat through the tragically periodic change of the planets, one is able to muster enough information by proxy to participate in conversations. In this way, we have become connected through the reputation & lore that these stories carry through the ages.

I have long watched the trilogy set to film from the original books. I was never a great fan of the Fantasy genre or of movies depicting scenes of catastrophic war but, within these visuals, I found something by which to tether myself. That being said, I am a bibliophile. On account of many of the ways in which my brain interprets the world around me, I am seldom drawn to film. It is a wonder that it has taken me as long as it has to endeavour to read this first book. However, it’s not so much a mystery to me as it might seem.

When I was growing up, I knew which books I liked. This is not something that has drastically changed as I have aged. On the contrary, I have become more certain that specific tropes, approaches to writing (stylistics, prose), etc. are not (generally) things that I enjoy in the written format. That is not to say that I avoid these things at all costs. Rather, my life is short. I have a specific amount of time on earth—time that I am unaware of—I do not want to be chasing after books that all but check the marks of works of literature I am sure to loathe. There are too many books in this world that I want to read, I have no time to spend reading that which is not meant for me.

I avidly believe that some readers are kept in the author's mind when crafting their work. I have come upon stories that I found to be great & horrible bores but, I know other readers who will love them—because they are not me. Part of being a reader is understanding what is contained within a book. A story is meant to be consumed by an audience. Whether this means that one person grasps the tendrils of the heart of the premise or a thousand readers share in circles of wonder; a story is meant to be told & appreciated.

Here we find ourselves at a crossroads. I did not think that I would be the target audience for this book but, I read it anyway. Halfway through, I found myself wondering why I was reading this at all. Should I push myself to finish a book that I was not very much enjoying, for the sake of boasting to have read it or, do I lay it down for the reader who will love it? I did finish this book but, will not be moving forward with the final two instalments at this time because, when all is said & done, this was not a story that I enjoyed.

It is always strange for me to be faced with an author who is a talented writer but a dreadfully uncharismatic storyteller. Tolkien is a phenomenal writer. It would not take a studied & learned individual of English linguistics to declare that Tolkien knew his way around the language. The story works only so much as his passion for translating experience into consumable words. If I have taken anything away from this experience it is that writing & storytelling are two different things; Tolkien would have been a glorious correspondent but a tedious conversationalist.

This criticism is said with tenderness. I am familiar with the reasons why he decided to write this story & I am not trying to take that away from him. As a fellow Sisyphus, a mountaineer in my mind & heart, I applaud Tolkien for taking the time to try.

It is very difficult to do anything when the world is shadowed to you by your own clouds, stapled to the crevices of your mind by terror. Here we have a long journey through a world that seems more eager to name the danger that exists than we are in our own. Tolkien brought to life characters who were ignorant & downtrodden but, they remain eager, to this day, to see goodness prevail.

One is left asking if this alone is enough. The parallels that exist between this story & the society in which Tolkien lived are enumerable. One might ruminate on the similarities between the Hobbits & the Frontline soldiers or the landscape that is heaving with darkened riders. I would have liked to be able to write a review that was critical of the comparisons but, I found myself bidding my time. The primary reason for this was that none of the characters emit a depth categorically necessary to the premise. Frodo is a Hobbit & that is what we know. The first book spends three separate occasions reiterating the history of the ring so that when the first book closes off to begin the second, one is left with nothing to remember but rambling in the woods & a tree that consumes everything that it hates.

This brings me back to my comment about being a good storyteller. When one writes, one either chooses to believe that the reader is smart or, chooses to pander to the mind of a person who is not paying attention. Tolkien wrote in circles about the same thing, over & over again, without reason for doing so. We understand the history of the Hobbits because he told it to us in the Prologue. This information is appreciated if a bit excessive. Why did Tolkien not approach the entire story in this way? This book was written during a period in time when the attention span of readers was not 15 seconds. Why is he acting as though the reader cannot remember that the ring fell into a river?

Did the author forget his own story or did he believe that after a thousand & one poems of sing-song nature, the reader might have forgotten why they should care? I am certainly not trying to be cruel but, I found my patience wanting. There is no need to have three separate occasions in which the entire history of the ring is reiterated down to the last detail—we already know this & now the information is redundant making the story dull.

I might have understood the need to draw out the details. Perhaps, when Gandalf first began to explain the history to Frodo he believed it best to keep some things hidden & when Aragorn was explaining his participation in finding Gollum to learn more about the ring, he was waiting for the right time to say everything that he knew. Instead, every character feels the need to dictate things that we have already been told.

Is the culture in this world that no one knows when to jump into lengthy retellings? Everything that might have been useful for Frodo is kept silenced because people believe that Gandalf is the only one who should be speaking the truth. Fair enough but then why are we all constantly ruminating on the ring—maybe if we made more tangible progress on the path we mightn’t need to regurgitate the same intention behind the journey every five minutes.

In all this story is boring. This is not the work of someone who understands what goes into an enthralling story. This is the work of someone intent on forgetting the world in which they live. I do not begrudge him for that. I do not think this story needs to be read to be appreciated. It is enough for readers to share their experiences to keep the book's essence alive.

Perhaps if we all remember that hardship can be found even in tender places, we are better set & ultimately prepared for the troubles that befall all of humankind. Perhaps in stories, even the ones we do not enjoy, there is something like a token we might keep with us. From this book, I am reminded of the gruesome terrors that loom over our world & the magic we create amid our days in the hope that when we close our eyes, the darkness might not reflect an iris that sears morbidly back at us.

Read this (and the rest of the trilogy) as a kid and didn't hate it, but I sure hate it now.

It feels as though nothing happens, despite all the side-quests and mini-trials; pages and pages of uninspired travel scenery. The incredible attention to detail I remember from the films re architecture, cultural symbols, fashion, weaponry etc apparently never came from the books, because there's no visual description to speak of, we have little to no idea how to picture ANYTHING - but it sure was important to make sure we knew stuff was on the left or right of the characters as they travelled!

Despite a great deal of pretentious info-dumping, the characters almost never say anything of substance and have very little personality: Legolas is barely a character at all, Gimli and Boromir are defined only by their patriotism, Merry and Pippin are interchangeable, Aragorn is extremely vague when he's not being weirdly indecisive (or referring to himself in third-person). Gandalf is an idiot (yes, he is! If he suspected the ring was the Ring when Bilbo found it he should have reacted immediately, not waited decades to do anything about it! There was no good reason for leaving it be, wtf!) Frodo is a sweetheart but also deeply vague. Sam is the only one with a clear personality. The omniscient perspective comes with a flattening of every character; we get so little of their thoughts and feelings that none of them feel like real, vivid people.

The book is littered with Cherkov's guns that are never picked up (Tom Bombadil, Glorfindel, etc). Characters like Elrond can’t do anything because Reasons. In fact, almost EVERYTHING is because Reasons; very little is done because it's the most logical path. They spend THREE MONTHS doing NOTHING in Rivendell instead of setting out! If you haven't read the Silmarillion there’s little to zero context or explanation for almost every Big Picture thing. And I still think Sauron and Saruman having such similar names is a bad writing choice.

I was so bored. Everything is put in the dullest language and light possible. There’s a biblical quality to the prose that put me to sleep, and I never got goosebumps, I never felt moved. The moments when something supernatural is happening - the balrog, what Frodo experiences while wearing the Ring, etc - are laughably under-described. This series has a reputation for immense beauty, but it’s all down to the imagination of the readers, because it’s not coming from the actual text. (Where does the idea that Tolkien writes really gorgeous nature writing come from? Give me Niccola Griffith any day!)

Just watch the movie again.

It is incredibly slow with all those descriptions of travelling and for some parts can turn into a true slog, most infamously the Shire and especially Tom Bombadil which are just about a 100 pages where for the most part nothing happens and it is almost devoid of drama.

I also couldn’t stand the dialogue in this book, it feels incredibly unnatural and dry and it kept me from getting immersed. The characters also weren’t all that great or witty and I felt their screen time was spread too thin over the many characters in the fellowship. Merry and Pippin might as well have been one character for the amount they differed from each other. I desperately missed some bonding and character building scenes where they talked about their hopes, doubts and dreams at the fire or something like that.

I think keeping so closely tied to Frodo’s perspective was also a mistake as there are chapters where the rule is telling over showing. The most glaring of these are Gandalf telling what he had been doing all these years between Bilbo’s birthday party (which, by the way, are 17 YEARS) and revealing Gollum’s tragic backstory (which playing it close to the chest and revealing that at the beginning of the third movie was a great decision) and, most frustratingly, Gandalf’s disappearance which results in an incredibly dry and boring council scene which just get exacerbated by the unnatural dialogue.

I was also truly disappointed that the few action/fight scenes this book does have are so sparse in description that they feel summarized which is a real shame.

Ultimately I think the movie is WAY better than the book can ever hope to be, as a lot of iconic moments from the movie (‘What about second breakfast’, Bilbo’s jump scare, Saruman summoning an ice storm, Gandalf talking to Frodo in the mines, the Orc fight in the Mines of Moria, etc) are missing or fall flat in the book. Making Merry, Pippin and Gimli more comic relief characters was also a great idea and actually makes them feel like different characters and they have some life to them.

The only thing I think the book did somewhat better is the Mirror of Galadriel which I always found a bit stupid in the movie with Galadriel pulling an angry Gandalf.

Overall, I can see a great story underneath but the boring travelling, unnatural dialogue and many other nibbling issues really needed an editor which was what the movies were.

Apologies to the fantasy gods before I write this review, but I'm just going to put it out there. I found this to be a slog. There. I'm not proud of what I said, but I said it.

You know that feeling when you see the movie, and it just doesn't match up to your imagination of the book? Reverse that, and that's how I'm ashamed to say I feel. Because this seemed like a gap in my book experience, I picked up this audiobook. I loved The Hobbit, and I loved the LOTR movies. It seemed a no-brainer. Well, I know it's an unpopular opinion, but I just did not enjoy this audiobook.

So, why is that? I think there are a number of reasons. First of all, it was a ton of exposition, and a ton of unnecessary detail. I'd been warned that the start of the book was basically a giant info-dump, and by the time I got halfway through and it was still going on, it felt like I'd invested too much time not to finish it. Second, the pacing was super-weird, and it felt like it ended in a strange place. Third, the songs. Oh, the songs. On audiobook, especially, there were a number of times I found myself saying, "Oh, no. I see. This song isn't over. There's another verse. Yep, and another one."

In all fairness, I think a lot of this is not on Tolkien, for a number of reasons.
1. He was one of the first fantasy well-known fantasy writers, and his writing either was in line
with or the source of the conventions of the time in the genre. Wordiness and info-dump and almost entirely male characters and the like was not out of the ordinary. Even if I don't think it aged well, I realize I might have felt differently if I had read it then.
2. The audiobook narrator was not my favorite. His voices blended together for different characters, his intonation wasn't varied enough, and he just couldn't quite keep my attention.
3. To my knowledge, Tolkien wrote the full LOTR series as one book, and then he split it into three installments. With this in mind, the pacing and the weird ending makes a ton more sense.
4. If I hadn't seen the movies and known what was going to happen, it would have been so much more interesting and suspenseful. As it was, I kept waiting for the next thing to happen, and nothing felt surprising.
5. I would have skipped over the songs if I'd been reading the book instead of listening. That would have saved me about a hundred pages.

I truly wish I had read this without having seen the movies a hundred times.

I read this with my son after reading The Hobbit which I have read before - but I didn't go full Lord of the Rings then so I thought I might do so now with him. We enjoyed The Hobbit, it is a good, fun story but there was a lot of lore, poetry, odd names and seemingly random asides, but not enough to ruin the plot. I am not a big fantasy fan but I have seen all the Lord of the Rings movies which I enjoyed, but I know it can distort how much you enjoy reading books after you have seen the film version of them.

Given the level of popularity of Lord of the Rings, I did have high expectations. There is undoubtedly a lot to like here - the characters of Frodo, Golum, Gandalf, Aragorn, Sam etc. are great. There are lots of enjoyable set piece bits like the Birthday party, Gandalf's 'They Shall Not Pass' confrontation, the attack of the Night Rider things, the meeting of the Elves, and when Frodo uses the ring. It is a big, epic quest that is tense and exciting at times (even if you have seen the films) and I respect the whole world that Tolkein is building.

What is much harder to deal with is how hard going so much of the rest of the book is. I was always told that you should wear your exposition lightly but Tolkein goes to such great lengths to give you the histories of everyone, long songs and poems, strange asides, minor characters that go nowhere, and some parts that I really didn't understand at all. I am not sure what the point of all these things is either - is he trying to make some kind of artistic point or is he just showing off?

Perhaps all of this extra explanation, ancestry and poetry will all pay off by the end of the trilogy and I will look a bit silly by complaining about all of this extraneous content in book 1 (and I am stubborn enough that I fully intend to get through all three books) but I doubt it. Genuinely I am very surprised that so many people absolutely love these books and they are one of the most read novels around as it feels like such hard work, and took us a very long time to get through this as a result.

It may be that watching the films first didn't help as I already knew most of the plot twists and developments to come, equally perhaps me and my son are the wrong ages to be reading this and really getting into it, but to be honest I was a bit disappointed.

Okay well. I really wanted to like this, I wanted to be a true Tolkien girly since I like the movies and TV show, but good heavens this a slog through the mud.

I understand that Tolkien is considered the father of fantasy or whatever, but there’s really no fantasy to this story besides the races of some characters. Most of the characters feel so interchangeable that I found myself having to go back and see who was speaking because they all sound the same. Sam and Gandalf are the only ones who actually have a personality and a distinguishable voice. The world itself seems to just be earth-adjacent. They go through fields and forests and mountains, which is fine, but I never get a sense of fantasy in his descriptions. The magic system is pretty much non-existent. I don’t think they ever interact with any sort of mythical creatures either? Which seems so crazy to me. I think they mention wolves, which is another example of it being earth-adjacent. The most fantastical aspect is of course the ring, and even that raises so many questions for me. This ring is so powerful and fearsome but all it does is make you turn invisible and go crazy? And draw the enemies attention to your location? That’s what all the fuss is about?

I know it’s a meme now, how wordy Tolkien is, but it truly does not seem necessary. It adds nothing to the story or world-building; it just made me feel like I was reading a social studies text book. He focuses way too much on histories and settings and can’t seem to give a real POV for any of the characters, which is the heart of a book for me. And all. The. Walking. By god, they just walk everywhere for pages and pages. I felt like I was being held hostage on a hike with the most boring people on Earth. And it wouldn’t have been so unbearable if Tolkien had spent more time building bonds between the characters, creating development arcs, giving them personalities, etc, but I think that’s just not something he’s capable of, at least based on this book. I kept asking myself WHY these characters seem so duty-bound to one another; why Pippin and Merry and Sam want to come with Frodo. It’s like everyone’s defaulted to being altruistic, and it’s boring.

This is the biggest exception to the idea that “books are better than the movie.” The movies are so much better.

No, no, no! I can't even bring myself giving this one 3 Stars.

I have all the respect for Tolkien, his work and his influence on the modern fantasy genre. I don't deny that there is a lot of effort being put into this trilogy, but still ... it just doesn't work for me. I already didn't like it when I read it as a teen - roughly around the time the movies came out - and it's not any different now.

Listening to the audiobook version of "The Fellowship" just felt like watching an old black and white movie that hasn't aged very well. The flourishes of making the story interesting just aren't that gripping anymore. It's not that they aren't there. In the early parts of the book, Tolkien crafts a lot of suspense around the ring and reveals it's hideous nature ever so slowly. That builds intrigue. Same thing with the mysterious riders who haunt the hobbits on their journey. There is also a lot of charm in the way the Hobbits are characterized as a people.

However, all the suspense and momentum the novel has to offer is almost completely buried under regular detours, endless travelogue descriptions and characters just hanging out and listening to poetry, songs and life stories. The chapter about Elronds Council e.g. has half a dozen characters report on their recent activities that takes far longer than it should before the discussion about what to actually do with the ring even begins. It doesn't get better by the end. Entering Lothlorien, hanging out there and finally leaving it takes three entire chapters that roughly span 10% of the entire book. Most of the chapters take far too long to get to the parts that are actually interesting.

I'm not even blaming the novel for being like this. Like I said, to me, it just hasn't aged very well. I find it very hard to find the same amount of enjoyment here than I do, for example, in a Brandon Sanderson or Joe Abercrombie novel. It's also not that I only read and enjoy modern stuff. I had fun reading Lovecraft and Robert E. Howard stories in the past. Tolkien just seemed to be obsessed with building his world and wanting to show the reader every nook and cranny of it. And to me, it just detracts from the sense of excitement and adventure that I want from a story.

This book does something I very much dislike: it describes the environment way way too much. About a third of the book is describing the terrain, the trees, what is north and what is to the west, to the south, and how the road slopes down and to the right ahead and the rocks and trees and more trees and the night sky with stars and without and the cool breeze and cold air. It's constant.

Maybe a fourth of the book is names of lands, towns, rivers, people, people of older times. We can do away with most of this part if the book, but I get that this story has a ton of depth and you do kinda need to know some of the history of people like Isildur, and some of the main terrains and locations like Mordor and Moria amd Rivendell. Thankfully, the map of middle-earth is in the book. But so many names of people throughout. The Council of Elrond chapter starts with Elrond talking about people from the past for maybe 6 long pages, and I had zero clue who these people were and no idea how they fit into the main storyline, and then someone else talked for many pages, and what they talked about actually fit with the story, so no idea why Elrond's part was in the book at all.

The prologue was mostly not needed; again just unnecessary detail. As I read it, I had no idea what I was reading until the part that summarized The Hobbit book.

I was fifteen when The Fellowship of the Ring was forced upon me by the educational system, a well-meaning but ultimately sadistic act of literary cruelty. Our teacher called it “an epic journey of courage and friendship.” What it actually was, was a 480-page endurance test featuring ten blokes and a ring that refuses to mind its own business.

The plot, as far as I could tell through the fog of adolescent despair, was this: a nervous little man inherits a piece of evil jewelry, a wizard with commitment issues tells him to get rid of it, and off they go on the slowest road trip in English Literature.

Now, I like adventure. I like swords, danger, moral ambiguity, all that good stuff. But Tolkien’s version of adventure is like watching someone assemble IKEA furniture while narrating the entire process in Elvish. Every time something exciting threatens to happen, he pauses to describe a leaf, or an ancient poem, or the genealogy of a tree that died in the Second Age.

Half my class didn’t make it. We lost them somewhere around Tom Bombadil; a singing nature sprite in yellow boots who, to this day, remains the single most inexplicable literary decision ever made by a sober adult. I remember thinking, if this is Middle-earth’s idea of fun, I’ll stay in the Shire and take my chances with gout.

And the names! Every rock, river, and puddle has six. Everyone speaks in riddles or riddled poetry. It’s as if Tolkien looked at the concept of pacing and said, “No, that sounds far too modern.”

Reading it at fifteen, I felt like I was being punished for something I hadn’t done. As an adult, I can at least admire the sheer lunacy of Tolkien’s ambition; he didn’t write a story, he built an entire religion with footnotes. Respect where it’s due. But teenage me didn’t want to be awed by the scope of creation; I just wanted something to bloody happen.

By the time the fellowship actually left Rivendell, I’d emotionally checked out and was rooting for the Ring.

Another two stars for Mr Tolkien; one star for inventing orcs (relatable, frankly), and one for the comforting knowledge that I’d never have to write another fucking essay about Frodo’s “journey of inner transformation.”

In the first eleven chapters I have no idea who Frodo, Merry, Sam, Gandalf, Strider, or Fatty Bulger really is other than people moving from A to B because of X. “La compagnia dell’anello” di J.R.R. Tolkien pag. 670

Direi che è difficile scrivere questa recensione è dire poco…partiamo dal presupposto che avrò fatto almeno 5 tentativi di lettura della trilogia, tutti abbandonati dopo poche centinaia di pagine, e nemmeno il film mi ha aiutato visto che immancabilmente mi addormento.
Questo tentativo è stato portato a termine, almeno per il primo volume della trilogia, ma non è stato per nulla facile.
Penso che la trama sia nota e arcinota…il caro Hobbit Frodo viene in possesso dell’Unico Anello lasciato dallo zio Bilbo Baggins e su consiglio di Gandalf il mago intraprende un viaggio per buttare l’anello nel monte Fato e liberarsene una volta per tutte. Insieme ai fedeli Sam e Pippin si mette in viaggio e lungo il percorso incontrano Aragorn che li porterà in salvo presso gli elfi. A quel punto alla compagnia si uniscono l’elfo Legolas e il nano Gimli, oltre ovviamente ad Aragorn e Gandalf che li ha raggiunti presso il regno degli elfi.
Mi rendo conto che Tolkien è considerato uno dei grandi della letteratura fantasy, ma io proprio non riesco a digerirlo.
Pagine su pagine su pagine per raccontare un viaggio che è talmente lungo e dettagliato da rendersi noioso al punto che si perdono un po’ i temi che in realtà vengono trattati nel libro come la battaglia tra Bene e Male, la speranza, il concetto di salvezza e sacrificio attraverso la morte.
Viene ovviamente toccato il tema del viaggio che in questo romanzo di Tolkien è di carattere misterioso perché, anche se i membri della Compagnia dell’Anello sono apparentemente spinti dal compito di proteggere Frodo e di distruggere l’Anello, viaggiano anche attraverso impulsi e desideri interiori.
Nel corso della narrazione è relativamente frequente imbattersi in canti e poesie che conferiscono maggiore solennità ma che personalmente hanno ulteriormente rallentato la lettura.
Tolkien non si è limitato a creare una storia fantasy, ma ha abbondato nei dettagli e particolari dando vita ad una vera e propria mitologia della Terra di Mezzo con linguaggi finalizzati a descrivere le caratteristiche dei personaggi che la popolano.

I began The Fellowship of the Ring (1954) back in July, and have read it in bursts since then (it's early February as I write this). It took me a very long while, but I've been putting off reading this book since I received the series years ago for Christmas, and so I knew that - if I wished to finally read these books - I needed to allow myself a lot of time to finally make my way through the series. Clearly, I didn't rush. I read a group of chapters every few weeks - or months - until I finally reached the end tonight.

And so I can now say I've read The Fellowship of the Ring, and am now one third of the way through The Lord of the Rings.

It may appear as though I hated the book, as I took so long to get through it. While that's not the case, I did have some very big issues with it, which in no way quickened my pace.

I won't bother getting into the plot since it's so well-known. Just know that the villain is after a powerful, magical ring, and our main characters are in possession of it, and must journey to the ends of the earth to destroy it. I will have some spoilers below, so watch out, if you do not already know the plot of Tolkien's acclaimed series.

My biggest issue with this book is its story. Tolkien has devised a plot I am entirely unattached to. The tale this book holds consist of one long journey, with a few stops along the way, which are actually less interesting than the endless walking that makes up the journeying.

The book reads like a movie montage. They go through forests, cross rivers, pass over mountains, go through tunnels that run through those mountains, etc. Tolkien includes sporadic exchanges of dialogue between the characters; and sometimes these are interesting, but sometimes they are only long paragraphs detailing the upcoming leg of the journey, such as how they will cross the river, or get around the mountain, or find their way into the tunnel.

Occasionally characters will receive a bit of development in the form of conversation or some action performed by them, but it is never very extreme, and for the most part the characters only have personality traits - and some don't even have these.

I am referring to Frodo, the unlikely hero of the story, who remains quite bland throughout the book. His struggles with the ring, which tempts him and gives off an appealing sense of evil, could have been engaging. But Tolkien doesn't mention them much - which is fine, as this only the first book in the series. There remain 1,000 pages for Tolkien to include some scenes of struggle between Frodo and the ring. But as it stands, at the end of Fellowship, there are only occasional moments of temptation. These few instances approach intrigue, but are never quite as weighty as they ought to be.

Instead of focusing on the characters' struggles and relationships - something I would have greatly enjoyed - Tolkien commits solely to moving the story along, and on the way does his best to mention hundreds of places and names. This forms one half of my problem with his writing: he loves to talk about the massive world he's created. I will not deny the creativity found in Middle-earth; it's amazing. But I can't focus on what I'm reading when I come across a section like this:
...The River flows in stony vales amid high moors, until at last after many leagues it comes to the tall island of the Tindrock, that we call Tol Brandir. There it casts its arms about the steep shores of the isle, and falls then with a great noise and smoke over the cataracts of Rauros down into the Nindalf, the Wetwang as it is called in your tongue. That is a wide region of sluggish fen where the stream becomes tortuous and much divided. There the Entwash flows in by many mouths from the Forest of Fangorn in the west. About that stream, on this side of the Great River, lies Rohan. On the further side are the bleak hills of the Emyn Muil. The wind blows from the East there, for they look out over the Dead Marshes and the Noman-lands to Cirith Gorgor and the black gates of Mordor."
This goes on. I understand his world is detailed and thought-out. But this is bad writing, in my opinion.

Now, my second problem with Tolkien's writing: it is, overall, not very good. His style is simple, which I usually like; I always enjoy writing that is clean, clear, and to-the-point. But his writing is rough at times, and not very smooth, and very plain. It would make the story more enjoyable if it were at least told by an engaging voice; unfortunately we're left with a bland one instead.

Many people criticize Tolkien for being too descriptive. I did not find that an issue. I do see how his writing could be taken as overly-descriptive. But I think what many people mistake as useless description is actually nothing more than a boring setting to place the story in. Yes, he describes a lot of trees - but that is because every location they arrive at is largely made up of trees. All writers describe the setting of the scene - except for some more "experimental" writers, of course - and Tolkien is no different: he is describing the area around the main characters. The areas just happens to be very similar and not very interesting, and so they appear as superfluous description.

The last problem I have with the book is the distance from which I felt I viewed the story. Because the scope of the story is so large, and the tale so epic and grand, everything felt very distant and blurry. We never get close to the characters. We never get in their heads. I know many epics are told in this grandiose way, but I do not like it. So while it may not be a flaw within the book, I would prefer to have been inside Frodo's head as he wrestled with the temptation of the ring - felt the fear the Company faced as they watched Gandalf die. The "montage" feel of the book got in the way of that.

There were a few moments when I felt like this could be something good, times when I stopped counting the pages. This happened when the characters stopped walking long enough to engage one another, and not to merely plan out their route, but to actually talk. When there was actually conflict between the Company, and not just talks of past battles from hundreds of years ago.

I see the appeal of books like these. You can get lost in the world if you want to. Tolkien's set it up to be lived in, and the door's open if you're willing. I just don't like epics like this, where world-building is placed over story and character development.

And so, after reading handfuls of chapters every couple of weeks over the course of the past six months, I have finished The Fellowship of the Ring. I'll probably read the rest, after I've gathered up some energy for the task. The only way I'll finish the series is if I keep up my snail's pace, reading many other books during the process.

One of the rare occasions in which the book is worse than the movie. Please do not attempt to read this book. In my head Tolkien is like a narcissist who is so obsessed with his own creative genius and whimsy that he simply rambles about things no one else has ever heard of or read about before, as if he can't fathom the idea that anyone would dislike FOUR HUNDRED pages of incessant and overly descriptive depictions of his imagined world, making it impossibly frustrating to get through. Not to mention the fact that LITERALLY NOTHING EVEN HAPPENS. I at least expected Frodo to get to Mordor and Mount Doom and make a little progress toward destroying the Ring, but ALAS, NO. Why did I even invest so much time and energy into this book??? I assumed there would be some payoff at the end but it was just a lousy cliffhanger. I guess that's probably why people read his other books, but honestly I don't think I could survive another Tolkien. This actually took so much life out of me and I kept waiting for something good but it never came. I struggled through 400 pages of this tale and still can't even tell you more than 2 things about each of the supporting characters or the landscape of Middle-Earth (I think that's what it's called) because Tolkien uses such inaccessible and incomprehensible descriptions of mythological places and people that just build off one another until a sentence or paragraph is utterly unreadable. I'm not even making any sense in this review because it's so hard to explain how badly this book was put together. There are just so many internal references to things that Tolkien made up that it's nearly impossible to understand what's going on unless one has a complete knowledge of Tolkien lore and all his vast ideas, which I clearly don't.

Gets two stars because I guess I liked some parts of the story, like the times in Bree and Lothlorien, and some of the characters were fun, but I definitely regret reading this book as I put a lot into it and got very little in return.

Just Watch The Movies (Part I)

I first watched the movies years ago when they came out. I thought they were great. So I tried not to let my like influence this reading, but it was hard.

The movies really do seem to take the best parts of this book and string them together in a cohesive story. So many of the characters missing from the movie were extraneous. So too was some of the adventuring. In some ways, it felt like Tolkien created a wonderfully elaborate world and then insisted on using every part of it.

This is most evident in the first book with the hobbits enter the woods just after leaving the Shire. Watching them wander aimlessly, only to be rescued by Tom Bombodile seemed pointless. So too was the white barrows. Truly, what purpose did they hold other than to let them find treasure?

As such, this is very much one of my main problems with the book (from a literary perspective). Most of the first book (and much of the second) are a series of happy circumstances by which Frodo (and the fellowship) come to rest at the tables of others by chance. It’s annoyingly repetitive and shows little character growth. So much so that it reminds me of a story my cousin tried to write (for school) in middle school. Only half way through the second book do we actually get some character development.

My other general dislike of the story is the extreme world building. I recall others complaining about this before, and in truth, it’s why I picked up (and then quickly put down) the Hobbit years ago. The long lineages and the ancestral existence of all the places is great (and thankfully Token didn’t create a catchphrase for “but it was different long ago”), but there are ways of incorporating or referencing these things without making us read the Bible.

Overall worth the read due to notoriety, but I’m not sure I’ll ever read them again… after spending $20-30 to own them in audible form.

2.5/5 stars

As a fantasy fan, it pains me to leave an average/poor review of a classic like “The Fellowship of the Ring” but as someone who tries to remain objective, I had to despite what I thought the book would be in my head.

Positives:

- Sam and Bill the pony, my beloved
- Gandalf (probably my favorite character in the book. I understand the intrigue surrounding him, and Tolkien conveys his personality incredibly well)
- The meandering feel that reminds me of travel writing
- The first chapter of Bilbo’s birthday party. It was very fun, and I think Bilbo is also one of my favorite characters
- This is THE book that jumpstarted fantasy as I know and love
- Gollum is one of the nastiest creatures I’ve ever read about, and I think it’s quite incredible how that feeling of inherent disgust is conveyed through the page
- It’s really fun to talk about the series with other fans

Negatives:

- Interesting worldbuilding is dumped on the reader in a way that’s hard to follow. I legitimately am going to sit down and watch a YouTube video explaining it all soon after I write this. I can’t tell whether the worldbuilding in this series is actually this hard to follow or if I’m just daft. Either way, it affects my outlook on the book, making it hard for me to understand the relevance of some plot points and characters. Since the world is quite sprawling, it’s hard to get a grasp on anything which makes the narrative feel substantial
- Plotting is slow, and characters are often conveniently saved in ways that begin to feel tiring
- Frodo is a fairly weak character in terms of characterization and development. Some of the others also feel weaker. The characterization I was hoping for in most of the characters just isn’t quite there

I’m planning on continuing with the series, as I do think it’s a must read for fantasy fans and I’ve heard it picks up in the next book. Hopefully some additional context and research will help my reading experience moving forward

The first book of the legendary, Lord of the Rings. This series has been on my mental "to-read" list for years. And overall, the book was very, meh.

The first third/half of the book is exceptionally slow and cumbersome. For lack of a better description, there's a lot of backstory and dialogue that is completely off-track from the story at large. Did you know the second cousins of the BlahblahBaggins family are the Hehogginses? No? That's right, because it doesn't matter! And it's not just one sentence here and there, but entire paragraphs and pages of useless information. This makes digging into the book a real burden. You really need to self-motivate yourself to continue reading. Your skim reading skills will be tested. And all that to say, when you get to second half, things don't entirely pick up all that much more than the first half. But there are some particularly exciting moments, arriving in Rivendell, trudging through the mines under the Mountains of Mist. These chapters stand out as particularly good.

The other major negative to this book is the dialogue. Somehow Tolkien has managed to make all the characters sounds exactly the same, with the exception of Sam. If I read you a passage from somewhere in the book and removed character names, I bet it wouldn't be obvious which character was speaking in that given moment. The result of this is that all the characters sound phony. And this creates a lack of attachment to any of the main characters.

This book operates in my headspace as a work of historical fantasy. Reading this through the lens of "this is the origin point of modern fantasy" is where the value is. Because let's be honest, Tolkien is an awesome world builder, but not a great writer. The Fellowship of the Ring makes this dichotomy readily apparent.

The writing is pretty, for sure. Everything else is fine.

That's how I found myself feeling for most of this book: fine. There are no "wow" moments, no excitement, no anything to keep a reader entertained. It's mostly a strange collection of bland characters walking around.

The characters in this book were the most underwhelming part. There is not a single personality between all of them. At least, not that I could find. Maybe it's the language, maybe it's the fact that this was written 80 years ago, or maybe it's just not for me. Either way, none of the characters made a significant impact on me. I didn't connect with a single one, and I wouldn't even say I liked any of them, besides maybe Aragorn. Frodo is irritating, Gandalf is also irritating, Aragorn and Boromir are bland, Merry and Pippin are the same person, Sam is infuriating, and the others hardly even exist. Also, where are all the women? I know, written in 1945 and all that bullshit, but come on! Two women, Arwen and Galadriel. Arwen doesn't speak, and Galadriel says nothing helpful, only talking about how powerful she is and how she can't take the ring because she would be too magnificent, and everyone would fall to their knees before her. OK.

The plot, just as lackluster. There is a vague notion of a storyline, but most of the time spent in this book is the characters travelling. From the Shire to Rivendell, from Rivendell to Moria, from Moria to Lorien, from Lorien to Gondor. Please stop. Please. I know everyone says that this book is just the set-up for the next two books, but there was no need for so many pages. It was completely unnecessary.

This book gets 2 stars, 1 of which is only because the world building is very impressive, to the point where it is difficult to keep everyone and everything straight because everything has five names. 1 star for the enjoyment.

It's not a bad book but it's really not my genre/style. First of all, from after Frodo left the Shire to ~40% of the book, not much happens. Frodo is just walking around with his mates if I'm being honest. All the scenic description with no major plot progression really wore me down. And from when Frodo met Strider, was injured, woke up and was reunited with Gandalf and Bilbo, etc., the plot does pick up its pace and things happen. However, the focus is purely external, not internal. It's all about quest, battles and journeys, and of course landscape and mythology, with very little character-building. The lack of emotional arcs, relationships, internal growth and character depth meant that I felt zero empathy for or connection with the characters, and so their danger, loss and heroism felt abstract and empty. Tolkien's style is very different from what I'm used to - this is a genre-defining mythic legend, not a character-driven modern story, and half way through I just started rapidly skimming because I completely stopped caring.

I am not much of a high fantasy person (I think). I cannot recall if I have ever read a similar novel. You can't go wrong with Lord of the Rings being your introduction to fantasy in any case. I somehow managed to avoid learning about the characters and plot in my 20 years on Earth, so experiencing everything for the first time was a blessing. 

This book was world building info dumps, travel sequences, and character monologues held together by the power of friendship and good vibes. I realized I am not built to read books where half the time is spent reaching a destination only for there to be a new one.

That being said, I didn't *not* enjoy it. The characters truly are the heart of the novel (the ones whose names I remember at least). I adore Sam, he is the sweetest, and he deserves every happiness. I am still salty he got separated from Bill (is that considered a spoiler?)

We will see if my opinion improves after watching the movie for the first time. As of right now, I am hoping the later books involve less travel. I want there to be more plot, but maybe traveling is just the plot of adventure novels? I am not exactly an expert on the subject.

On the bright side, I now know new words to describe marshes, hills, and streams. They will totally be integrated into my vernacular. Totally.

Me da pena admitir que dejé de leer este libro cuando llegué al final del “Libro 1” dentro de la primera parte de la trilogía, y que desde entonces no lo he vuelto a tomar. Cada vez que pienso en retomarlo, me invade una sensación de flojera y evitación. Después de semanas pensándolo, me di cuenta de que no quiero seguir leyendo este libro.

Es innegable la enorme influencia que esta trilogía ha tenido en la literatura, y la experticia de Tolkien en lingüística y mitología emana fuertemente en esta novela, además de que es admirable que haya podido crear un mundo tan rico y complejo. Sin embargo, el libro es sumamente lento, y lo único que narra, al menos hasta la parte donde yo llegué, es cómo los personajes van avanzando por distintas partes, tratando de llegar a un sitio. Pero siento que falla en generar interés, tanto por el mundo como por lo que está sucediendo.

Sé a dónde va la historia porque me la han spoileado, pero si no me lo hubieran spoileado, todavía no sabría de qué se trata el libro, o qué están haciendo los personajes y por qué. Incluso, creo que si no me hubiesen spoileado la historia, habría dejado este libro mucho antes. Intenté tener paciencia con esta lectura porque siempre se lo ha clasificado como un “must read” para los amantes de la fantasía, pero no puedo luchar contra lo que realmente siento al leer este libro: Aburrimiento. Me aburre la narración sin una dirección clara, y personajes que, si bien tienen sus características, siento bastante planos al menos hasta la parte donde leí el libro.

Debo decir que El Hobbit es un libro que sí disfruté, por lo que estoy segura de que Tolkien creó una historia fantástica. Simplemente, el delivery, para mí, es insufrible.

Con algo de decepción, decido dejar esta obra de lado, para darle lugar a otras obras de fantasía que tengo en mi backlog de lecturas pendientes.

Останах доста разочарован. Имах високи очаквания, имайки предвид, че повечето книги в този жанр се сравняват с Властелина и никога сравнението не е в тяхна полза. Книгата ми беше скучна и единствено успяваше да ме приспива. Историята има огромен потенциал, но в тази книга не се случи нищо. Дано това е просто въведение и интересното да е оставено за следващите книги (силно се надявам). По-голямата част от книгата представлява описание на пейзажи, метеорологични условия, както и инструкции за навигация. Непрекъснато се повтаря следния шаблон: "Слънцето изгряваше от изток, времето беше ясно (или пък беше облачно и мъгливо), поеха на юг, вървяха 20 мили, спряха да хапнат, продължиха, завиха наляво, после надясно. Слънцето вече залязваше на запад, спряха да починат през нощта (в някои случаи продължаваха и нощем). Пътят ми до офиса в задръстване е по-интересен и по-разнообразен. Останалата част от книгата е песни, които лично за мен бяха доста дразнещи и към края ги пропусках, за да се свърши по-бързо с тая мъка. Цялата работа с родствените връзки и хилядите имена, които на всичкото отгоре си приличат, също ме напрягаше. Най-вече защото повечето имена просто се споменават и не се казва нищо за тях. Светът, който развива Толкин, е огромен, Средната земя има хилядолетна история и тези хора, очевидно играят някаква роля. Но в случая, самото им споменаване не допринася с нищо. И за съжаление, не са само родствените връзки. За всяко нещо бяха давани куп детайли и все излишни и с нищо недопринасящи за историята. Както казах, историята има огромен потенциал, просто не ми хареса начина, по който е разказана.
Иначе пък, по книгата се е получил доста добър филм. Всъщност за първи път филм ми харесва повече от книгата, по която е направен.

Three reasons to read The Fellowship of the Ring:

1) I very much love the optimism and the pure belief in the strength of being good that the main characters possess.

2) There are a lot of great quotes you might find if you're willing to sift through the not so great ones.

3) I do love books that reference prequels.

Six drawbacks to The Fellowship of the Ring:

1) The worldbuilding is extensive, detailed, and impressive, but it fails to add depth. Description and backstory are essential elements of fiction. They are not decorative; they must serve a purpose in the narrative to expand upon the story's message, in this case, that unchecked desire, even if it seems harmless, leads to evil.

2) Tolkien wanted so badly to be a historian for this made-up world that he forgot he was supposed to be, first and foremost, a storyteller. A storyteller knows better than to burden readers with too many names, especially similar-sounding ones, and historical details that have no bearing on the story. A storyteller knows that less is more.

3) Sauron's quest for absolute power makes him an incredibly dull, one-dimensional villain. The story's black and white nature removes any possibility of depth from the moral argument.

4) I do not like Tolkien's style of writing. I find it heavy and dispassionate.

5) The simplest task requires paragraphs upon paragraphs of thought, debate, and the odd history lesson. The obstacles become repetitive. Characters are frequently saved from disaster because they have a "bad feeling". And vital information is often withheld for a few pages for no reason other than a poor attempt at creating suspense.

6) I have little patience for media that has so few female characters.

I was a bit surprised with my thoughts on this book. I love fantasy, and was expecting to eat this story up. Before reading The Fellowhip I read the Hobbit, and I honestly ended up liking the Hobbit more. Maybe because the Hobbit felt more like a long bedtime story, and this one felt like a 400 page prologue.

The main character in The Fellowship, Frodo, doesn't have a lot of dimension for me. I can't think of any defining characteristics other than the fact he's the one with the ring. Tbh, the only characters out of the main 9 that have defining personal traits would be Sam & Gandalf. You get a little bit of personality from Dimli & Aragorn throughout, and then a good chunk of personality from Boromir, but not until the end. Merry, Pippin, and Legolas might as well be nonexistent as they don't really contribute to the plot at all. A lot of the book is focused on describing scenery, which don't get me wrong I love an author beautifully setting a scene, but after awhile there's only so many hills & streams & plains that I can imagine.

I saw one review that said you could zone out for a couple of pages and not really miss anything due to this, and I sadly have to agree. I really wanted to love this book - I even preemptively bought all the books in the series because I thought I'd love them. The pacing is what gets me and makes me not as excited to pick it up.

I will say the premise is great, and I am very intrigued by the story. The world building is phenomenal, and I can see why there is such a cultish following. I'm definitely going to start reading the next book and try to finish the entire series, but if it starts to pan out like this one I may give up. Overall not as thrilled as I thought I'd be.

I have a feeling this review is going to invite more disagreement than any other I've written.

The strange thing is, I don't actually have a solid reason for not enjoying this book.

I found Tolkien's writing fresh and surprisingly readable. I liked many of the characters. I didn't think the prose was as impossibly dense as people often claim. And yet, somewhere along the way, the magic and the sense of adventure that so many readers talk about just never reached me.

I kept trying to figure out why.

Maybe I just don't enjoy fantasy? That can't be it—I love *Harry Potter* and *A Song of Ice and Fire*. Maybe I wanted more political intrigue? But I've happily read children's fantasy with far simpler stories. Maybe I was bothered by unanswered questions or worldbuilding gaps? That doesn't feel fair either; I've only read *The Hobbit* and *The Fellowship of the Ring*, so I'm probably judging an unfinished story.

Every explanation I came up with fell apart.

That's what made this such an odd reading experience. On paper, it has so many things I normally enjoy. In practice, I never felt immersed. I admired the book more than I connected with it, and I found myself appreciating what Tolkien was doing rather than feeling caught up in it.

I'm fully aware that I'm in the minority here, and I almost wish I loved this as much as everyone else seems to. Maybe something will click when I continue the trilogy. But as a standalone reading experience, this simply didn't work for me—and sometimes, despite our best efforts, a book and a reader just fail to find each other.

That's why this ends up as a 2-star read for me. Not because I think it's a bad book, but because I never found the magic everyone else did.

Boring. Too many coincidental events. Too much magic just in the nick of time. I liked Harry Potter magic, but not this. Too many feasts where someone blabbed on forever about how his great-great-...-grandfather did such and such to so and so, blah blah blah, and nothing in the story had anything to do with anything else in the book. I just don't get it.

Too much inscrutable stuff like this:
"So it was that Frodo saw her whom few mortals had yet seen; Arwen, daughter of Elrond, in whom it was said that the likeness of Lúthien had come on earth again; and she was called Undómiel, for she was the Evenstar of her people. Long she had been in the land of her mother’s kin, in Lórien beyond the mountains, and was but lately returned to Rivendell to her father’s house. But her brothers, Elladan and Elrohir, were out upon errantry; for they ...."

Then there are too many things like: they were on the path and something bad happened but X saved them in the nick of time and they went to X's house and had a great feast and woke up refreshed and went back on the path and the trees started to swallow them and kill them but, just by luck, Tom B came by whistling and that stopped the tree deaths and they went to Tom's house and had a great feast and woke up the next morning refreshed and went back on the path ...

Or they were in a giant cave system, lost, then found a stairway with a zillion steps down, and Gandalf said to be sure to look for a left path for that will be East. Huh?

On and on.

I remember someone (Isaac Asimov?) said he had to read it 5 times before he liked it. I'd rather go to the dentist.

The movies were excellent, way better than this book.

2.5 rounded down.

The background information and the influx of characters was just SO overwhelming. I was genuinely so relieved to finish this book.

A few months ago, I decided to finally watch the Lord of the Rings movies. My family is obsessed with them and I wanted to see why they were so revered. To this day, I’m still not sure why they are. I gave up halfway through the first film out of sheer boredom. So I looked online and saw numerous people saying that the books were far better because they focused more on the folklore and fantasy that the films swapped out for ludicrous action sequences (Saruman spinning Gandalf on the floor still haunts me in my nightmares.)

In January, I decided to buddy read the entire Lord of the Rings with a small group of bookstagrammers. It has definitely proved tough, but we’re powering through! I think we would all agree with the general consensus that The Fellowship of the Ring was, simply put, boring.

While it can absolutely be agreed upon that The Fellowship of the Ring contains infinitely more folklore and fantasy than the films, the online reviewers didn’t necessarily say it would be interesting folklore and fantasy. A lot of the time it was hard to keep reading because there were pages upon pages of information I just didn’t care to read about. Still, it was more captivating than the films. I found that there was just a little too much detail about things that were irrelevant or that we would never hear about again. We learned so much about characters and, while I will always love solid character development, I thought that the development wasn’t particularly useful to the plot.

On another note, I can’t even guess how many songs there were in the first book alone. You couldn’t read three pages without encountering another one. I’m not ashamed to admit that I skipped most of the songs. Those were perhaps my least favourite aspect of the entire book.

Currently, we are working through The Two Towers. It’s proving to be better in terms of having more intriguing events than background knowledge of characters and places. Sadly, I think I would have DNF’d The Fellowship of the Ring had I not been buddy reading it with friends!

The second star is for being an inspiration for the Harry Potter series. The foundation of fantasy, or whatever.

Some faceless dark-lord-assistant-type thing attacks them, every once in a while.
One servant-type friend. Two other friends - whose names if interchanged and read, you wouldnt notice the difference (except that Merry knows to handle a boat). And a few others. They meet a few people on the road, who treat them kindly. Umm well, that's it. Oh yeah, and a few songs too... which I just can't make myself care about.
2. There are no emotions. Something happens, sun westers, river flows, golden larks cry, some guy who is the son of some other guy.. idk, sleeps. I feel so disconnected from the characters. I just can't care about them. The only time I saw emotion, is in the final chapter with Boromir.
3. There are so many places. Why?
4. Apart from very few situations, it's very linear. Maybe when Frodo suspects something, or Sam sees something - we have something to look forward to. Otherwise it's just boring narration, that once becomes past, no longer matters.
5. Not relatable. Obviously
6. Appreciate Lady Galadriel, and the other river-lady( though I didn't get her point). But where are all the other women??
7. Nobody has a personality. Aragorn's sort of nice. Everybody else is borrring..

Es tut mir leid! Es tut mir so leid!!! 😭

Ich hätte es doch gerne gemocht, aber das war wirklich mit Abstand das langweiligste Buch, das ich jemals gelesen habe. Die ersten 2/3 ca haben sich angefühlt wie ein Geschichtsbuch, nur mit weniger Jahreszahlen, dafür mit mehr Liedern und Gedichten. Es gab mehr Monologe als in jedem Shakespeare-Buch und das muss man erstmal schaffen!!!

Danach wurde es irgendwann etwas besser, aber leider immer noch nicht mega spannend.

Ein Punkt, der mich wirklich gestört hat, war der ständige Rassismus von allen Parteien in diesem Buch. Es wurde so oft was gesagt von wegen "Alle Ausländer sind dumm und komisch, gib dich bloß nicht mit denen ab" oder mein Highlight "Zwerge dürfen nur mit Augenbinde durch unser Land" Excuse me?? Geht's noch 😂 vielleicht sehe ich das ja zu kritisch, aber immer wenn das Wort "Ausländer" gefallen ist, und das war mir wirklich zu oft, wurde ich komplett aus der Story gerissen und in die Wirklichkeit geholt. Aber vielleicht liegt's ja auch einfach an der aktuellen Weltlage, dass mich das so massiv stört.

Zu guter Letzt habe ich noch eine Frage zur Übersetzung. Wie kommt man auf die Idee, "leader" (ich nehme an, dass das das englische Wort war) mit "Führer" zu übersetzen, bei einem Buch, was im 2. Weltkrieg geschrieben wurde!!! Gandalf und Aragorn sind doch keine Führer!! Nenns doch bitte wenigstens Anführer, ich kann nicht mehr :( Wahrscheinlich bin's nur ich, die diese Wortwahl schrecklich findet, aber das fand ich auch wirklich ne sehr spezielle Wahl...

Ich weiß nicht, ob ich die Reihe weiterlesen will. Wenn dann muss mir jemand sagen, dass der nächste Teil spannender wird.

I think this will be the most controversial take I have in my entire life. Ughhhhh. I seriously questioned about half way into this if I was even a fan of fantasy at all. But then I remembered that the Inheritance cycle is my favorite book series of all time. So that wasn’t it. So I thought maybe I just don’t like long books? But no, The Shining, IT, Inheritance, Dune, Don Quixote, and House of Leaves are all longer than this and I adore those books. Maybe it’s the story? Well, no. I consider the lord of the rings film trilogy to be up there with the original Star Wars trilogy as the best film saga of all time. So I guess that just leaves Tolkien. Ding ding ding. I HATE the way this guys writes. Why do we spend the first 25% of this story dicking around in the shire? Why do we take extended breaks to lore dump? Tolkien strikes me as a guy who can’t stand the idea of people interpreting or theorizing about his text so he just crams in every little bit of info he can. We get it. You spend too long building this world so you have to tell us every single detail about it even if it doesn’t matter. The tone also does not work at all. It feels like nothing matters in this book. Every other chapter is dedicated to people standing around talking about how dangerous the journey will be ahead and then it’s the tamest shit. Gandalf dies and nobody seems to care? They’re all like well he’s gone let’s keep going. I was going to try to go through the next two of these but I just don’t have it in me. Maybe in a few years I’ll try again once I’ve read a couple more fantasy series and I can really appreciate the influence. Idk. I’m gonna go reread slaughter house 5 as a pick-me-up 👋

Hace muchos años tuve un intento de leer la trilogía y fue un desastre. Llegué a los primeros capítulos del segundo libro y lo abandoné.
Que conste que amo las películas y le quería dar otro intento a la saga, porque como fan de la fantasía, hay ciertos libros que son un MUST de la vida.

Opté por la versión audiolibro porque ya había leído este libro, la historia la conocemos todos y tiene mucho relleno para mi gusto. De todas maneras no lo padecí tanto como cuando lo leí en formato físico. Sigue sin atraparme del todo la historia, lo sentí como un viaje eterno en la búsqueda la nada misma, y capaz es un poco demasiado honesto y brusco de mi parte, pero hay capítulos enteros que son innecesarios y no aportan absolutamente nada a la trama, o partes como las canciones, las descripciones en detalle de los paisajes y los diálogos con metáforas eternas.
Entiendo que la fantasía se escribía de forma distinta antes, que las historias se construían en base a un viaje en donde los personajes tenían una meta común y no era tan relevante el desarrollo de los personajes en forma individual, pero claramente no es lo que yo busco en un libro de fantasía. Siento que no hay desarrollo de la magia, que las cosas son y uno no se puede cuestionar ni cómo surgieron, ni cómo mutan, simplemente son así y se acepta. Conocemos muy poco de la historia de la mayoría de los personajes, como si la gracia es que todos coincidieran en el tiempo y el espacio para realizar una misión específica y el antes y el después fuera irrelevante, y el no poder conectar con los personajes afecta bastante mi opinión de la trama en general.

En conclusión: sigo desilusionada.

😴😴😴 I think everyone in my house must have felt the cosmic shift this morning when I FINALLY finished this book. I simply must see the movie to figure out how they make this exciting.

I've wanted to read these books for a long time, and they've been taunting me on my shelf, BUT, I was finally struck with the desire to pick it up (and was pushed into it by a coworker)....it was certainly a choice. It just felt like I was dragging through the mud trying to finish it. And I know people keep telling me the 2nd book is the best one, but I don't love media where I have to "get through" the first part to get to something good.

I understand that this is a classic to many, but this man does not know how to write conflict. Any threat of action is immediately squashed.

This all-powerful Gandolf doesn't seem to be all that. He literally said he had nearly been destroyed by blocking a door from orcs. Maybe they're more powerful than I'm imagining, but the descriptions aren't that vivid for me to know. I finally got to the infamous "You shall not pass" (actually "you cannot pass" in the book--- the movie did it better) and it was so anticlimactic that I kept reading on and had to do a double take back to make sure that was what I had just read.

I will eventually be watching the movie to compare (I imagine the movie is better, which is rare to say), but it might be a while until I read the next book. Because yes, despite my distaste, I need to see what happens next. I also, may I add, had NO idea how old these books were, so I am impressed with Tolkien creating this concept at that time and starting a movement with these works.

No me ha gustado. El libro desde mi punto de vista tiene dos grandes problemas: el ritmo y la acción.
El ritmo es muy lento y pausado, esto debido a la gran cantidad de descripciones que hace Tolkien. Esas descripciones, más allá de dar un buen ambiente estético al escrito, hace que este se torne pesado y aburrido. Este señor describe la mínima cosa que hay en el ambiente.

Otro punto negativo es la acción, y no me refiero a una pelea de espadachines o Goku vs Cell, cuando yo hablo de una buena dosis de acción en un libro siempre voy a “El nombre del viento” Donde siempre están pasando cosas importantes y la acción es ver a kovhe (espero este bien escrito) tocando o los diálogos que revelan secretos. Aquí carecemos de esos momentos y los pocos que tenemos llegan después de una parrafada innecesariamente larga.

Un punto positivo es prologo y yo diría que las primeas cien páginas son amenas y hasta disfrutables, pero una vez pasamos ese límite se hace difícil seguir. Esta novela esta dividida en dos libros, el libro uno por si solo sería un tres para mí, pero el segundo libro me tumba todo.

Es muy fácil, ¿te gusta la fantasía épica? ¿quieres estudiarla? ¿escribes fantasía épica? Pues léelo, es imprescindible. De lo contrario no lo recomiendo para nada. Si eres un casual y quieres leer un buen libro de fantasía lee a Martin, Sanderson o Rothfuss.

Nota: Se que se escribió en otra época y para otra gente, pero eso a mí no me va ni me viene. El libro es pesado y aburrido.

El Hobbit sin duda alguna fue de mis libros favoritos, me pareció una excelente introducción a esta saga. Por eso esperaba lo mismo de este nuevo libro, que a mi parecer se quedó demasiado corto.
Para comenzar, los primeros capítulos donde nos dieron un poco más de introducción sobre lo que pasó en el anterior libro, me encantaron, tuvieron la información justa para captar la atención. Después de eso el libro se fue volviendo más y más lento, hasta el punto que algunos capítulos me parecieron solo de relleno y sin ningún aporte real a la trama principal.
En el Hobbit me encantó el viaje y las aventuras que tuvo Bilbo, siempre fueron interesantes y mantuvieron mi atención. Ahora en este libro todo fue solo "camino" que si llegaban al río, que el bosque y demás... Nada interesante pasaba en ese viaje. Gandalf es uno de mis personajes favoritos y me hubiera gustado que tuviera más participación.
A pesar de todo esto, me sigue dejando asombrada la manera en que el autor conecta los tiempos y las fechas para que todos los acontecimientos encajen a la perfección. Como ya lo he mencionado me encantó ver al inicio a Bilbo para que pudiésemos entender mejor el giro que iba a tener la historia.
Este libro más que entretenido me pareció "informativo" por que aquí es donde verdaderamente se conoce el inicio de esta magnífica saga.
Se que en las siguientes entregas volveré a ver un poco más a Gandalf (es algo que espero con ansias).
Sin duda alguna este libro deja una gran apertura para el siguiente.

The LOTR is such a popular series and this is why I decided to read the books to see what the hype is about and form my opinion on it. Unfortunately, just like with The Hobbit, while the book does have some interesting moments, most of the book is incredibly dull and hard to get through. There's so many unmemorable characters it's hard to remember who is who, especially since I don't particularly care about any one other than Frodo, Bilbo and Sam.

The most interesting aspect of this book is the the One Ring itself and its effect it has on its bearer. Ofc, seeing these effects and the history of the ring is just a very small part of the book. Hardly anything interesting actually happens. It's all just a long and boring perilous journey to get from point A to point B with many stops and rests along the way. Particularly these rest stops are with the elves and honestly, despite being a fan of fantasy, I have never liked elves. Elves, dwarfs and orcs have always been a boring concept to me and LOTR doesn't make them any interesting at all whatsoever.

I will say though, that I have really come to like the relationship between Frodo and Sam. I can definitley see why people ship them. Sam's loyalty and love for Frodo is so adorable. He really knows Frodo well and that ending boat scene. Nice 👌

All in all, the book got more boring, imo, in its second half which isn't good at all since the series itself, again, I have found pretty darn boring.

Still, despite this, I do want to keep powering through just to say I read the series and see what ultimately occurs.

Somehow, for reasons I can't quite understand, this fantastical little adventure series has been elevated into the realm of "high literature" by many. I won't call this first in the trilogy, The Fellowship of the Ring, a masterpiece, nor will I concede that it bests The Hobbit's well-rounded, imaginative prose or compares at all to J.K. Rowling's Harry Potter for fun, adventure, or excitement. Fellowship is basically a pleasant fantasy adventure, strong in story, well-shaded, and colorfully written. Several patches of the book do well to stir the imagination. But it's got problems.

Tolkien has a terrible compulsion to get sucked into meaningless tangents. The songs, a controversial element, are the least of the book's troubles. More frustrating are the endless pages dedicated to planning the march to Mordor; deciding who goes where, with whom, by what method, into what territory, and why. And once the Company does get moving, you must prepare for an onslaught of granular landscape description. Tolkien gets so specific with the dozens of valleys which overlook dales seated opposite paths that bend to the east beside streams running down from mountains that it becomes an exasperating ordeal to properly picture his Middle Earth.

I have loved The Hobbit since I was a kid. I love the simple whimsy of that self-contained fantasy story. The Fellowship of the Ring has the DNA of The Hobbit, which occasionally shines through in its best moments, but it is littered with winding paths that do nothing but crowd and diminish the story's power.

I expected more from such a foundational piece of literature. Of this 400 page tome, I found myself engaged for maybe 60 pages in total. Tolkiens autistic world-building obsession dominates the narrative, and as an autistic world-builder I can appreciate the detail however detail does not create depth. Instead, any pacing and flow of the story is drowned in a dozen poorly executed songs and a hundred Proper Nouns™️ that remind me of reading the Jacob-begat-Judah portions of the Bible yet significantly longer. There is very little actual plot happening in the book, much of it is expository dialogue about what happened in the past. Characters are thin, poorly fleshed out archetypes that act more as personifications of the social order than actual people. The hobbits are presented as a fetishization of the rural countryman whose “natural innocence” shields them from evil, the dwarves as haughty bourgeois urbanites obsessed with coin and honor, and humanity is shown to be prideful, violent, and eminently corruptible with the only exception being a nobleman of “respected and ancient bloodlines”. I could go on all day about the elves.

It’s a shame because I can see the diamonds in the rough. The sections in Moria and the confrontation of the threats within is one the best sequences I’ve read in fantasy, but it feels almost like a different book entirely when taken in full. I promised myself I would read the whole trilogy, I only hope the next ones aren’t as slow and meandering and that some personality gets injected into the characters.

I have never met a person who said that these books are enjoyable. They’ve always said that they are tough, hard, descriptive, etc. Did other people’s opinions taint my experience? Not necessarily, I mean, I was prepared but I’m able to formulate my own opinions, thank you. Having read Game of Thrones and liked them, I had hopes for this. Not high ones, but hopes. Passed the birthday party, I was really liking the first hundred pages. I loved reading about the ring, the backstory, about Smeagol. I’m already obsessed with Ringwraiths so I had that going for me but beyond those subject matters I found these 500 pages to be very boring. I know that there are people out there who aren’t so I just have to reinstate that I’m the type of person to read every word out of respect to the author and I couldn’t believe I read every word describing the birds and trees and grass. Also, pretty much nothing happened in this book so that’s great. I will be rewatching the extended edition of what I just read because it’s amazing and I’ll be taking a significant break before reading two towers.
Now that my rage writing is out of my system, I can say that it is without a doubt that the plot of this story is fantastic. How quickly evil can taint the hearts of lesser and greater men alike. The intention to do good being disguised by evil. The least assuming person having the ability to carry such weight. It’s beautiful. Just about 200 pages too long.
