…I admit it is blasphemy, but I prefer the movies.

Growing up seeing the journey unfold on the big screen, I became a large LOTR fan. Planning my upcoming honeymoon to NZ to see filming locations, I decided it was about time to read the book. I hoped for the excitement of the movie, obtaining more depth for my favorite parts. I knew to expect differences, more characters, and a longer plot, but my blasphemy is how bored I became.
I persisted because I felt it was important to know the core story; and I was shocked at how long it all took. The real amount of lag within the journey; the years after Bilbo’s party, the months at Rivendell, it was all just so drawn out. I felt this took away from the immediate danger of the One Ring.

I do not think I disliked the writing. I saw the value in the amazing world Tolkien created. I realized, for its time, the pages and pages of descriptions were gorgeous to those needing a new world of imagination. The endless discussions, created a classic. But going backwards, there was a magic lost. The extra parts were gladly removed to pace the story better, and the songs went on and on. I even found some of the mythology harder to follow as it was drowned in setting. It’s apparent how much time and love it took to create this world, so I’m intrigued if the next novels quicken in pace and story since all the fantasy is laid out.

I have to be honest, I was really disappointed by this book. I brought this book because it’s one of the most popular fantasy book series out there. I had very high expectations because I read “the hobbit” and really enjoyed it, I liked the writing style, characters, and the plot. It was really interesting. But I’m not here to talk about “the hobbit” am I?

The only reason I didn’t enjoy this as much as I should have is because it didn’t have much of a plot. The story started off with a bang, all that stuff that happened with bilbo and him disappearing in the party, it really got a hold of me and pulled me into the story. But the further in I got to story I realized how it didn’t really have a plot, all Frodo ever did was travel, travel, travel. With occasional danger and the inn, but nothing other than that ever happened in the story.

Now, as I mentioned before, I really liked the writing style in “the hobbit”. But in this story, it was just too descriptive. Some of you might like really descriptive writing styles, but it’s just not my thing. There was a whole page of dialogue from this one character explaining some kind of history, and another whole page explaining Frodo’s surroundings, and it was really unnecessary and could have all been stuffed into one or two paragraphs. I don’t know how Tolkien made a whole book that was so descriptive and just about traveling, but props to him.

I'm sorry to say that I haven't completed this book, for reasons I will state below.

First of all, let me start of by saying that I don't think this book is bad. In fact, I liked many parts of it. But it isn't perfect either. Even though this was excellently written, and I could easily tell that Tolkien had a great passion for the story, there were a few problems that made me not want to finish it. I can already hear the fans gasp in terror at such words, and I understand why so many people love it so deeply. But to me, there were just way too many pages where not much happened at all. The hobbits would travel, they would find a place to eat, they would stay there for the night, they would continue their travel. They find another place to eat, and... it just goes on and on.
The characters too, didn't feel too special too me. I couldn't tell the difference between most of the hobbits, and those I could, were the ones I rarely read about. It made it hard for me to get fully invested in it.
I reached page 338, when I decided this was enough for me. To specify, that's about halfway through. And I feel ashamed for dropping the book so quickly, but I had just decided that it wasn't for me.

Let me repeat myself: I don't think this book is bad, but when reading, I had an increasing suspicion that Tolkien tried to drag this fight with Sauron out as long as possible. That notion threw me off a bit, as much as I wish it didn't. Now, if you'll excuse me, I need some sleep.

I can understand people who say they like The Lord Of The Rings.

I just don't agree with them. I didn't like it.
Why ?
Let me explain in this review.

Firstly, The plot.
I don't think that the story is bad, I found that plot great. I just hate the way it is told. It's very slow and not enjoyable for me.
There are a lot of passages where nothing happens, people are just talking all the way to say things that are not very interesting or important.

It's like the ironic point : ⸮
It's useless.

There are some good passages, though they are rare.

Like the ironic point.

Secondly, I don't like heroic fantasy,
and I think it's the main reason why i didn't like this book.

Trolls, Elves, dangerous worlds, swords, magic... It's a no for me.

They never attracted me. I can understand that people love this, but it's just not my cup of tea.

Some people will also say Tolkien created a rich universe, full of original creations.

I totally agree with them ⸮

Thirdly, The characters,
I don't think they are bad, but they aren't developped enough.
And some are badly introduced to the story.
So I didn't get attached to them. They were like the homeworks from school, I forgot them quickly.

In conclusion,
I don't like The Lord Of The Rings, but some people do.
But you have to read it to make your own opinion.

Will I read the next volumes ?

Surely ⸮

2.5 stars.

I'm torn giving it this rating, but I have to be honest with myself and I just didn't enjoy it that much. The story itself is excellent, but the writing is just too much for me. Also, I found that the characters had no distinct personality - literally any character could have been talking and there would be no giveaways except for the fact we are told who is speaking. The story didn't keep my attention, and many times I felt like I had to read it just to make progress so I can be done reading it.

But, as I say, the story behind all that criticism is very interesting. I feel disappointed it's masked in all the writing, but I do find myself interested to see where the story goes. I've seen the movies so I know where it goes, but the books often have more information or pieces left out in the movies.

As far as the characters, I haven't noticed any real development except that they are brave. They all sound the same and almost act the same except where there are limitations of their species. Because of that I don't have a favourite, or really care about any of them, rather I care that the quest is successful. If everyone dies along the way, meh.

I know this is a favourite for many people, but unfortunately it just didn't work well for me. I will likely read the sequels (I own them) but it won't be any time soon. Time to reward myself by watching the movie!

I really wanted to like this book. The Hobbit is one of my favorite books of all-time. During the pandemic I led a virtual reading club for my daughter and her friends where we studied The Hobbit in-depth. They loved it so much they begged me to do another one for The Lord of the Rings (which meant I had to read it) this coming summer. I’ve already agreed to this, which means I’m still going to have to analyze it, despite my general disappointment.

One of my issues with this book is that the reading level of this book is far above that of The Hobbit, which concerns me about whether my daughter and her friends will really be able to follow it. My other issue is how the book goes on and on with far less action and adventure than its predecessor.

Yes we meet lots of characters, but most are far less developed than anyone in The Hobbit. I had to keep reminding myself who Boromir was. Every time they mentioned him I’d be like “wait, who is he again?”

Having watched the movie trilogy, I recall that this book was the worst of the three. Both The Two Towers and Return of the King were far more engaging than the first movie. My hope is that is the same for these books.

I also hope that as I prepare for the reading group, my appreciation of this book will grow. If it does, maybe I can update this review.

I know I'll be in the minority when I say that I didn't enjoy this book. Part of that may be that it took me so long to read it. (I read for work; when I read for fun, I want to be entertained, and I'm very critical. If I'm going to read for fun frequently, the book has to drive me to pick it up.) But nothing about this story screamed "Read me!" after the first three or four chapters.

This book reads like a travel memoir, and while a few spots gave me a lovely, creepy tingle up and down my spine, for the most part, I was bored. I finished it so I could say I had read it. That's all. Reaching the end and discovering that I had read merely the first third of the story was discouraging. I have the next two parts of the trilogy in my library, along with The Hobbit, but I don't know whether I'll read them. I'm certainly not aching to dive into the next volume right away.

Lots of "fantasy" names and a plethora of characters make things tough to follow if you're not devouring large chunks of the story every day. I'm not a fan of multitudinous and complex maps at the back of the book—repeatedly having to flip and look at those decreases my enjoyment of the read. If I had put in the effort, perhaps some things would have made more sense to me.

Overall, this is a slow and cumbersome read, in my opinion.

To be completely honest, I did DNF this book

DNF, and I feel like I need to turn in my reader and nerd credibility for that fact. This book was a slog. I gave up around page 300 of my edition and they had JUST met Aragon.

Credit where it is due - Tolkien created an entire universe and told a single story there. Everything has lore. For example at one point, Tom Bombadil picked up a necklace and thought of its previous owner. I am willing to bet there is a long backstory to the necklace. There is more description than plot though, which feels self-indulgent.


The story moves glacially slow. I have seen the movies, so while I know the general plot is "group goes on a long walk to return jewelry," I also know that STUFF happens. Literally anything. The biggest plot development in my 300 pages were that some trees tripped the Hobbits and someone stole their ponies.

I feel bad about this review, but I think that LoTR suffers what I have named "The I Love Lucy" effect. I Love Lucy was an original and wacky sitcom, but its ideas were so popular that they were all co-opted and became tropes. Going back to watch reruns feels boring, because it has all been done (and better). Even though that was its originator.

In the same vein, LoTR may have been original when it was first published, but others have done better and more exciting spins on the concept, so the original just feels old and cliche.

To preface, I watched the movie 10+ times before reading the book. Despite it being my favorite movie of all time, The Fellowship of the Ring was a dull, slow tale that lacked the excitement and personality in the film.

Where do I start? The most obvious sign that Tolkien has no regard for his readers’ experience is in his random poems or songs. Sometimes taking up multiple pages, the poetry added nothing to the plot expect confusion and watering eyes.

The random descriptions were worse. Meaningless details of Frodo’s journey prevented any rhythm in the plot. Tolkien will describe a trail for like 200 words and then go into a lengthy description of some historical event surrounding the area in some distance age.

Here’s the bottom line: It takes almost 300 pages for them to get to the Mines of Moria. Beyond the previous observations, this slow unwinding of events is also due to boring chapters and excerpts. Why is Tom Bombadil in the story? He provides nothing. Why is there a three page song that Frodo sings at the Prancing Pony? The four hobbits should have reached Rivendell by page 150 at the latest. But no—Tolkien had a word count to hit apparently.

I was very disappointed. Don’t let Middle-Earth super fans trick you into thinking this book is literary genius. I promise, you’ll be fine just watching the movie.

I thought this was going to be the kind of book I loved. I mean, a book that's important in making fantasy, my favorite genre, what it is today? I'm sold.

And then I realized the book was utterly boring. I borrowed the e-book, and quickly (the only quick thing about this book) figured out that it would not work. So, I got the audiobook and slogged through it. And, by slogged, I do mean I started reading the book in July. I've finished 24 books since I started this one.

Anytime I started listening, I just suddenly felt so bored. While there is epic worldbuilding, I didn't get swept up in it like I thought I would. I was just, bored. The characters didn't feel interesting, and the storyline moved at a glacial speed. I know a lot of modern books move at a much faster pace, and while I can respect that older books are important, that doesn't mean I personally need to enjoy them.

And, yet, there is still a part of my nerdy heart that is so disappointed that I didn't like this book. I wanted so badly to fall into it and never want to leave, but that's not what happened. Even after disliking it most of the time and celebrating when I finally finished it, a part of me still wishes I loved it.

So, The Fellowship of the Ring was a disappointing read that has crushed my dreams of loving this series. Woohoo.

What can I say, it doesn’t pass the Bechdel test. Unless there is a conversation I am not recalling between Bilbo’s female relatives, but even then it would only pass on a technicality. The lack of female characters made it really hard to get through. Women only seemed to be consistently acknowledged when there needed to be a womb to propagate a family for more lore about generations of men. Or there needs to be a mystical and beautiful character like Goldberry. I suppose that Galadriel is the keeper of a ring which is significant, but I’m looking for redeemable scraps here.

Much of the excitement in the story comes from travelers covering great distances on foot without delving too much into their inner worlds, or revealing very much about the nature of the enemy. I loved the specificity of the map and the descriptions of the lands they travelled through. However I did get tired of the adjective grey. Grey clouds, grey mountains, grey dew, grey cloaks, grey grass, and there was even grey wind at one point.

The story did slowly build into a page turner, but it does still feel like a slog a lot of the time and I’m not sure if I will continue. There is just so much fantastic, diverse, and compelling fantasy out there that I don’t feel the need to complete this classic. But I did just check out the next one from the library so maybe I will continue!

2.0 ⭐️
slow, slow, slow. There are definitely great adventures to be had, but I feel like those moments of action were so vastly hidden beneath lore & worldbuilding. I wanted to love this more than I actually did. I respect The Fellowship of the Ring for what it is—a cornerstone of fantasy, deeply detailed, and obviously groundbreaking for its time—but reading it felt more like work than adventure for me.

Tolkien’s world-building is rich, no doubt. Middle-earth feels lived-in and layered, and the lore is unmatched. But there were so many moments where the pacing dragged under the weight of description, songs, and histories that felt like detours from the actual story. I kept waiting for the plot to pick up momentum, and it just… didn’t, at least not consistently.

The characters had their moments (I loved Sam, and Aragorn intrigued me), but many of them felt distant or overly formal. The emotional stakes didn’t hit me as hard as I’d hoped. And I know this is a controversial take, but I struggled with Frodo as a main character—he’s brave, sure, but also kind of flat at times.

That said, there is a quiet beauty in the writing, and I can absolutely see why so many people fall in love with it. But as a modern reader who enjoys a faster pace and more character-driven stories, this one didn’t quite sweep me away.

I appreciate it more than I enjoyed it. Solid foundation for a trilogy—but I’ll be honest, I’m hoping the next book moves faster.

I’ve read time and again that the Lord of the Rings Trilogy (which is actually not a trilogy, but one massive book published in 3 parts) has all kinds of allegorical content and contains a lot of stuff Peter Jackson had to leave out of the movies. Well, they’re certainly right about Mr Jackson leaving material out of the movie. I’m on page 160 (reading during my lunch breaks) and I’d have to say that roughly 90% of what I’ve read does not appear in any form in the movie. I’m about a little less than halfway through the first book (in the size they’ve printed) and the main characters JUST got to The Prancing Pony. I think this happens in the first 10 or so minutes in the movie. And what a great idea to cut all that chaff was!

I have absolutely no idea how the Lord of the Rings became such a revered book amongst the fantasy crowd. Tolkien appears not to have had an editor, or perhaps his editor was a pushover. If I were his editor I would certainly have made him remove the stupid chapter and a half about Tom Bombadil. This chapter does not further the story in any way and just leaves you with the same feeling as when you thought you’d be getting lucky to realize that your girl was only wearing the sexy panties because everything else is in the laundry basket. I kept reading thinking that Tom Bombadil would drop some bombs about some key part of the story or that the Black Riders would show up and tear his place apart and kill his wife. Oh, and the insufferable singing! It didn’t even make any sense! What’s with everyone speaking in the third person? Eric doesn’t like that.

And the hobbits are always breaking into song. One could be forgiven for thinking that Peter Jackson would have make Lord of the Rings the Musical. They sing songs about everything from travel, to hotels, to taking baths. And I’ve found out more about hobbit genealogy than I ever cared for.

Interestingly, the relationship between Frodo and Sam doesn’t seem to have the same sexual overtones that it does in the movie. And, I’m pretty sure Peter Jackson didn’t do that on purpose. It just came out so ridiculous that TBS had everyone almost literally rotfltao when they had a commercial for their broadcast of LoTR featuring clips of Frodo and Sam and the song “Secret Lovers”.

At any rate, this is mostly a rant about how slow-going this book is. Had it not had so many decades of reputation to rest upon, I would have probably returned the book to Borders and not even attempted to finish. Then again, I found the movies really boring, so perhaps the Lord of the Rings just isn’t for me. Ironically, I’m loving Terry Prachet’s Discworld series which is, partly, a parody of the Tolkien universe.

A few days ago I finished The Fellowship of the Rings. Things picked up in the second half of the book and they accelerated in the last quarter. I’m enjoying The Lord of the Rings a lot more now that Tolkien has gotten Tom Bombadil out of his system. In the Wikipedia article, even Tolkien seems to understand how much Tom annoys the crap out of people.

“Tom Bombadil is not an important person — to the narrative. I suppose he has some importance as a ‘comment.’ I mean, I do not really write like that: he is just an invention (who first appeared in The Oxford Magazine about 1933), and he represents something that I feel important, though I would not be prepared to analyse the feeling precisely. I would not, however, have left him in, if he did not have some kind of function.”

“And even in a mythical Age there must be some enigmas, as there always are. Tom Bombadil is one (intentionally).

Tolkien did go on to analyse the character’s role further:

“I might put it this way. The story is cast in terms of a good side, and a bad side, beauty against ruthless ugliness, tyranny against kingship, moderated freedom with consent against compulsion that has long lost any object save mere power, and so on; but both sides in some degree, conservative or destructive, want a measure of control. But if you have, as it were, taken ‘a vow of poverty’, renounced control, and take your delight in things for themselves without reference to yourself, watching, observing, and to some extent knowing, then the questions of the rights and wrongs of power and control might become utterly meaningless to you, and the means of power quite valueless…

“It is a natural pacifist view, which always arises in the mind when there is a war… the view of Rivendell seems to be that it is an excellent thing to have represented, but that there are in fact things with which it cannot cope; and upon which its existence nonetheless depends. Ultimately only the victory of the West will allow Bombadil to continue, or even to survive. Nothing would be left for him in the world of Sauron.”[3]


At any rate, what I like about the book over the movies in the last half to fourth of the book is that a few of the plot elements get explained a little more clearly. Sauron’s origins are explained a lot more clearly. Gandalf and others talk about how he came to power and why he’s just an “eye” now. Gollum is a lot more treacherous in the books. The characters know who he is and he menaces them a few times. I think this elevates his dangerous aura and prepares the reader for the fact that Smeagol has been following our protagonists. Finally, the elven queen Galadrial is given a much more cohesive treatment in the book. In the movie, from what I can remember, she just talks to Frodo in a dream. In the book, all of the characters leave the forest changed in some way because of her. Also, she gives everyone a special gift.

So, perhaps LoTR can be enjoyable….if you can get past Tom Bombadil…

I understand that J.R.R Tolkien was a British author, however, I was not used to the way how the British English write dialogues. Regardless, I did like some of the characters from the book since they made it amusing for me to read. Specifically, I genuinely enjoyed Gandalf and Pippin’s characters. All in all, I would rate this book a 2 out of 5. I recommend this book to those who can handle reading very descriptive paragraphs and those who enjoy fantasies and adventures together.

Sooo boring... and I've spent the better part of the last 18 months plodding through old "classic" literature from the 18th and 19th centuries. (Just before this I trudged wearily ALL the way through The Tenant of Wildfell Hall, for heaven's sake.)

I gave up on The Hobbit because it was so impossibly dull, and for some reason I thought this book would be better. Hahaha! I forced myself through this because I almost never DNF books, and I thought I couldn't possibly give up on two Tolkien books in a row.

His work is supposed to be so amazing, I thought maybe it just took awhile to get going... hah! I listened to the audiobook, and I checked the timestamp when the first interesting thing happened in the plot - I'd been listening for 7.5 HOURS! I excitedly thought perhaps the pace was about to pick up. But no, it was back to dreariness for much of the remaining TWELVE hours.

Obviously many of Tolkien's ideas and characters are quite interesting, and eventually even I became ever-so-mildly invested in the story of the ring, but the good bits were mostly buried in an avalanche of tedium.

To be honest, maybe I just don't understand the beauty of this book, but it was kind of just ok. Lord of the Rings is supposed to be the epitome of fantasy, like the classic, great medieval-style fantasy, and I was a little unimpressed.

This was only the first volume, but my main complaint is that it's long. So so long. And sometimes, that's great, but here it felt really boring in places. Like, the first hundred pages or so I took over 4 months to read because I could not get into it. Do we need every single detail about the travel? Probably not.

And while there's definitely some beautiful prose, including poems/songs and really quotable sentences, it was just buried beneath so much else. And, I suppose that it's the point, but the whole text reads like an idolization of heroism rather than a glimpse into reality. There's a clearly defined good and evil, and the characters discuss hope, persistence, and doing the right thing, but without any acknowledgment of how complicated these things actually were.

I'll probably continue onto the next volume, but I also feel that I won't be rushing to it.

~2 stars~

Finishing this book is one of my proudest accomplishments in life. I got a little $7.99 paperback from barnes and noble and never once fathomed how long this book would take me to read. Reading more than fifty pages at a time felt like an accomplishment.

I simply don’t understand why this book is considered to be so great. The worldbuilding is interesting, but I could have used a freaking glossary based on how many names I didn’t know.

There was a lot of deus ex machina. I would say 90% of the problems were solved by someone powerful showing up and saving Frodo & company. On that note, why on middleearth is Frodo (or any of the hobbits) on this quest? Maybe it was explained and I slept through that page, but it seems to me that based on the gravity of the situation, this should be an elite task force from Rivendell, not four random hobbits plus some helpful people.

Also, I’m literally Catholic but did not sense any Catholic philosophy in this book? I’ll probably watch some analysis video about that.

I might read the second book someday, but that day will not be in the next year.

As celebrated and influential as this has been, to get through what is one-third of a story proved to be a slog. Anything that takes almost a year of putting off continuing cannot be recommended.

The pace right from the off is slow, front loading lore, which one can easily skip but may feel guilty doing so. As the story actually starts, despite the intrigue and threat setting in fairly early, very little seems to happen beyond travelling and singing to a tune I can never grasp. A meme in itself, the constant walking offers very little beyond nice views that I have witnessed largely in person. This does create a longing to travel again but not for reading.

The saving grace comes when we hit cities. The social interactions of such and the effortless blending of the societies politics with the treatment of the fellowship offers a satisfying nuance that I did enjoy and seems to contain commentary on Conservative attempts to shelter oneself from the larger world. A bigger shame that one must hike through 100 pages to get this crumb of enjoyment alas.

In all, while an expansive story can enthral, there proves to be a reason why we do not dedicate 400 pages to act 1.

It took me a really long time to read this book, and it wasn't because I enjoyed it and didn't want it to end. I can see why people enjoy it! It's very detailed and the characters are sympathetic. The plot can be interesting. At times, I was really engaged - there was about a hundred pages that I flew through and found myself really enjoying. And seeing how elements of this book (which is beloved by some of my favorite writers) influenced them was really cool.

But I also found this really tedious. I feel like the details could really weigh the book down. Instead of making the world feel very rich and open, I found myself wondering if it was necessary to always show the world and dump all this info onto the readers. I wish that there would have been more happening - or felt the urgency of the events happening. Obviously, I have to acknowledge that this was written a while ago and the writing represents that. And I also appreciate how there was a lot of research and planning put into this. The execution just didn't work for me.

Proud of myself for finishing this, even if I won't continue this series! Maybe I'll finally watch the movies now.

I wish I could have given a high review of this book but I found myself struggling to carry on, it almost felt a chore which reading has never been like that for me.

I loved the movies, wanted to read a classic book and when I bought it I thought the Waterstones employee was going to jump for joy at hearing I’d never read it before “you’re going to love it so much”

Sadly I didn’t. I do have the other two books to read and feel they may be better due to the first one mainly being the journey part. However, I’m reading other books first because it simply didn’t grip me enough. I’ll go back to it though, one day.

I usually like detailed books, my imagination is very vivid but this felt almost too much of over explaining small details but again, I get that it was needed as Tolkien’s world is huge.

I will say, it was sometimes a struggle to read mainly because I would often fall asleep reading it, my boyfriend had to pry it from my grasp more times than I’d like to admit, you could judge this as being boring or that it was so soothing and calming I fell into a deep sleep within 4 pages, you decide.

I wish I loved LOTR. I thought I would when I began reading The Fellowship of the Ring, but after the first sixty pages my opinion shifted, and when I reached part two I decided to just quit.
The problem? It's just okay. Whilst I found the story absorbing initially, I found myself becoming more bored as I continued to read. There isn't much going on -- 220 pages of walking, eating, singing, black riders appearing, and then that cycle repeating.
The characters also weren't the most interesting. Gandalf was easily the coolest, but he isn't in it much and I thought Pippin and Merry were interchangeable with each other.
My biggest complaint? All the singing. I swear, every chapter had at least one paragraph of singing and the songs just get longer and longer as the book continues on. I hate Tom Bombadil. Can a book be considered a musical? If so, this is a musical.

I know Tolkien cared the most about world-building and his favourite part was creating all the different languages, and I can understand why some people love this but it isn't for me. Anyway, I'm glad I gave LOTR a shot, even if it wasn't my thing.

The world of Middle Earth is introduced in Tolkien's The Fellowship of the Ring, where young Frodo Baggins and a motley crew from the Shire are thrust into the world of elves and men, wizards and orcs, dark lords and the ever present temptation of The One Ring as they embark on their epic quest to destroy the last vestige of true evil left in the world.

I know, you're disappointed and shocked, mayhaps dismayed, by my rating but let me explain...Should Tolkien be credited as the veritable grandfather of fantasy? yes. Are some original fantasy concepts, such as Orcs and Mithril, still used in modern fantasy writing today? sure thing. Is Tolkien a good writer? not at all, especially when compared to modern writers of the genre such as Brandon Sanderson, Christopher Rowley or Sarah J Maas. The infamous writing style of Tolkien shines strong in the night in The Fellowship, where we had three or four pages worth of detail regarding the village of Bree. I found myself skimming through the vast descriptions of valleys and mountains which, while some may love that in order to really "build" the imagery, it's truly distracting and unnecessary.

I did not want to read this book but felt that it was a book that every fantasy reader should tackle. I had hoped that despite my hesitation, I would discover a new favorite, or at the very least, be satisfied with the read. The only satisfaction I received, however, was finally finishing it.

I’m sorry to say but this book was just boring. I feel like they did a whole lot of walking and nothing more. The world building was intense but it was delivered in a way that made it hard to decipher whether the characters were on some acid trip or truly experiencing certain events or environments.

I really really tried to love this. I wanted to at least like it but I feel like the content of this book could be summed up in about 10 pages. There was no great reveal or puzzle to be solved. The characters were shallow and I don’t ever want to see another exclamation point in dialogue again. All this book had was epic world building, which was so abundant that you end up walking away with none of it

I am willing to try the next book and see if my opinion is swayed but this series could be one of my first DNFs.

I'm sorry, but I really did not enjoy this book. I tried to like it because it is so widely acclaimed. Yet somehow it simply bored me. I don't find fault with the author or readers who love it. The issue is with me, not them. I found all of the Star Wars films unwatchable and always fell asleep during the interminable battle scenes, laser lights nowithstanding. We all know just how weird that sounds considering the great popularity of that series.

This book was the same kind of experience for me. I forced myself to finish it because I was sure I would change my opinion by the the end. Sadly, I did not. But I've done my duty now and don't feel an obligation to complete the Trilogy or suffer through the movies. Usually fantasy is not my genre, although I did read and enjoy all five of the Song of Ice and Fire books. I guess I cared more about the characters and connected with them.

Many people love this Trilogy, so I encourage others to give it a try. I did, and I'm glad because it is such an important cultural element. Now I know...

I do not think that this is a very good book, unfortunately. After not liking the films too much, I actually enjoyed 'The Hobbit' quite a lot. I thought the final third was a bit too ambitious for such a short book set in such an un-fleshed-out world, but it was well written and had lots of personality. However, I really struggled with The Fellowship of the Ring, and can't see myself jumping to The Two Towers and Return of the King too soon.

Here is a message I sent to my friend (big up Dipayan) while reading it, I think it sums it up.

"the characters don't have any personality like they do in the films"
"it's just a bunch of made up names of places and ppl and I'm like c'mon challenge me a bit"
"asoiaf is a million times better"

The actual 'fellowship' is essentially nine blunt instruments to explain the plot and the world around them, with no sense individuality or charisma. You often forget who's monologuing exposition, as everyone's dialect is identical. Sorry, but this just wasn't an enjoyable read at all.

This is not fantasy/adventure fiction, this is boring.

-Barely any character development
-On the back of the book it literally says “Frodo and Sam, with a small band of companions, to carry the Ring to the one place it can be destroyed” BUT IT TOOK 270+ PAGES FOR THEM TO REALIZE THAT THEY SHOULD DESTROY IT FIEJE YOURE TELLING ME THEY WERE JUST FROLICKING AROUND IN FORESTS NOT KNOWING WHAT TO DO WITH IT???!:&/&/&
-No romance
-No politics
-The writing is so boring literally most of it is just talking about the nature and the weather
-Plot doesn’t come in for almost 300 pages
-Pacing is TERRIBLE
-Action scenes are fast, descriptions are so long whyyyy
-How is this an “epic adventure?” Once again, b o r i n g

Sam, Aragorn, and Legolas are the only ones that deserve rights. If anything happened to them, then I would probably feel emotions JAJEN I didn’t even care when Gandalf died

Wouldn’t recommend, don’t think I’ll reread it. Skimmed through like the last 100+ pages bc it’s so b l a n d . Only reason why I’m continuing on with the series is for Dad.

I have some mixed feelings on this one. I definitely won’t be continuing the series anytime soon.

What I loved: The descriptions of nature. Honestly just listening to the way Tolkien would describe the chill in the air and the way the sun hangs low in the sky felt like food for the soul.

I appreciate the amount of effort Tolkien put into the world. It’s so rich and I can see why people love it so much. You could easily spend your whole life pouring over the pages and learning about Middle Earth.

The characters were fine. I understand that fantasy has evolved quite a bit since Tolkien and characters are often the focus of modern fantasy. And that’s just what I like and what I’m used to. I’m very much a character driven reader. If I don’t care for the characters I won’t care for the story.

The plot is very slow and meandering. And the action just seemed to be skipped over that I didn’t have a chance to know what was happening.

All in all, while I admire what Tolkien has done for the fantasy genre, I was pretty bored by this.

Title: The Fellowship of the Ring - the lord of the rings #1
Format: secondary source: physical book 2020 edition (paperback) + primary source: audiobook 2020 edition
Rating: 2.5 ✨
Reading dates: 15.02.2022 - 18.03.2022

Overall, the lord of the rings - fellowship of the ring is the typical fantasy adventure book. However, although there was some character development throughout all the characters I didn’t feel like I knew the characters? If that makes sense. So, a little bit of controversy with this one! I know I have rated it quiet low but there is a few reasons why. I found all of the singing and poetic elements that would take forever to pass rather annoying and pointless.

I understand it’s probably meant to be insight into who the characters are and how the come to be etc etc but honestly it felt more as though these times were used to fill time and space.

I did enjoy the last few chapters of the book due to their anticipation for the next and the beginning of the new adventure but I’m slightly concerned that this series may be one of my first DNFs 😓😅

Fingers crossed.

OK, so before you start hating me for not enjoying such a popular book, hear me out. I totally understand why people like this book. If you get into the lore of this book and relate to the characters and are the target audience then this book is wonderful. However, I just personally didn't have a good experience. I really dislike the writing style and that made the book unenjoyable. Also, this book has no characters I can even vaguely relate to, partially because it has about 2 female characters neither of which are central to the plot. There are 8 members of the Fellowship, why couldn't even just one of them be a woman? In addition, the lore in this book is SOOOOO complicated and is often explained in info dumps. I totally understand that if you hyper fixate on this text then its probably fascinating, but for your casual reader it's quite intense.
However, I am one reader who disagrees with the vast majority. This book isn't bad, it just doesn't have any features that make me as a reader feel any connection to this book.

Some books or movies don't sit right at a certain time in ones life. I can vividly remember pieces of art that I've come back to that I've hated and came back with context from others or myself that have transformed a work into one of my favourites. I hope that happens with Lord Of The Rings.

I loved Fellowship the movie and thought it would be fun to read the books before finishing the rest of the movies. Sadly I just couldn't love it.

I can appreciate the world building and impact these books have had and I can see the appeal but it's not for me at this point. I love fantasy and have spent hours reading lore of books and video games, probably the same amount of time it took me to read Fellowship or more. I like slow burn books. I really like the characters in LOTR.

Something isn't striking me with this book and I think I'm going to take a break from the series, go against my plan, and watch the movies first, which so far I've enjoyed.

I feel like a heretic putting down such a beloved work so while I'm here I thought the Godfather was MEH.

Had to audiobook this one (my first audio book!) and it was still a hard trek.

There were a few amazing scenes scattered in, but this was predominantly a book about a group of misfits going on a long walk together in the forest, occasionally pausing to tell long stories or sing long songs or argue about which way to go. Throw in some incredibly detailed descriptions of trees and rivers and rocks, and you’ve got The Fellowship of the Ring.

The scenes I did like were Aragorn’s entrance, the Mirror of Galadriel, Sam saying goodbye to his pony (heartbreaking!), and the final chapter (and not just because it was the last one haha).

Andy Serkis’s narration is perfect and was probably the only reason I managed to make it to the end. If you are going to embark on this journey, I highly recommend Serkis’s audiobook.

I do wonder what it might have been like to read it without having seen the films / already being so familiar with the story and the characters. But as it is, I found it a long, hard slog, and one I’m not sure I want to repeat with The Two Towers.

Finally I am continuing my LOTR journey…I’m sorry to say that The Fellowship of the Ring was almost as boring as The Hobbit! It was not very engaging…too many random songs/poetry that just slowed the story down even more…blah blah walking blah blah mountains blah blah Elves and rivers. Gandalf is almost as annoying as Dumbledore tbh…why are wizards always keeping everything a secret? Ugh. Also-Tom Bombadil was frankly so annoying to me.

I like stories that you can’t put down. This was not one of them. I honestly don’t care about any of the characters…characters are boring, plot is also boring…Honestly I enjoyed Harry Potter way more. Lol! Sorry LOTR stans!

Also…I HATE the maps that are included in the book. They are difficult to read and also a lot of the landmarks that he writes about aren’t labeled on the map…??? Why??? How am I supposed to figure out exactly which mountain Frodo is on when he runs away from Boromir?? They couldn’t come out with an update version of the map and have to use this old one that is HORRIBLE?

11/19/2023 Update: After a few days I decided to knock this down to two stars. This was really boring for me and I honestly don't even know if I will continue this series. A real shame because its prequel is one of my favorite books too :(.


I was teetering on giving this a three star rating because I only merely liked this book... I LOVE "The Hobbit" and was excited to get to this one. I could not remember why I didn't finished LotR when I started the series years ago, now I remember.

For me, this book was quite dull. Charming, but dull. It took me so long to read it because I kept loosing interest after a few chapters. The reason why I'm still giving this novel a four star rating is because I love the writing itself. It is magical and the only thing really and a few scenes that kept me engaged enough to finish this book. I'm really hoping book two will have a bit more going on with it and I will enjoy the series as a whole. Perhaps I should try the films... but they scare me off from watching them since they are over three hours long and I would need to watch them in chunks haha.

Either way, this series is an important one to modern fantasy series, so I will still give it a higher rating because of that. For personal enjoyment however it would be more like a 2.5 rating. Here is hope to book two being more exciting for me!

TLDR: A bunch of dudes walk forever and sing songs at nonsensical times. Meh.


---
I am not surprised I didn't love this, as I found the Fellowship of the Rings movie relatively boring. However, I was disappointed even with middling expectations. This book drags on and on and remains rather uninteresting throughout.

I am somewhat confused by Tolkein's writing style and pacing. There are times when he expounds on a chunk of dialogue that does not drive the story forward at all, but then there are significant plot points he just quickly summarizes and moves on.

Also, what's with the constant singing? SO MUCH singing. It just seems like Tolkein wanted to write some random poems?

There is not a great deal of variety amongst the characters' personalities (except Gandalf). I lost track of who was speaking at times because they all sound the same.

Overall, it's a bit of a sophomore slump compared to The Hobbit. If I had not watched the movies, I doubt I would have finished this book. Hoping the second book of the LOTR trilogy is an improvement!

Finally finished! This book was really long, which I knew it would be. But I had hoped that I would think better of it. But unfortunately that was not the case. The text was long-winded and not further interesting. The problem with it was that I didn't feel the characters.

The whole book was confusing as new little stories and names kept being told which I didn't find relevant at many points. Most of all, I felt that it was a book where half was relevant and where the rest was not. There just wasn't enough going on to hold my interest.

I'm still sitting, and am a little confused about what the meaning of the ring actually is? Because how does it make Sauron stronger? I might find the answer to that at some point, who knows?

The book had the potential to be good, but this doesn't really work out for me. But I can see why people thought it was exciting when it came out. I wish the best of luck to others who try to read it. And I hope that there are some who find it more interesting than I did.

Queria dar 2,5 estrelas.
Sofri muito lendo esse. Não me venha com "Tolkien é difícil". Não é difícil. Só é CHATO.

Começou bem, eu estava achando bacana e interessante. Mas aí todo mundo começa a cantar?? Toda decisão precisa ser discutida por horas, dias, meses. Os diálogos. Meu deus, os diálogos são esquisitíssimos, parecem que estão fora de contexto.

As descrições são longas, mas batalhas são resolvidas em UM PARÁGRAFO. Os personagens parecem que têm uma emoção e ponto. As decisões que o grupo toma são meio ?!?!? Estamos atrasados e o mundo em perigo, mas vamos parar aqui para apreciar a vista.

O universo é de fato bem desenvolvido e a escrita é bonita. A leitura é arrastada, mas é uma prosa de qualidade.

Eu amo fantasia, mas o que acabou comigo nesse aqui foi o fato de ser insuportavelmente chato. Eu só queria muito terminar, para poder ler algo que me desse VONTADE. Empurrei com a barriga mesmo. E eu queria muito gostar, mas não deu.

Disseram que os outros dois são melhores, quem sabe um dia...

I have to be honest, after what was a sweet and adventurous introduction to the world through The Hobbit, Fellowship took a steep nosedive in entertainment value for me personally. The story takes roughly 150 pages to truly start, as we set up our characters and their mission for far too long. There is very little direct conflict for a good while since the companions are only lightly followed by the black riders. I am also still not completely sold on this cast of characters save for Gandalf and Sam. They have yet to convince me of being likable individuals who look out for one another. I have to respect what this book series means for popular culture and fantasy as a whole, but Tolkiens wordy prose, abundance of crazy names, locations song-singing and so so much walking make this journey a bit of a slog to get going. I’m hoping the action turns up in two towers. If it wasn’t for the thrilling few scenes like the Balrog fight and the sprint to Rivendell, I would have lost interest. But I’m seeing this story through to the end!

Can I be so honest? And it hurts to say this because all my friends love LOTR, but this book really just isn’t great.

Don’t get be wrong, world building is absolutely incredible. The details and the different races are so creative and unique. This book is just plain ol BORING. The storyline moves so slowly. Tom Bombadil makes me want to end my life everytime he says anything. Why is he there?

The hobbit songs prove that Tolkien is a great poet, but guess what, if I wanted a poetry book I would have gotten a poetry book, not an epic fantasy book.

All in all I got about 80% in before I realized that I wasn’t enjoying myself reading this book, and if an author writes something that isn’t enjoyable to read it’s pretty tough for me to call him a good author and it’s tough for me to call his work a good book.

The LOTR movies are enjoyable and cut out all the boringness and Tom Bombadil who is the bane of my existence. This is one of the few times where the movie is better than the book. Please just watch the movie. This novel is not worth your time.

I tried to read this book as a preteen because I loved the Peter Jackson films so dearly, I wanted to read the source material for my favorite story of all time. I ended up putting it down shortly after the hobbits left the Shire and didn’t pick it back up until years later. As an adult, I completely understand why I was unable to read this book. Tolkien is hailed as a literary genius for his imagination and descriptive writing, but for myself, reading a page long description of a river is a drag. Were it not for my love of the films, I would have put this series down again, just around the time Tom Bombadil shows up. Fortunately I was able to push through the initial boredom of the first half of the first book. After the fellowship unites, the true adventure of the story begins. I began to appreciate the pages of description surrounding my favorite characters because it lent context to their actions. Ultimately, this book is my least favorite of the trilogy, but I accept it for what it is due to it being the foundation of the later, more exciting books.

As a big fan of the film trilogy and its prequels, I wanted to like this one so badly, but unfortunately, it’s just not to my taste. This does not, by any means, discredit Tolkien as an author. I think his writing is brilliant (maybe just not for someone who has a really low attention span like I do).

I found the book unbelievably dull, with too many unnecessary details and plotlines thrown into the mix (Tom Bombadil, I’m looking at you). One more thing I found off-putting was the multiple times the characters broke into lengthy and boring songs. Maybe Tolkien wanted that to be one of the charms of the universe he created, but good Lord, was it boring to me.

At one point, I had to resort to listening to the audiobook while I’m driving in order to finish the book. Even then, it bored me to the point of microsleeping while driving.

Never mind that; perhaps I will try to read the first few chapters of the next book. If it still doesn’t suit my liking, I shall protect my peace and just rewatch the movies.

There are undoubtedly TONS of metrics by which lotr is a 5/5. If I were to rate it based on how good it was in the 30’s, for the authors kids, based on the level of detail the author imagined when making the world, its influence on the fantasy genre, or by its linguistic art then it’d be a perfect book.

Unfortunately, in terms of pure enjoyment, I found fellowship to be a slog of a book where, for obvious reasons, the whole book felt far more like an excuse to recount the lore of an imaginary land than to actually tell a story.

My previous knowledge of the story may affect my feelings here but I never felt like the characters were in any danger. Additionally, and I know nearly everyone will disagree with this, but I didn’t find any of their goals or characterizations particularly interesting. Everyone felt extremely one dimensional and altruistic simply moving from point a to b to c with no clear direction or purpose.

The world Tolkien made seems very well thought out and cared for, it’s just too bad nobody lives there.

The only reason this isn’t 1 star is because of how much of an impact these books had on the fantasy genre.

I hate to say it, but this was a chore to get through. So many inane side plots it killed me.

Love this world so much, grew up being obsessed with the movies, but OH MY GOD. Prepare yourself for the LONGEST, most pointless pages of writing so descriptive I wanted to bang my head against a wall. We didn’t even get into the forest to begin traveling until 6 hours into the audiobook. 6 HOURS. And they didn’t meet Aragorn until halfway through. The fellowship doesn’t form until 13 hours in, or 66% into the story. The characters felt less like individuals with differing personalities, and more like they were there to be there.

The pacing was actually hell on Earth and I fell asleep a concerning amount of times. Maybe I was just not in the mood for a book like this, and if I had been prepared for the word vomit I may have been more amenable, but I was not and I did not enjoy my time.

I finally finished it. I've been trying to finish this book for months and only finished it this weekend so I could watch the movie with my husband.
The best way I could describe reading this book was like reading a textbook. Specifically the second textbook in a series. Sure, you're interested in the subject matter, and you want to want to read it, but actually reading it feels like a chore. The writing itself switched between scenes of the hobbits on their journey (the parts I liked most of the book), textbook descriptions of the history of Middle Earth (the parts I liked least of the book), or characters/places/creatures that were thrown at me like I was supposed to know what they were but had no idea (like I'd missed a textbook I was supposed to read before starting the book).
I want to know how the story finishes, but I can't subject myself to reading another two books to figure it out. I completely understand I'm in the minority for my opinion but I really just didn't get this book and was not a fan.

Did not live up to the hype. I know a lot of LoTR fans (Like A LOT) who all told me it was a great book, and it was, I guess, I read this maybe in 2022 so maybe I need to re-read this now that I am older... but overall I liked the Hobit a lot more than this. There may have been parts when i was invested but never so invested I would forget where I was. It takes a lot of commitment to read this because it's very long so unless you have a good attention span, this book will kinda drag on.

I cannot do this. "They go here, then they go here, then they meet this guy, then the go here." I'm sorry. I understand why the series is so beloved. I don't have the audacity to call it bad, but it didn't captivate me.

Gandalf is awesome. Specifically when he argues with Saruman. His avoidance of the ring is the coolest part of the book in my opinion—the fact that he doesn't "trust" himself with all of that power. He believes it's something to be avoided altogether, not something to be harnessed by the good, because the act of harnessing the ring is itself wicked. I get that, but I just can't do all of the sing-songy travelling and generic characters.

That said, perhaps the work seems generic because of how classic it is, because of the hold it has on the genre, so I respect it, it's just challenging to invest in. It's like listening to classical music. I don't resent it because it's established some of the things that I love; I'm just not compelled to engage with the material itself.

Let me start this review with saying that Lord of the Rings is an absolute masterpiece...the movie that is, the novel not so much. Whilst Peter Jackson had me glued to the screen, Tolkien couldn't keep me very interested in his narrative.

I did enjoy the quest part of the novel, but the extreme slow pace and highly telling form of writing had me begging for it to end. Even the few action scenes where so blandly written and full of useless adjectives that I was glad to be able to rewatch the movie scenes in my head whilst reading them.And the very black and white duality gets boring real fast, I get it shadows are evil, Elves are good. And character dynamics are so non existent or so rushed, that some characters could be easily removed from the story without much effect, Bombadil and his wife come to mind.

I am really thinking about skipping the entire rest of the trilogy, because this first part left me with such a bad feeling.

I read these books when the Peter Jackson movies came out as I felt it would be wrong to watch the movies without having read the books. I'd had The Hobbit read to me as a child, and wasn't drawn into it like many of my friends were, so had never bothered to read LotR. Because I like fantasy novels goodreads keeps recommending these, so I feel the need to shelve them as read.

When I talk about the things I do and don't look for in books I often say 'I don't like books where the author describes the tree.' That came from this book. There was a lenghly description of a tree, right down to it's bark at one point that I just found painful, and that sums up how I felt about the whole series.

Perhaps if I hadn't previously read so many plain text fantasy novels that had been inspired by Tolkien I would have been swept up in the magic like everyone else I know, as it happens I just found the series a bit of a slog. For the record, I felt the same way about the films.

I gave the old classic another go after several attempts it in my youth because it always tops my recommended lists and the Hobbit is one of my favorite stories of all time. I made myself finish this time around, which was a massive struggle. Its just not for me. I need a little less world building/lore/poetry in the narrative, though I respect Tolkien for developing his world so deeply and I'm absolutely in awe of his linguistic accomplishments. The story is bogged down by so much unnecessary, boring, and complex detail which is such a shame because it's a great story and the interesting parts had me learning forward in my seat. Anyway, I'm not trying to hate I'm still a fan of LOTR and Tolkien I just found Fellowship really hard to read and that's rare for me. I'm probably still gonna force myself to read Two Towers and Return of the King someday.

I remember loving this story as a child, but it may have been the old Rankin & Bass movie, the records, the abbreviated versions and everything except this book.

This book is good. Good at best.

Tolkien's overly descriptive writing doesn't really hold up today. I am a huge fan of Twain, Steinbeck and Vonnegut, so it isn't like I dont appreciate older authors.

This just wasn't as good as so many people think it is. Tolkien is happy to set up a scene for pages, but not too much happens. The hobbits leaving The Shire is all pretty interesting, but once they start meeting the pretentious Elves, everything starts to head downhill.

Give me this some thought: there is a ring of power that Sauron needs so he can rule the world. The most notable thing it does is turn its wearer invisible. Huh?

Unfortunately, this was not a book that I really enjoyed reading, due to the overall dullness and slightly boring storyline. I think that the book was too long to just be focused on the journey of Frodo and the Ring. I also didn't understand the purpose of the poems and songs in random parts of the story, and I think the part that was most boring for me was that they were just walking 95% of the time! It was quite exciting in the beginning, learning about the effects of the Ring, but then after that, it just seemed like a drag on.

However, this book was useful for the worldbuilding projects as it touched on the topics of different castes/groups, powers/abilities of characters, and the significant landmarks/places.

All in all, I don't think I will be reading the rest of the books of the series.

I gave up on this book. I tried so hard to like it but I just cannot. All the characters do are just walking, talking, singing, and composing poems which are just not my cup of tea. I want some mind-bending plot twist but it seems to take forever for me to get to that point. I don't have a problem with Tolkien but I think I won't be able to absorb his style of writing. The fantasy world he creates is absolutely amazing and full of magical elements, which I admire and take inspiration from. But the way he depicts it is bland and tedious. I care about the plot much more than how the jungle looks like or what the Hobbits do for their daily monotonous routine along the journey. I haven't watched the movie either but I will and I hope it'll give me some motivation to finish this book later because I don't like abandoning my books.

This book was not for me, and here’s my reason why:

The pacing is weird! You can go from reading well-paced bits, to overly descriptive parts (I don’t need to know about a specific tree which has no part in the actual story other than it exists), to skipping over the really interesting parts. This completely detracted from my ability to become immersed in the story, or to care about what’s going on.

I have no issue with it being a bigger book, I enjoy longer titles (see Les Misérables from the beginning of this year’s reading list), I really enjoy fantasy, and I like an epic. However, this book was not for me. I found it tedious, and I should’ve known this after attempting it multiple times in my lifetime and only now forcing myself all the way through it. I would, however, recommend The Hobbit.

Very rare do I post a DNF, but after trudging halfway through this I just couldn't take it any more. I'd previously enjoyed The Hobbit, minus the very flowery language, and was under the impression that this was written in a more adult way, but as far as I read it's almost retelling the exact same story in a much slower way and still including more tediously stupid poems and songs every half dozen pages to interrupt and detract from anything interesting that was actually being built up. Having endured this overlong and boring affair, with a developing apathy towards reading the second and third books, there was little sense in subjecting myself to the rest of this one. It will sadly be one of those somehow iconic works that I just don't get; although I'm starting to think that it is so revered simply because Tolkien got there first.

This book was on my tbr list for SO LONG, and I was SO DISAPPOINTED.

I absolutely love the LOTR movies, and I expected to feel similarly to the books, even though I had been warned from the internet that there would be lots of long descriptions throughout. Those warnings did not do the book justice.

Not only is the book filled with long, boring descriptions, but even its action-filled scenes that should be exciting seemed slow and boring.

Add on to that the fact that I didn’t feel a connection to any of the characters except for Aragorn and Sam, and I was not having a good time. It’s crazy because every character talks about how great Frodo is, and he’s my favorite character in the movies, and yet none of his actions or dialogue in the book made me feel any strong emotions toward him while reading.

This is one of those rare cases when the movies truly are better than the books.

Endless; Descriptions; Of; Landscapes; With; Semi; Colons;
There is no doubt that The Lord of the Rings has been one of the most innovative books of all times for the fantasy world, but it is also crystal clear that innovative does not equal enjoyable. This has been one of the most tedious books I have ever read, and it felt like a shore to get through each page. Boring landscapes that could just as well be on earth instead of in a fantasy world are way too thoroughly described without any purpose whatsover, and are usually followed up by unnatural dialogues in which the 50-year old hobbits sound like toddlers. In the end, barely anything has happened at all throughout the plot of this book except for me being left dissapointed by a book that is supposed to be one of the greatest of all time.

I am so confused by this audio book. It's almost as if they are trying to see how many people would give up within the first hour.
I was excited to find an audio version narrated by Andy Serkis. Then I started listening...and I barely made it through the first hour. The first hour, the prologue, give the history of Hobbits and the Shire. And Serkis read it as if we himself were incredibly bored. He is monotone and draws out each word for an eternity. I hoped that when the actual story began, he'd at least do different voices. Maybe that way, I could make it through the book.
As soon as the prologue finished, his narration completely changed. It was energetic and everything I had expected from Andy Serkis. He is such an amazing narrator. So who in the world decided he should read the prologue like a half-dead, old history professor?!?!

I am so sad to write this review because I LOVEEEE the movies. They altered me as a human. But this book……

So slow. And yes I realize these books were written in the 40s but it wasn’t the old style of writing that made it boring, it was the way the story was written that makes it so dull. I feel like over half of the crazy adventurous stories are told over dinner or breaks the characters are taking, so there are no stakes…You know it’s going to end up fine because the person involved is telling the story! It’s the old show- don’t tell rule that Tolkien DGAF about.

Also the amount of singing made me want to go insane. I had to skip it, it never added ANYTHING to the plot.

Also ALSO. Tom Bombadil? Just why. Literally went on for SO LONG and it was hurt them hanging out with him but no one knows what he is or does except for he’s magically all powerful in the woods??????

Tolkien hat zwar eine unglaubliche Welt erschaffen, aber mitreißen konnte er mich zumindest in diesem Teil noch nicht. Allein, dass ich fast 2 Jahre lang auf Seite 200 rumgedümpelt bin, spricht nicht gerade für das Buch. Die Handlungen waren so ausschweifend beschrieben, dass selbst die spannenderen Ereignisse nicht wirklich spannend zu lesen waren. Ich habe mich gefühlt, als würde ich das Geschehen von einigen Metern Entfernung betrachten, anstatt mitten drin zu sein. Allgemein hatte ich große Probleme, mich auf die Handlung zu fokussieren und ich musste mich wirklich konzentrieren, nicht mit den Gedanken abzuschweifen. Die ewig langen Landschaftsbeschreibungen haben da leider auch nicht geholfen. Und außerdem - wieso hat Gandalf so Stimmungsschwankungen??
Ich hoffe, dass die Geschichte in Band 2 endlich mal richtig in Fahrt kommt und mir dann auch besser gefällt!

Fue una tarea ardua avanzar, entiendo que se alaba la habilidad y dedicación del autor por brindar gran cantidad de detalles, pero alcanza un punto en el que esto se vuelve más perjudicial que ventajoso. Para ser un mundo tan creativo da poco espacio a la imaginación por su naturaleza enciclopédica.

Veo cómo hacer una película de este libro es soñado, con tanto lujo de detalle se puede hacer de cada personaje el protagonista, pero el coste es que se dificulta formar una conexión con estos. Los momentos que más me entretienen y conmueven son las conversaciones entre Sam y Frodo, se sienten genuinas y no como que el autor me este llevando de la mano y contando que es conveniente sentir y pensar en cada momento.

Creo que ya es momento de ver las películas, pero por no creo que lea el resto de la saga.
