reviews.text:
Wanted to enjoy this, to get swept along the journey, but I kept getting pulled by long stretches where the book devolved into nature descriptions and history lessons. I love lore as much as the next fantasy enjoyer, but a lot of it felt disconnected, not adding much (or anything) to their quest.

It became very repetitive, which a journey like this would, (points for realism) but for me, that didn't translate into an enjoyable reading experience. For example, after some very important plot happens at the end of a chapter, within five pages of the next chapter they are talking about dwarven landmarks.

I think my main criticism is the lack of tension throughout. Its established in the beginning quite well, but over the course of the novel it is stretched the point of being translucent.

2.5 stars I feel obligated to like this book more because it's such a cult classic, but I really didn't. I read this book out loud with my 11 year old son after reading The Hobbit. It took us *8* months to finally wade through it. Tolkien spends far too much time on describing settings and getting me lost with elf lore that I was bored until the action picked up. Once the action starts, it certainly is good, but it's far too spaced out. We allow ourselves to watch the movie after finishing the books, and have been happy to see that for the most part, the movies are a fair representation. But I have mixed feelings wading through the next 2 novels to the finale. Feeling obligated . . . but dreading it (especially if they each take another 8 months).

i am not going to review lord of the rings y'all have already made up your mind but i do have a genuine question. do people like it because of the movies? or because they think they have to because it's a classic? or because when it came out there wasn't much else to read? or do people actually genuinely enjoy reading it?

i promise i'm not being snarky i'm only trying to sort out if i'm like. deficient when it comes to telling what good fantasy is. because i was bored for 90% of this book. i'm gonna read the others (because of the whole classic thing). but um the scene with so it wasn't totally a bad experience.

2 stars because i am Being Honest i'm sorry.

Listen, the worldbuilding is of course fantastic and what most fantasy aspires to, but the book gets progressively more tiring to read because Tolkien is so hell-bent on making you understand exactly where the characters are on the map in every. single. paragraph. I WANT to love this book, some parts of it are beautifully written, but... the *story* is wonderful. The prose however borders on exhausting, and 90% of what you learn about the characters is told to you by either the narrator or other characters, it's not shown as the story progresses. They also don't develop unique voices - if you were to cover up the dialogue tags, you'd have little to no clue who is talking unless it's Sam, especially in the second book.

I’m sorry this is rated so low I’ll give Tolkien’s story/world FIVE STARS but the enjoyability of the book was only a 2.5 max for me. It was so painfully slow to read and at times very hard to follow /: I wanted to like it so bad, and I did at the beginning but it really dragged in the middle and the end was so unsatisfying (I think it’s UNFAIR to leave the main plot unfinished in book one, even when it’s a trilogy, at least give me SOMETHING). That’s the majority of my rant, I also think that a book being published in 1954 could’ve had at least one major female character— that would not have killed you, Tolkien. Anyway, I will be watching the movies for the rest of this series bc I don’t think I have it in me to read two more of these !!!!

I didn't enjoy this book as much as I did The Hobbit.

1. It was pretty dark ( I'm not one who enjoys scary movies or books)
2. I felt like it was less "exciting" than the hobbit was
3. And even though the story line was good, it wasn't my type of book

Though some people will like the adventure in this book, some of the scary creatures/people, I don't think this was the book for me

This book follows the story of Frodo Baggins and his friend Sam taking The Ring of Power somewhere to be destroyed before the Ringwraiths could get hold of it. This ring held one special power- it would enable Sauran to destroy all that was good in Middle-earth. Now it was up to Frodo and Sam to take it to the very center of Sauron's dark kingdom.

I really wanted to like this book after reading so many good reviews, but I just did not unfortunately. The plot of the book is basically this;
walk, eat, sleep, destroy the ring. Also Tolkien writes so much descriptions and over describes everything to the point where I was bored out of my mind. The pacing was extremely slow. There are many, many chapters were its just walking, and when characters just talks about history, its just so BORING omg.

Also I wasn¨t invested or attached to any of the characters. Aragorn, Boromir, Merry, Pippin and Legolas are just boring characters.
There was very little character depth in my opinion.


I will try to read the second book Two Towers, just because the end of the first book got interesting. The last 5 pages or so. Maybe Two Towers will change my mind.

Boring, boring, and more boring

It surprises me that this is considered one of the best works of fantasy, ever. The Lord of the Rings is filled with unnecessary descriptions, unnecessarily difficult and complicated vocabulary, and an awfully slow pace. This book could easily be around 250 pages long, and it would still not feel rushed, that's how much unnecessary detail it contains. And that's not even the full story. Tolkien doesn't know how to build tension and suspense AT ALL. In the first place, the story doesn't have many "intense moments", but even the "intense moments" were so boring that they literally put me to sleep.

I will just say this with my chest out, this is a 3/10 book, at best. Absolutely not worth anyone's time

I have tried and tried and tried to read this book several times, both physically and with the audiobook. I finally made it through, but barely.

Tolkien is an amazing writer and I understand what he's done for the genre. I absolutely can not get into his writing, though. It's so dull...I was bored to TEARS the entire time. Even switching from the Robert Inglis audiobook to the Andy Serkis one did not help.

Perhaps because I went into it (again) this time while Rings of Power is still airing, my full potential of enjoyment factor went down. I don't know.

I'm going to continue with the next two as well as The Hobbit, but I'm going to need to put myself on Tolkien time-out before I do.

You get the point of the story within 45 pages. Then it takes 350 pages for the story to start. I also hated that the council just recounts their adventures like they are telling a story for 150 pages. Tolkien could have written all of their perspectives within 150 pages and had them all converge at the council. Just terribly structured. Unique story but not really at the same time - it just takes the Hobbit and expands it. And the Hobbit was just his rip off of all of the old fairy tales. And it took him 20+ years to finish when he had already written the whole premise in the Hobbit? Jesus, Robert Jordan and GRRM would like a word.

Not good. I may still finish though, if only just to be able to reduce these very high ratings I scratch my head over.

I'm a die hard LOTR fan but have tried to read the books several times but for some reason always struggled. Finally got all the way through and yeah I was unimpressed.

Unpopular opinion but I think a lot of older pieces of literature have mediocre prose. Writing styles were just different in the 70s and I don't think it aged well. Important events will often be glazed over, but then Sam wishing he brought rope on his journey was pointed out several times? It is a shame because the details and lore that Tolkien put into this world seems barely touched upon in this book. I was left feeling disconnected from the characters and the tale itself.

I never say this BUT THE MOVIES ARE SO MUCH BETTER

I love fantasy. I've enjoyed books with lots of description and books where the majority of the narrative was a journey. This had a few interesting nuggets, but overall it was awful. Maybe because I already love the movies it felt like we were taking forever to get to the interesting parts that I knew, but I don't think that's it. Tolkien's narrative style was droning rather than engaging for me. Except for the first couple chapters, the whole first book felt irrelevant and disconnected (this is two books in one). Maybe the rest of the books are more interesting, but I'm not going to take that risk and waste my time. I will stick with the movies in this case and find more modern fantasy to enjoy.

I know it's sacrilegious for me to say, but what a snooze-fest. I wanted to check off reading *The Hobbit* and *The Lord of the Rings* from my bucket list. I love the movies and have immersed myself in Tolkien lore for the past 20 years. However, I found the book to be incredibly long-winded. It might be the writing style from 40s and 50s or perhaps Tolkien's tendency provide too much information, but my God, this could've been SO much shorter without losing any of the plot points. It took six hours of reading just for the Hobbits to get from Hobbiton to Bree. All the extra, superfluous detail felt completely unnecessary. I'm really not looking forward to reading the other two books. How Christopher Lee read this every year is beyond me.

I tried reading the hobbit as a kid and found it very boring. I watched the movies as a teenager and also found them to drag. I love fantasy and I love magic so why don't I love Tolkien!? Some of my fave people are hardcore LOTR stans so this is my last attempt before admitting defeat. I intend to read the trilogy and am glad to have this one out of the way. I think I hate Hobbits as they remind me of what American's used to romantically imagine what Ireland was like. (I may have some internal cultural stereotyping to address in my next therapy session) I NEVER thought we would leave the Shire and quite possibly my soul is still there withering from the constant bombardments of twenty verse songs.

I really really REALLY wanted to enjoy this. I just thought the first 50% of the story was just… boring 🫣there was just A LOT of walking, which would have been fine if there was something going on at the same time. I didn’t feel like I learnt anything about the characters or grew attached to any of them, they just talked and walked and felt really 2 dimensional to me.

I thought the book was going to add an extra layer from the film (as the book is normally better) but I just think as a lover of the films the book fell flat.

I did have to switch to an audio book about half way through just to get through it. I’m going to carry on with the series in the hope that there’s a bit more action.

This was a tough one to get through. I know that many love this book, but honestly it was so boring to me. The beginning was intriguing, and I found good nuggets about leaving what’s familiar. But then Frodo and co left and just kept plodding on, and on and on. I ended up listening to the audiobook (on 2x speed - it was that dry) halfway through, which helped me finish but was maybe to my detriment. The main reason I read this was because I’ve heard people liken it to Narnia in its spiritual depth and deeper meanings. So listening to it sped up probably didn’t help with that. Unfortunately, I have little to no desire to continue with the series, but hopefully I will someday so I can check it off my list.

it actually kills me to give it two stars. i am genuinely confused on what i missed and why everyone else loves this so much 🥺 i felt bored 98% of the time. confused? nothing made sense and honestly it could be because i was so bored, so i started skimming and then eventually it was too late and nothing made sense.
too much description, too much “follow the yellow brick road”, no action. am i spoiled in thinking fantasy should have action????
i will be watching the movies because i think it will help better understand also because of FOMO. But… as of now, there is a good chance i will never finish the series.

all this to say - i always did the worst in all of my English class comprehension tests. maybe it’s a me problem 😂

It could be a good book, but it's not my type of book. I was too bored and just could not get into it. Having a Foreword AND a Prologue that was longer than a page or two just seemed unnecessary to me before even getting into the book. That's probably what turned me off. I wished I would like it because I was told by a lot of people how much I would love it since I love Harry Potter, but they are just not the same. I don't feel bad about my rating because that was my personal opinion, but I can see how others would love it and give it a 5 star rating. Again, it was just too much background before getting into the main story. I might come back to it later on and find that I love it, but for now, this is how I feel.

Initially interested, but that soon took a nose dive, after all of the resting breaks and tons and tons of descriptions of the forests, trails, and roads, just to name a few! Often zoned out as I read the ramblings of the Tom Bombadil, or however you spell it. Whenever they wanted to "sing" a song, I'd roll my eyes and just skim. I'd skim those song passages as well as the endless times the hobbits would complete a path and then get on a hill to observe the land, only to realize they weren't exactly where they needed to be! So then, I would grit my teeth when they would set out for yet ANOTHER route, and then another. This wasn't my cup of tea, but I do find myself wanting whatever it was Tom Bombadil was on!

Lacks depth and good storytelling skills in general

The best way I can describe the book is that it's meh, not the worst thing I have ever read but comes close to it. Ironically (considering the great deal that went into building the lore and the fantastic world), the characters and the plot are too two-dimensional, making it extremely difficult to care about what happens to anyone and to empathize with them. The characters are so bizzare and interact with each other extremely weirdly, and don't mistake that with attractive ancient-tales style of interactions.
It gets deeply boring a lot of the time, and when it's not boring, it has the level of excitement of a children's fairytale at best.

Even though I love the movies I've never had much of a desire to read the books. The overwhelming response seems to be that they're boring. I remember a friend of mine tell me that she stopped reading because of all the songs. Unfortunately I have to agree with all of these critiques.

I found the pacing to be absolutely atrocious it feels like everytime something interesting is going to happen it's violently halted for some random character to cameo for. It's very hard to get invested in the story when it just keeps stopping every 10 pages to have yet another song. Do we really need that many songs??? Tolkien pls. Only reason this isn't lower is because it inspired the movies and gave some backstory on Frodo.

🇸🇮 (slovensko zgoraj) // 🇬🇧 (english below)

----
🇸🇮

Gospodarju prstanov sem dala že ogromno priložnosti, pa me ne prepričajo ne filmi, niti knjige. Očitno fantazijske avanture pač niso zame. Preveč likov, preveč popotovanja, preveč lokacij, preveč preskakovanj v času. Res škoda. Rada bi videla, da bi mi ta serija bila všeč, a kar ne gre, pač ne gre.

----
🇬🇧

I’ve given *The Lord of the Rings* plenty of chances, but neither the films nor the books have won me over. Apparently, fantasy adventures just aren’t for me. Too many characters, too much travelling, too many locations, too many leaps in time. It’s a real shame. I’d love to be able to enjoy this series, but if it doesn’t work for me, it just doesn’t.

Tuurlijk, Tolkien heeft een mooie wereld bedacht en ik kan de fantasie ervan waarderen. Elventaal, runes etc. Maar er zit in alle 540 bladzijden maar één vrouwelijk personage die wat zegt. En dan is het Galadriel die als mythisch figuur wordt neergezet (classic).
De eerste helft van het boek is ronduit saai, ik heb meerdere fantasy boeken gelezen met een beter uitgewerkt plot dan dit. Verder doen de personages domme dingen, echt get a grip. Maar hè, het zijn allemaal mannen, dus dat verklaart.
Het lukt me ook niet helemaal om het verhaal in de tijd te zien en dus te begrijpen waarom het verhaal alleen mannen omvat. Ik vind het hinderlijk, en al helemaal omdat dit “the epitome” of fantasy zou zijn. Misschien had ik ook gewoon te hoge verwachtingen van het boek.

It’s fair to say I have had a long relationship with this book. It’s one of those unfortunate ones where you drift apart without quite being able to let go, but it’s lasted decades. And then you start stalking them on social media, you forget why you loved them in the first place, terrible, shameful things are said to their new partner and it all goes a bit wrong. So, to stop myself from putting regrettable comments under hyperbolic five-star reviews that, twenty years ago, I might have been guilty of myself, I feel the need to vent a bit. It’s not as if anyone will read this. In the unlikely event a rabid, “greatest book of all time!!!!!” Tolkien fan does stumble across it, please bear in mind that I am a horrible, evil troll, and I am typing this whilst dancing by the light of a burning orphanage. This will save time.

So: The Mysteries of Udolpho is a huge, often rather slow, structurally clumsy novel, weighed down by a good deal of uneventful travel, tedious landscape description, and poetry written by someone not as good at it as they think they are. It takes hundreds of pages to get going, and some of the characters might as well be made out of cardboard, but it is still something of a landmark in the history of the gothic novel. Udolpho may not be the earliest, it certainly isn’t the best, but it is one of the better known of its type.

Oops. Sorry. Wrong review. Just substitute Lord of the Rings for The Mysteries of Udolpho and fantasy for gothic, would you? I think the points still stand. And apologies if you’re a rabid Anne Radcliffe fan. There must be at least one.

Excuse me while I twirl my moustache.

But the thing is that although there is a lot wrong with Udolpho I still enjoyed it and still intend to go back for a re-read. Yes, really. The other very big book, on the other hand, I probably won’t. I’m not going to get rid of it either – I feel physically bereft if I don’t own a copy – but I don’t feel the need to trudge through it yet again. I like The Hobbit, I love The Silmarillion, but I really can’t be having with The Lord of the Rings. It falls down a big crack between the two.

Now why? And why do I prefer some of Tolkien’s contemporaries?

Well, bizarrely, I think it’s probably down to things that make it more accessible, and perhaps more popular, than its antecendents. The Lord of the Rings doesn’t use a huge amount of arcane vocabulary, it isn’t very creative in terms of sentence structure or even plot, you don’t need to bring very much in the way of general knowledge or psychological insight to the party. Compared to something like Eddison’s The Worm Ouroboros, Mervyn Peake’s Gormenghast books, or even some of the works of James Branch Cabell – all of which are immeasurably better written on a sentence-and-paragraph level – The Lord of the Rings is a doddle to read. Personally, though, I find the thing too easy to read to be interesting to read. I find the sparseness of the book an effective barrier to enjoyment. I find Tolkien’s style is often neither transparent enough to ignore, nor dazzling enough to admire. It plods.

Now, I’m not talking about Middle Earth itself there. Middle Earth, which is a remarkably self-contained, self-sufficient entity, whilst not remotely as detailed as his fans make out, is quite detailed enough for one man to produce in one lifetime. I’m talking about a single book. Middle Earth may not be sparse, The Lord of the Rings is. It’s the result of one man doggedly churning out page after page of something that, at some points, in some ways, he wasn’t very interested in, to produce a very large work of fiction. He was more interested in the world itself than in the story he set there, and he was more interested in telling that story than in polish. It shows. Parts of the book shine, but much of it is what would happen to The Hobbit if you inflated it with a bicycle pump. Or at least that’s the way it turns up in my head.

And, as we’ve established, I’m a terrible human being who spends his spare time tying kittens to railway tracks. You should ignore me, and if you’ve read this far it is entirely your own fault.

To my mind, then, The Lord of the Rings isn’t Tolkien’s masterpiece. Tolkien’s masterpiece, so far as I can tell, is that extended exercise in hyper-nerdery that is The Silmarillion, the concentrated essence of what, outside of linguistic experiments I have no desire to comprehend, the man was interested in writing.

To my mind The Lord of the Rings isn’t the great fount and origin of modern fantasy; it’s a distended monster of a thing that, if you look at the publication date, turns up really quite late in the game.

To my mind not only is it not the best book of all time… which raises the interesting question of how, without reading every other book across the whole of time and space, anyone could possibly tell; and whether it might not be rather depressing, having found that book, to realise that anything else you can possibly read is going to be a let-down… it isn’t even the best book by Tolkien.

And yet…

And yet I can remember, just about, being ten years old, sat on a riverbank, and losing myself in this massive work of fantasy with a map in the back. I can remember reading it in three days without once having to think about angling. I can remember discovering, for the first time, that adults read this stuff too. It opened a door. I should be grateful.

The good times were good, but I can’t let go.

I never read The Lord of the Rings as a child or as a teenager. I tried to read it in my teens but I got part way through the first few chapters and gave up because I was bored to tears. I'm glad to say that by listening to the audiobook I was able to move beyond my previous stumbling block and I'm glad I did.

While I love the world that Tolkien created and its embellished history, I can't say I enjoyed the pace or the characterisation all that much. A lot of the characters felt quite samey in their dialogue and lacked distinct personalities. Thankfully the narrator was able to bring distinct tones to everyone's speech which really helped filter out who was who. As for the dialogue in general it was very drawn out. I get that Tolkien was evoking Ye Olde Speach but most of these conversations could have been cut in half without losing their meaning and purpose.

The pacing for the first half of the book was far too slow. I really zoned out when the 23493th song started to be sung, and 23451 of those songs were just from Tom Bombadil. I started skipping passed the songs out of principle after I realised some of these songs were taking up to 5 minutes to sing because the verses would go on for pages and pages. I realise that the songs comment upon and expand the history of the various places of the world but they really bog down the pace and flow of the story. I actually enjoyed them at first but they soon outstayed their welcome. If they had been sprinkled here and there throughout the story I would have been fine, but having multiple per chapter was just a huge NO from me.

I was a little sad that there wasn't nearly as much action as I was expecting, but the few we did get I thoroughly enjoyed. I do wish there were more scenes outside of Frodo's PoV, because simply having the other characters painstakingly retell everything they've done in their absence also slowed the pace, though the meticulous detail that the characters recall does help set the scene.

Tolkien's descriptions are lush and vivid though sometimes a bit overblown. However, I can't deny that they took me straight to Middle-Earth and didn't want to let go.

I can definitely see how this absolutely changed the landscape when it came to the Fantasy genre but it doesn't really hold up as well for me as a modern reader. Though, I wonder if I would have liked the book more if I had read it before I saw the films. I still adore Middle-Earth and Tolkien (and J.K.Rowling) inspired my love of the genre ... but I can't help but feel that the films were better.

There is one rule that I love about good storytelling, Show Don't tell, and this book is a whole lot of telling, What should have been the most interesting part of the book (The telling of the ring's history) was incredibly boring because rather than showing us this history it's reduced to a bunch of guys sitting around a table telling you what they know. And don't even get me started on the flowery language and hypnotic cadence of the writing, It's so hard to concentrate on anything that's going on, I even tried listening to the audio book and passed out in a heartbeat. So I guess this was a great sleep aid, better than Ambien! I can only hope that the next two are better.

Ugh. I wanted very much to like and rave about this but I will stay true to myself and say "No, this is not for me." It started promisingly enough; I actually enjoyed the intriguing bit on Bilbo, his party and its aftermath. Was following the storyline pretty well right until Frodo & Co's departure from Crickhollow, after which I almost had a fatal overdose of descriptions about EVERYTHING related to nature, topography, sky and trees. Phew... could we just get on with the story already?? 😂 The cliffhanger at the end was pretty clever though, I may feel inspired to attempt the next book in a couple of month's time!

It took me like a year to read lol but honestly thought it was a slog. I get that Tolkien wrote a glossary for these books but at least every few pages had some nonsensical place name, side quest, song, or overly long description of a nature scene, with no bearing or connection to what was going on. It wasn’t quite enough for me to be completely lost like I was at the beginning of reading Dune, and granted sometimes I’d go like a month without opening it, but I threw up my hands often enough to the point where whenever I picked up my place in the book again I stopped caring to figure out what had happened beforehand. At least with Dune you could tell all the details had world-building purpose; this at times just felt like winding nonsense that an old British man wrote 75 years ago.

All that said, Tolkien’s prose at points (especially towards the end) could be charming - reminded me of his buddy C.S. Lewis, very contemplative and calming - and I was kinda invested by the very end. I think the more you read in one sitting the more you want to keep reading.

Gandalf seems kinda nerfed compared to what I was expecting. This is supposed to be the precursor to Dumbledore but he’s just a wise learned old man with some cool fireworks?

I couldn’t handle the writing style, there seems to be no character development/thoughts and feelings, just a series of actions and reactions and going from place to place, I just couldn’t immerse myself in their world like I was expecting to. I think I’ll just watch the film before I think about reading the next two in the LOTR series, maybe they’re just not for me!

I had been saving reading LOTR for when I'd have a lot of time on my hands. Thanks to the lock down I picked it up and I am utterly disappointed . The writing is not engaging at all. The characters lack depth and thus I felt nothing for or against them while reading. All I can give is that the landscape and setting descriptions are vivid but also too long and ultimately became boring. Oh, and I like the idea of having poems in storybooks but they, too, were a drag at most places.

Absolutely abysmal!

I was very excited to read this book knowing that Tolkien is considered father of fantasy. But I didn’t enjoy reading it all. I felt lost many a times amongst so many names and journeys that the characters take. Names of mountains, valleys, rivers- After a while I stopped caring.

I enjoyed reading the songs though.

One of the blurbs say that the English speaking world is divided into those who have read this book and those who are going to read them. If we are to divide the world who has read further into those who like this book and those who don’t. I would be in the latter.

I really struggled to get through this book. I love fantasy books, games and movies and I really enjoyed the LOTR films on multiple occasions.

I just couldn’t get into this book, it is so long winded with a million different ways to describe landscapes as they walk from one place to another.

This was my second attempt to read the book and I managed to finish it and I really wanted to enjoy it but I couldn’t. I can appreciate the way the book is written and use of language is fantastic but it’s just not for me.

Sorry!

finally managed to finish reading this book after 2 failed attempts 7 years ago, but still unable to read the last 20 pages because the story and plot are so slow, so i read quickly only at a glance . the storyline of the journey is so slow and complicated, boring because there are too many details that I don't think need to be explained. maybe book 1 is just a prologue because there are almost no action stories. and maybe the Tolkien style just doesn't suit me. but still I will continue reading books 2 and 3, hopefully it will be good and interesting

I wanted to enjoy this book... I truly did... but I did not. I don’t seem to appreciate poetry or flowery language, spontaneous nonsensical songs, and conversation that goes on and on and on yet gets nowhere. Thank goodness I watched the movie years ago and every so once in a while had touch points to draw me back in to what was currently happening. I struggled so much to imagine the characters and scenery. I had hoped to continue the series but as I often had no desire to even finish this first book I shall not... maybe one day I’ll try the hobbit though.

I finally finished it. This was one heck of a book and to be honest it was kind of dull. I was thinking it had more action but I may have thought that because I’ve seen the movies. It was very, very unnecessarily wordy and I don’t think I would have finished it if I wasn’t listening to the audio version. While this is supposed to be a grand adventure and it did have moment of peril the plot just seemed to plod along. The characters also seemed sort of bland and were difficult to separate. Anyhow, I think this will be my first and last foray into Middle Earth at least in literary form.

Una saga que tenía siempre en mente pero nunca me animé a empezar a leer. Le doy solo 2 estrellas porque no ha conseguido engancharme, no tengo claro si por ya conocer parte de la historia o por no estar 100% segura de querer leerlo.
Se me hizo bastante largo, entiendo que por el desarrollo de la historia, aunque aprecié un montón la imaginación de J.R.R. Tolkien (esa capacidad de describir diferentes paisajes y terrenos cada vez, así como de dotar de nombres a las cosas en 2 o 3 lenguas distintas....wow!).
Esperaré un poco para leerme el II y III

I’ll be honest. I couldn’t bring myself to finish this book. I gave up with about 100 pages left, I couldn’t find the motivation to push through what I felt was a dense, dull and difficult read. Descriptions of vast landscapes in the book are extremely hard to imagine and never mind the densely packed lore and map directions. I found myself referencing the movie wherever I could but it all became quite a slog.

Maybe I’ll finish it one day?? I heard the second book is where things get really interesting..

I have been wanting to read this series for quite a long time, but after reading it I feel disappointed. Besides being hard to remember the several names of places and people, there is really nothing wrong with the book itself. It has a lot of great elements and I understand why it is so well renowned. It's because of this that I feel so disappointed. I thought I would really enjoy this series and although I have been assured that it is an acquired taste, I almost feel as if I have somehow failed by not enjoying it.

Not a fan.

I actually think the story itself is a really good one. I love the film franchise. BUT there are soooooo many songs. I just couldn't get through it. Maybe it is because I listened to it on Audiobook and they literally sang all of the songs, but I just dreaded turning it on.

I really enjoyed The Hobbit and was so excited to read this trilogy, but I don't think I will ever pick this book up again.

I gave it two stars simply because I believe the story has so much potential, but I will stick to the movie thank you very much.

Did not finish. I really wanted to love this book and be a Tolkien fangirl but it just wasn't for me. I understand that this book and this series made huge strides in the world of fantasy novels, but if we are being honest, the first half of the book is extremely boring. It's one thing to set up storylines and characters, but it is another to write 200 pages where not much happens. I didn't have a chance to read the last half, as it was too much fluff to keep going. Unfortunately, I will be sticking to the movies from now on.

I know, I know. This is known as one of the greatest books but honestly it was boring. The story was interesting, I liked the characters, it was just the writing style I couldn't deal with. Tolkien did a great job creating a spectacular world and characters in the Hobbit, while still managing to keep it engaging. I cannot say the same for this book. For instance the famed Council of Elrond, was purely info dumping. There are other ways to give backstory than creating a thirty page chapter where nothing happens. He has never heard of "showing not telling" and that is clear.

I listened to the audiobook version, and I appreciated how magical and lyrical the book was in that form, BUT I really had trouble focusing on it and missed 90% of the plot. I really only remember particular scenes, but tbh I have no clue what actually happened… I hate to say that I didn’t enjoy this book because my dad looooves Tolkien and LotR, but I just could not get into it. I mean I started this book back in 2018 and didn’t finish it until 2022… I would listen to a few hours over the course of a week then not go back to it for months…

The Dark Lord, Sauron created one powerful ring to rule them all and hobbit, Frodo Baggins happens to inherit it from his uncle Bilbo Baggins. But with this powerful ring Frodo has enemy’s coming to take it from him. He must go on a journey and destroy it.

In my opinion, a lot of the book has too many details that are very unnecessary. It takes around 200 pages to actually get to the main conflict. I think it would be hard to understand the book if you hadn’t seen the movies beforehand. But the second part was definitely more engaging and interesting. Overall i give this book 2.5/5 stars.

Jag FATTAR inte att jag ÄNTLIGEN läst ut denna! Efter att ha påbörjat den säkert 4 gånger genom åren, har jag tidigare aldrig tagit mig förbi värdshusbesöket där (*spoiler?*) sällskapet träffar Vidstige. Nu läste jag i alla fall klart till allra sista sidan och kan konstatera: Sagan om Ringen är inget för mig. Det är för långsamt, för högtravande, för märkligt tempo och, ibland, helt enkelt för cringe. Egentligen 2,5 stjärnor, och men den där halva består bara av att jag tycker det är så gulligt med Sams crush på Frodo (även om det är skevt med maktobalansen de tu emellan).

Respeto muchísimo el trabajo de J.R.R. Tolkien, porque por algo representa lo que representa. El universo que creó es algo tan maravilloso, pensado y cuidando cada detalle que no encuentro palabras para describirlo. Peeero no le encontré la esencia a los personajes, me parecieron blandísimos y eso, desgraciadamente, no ayudó a mi conexión con el libro. Hubo pocas partes en las que realmente quería saber YA que iba a pasar, quizás no ayudó haber visto la película aunque no recuerde nada. Como dijo Jack Edwards el libro es solo gente caminando, en su mayoría gente talla baja.

I read until page 400/480. While the book certainly has it's charm, and I really like the first 200 pages, the endless environmental descriptions made it so I was less and less motivated to pick the books back up again. For me immersion isn't: being told what lies south, north, east and west of about every location. Also, the characters felt very flat to me a lot of the time. It's a shame because I really like reading fantasy and, considering the Hobbit is one of my favourite books, I really expected to have a great time reading this.

It was way too boring. It took them 200 pages just to get to rivendell and decide what to do with the ring. Too much descriptions. None of the characters have any distinguishing personality, I couldn’t even tell you half of their names. Waaaayy to many songs, I still don’t understand why therer were so many. The book was like 50% worldbuilding and i still could not tell you a single thing about the world.
The writing was also boring? I was forcing myself through. I really hoped to live this because I am a huge fan of fantasy but this was really a slog

It really wasn’t all that interesting to me. The world building was wayyyyy too much in certain parts so I would skip ahead a few pages until I had gotten past section that just gave details about the trees or the grass. I like details and world building but there was just too much in this book. I also just found the story to be particularly dull when written out like this. I don’t know what I disliked about it but I found the movies to be way more enticing than trying to sit down and read the book.

girl this was so hard to get through. i ended up reading it alongside an audiobook because i could not get past the middle of it and that helped to keep my mind from wandering. it’s frustrating cause there’s clearly a solid story in there and i love the movies but im begging mr. tolkien to shut up and get on with the ACTUAL STORY. i have read enough landscape descriptions and travelogues for the rest of my life

it was so hard for me to get immersed in this or relate to any of the characters. the writing style made me feel a million miles removed. but idk i will probably read the rest

This book was really indepth but very slow in developement for me. The whole world and agenda has a really interesting and intreaging feel to it but in terms of character developement I feel like it was just too slow for me. I also feel like the main character was too scrony and helpless. They didnt really help him to bulk up or give him any added hero like qualities after the book starts rolling. The whole time the rest of his team seems to be carrying him along. Overall this im sure is amazing and I know many people love this book but it just wasnt a good fit for me.

The world that Tolkien built is the work of a true genius. His imagination is unrivaled. This story is incredibly compelling, and there’s a reason it’s still so famous.

That being said, I’m shocked how terrible Tolkien is at the actual writing. His prose and dialog are both severely disappointing, bordering amateur. There are moments where the writing is good, but it’s typically when he has a character just giving a factual recounting of an earlier event. I was looking forward to reading this series, now I’m kind of dreading the rest of the books.

Actual rating 2.5*
I think I made a mistake listening to this on audible. Hearing a merry song every 5 mins which is how often it felt like it as there were that many and it just got on my nerves. If I read a book I imagine I could clearly see where the song ended so I could skip but on audible I didn't want to skip 30 seconds in case I missed anything after it.
Just boring. Didn't excite me at all. Last few chapters were okay. I plan to read the others at some point but definitely as a physical book. Disappointed as I really wanted to enjoy this well loved franchise.

I don't see the value of this outside of purely a historical novelty. Mostly it's songs, poems, genealogies (really lame ones where every father and child has almost identical names - wonder why "Arathorn" was never mentioned in the movies), and myths and stories that characters all describe to each other. Tom Bombadil section is incredibly lame. There is a shockingly small amount of plot for such a long fantasy epic. It's honestly amazing that Peter Jackson was able to pull off what he did with this source material.

I can see why so many people enjoy this series since it is not only well written but it manages to paint beautiful, albeit painstakingly detailed, images and landscapes in our minds. However, I found it difficult to immerse myself in this otherworldly fantasy; much of it appearing to be senseless wordplay rather than storytelling. I attempted to continue the tale but after finishing the Two Towers, I believe here is where the journey ends for me.

It's a shame not to be able to savor such a beloved series. These books are like a song I just can't seem to hear yet. At a later time, perhaps.

الصراحة ما اعرف اش اقول…

الكتاب خيّب ظني ولو أني ما اعرف القصة ولا اعرف الأحداث كان ماكملت السلسلة ابداً ولا قرأت الكتابين الثانيه

LMAO I MADE IT😍😍😍😍

It’s not bad at all I just got sick of the indefinite description but that’s what the author’s known for and I knew what I was getting into😔

I absolutely love the movies so I know the story and yet it was still exciting rereading about Aragorn🫦 loml 🤭🤭🤭🤭 but the description WHAAAAAAAA it was never ending.

I stopped reading like 7 months ago and restarted few days ago and finished FINALLY🤩 I’ll read the others one day but not now🖐️

BYE 2023, you’ve been good on a reading scale and life one😘😘 kisses to everyone and happy new year loves

En mi opinión, no es un mal libro, pero a mí me aburrió bastante. Siempre empezaba otro libro para no tener que seguir leyendo este. Aparte de haber tardado como dos años para terminarlo, no me gustó que no hubiera casi personajes femeninos. El único personaje femenino fue la Dama Golondriel y por supuesto era hermosa y delicada, además solo aparece en un capítulo al final del libro. Aunque tenga muchos aspectos negativos, no me parece mala la historia. Me habría gustado tal vez un poco más de suspenso y batalla.

I read this book because I thought I should know some Tolkien, given his cult following and impact on culture and literature. But I absolutely HATED it! My mind kept wandering, so after three weeks of gutting my way through it all I can really tell you is that there was a ring, a lot of walking through the woods, and singing. Lots of singing.

I’m giving it two stars instead of one because I can appreciate that the language Tolkien uses is beautiful and because reading this book did help me answer a NYT crossword answer last week.

I really wanted to give the Lord of the Rings a try as I've generally been reading a lot of high fantasy lately, but perhaps the Fellowship is for a reader of more distinguished taste. It was a bit of a slog for me. It moved very slow without a build to anything specific -- felt like a video game full of side quests. Frodo hasn't had much of a character arc yet -- his seems similar to Bilbo's in the Hobbit, but ... Bilbo actually arrived, and we still have yet to see Frodo evolve. I'm going to slog through the rest, so we'll see.

I wanted to like this book so badly, but it felt like trudging thru sludge to get to the end.

Perhaps I went in with the wrong expectations, thinking it would be a tale of adventure and battle. But really it was a book about depictions of scenery, historical lore and lots of songs. The writing was good in theory I guess, but the overwhelming feeling I had throughout this book was boredom. Huge bummer because I did really enjoy the movies and I love the idea of the world Toliken built, but I can’t bring myself to read the rest of the series.

As much as I love Tolkien for paving the way for mainstream epic fantasy (that’s not to say there haven’t been other authors before him) - I’ve never been a fan of his writing. If you know me, you know that I love epic fantasy. I love all of Brandon Sanderson’s works. I love Brian Staveley, Pierce Brown, Joe Abercrombie, Patrick Rothfuss, George R. R. Martin, etc.

It is a shame that I find Tolkien’s works to be very dragged out, in a way that does not put me to the edge of my seat. They do not have the epic world building that more contemporary epic fantasies have.

Sadly disappointed. I have had friends for more that 25 years tell me how amazing the books are, and I have loved the the movies since they came out so I finally decided to attack the main trilogy. I have been so utterly bored. I understand why so much was cut for the movies, so many side stories that do little to advance the main story line and seem to serve as excuses for random poems and song lyrics. If I ever finish it will be via audio book. I see no way that I could finish these on paper. I am so disappointed as I was hyped to finally ready them.

Oof oof this book was hard to get through. Still an interesting and adventurous read but was much longer than it needed to be. It dragged out every needless detail and all the songs were a bit much. I don't mind a lengthy book but really felt like he was writing just to write and felt myself dragging to get through the story. I really wanted to get into this series & the plot itself was so good but it was hard to follow. I almost hate to say I'd rather watch the movies than read the books. Forgive me 🫢🫣

I love the lore, I love the movies, I love that he invented a genre, I love tom bombadil.

Maybe its because I also generally dont like fiction but this was the most boring book I have experienced in my life, its just walking and then walking and them some more walking. Its the people saw a mountain, and walked up the mountain and set camp in the mountain and slept in the mountain and so forth with specks of interesting things in between long overly detailed accounts of some journey in nature. Just not for me

I had to read this for my English class, which definitely hindered my ability to actually enjoy it (unfortunately this always happens with books that I'm forced to read). I go back and forth on fantasy books but couldn't really get into this book (curse the daily reading quizzes I had to take on this book). The story was overall engaging but I really focused on minuscule details that I was going to be quizzed on. An alright book, but not one I necessarily liked. Probably not going to read the other books.

I’m honestly so sad, I wanted to love this so much but I just couldn’t get past the writing style. So many people love this story and I wanted to as well! I have no sense of nostalgia for this world & I believe thats why a lot of people like this story so much so I am sure not having that affected my enjoyment. It just was not for me. That’s being said it was nice to actually understand what was going on in the book/movie because of my book club. However I will not be continuing on with this world. 🥲

I wanted to like this so much…

I guess the writing style is just very much not for me. Instead of feeling enchanted and intrigued by all the weird names and places mentioned once, never to be relevant again, I just got annoyed at them.
The character work itself is on too simple of a level for me. I like to see deeper dives into the personalities of characters in order to fall in love with them.

I guess I am the odd one out here as everyone else seems to love these books and everyone deems them fantasy royalty.

Where did I (or it) go wrong?!

This was not the book that was promised me :(
I understand what the book did for the genre was quite a big deal and that deserves respect but enjoyment wise this was not it at all... how sad I am to say so.

Too many songs for my taste, too little of interest happening and far too many descriptions of scenery that did nothing for MY imagination.

I (maybe desperately) wanted to like this book and belong to the Tolkien fanbase. As of now, thats nog happening :'(

Consegui acabar depois de ver os filmes, porque pelo amor de deus que livro chato e empurrado, escrita difícil sem a mínima necessidade e tipo para que eu vou precisar saber do detalhe da parede de uma casa que nunca mais vai ser citada, sério 2,5 páginas disso?¿dps da primeira metade não acontece nada nem no livro nem no primeiro e segundo filme, o mundo é bem interessante mas é doido como Nárnia é tipo mil vezes melhor, mas com certeza world building é maravilhoso mas desculpa Nárnia continua sendo o melhor e o Edmund continua sendo o maior.

2.5 stars.

I'm undecided what to make of the Lord of The Rings series so far. For all the hype this series has gotten over the years, going into this first book mostly blind I can't say it was anything resembling a 4-5 star book.

The concept is good, and there was plenty of good throughout the story, although it is hard to follow along with at times, and hard to stay engaged with at others.

I will give it this, the ending does give me hope for the rest of the series and I'm interested to see where it leads to.

good worldbuilding does not necessarily make a good story. they visit so many places but spend too little time in each to get properly invested. the volume of infodumps makes me unsure of what i should actually pay attention to and try to remember (don't say everything because i'm here to read a story not study for an exam). and i wonder how these populations continue on through the sheer lack of women!
generally, there is too much just happening all the time and there is not nearly enough character introspection and interaction for my tastes. i hope i will like the next books better.

Bardzo nie podobała mi się pasywność postaci. Przez całą pierwsza księgę wszystko co osiągnęły postacie można zawdzięczyć przypadkom. Nic tylko deus ex machina. Postać Toma pod żadnym względem nie była interesująca ani przyjemna w czytaniu. Dopiero pod koniec w ostatnim rozdziale Frodo podjął jakąkolwiek decyzję samodzielnie. Wszystkie postacie w drużynie pierścienia są jak wydmuszki na razie. Może Gandalf jest wyjątkiem, ale pewnie po prostu go lubię bo jest tajemniczym magiem i sam wypełniam sobie luki w jego historii. I do tego te piosenki, jprdl.

Booriingggggg. This book was dull, though still leaps and bounds better than The Hobbit, which is an extremely low bar. I love complicated fantasy world building, but that was sort of all this book had going for it, and it wasn’t even that in depth. The characters were very very one - dimensional and flat, and barely even likeable. All the female ones felt sort of weirdly depicted. The plot was good, but slow. The first half was just awful, but the second half was so much better, and kind of enjoyable. The writing style can be a little charming, but just gets grating over time.

Not my favorite fantasy book I've read but this is also coming from someone who's read a lot of romantasy series. I prefered the action packed nature of the Hobbit. Honestly, it's a lot of walking and singing which I'm sure could be a bunch of people's cup of tea but I felt like this book was really meant to set up the rest of the series. One thing I noticed is that compared to other fantasy series, like the Witcher series, the Fellowship of the Ring is lacking comedic relief to break up a realtively bleak plot.

Essa primeira parte até tem alguns elementos interessantes para a literatura de fantasia, considerando que é uma obra seminal para várias outras. Porém, não sei se é um problema da minha tradução, mas achei a narrativa muito pobre: repleta de adjetivações, quebra da atmosfera sombria em vários momentos, diálogos esquemáticos, o que acaba tornando os personagens robóticos. Em suma, não foi uma leitura das mais agradáveis, sobretudo pela expectativa gerada em torno de toda uma fanbase fiel em torno da obra. Mas vamos ao segundo volume. Pode ser que melhore.

I listened to this after Alchemised and I’m almost ashamed to say I enjoyed that more than this. I wanted so badly to like it. It had its moments. I genuinely enjoy Tolkien’s writing, but I couldn’t get into it. Except for Tom Bombadil, favorite character hands down. Weird little guy.

I could do without the singing. Is it a cool way to develop the canon? Yes. Do I want to hear a song for 3+ minutes in every chapter? No.

The narration of the audiobook was 5 stars. Incredible. Maybe I’ll continue the series just to see if it’s me?

There are definitely strong elements here. J.R.R. Tolkien creates an incredibly rich and fully realized world, and the attention to detail is impressive. Certain moments, especially those involving the Fellowship coming together, do feel meaningful.

Still, the pacing didn’t work well for me overall. Large portions of the book feel like travel and description rather than emotional progression. I also found some sections repetitive in tone and structure. It’s clearly influential and well crafted, but I wasn’t fully drawn in emotionally.

I feel like quite a lot of this book was lore dumping and info dropping and was kind of hard to follow, I found myself falling asleep quite a lot trying to get through the book. It felt like the longest 400 pages I have ever got through and frankly I’m glad to be finished,


Gollum following was a fun thing, it is a shocker that Frodo just abandoned everyone but sam to pursue mount doom, I feel that I don’t resonate with many of the characters in this as I did in the hobbit, especially now without Gandalf I have just Frodo and Aragorn.

45/100

If I had to describe this book it would be endless descriptions of paths and topography. Hundreds and hundreds of names. Some characters which had minimal connection to the tale, had three names. Tolkien then thought we needed to know who they were the son of and where they were from and its proximity to some other place that had no bearing on moving to plot along.

I’m glad so many people can get so much from this book and I realise I’m missing a great deal of what people love about the genre whether through ignorance or disinterest. But, I found it very hard going.

My second attempt to read LOTR and I can’t say I enjoyed it. I nearly DNF’d out of sheer boredom, but then I would be responsible for attempting it again in 3-5 years (because it’s my belief that good English teachers have at least a grasp on the classics). Maybe it was the astounding amount of description with really very little plot, maybe it was the narrator of the audiobook I had, or maybe it’s just me, but I really don’t get the hype and will not be continuing to read the series. I’ll watch the movies someday and that will be good enough for me.

i thought the four hour extended version of the movie was bad (long) and then the book started the first act with frodo moving houses for about eight chapters. (longer and somehow feels even less relevant)

it’s long the pacing is shit i fell asleep multiple times reading it and i genuinely feel like this is the one instance where the movie is better than the book (and let it be known i fell asleep watching the movie. multiple times)

“i always fall asleep in the movie so maybe if i read the book ill be more invested” and i fall asleep while reading the book. speaks for itself.

Not. A. Fan. I had to force my way through this, since I don't like to leave books unfinished. This book has more descriptions of the terrain than anything, which was dull and annoying. So much talk of how perilous this journey was going to be, but when anything remotely exciting started to happen, it was over in less than 2 pages. This book is basically all talk, barely any action. I doubt I'll continue with the series.

A close friend recommended this book way back in junior high. The film wasn't out yet and it was the first time i've ever bought a novel...

Guess what?... it took me 2 years to complete! My imagination wasn't high enough to absorb the fantasy story. Eventually, I finished the book but feeling confused and (kinda) traumatised. For a few years after that, I didn't pick up any other novel...:(

Finally, I understood what I read after watching the movie.

I don't usually enjoy these books (although Harry Potter is one of my favorites)-- but I know how popular they are so gave it a chance. Maybe going into it with that attitude I didn't give it a fair shake; although I really wanted to like it! Also the commitment to more books was something that was not thrilling.. at all... to me. I may like the movie better, but the book just moved slow and I couldn't really get into it.

The first 200 or so pages of this classic are just an absolute waste of time. I don't know how this ever became a classic because I don't understand how a critical threshold of readers actually made it to the good parts.

That said, the good parts *are* good. Tolkien had a talent for ominous imagery, almost to the point of horror. Fellowship of the Ring is technically split into two internal books, and my rating of the second book would be four stars.

This is one of those reads that leaves me conflicted and the review is hard for me to write. I know that I want to like the book but I found it very dull and the writing difficult to stick with and at times long-winded for little reason. The Lord of the Rings is a book that time has served well, but not because it's a good book. In my opinion, you either had this book read to you as a child, or you haven't actually read it. It's boring. Slow. Tedious. Tolkien was a linguist and historian, so while his world building is exceptional, the narrative just doesn't compete. Seeing masses of adults rate and love this book just doesn't make sense. You're all lying if you claim this book holds a candle to many novels published today. If this was submitted for publication in the 21st Century, it would be sent back with a large, red REJECTED stamp, no ifs, ands, or otherwise.

The ensemble is largely forgettable, with characters slipping into each other very easily.

Merry and Pippin have no defining attributes besides twinning, so even they admit they don't know why they insisted on going.

Aragorn is not a ”book boyfriend”; he is a confused leader with zero real personality. He does have good working chemistry with Boromir, as they struggle for the leadership they both think they want, but that doesn't go too well does it?

As for Arwen, well, at least she’s pretty AND a princess, but she’s not really a bun for this sausage fest.

Legolas is a fruit. We get it, you're an elf.

Frodo is not a good main character, he's a douche. The only father figure in his life wants to give him two special heirlooms of adventure, believing they will keep Frodo safe. Naturally, Frodo scoffs and acts like a “too-cool-for-school“ teenager receiving a present from their Nanna. He's rude to his friends, he's rude to those who save him, and, of course, he's rude to everyone in the background who helps him through his journey. He's not rude to Sam, but no comment there. He was the prince of Bagend and he's way to cool for this shit.

Gandalf and Gimli are slightly refreshing though. They’re strong yet they make mistakes, unlike the others, who are borderline Gary Stus. In the first book, they give themselves a rememberable presence and an identity. Gandalf’s showdown with the Balrog of Mordor was, however, quite underwhelming …

The story itself also raises a few concerns. On the first evening after I started reading, my fiancé asked me what I thought of the story so far. The only answer I had was: “What story?” Up until Aragorn’s escort service guides our heroes to quasi-safety, it’s just the story of a hopeless hobbit struggling to leave his hometown, and when he finally does, it’s a slow, procrastinating road trip. They find many, many excuses to put a halt in their journey, and even with death on their tail, there’s never a dull to time to miss out on a jolly jingle. I’ll present this particular scene that made me laugh, but not for it’s comedic value:

Chapter XII — Flight to Ford.

The Hobbits and Strider are having a meal under the old stone Trolls that Bilbo encountered on his own adventures in ‘The Hobbit’, when the following, ridiculous conversation ensues.

‘’Won’t somebody give us a bit of a song, while the sun is high?’ said Merry, when they had finished. ‘We haven’t had a song or tale for days.’
‘Not since Weathertop,’ said Frodo. The others looked at him. ‘Don’t worry about me!’ he added. ‘I feel much better, but I don’t think I could sing. Perhaps Sam could dig something out of his memory.’
‘Come on, Sam!’ said Merry. ‘There’s more stored in your head then you let on about.’
‘I don’t know about that,’ said Sam. ‘But how would this suit? It ain’t what I call proper poetry, if you understand me: just a but of nonsense. But these old images here bought it to my mind.’ Standing up, with his hands behind his back, as if he was at school, he began to sing an old tune.

A song about Trolls eating bones then follows, and the song, while cute, peppers the scene in all the wrong ways. It feels like an excerpt from a daytime children’s television show. For Melkor’s sake, puppets may as well have asked their gleaming hosts to perform a song to the tune ‘If you’re happy and you know it’.

Countless people have praised this book to me through the years as a fantasy epic, or a grand adventure, but there has not been a single chapter so far that hasn’t included a song. I wasn’t from a household where bedtime stories would include books like these, and I honestly feel as if I missed out on something. I can’t see any child under eight hating the magic and gayness these books present, because in all respects, they are written like an epic fairy tale. A far cry from serious fantasy though.

Tolkien was, as we all know, a master linguist and historian, and the world he has built is beyond exceptional. I’m thoroughly enjoying the history behind all of the landmarks they encounter, and the many languages are both intriguing and engaging. Middle-earth is an immersive, magical land, and I love the expositional history of fabled landmarks like the Mines of Moria, or Lothlórien.

I was initially considering abandoning this adventure, but I persevered, and as this appears to be the largest instalment, it seems as though the hard work is over. The ending was somewhat redeemable, with a little slice of action and the start of a real adventure, so I’m mildly interested to see if the story maintains its newfound maturity.

Also, Tom Bombadil sucks.

The Fellowship of the Ring has impressive world-building, but I found the story painfully slow. The long descriptions and frequent detours made it difficult to stay engaged, and some characters felt distant rather than compelling. I appreciated the imagination behind Middle-earth, but the pacing made this a much less enjoyable read than I expected.

The Fellowship of the Ring is undeniably patient in its buildup, but the slow-burn approach felt more drawn out than rewarding for me. Tolkien spends a great deal of time on descriptions, history, and travel before the story gains real momentum, and I often felt the pacing dragging. I understand the purpose of the gradual immersion, but it required more patience than I was willing to give.

2.5 ⭐ Started: June 24, 2024. Ended: July 31, 2024.

The Fellowship of the Ring follows Frodo Baggins after his cousin, Bilbo, leaves a powerful ring in his care. Danger follows him like a shadow, and he's forced to leave behind everything he knows—but not everyone. His closest friends and longtime mentor are there to see to his survival and success. Where will the ring take him next, and what new friends (and foes) lie waiting for him?

I am not much of a high fantasy person (I think). I cannot recall if I have ever read a similar novel. You can't go wrong with Lord of the Rings being your introduction to fantasy in any case. I somehow managed to avoid learning about the characters and plot in my 20 years on Earth, so experiencing everything for the first time was a blessing.

This book was world building info dumps, travel sequences, and character monologues held together by the power of friendship and good vibes. I realized I am not built to read books where half the time is spent reaching a destination only for there to be a new one.

That being said, I didn't *not* enjoy it. The characters truly are the heart of the novel (the ones whose names I remember at least). I adore Sam, he is the sweetest, and he deserves every happiness. I am still salty he got separated from Bill (is that considered a spoiler?)

We will see if my opinion improves after watching the movie for the first time. As of right now, I am hoping the later books involve less travel. I want there to be more plot, but maybe traveling is just the plot of adventure novels? I am not exactly an expert on the subject.

On the bright side, I now know new words to describe marshes, hills, and streams. They will totally be integrated into my vernacular. Totally.

I found large parts of this book to be exceedingly dull. The first 100 pages or so were painful to read. I also dislike how often characters are telling each other about things that have happened, it is a very boring method of exposition.

Like many people in recent years, LotR has been on my list of books to read ever since I fell in love with the films upon their first release. And after reading The Hobbit earlier this year (which I absolutely loved), I was truly excited to start the trilogy. Tolkien is at his best when his characters are in action, and sometimes even the dialogue is unexpectedly witty. I knew Lord of the Rings would be a darker tone, and lengthy, but I figured if I tackled The Hobbit, I might enjoy Tolkien's masterpiece.

And for part of The Fellowship of the Ring, Tolkien has those aspects. Especially in writing about the hobbits and the Shire (the first 100 or so pages of the book, which was my favorite part). Like what many other reviewers have pointed out, Tolkien's writing does get long-winded and - dare I say it - boring. He goes into detailed from the smallest hikes or stops the Fellowship members take. Some of the adventures the characters had I found a bit random and out of place (I don't think I fully understand Tom Bomdadil, yet at the same time I'm not sure the reader is really suppose to...). Or I felt details were described unnecessarily and would of been better if written later on. For example, the prologue "Concerning Hobbits" would of been best if brief or at the end of the trilogy. Tolkien could of just recounted Bilbo's adventures or more specific things related to those adventures. But he goes more in-depth about a made-up history of characters who, as readers, we have not encountered yet/never will. Eventually, I also found myself skipping many of the songs, many of which just seemed to rehash what has happened or what is about to happen. So why should we care to read it?

The characters of the fellowship, especially the hobbits (can you tell I really love hobbits?), are depicted as heroic, brave, and loyal. It is Tolkien's goal in creating the underdog hero as seen through Frodo and even Sam. Frodo's line "I shall take the ring, though I do not know the way," will always ALWAYS break my heart, no matter in what storytelling medium. Of course, there are some slight character differences from the movie as expected. Yet nothing too major. For example, Legolas is different - meaning he has more to say and do than in Peter Jackson's films. Or Frodo is less quiet than Elijah Wood's portrayal. He is, to me, even more heartbreaking as Tolkien describes how Frodo longs to be with Bilbo and the Shire after starting this burden several times. And as a reader, I couldn't help but felt the same way - though for a much different reason.

With that said, I still admire the characters and mythology Tolkien independently built despite the his garrulous writing style. I would sometimes just google certain terms or characters in Tolkien's world only to spend 2+ hours reading more about hobbits, wizards, elves, and men of Middle Earth. The influences of Norse and Western mythology are beautifully done (when you discover them), and I could only wish I knew more about the topic to appreciate the work even more.

Overall, I am disappointed with Tolkien as a writer. Similar to C.S. Lewis' Out of the Silent Planet, FotR gets wordy and lost my attention many times. However, unlike Lewis' book, there is a more epic story to be told. I hate to be one of those people who like a film more than a great work of fiction, but I can't help it. If anything, though, reading this made me fall in love with the film even more. If you are a lover of Jackson's interpretation, reading Tolkien's original books will make you appreciate how creative, detailed, and close the films and the original story can be. I still want to finish the trilogy due to my love of Middle Earth - I just wish I fell in love with the books more.

Before I begin my review, I'd like to specify the exact amount of time it took me to finish this book: one year, seven months, and eleven days. Yes, you read that right. It took me nearly TWO YEARS to complete a book with only 576 pages.

After a long and arduous journey I finally closed it for good last night. And when I say for good, I mean for good. I never, ever, EVER want to read this book again. Perhaps some day, very far into the future when I'm old and knobbly and have nothing better to do but fly around the house in my hoverchair, I'll pick it up one more time and see if I like it then. But I can say without hesitation that as of now, in this moment in time, The Fellowship of the Ring is the most boring book I've ever read. Not even kidding. The only reason I gave it an extra star is because I love the story itself and find Tolkien's world-building absolutely fascinating. He was no doubt a genius of a man and created something profoundly exquisite, an accomplishment that even the best fantasy writers have trouble emulating. The geography, languages, mythology, history, and culture of Middle Earth are presented strategically throughout the book, although the vast amounts of information are sometimes a bit much. And honestly, the amount of detail he put into Middle Earth overshadowed the characters and main plot.

I've found that a lot of fantasy writers have one of two problems: either they have three-dimensional characters with an underdeveloped world, or a three-dimensional world with underdeveloped characters. Tolkien suffered from the latter. If I hadn't seen the movies, I wouldn't even know what to say about the characters. Just that they're on a quest and form friendships and stuff. Frodo is quite drab as a protagonist and the supporting cast isn't all that interesting either. Aragorn is really the only one who seems to have a complexity about him, while everyone else is just there and helping out in whatever way they can. Gandalf is cool but it's almost as if he has no faults. He's too perfect. To me that's just as bad as creating a useless character; instead of offering nothing to the story, he offers too much. He saves the day constantly and acts as a deus ex machina, leaving much to be desired from the other characters. He literally has to be captured and/or dead so that the others can show their own wits and strength. Same thing happens in the movies, but at least in that case the characters are developed enough so that he doesn't always steal the limelight.

Aside from the lame character development, there's wayyyy too much description that goes on. I understand that Tolkien was from a different time and that he was deft in creating his world piece by piece, but his lengthy exposition is wearisome and distracting. The book could easily lose 100-200 pages and still prove to be an excellent read. In fact it would be better because there wouldn't be a bunch of inconsequential filler that puts you to sleep. There's too much traveling and too many details of trees and rocks and grass. I know what trees and rocks and grass look like. Unless they provide some significant detail to the story then we don't need to hear about them over and over. It would be one thing if he mentioned the setting briefly but he describes inanimate objects for two to three paragraphs at a time. And the songs! Don't even get me started on the songs. I have no idea why he felt the need to include so many, especially when they add nothing to the plot. It's insane how much time he put into something so trivial. That was his way I guess. He obviously wanted to give the reader a unique, vivid experience, but the good parts of the story got lost in the process.

I still love this series as a whole and I always will. Unfortunately the writing is unbearable for me. If Tolkien had condensed the book into something more streamlined - like he did with The Hobbit, for instance - I would enjoy it immensely. Alas, that was not his intent.
