The world is changed. I feel it in the water. I feel it in the Earth. I smell it in the air. Much that once was is lost, for none now live who remember it...."

So begins The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring, directed by Peter Jackson and based on the book of the same name by J. R. R. Tolkien. The first installment of the famous Lord of the Rings trilogy, The Fellowship of the Ring is set in the fantasy realm of Middle-Earth, where the races of Men, Elves, Dwarves, and little people known as Hobbits live among each other. However, the race of Men is in decline with no king to rule, and tensions have risen between Elves and Dwarves. The Hobbits live in peace in the Shire, and they (mostly) keep to themselves. But all of these races must unite when a long-believed-dead ancient evil rises once again: the Dark Lord Sauron, ruler of the fiery lands of Mordor.

FotR is centered around Frodo Baggins (Elijah Wood), a Hobbit who lives a peaceful life in the Shire with his uncle Bilbo (Ian Holm) and his friends Samwise "Sam" Gamgee (Sean Astin), Peregrin "Pippin" Took (Billy Boyd), and Meriadoc "Merry" Brandybuck (Dominic Monaghan). Together with his fellow Hobbits and the wizard Gandalf (Ian Mckellen), Frodo begins a long, torturous journey to Mount Doom, a dangerous volcano deep in Mordor, to destroy the ancient One Ring, the source of Sauron's power. Other cast members include Viggo Mortensen as Aragorn, Liv Tyler as Arwen, Orlando Bloom as Legolas, John Rhys-Davies as Gimli, Cate Blanchett as Galadrial, Sean Bean as Boromir, Christopher Lee as Saruman, Hugo Weaving as Elrond, and Andy Serkis in a brief appearance as Gollum.

I'll be honest and say that I hadn't seen any of the LotR movies until a year ago, and I've never even read a page of Tolkien's works. However, these films are quite entertaining, and they hold a special place in the hearts of many people. A little refresher course for newcomers: the whole trilogy was filmed back-to-back in New Zealand over several years, and production had begun even years before then. Peter Jackson and his team went to great pains to make these films a faithful adaptation of Tolkien's text, and it comes through in each frame of this trilogy. The costumes are beautifully detailed/handmade, the weapons are real, and a vast majority of the locations, such as Rivendell, Amon Hen, Lothlorien, and the Shire, were filmed in real places in New Zealand. It's also noteworthy to mention that very little CGI was used, mainly as a last resort. And while some of the visual effects show their seams, they largely hold up, especially when it comes to the Balrog in Moria.

Also deserving of praise is the music composed and conducted by Howard Shore. From the opening notes that play over the beginning logos to the main theme of the film, Shore does a bang-up job of capturing this fantasy realm and its inhabitants. Without giving much away, a personal favorite track of mine would be the music that plays after the Fellowship escapes Moria and they've just lost a comrade; the choir that plays in the background along with the soft instruments really bring you into the pain and sadness of such a terrible loss.

The performances in this film are also worthy of mention. Wood perfectly captures a bright-eyed Hobbit being thrust into a high-stakes adventure, and he has a great dynamic with everybody around him, especially McKellen and Astin. Speaking of which, McKellen sells Gandalf as an aloof, goofy wizard with knowledge and wisdom beyond his years, while Astin perfectly conveys Sam's initial bumbling demeanor and later bravery as he resolves to help Frodo in his quest. Mortensen is more calm and reserved as heir to the throne of Men, but with a strong moral compass. Bloom and Rhys-Davies fill their respective roles as Legolas and Gimli quite well, and Bean's conflicted performance as Boromir makes the ending of the film all the more impactful.

Give the trilogy a watch, and I hope you enjoy it as much as countless others.

I tried unsuccessfully tackling this book 4 times before. This time I finally finished. I don't think I would give any other series that sort of treatment, so I guess LoTR gets brownie points for that. Not that that's an indication of how good the books are in content, just an indication of how important they are to the genre that I felt I had to try to read them so many times.

So I didn't love it. I think that's obvious from the fact it took me 5 tries to get through the first book. But I did find I enjoyed it more than I thought I would from the first 4 tries. It took a different mindset to get through this book, one that I maybe wasn't mature enough to adopt the last few times I tried conquering it. I read Fellowship like I would any scientific paper. Not to entertain me, but to learn. And I'm glad I took that mindset, because the entertaining moments were few and far between. But there was a sort of entertainment in going on the wiki and clarifying points, looking up locations on the map, and googling Middle Earth folk legends to learn about the history of the world. So the best part for me wasn't actually the reading, it was the extra wiki-ing about in between reading.

There are some parts I can't complain about. Tolkien was obviously a smart dude who crafted a unique world. I don't get any Christopher Paolini vibes from him. The world building is monstrous, the world is, without a doubt, lived-in, and the writing, beyond some weird stylistic choices I'm chalking up to time differences, is solid and sometimes even beautiful. I can't really complain about the clichés either, because people imitating Tolkien are the ones who made them clichés in the first place. Though my limited knowledge of the history of Fantasy does let me know that some of the stuff Tolkien is thought to have invented was invented before him. But there's a lot of parts I can complain about.

There's the poetry. I skipped nearly all of it. I'm not highfalutin enough for that. To borrow a phrase from a friend of mine, I'm straight up Piper Smurf (low flutin'). Characters are always breaking out into song or verse at weird times, and maybe that's how the world worked before we had the internet, but now we have the internet, and I'm going to use the time I saved by not reading poetry to watch Netflix instead.

The plot is one big travelogue, which is great for learning about the world, but not so great for the actual plot. Travelogue Fantasy is my least favourite type of Fantasy because nothing interesting happens. There's too much description about things that don't matter. Tolkien likes to tell, not show. The pacing and focus feels weird sometimes (like a whole chapter in Lorien, but a couple paragraphs on Gandalf versus Durin's Bane. Or Boromir dying quickly essentially offscreen [I know that happens in Book 2, whatever, and maybe there's a POV chapter later, I haven't got there]). The first couple hundred pages are a slog (that took me 5 tries to get through), infodumps are frequent, there's this pathological focus on genealogy that hasn't quite disappeared from the genre yet, the dialogue is comically bad at times ("Yeah... he died." "Hark! Bad news you bring"), and there are about 4 different synonyms for every made-up word.

It seems to me that the book was written, not to be an engaging story by itself, but rather to showcase a world Tolkien had already built, and to let him explore a couple of basic themes that have since (or arguably 'already') been beaten into the ground in Fantasy, like good vs evil or corruption of power. I prefer my stories written the other way around. So my take away? Tolkien's a great worldbuilder, even a great writer, but he's not a great storyteller. But I'm just some idiot who likes reading Fantasy in his spare time. Tolkien studied English and poetry and stuff (see, my vocabulary screams "I studied science") and sold a buttload of books, so obviously he's doing something right.

Needless to say: DULL

Obviously it’s an old book, but my review is purely my opinion based on what I like not how revered a classic it is or how extraordinary it was for its time.
First it’s very slow paced, it takes 100 pages for Frodo to even leave in the first place. It does mean there is nice descriptions and depth but it makes it really hard to get interested when nothing happens. It also makes the characters dull because they barely do anything, they have personalities that could be described in a sentence. This could all be explained with the fact it is the first book, but I will not be reading the other books any time soon because of how this book was. I personally believe that the first book in a series should stand alone fine and not rely upon its sequels to complete a full story, as if the first book cannot captivate a reader to want to read the next ones then they serve no purpose at all. Building on the point of how long this book is for such little content, it is such a shame that there were points where it was all talk no show. So many things were plainly said when it would have made the story much more immersive to represent such things. For example it was just said that Gimli and Legolas became friends. Their friendship would have been so easy to root for if it was just described slowly throughout the book, them doing actions that friends would do. But instead they have little dialogue together, rare scenes of them interacting as friends and the reader is just supposed to understand they are friends now. There is simply too many characters that are all one dimensional, so there is little space to build any meaningful relationships between them. Bilbo and Gandalf were the only two that actually felt realistic in their dynamic, and their relationship was mostly shown through actions towards each other and dialogue. But what about Sam and Frodo? Well Sam is a default sidekick which makes sense, he also does have personal interests and hobbies. He has a motivation other than just serving his master, he wants to go on an adventure and meet elves which gives him so much more depth than Merry and Pippin who are just there and loyal to Frodo just because. If Frodo was shown to use his riches to help hobbits in need or was a valiant leader it would make sense for them to follow along but Frodo doesn’t even seem all that good of a friend. Frodo doesn’t seem to be all that much of anything. He spends the entire book doing whatever he is told and never making decisions for himself, only when Gandalf who was telling him what to do is gone, and he is forced to make a choice does he ever decide something. And even then he takes days to come to a conclusion, which was fairly obvious and he only decides because Boromir basically attacks him. He has no interests, no hobbies, no job, no personality and no uniqueness at all. The only thing is that he has the ring, which he did not go on an adventure to find, he did not win it in battle, he did not discover it while searching for treasure, he was given it by an uncle. That would be fine if he was interesting in the slightest but unfortunately he could be replaced with a mannequin and the story would be the same. The names are so perfect though, the world building is obviously unmatched and it’s an icon. I would give 4 stars but I will never be touching this book again.

First of all, I'm sorry. I'm sorry that I didn't love this book. I understand completely why others love it so much and it certainly deserves the great reputation it has earned. The plot is interesting, the writing gives everything plenty of detail, and the world Tolkien has created is legendary! I still can't get over the fact that he made an entire language for the books, not to mention the centuries of history he has written.But all this being said, I didn't really enjoy this book. Once again, I'm so sorry.

Honestly, I don't think I would have finished this book if I hadn't been reading it for school. There were chapters here and there that I found really interesting but just not enough for me to love this. I wanted so badly to love it, but I just don't. After a while the story just felt kind of slow, like so much was happening yet so little at the same time. Many things in this book felt very drawn out to me, and the amount of details seemed excessive. Of course I don't dislike descriptions, I just couldn't understand these very well. They weren't helpful to me, because I still could not picture what was going on or what the setting looked like.

I think I might have had more luck with this book if I went into it with an understanding of what it was like. I imagined this series as being quite different than what I've read so far. I think I'll still finish the series but after taking a bit of a Tolkien break for a while.

Once again, I entirely understand why so many people love this and I'm sorry that I don't. Maybe someday I'll read this again and understand the genius that is The Lord of the Rings, but for now I'll stick with The Hobbit.

Also, I've heard that a lot of people don't like Tom Bombadil, but for me he was the best part of this book.

Real rating: 1.5

Tolkien couldn't write worth a damn. I could say that, but it would mostly be a lie.

He is revered as the father of the modern fantasy genre; praised as a literary genius like no other has been or ever will be. And you know what? He deserves some of that praise. The imagination and devoted research, and sheer, obsessive attention to detail put into this book has made Middle-Earth a world as complex and enormous as our own. And only Tolkien could have done it; he is the only one in the world who could have created the intricate web of family lines, wars, legends, myths, species, and folklore that makes Middle-earth the world it is. He is also the only person who could create an Elvish language that actually sounds like a language and not incoherent, drunken nonsense. He should be applauded for that.

If I wasn't so completely apathetic to this freakin' doorstop, I might even clap for him.

420 pages. 420 pages spent on naming the cardinal directions and desrcibing hills instead of developing characters beyond their name and species. The only people (out of eight main characters in the Fellowship)who aren't completely interchangeable are Gandalf and Sam. Gandalf because he is the Old Wise Mentor and Sam because of his complete devotion and loyalty to Frodo. And occasional bursts of humor. And mad jester skills. You know what? Fuck it, Sam is awesome. He is a shiny red pebble among gray stones.

Seriously, Tolkien; what the hell is the point in all of this? Why do you expect me to care that Frodo is the Ring-bearer and the only hope for an entire world when the only reason I can even tell him from a tree is because of his name and the fact that he's a hobbit? Why do you expect me to care about Middle-earth, for that matter, when the only people you've shown me who live in it are as sympathetic as dust?

And don't get me started on Sauron; the one hope I have of some excitement in this wasteland of boredom does nothing more than sit up in his DARK AND SPOOKY FORTRESS in his DARK AND SPOOKY FOREST, leaving his less-menacing-than-a-newborn-kitten minions to do all the work. Damn him. Why couldn't he fly down in a rage of hellfire and brimstone and just burn everyone in the Fellowship? That would have been spectacular, and awesome, and a total cop-out from even pretending to want to write an epic quest - but I wouldn't have cared, because the book would be over.

The Fellowship of The Ring reads like my middle-school history textbooks: long, depressing to read, history that stretches on forever with a confusing amount of names and events, half-hearted attempts to make the reader care about whatever it is explaining in the first place and how it relates to the present day and, most importantly; a sense of overwhelming relief warring with drowsiness when I reach the last page. I think I might even feel nostalgic...

My first experience with The Lord Of The Rings was when my father showed me a new movie he had bought. I was still very young but remember vividly how i watched a few hobbits undertaking a dangerous and interesting journey. The hobbits faced quite a few challenges while still retaining a sense of humor. They encountered other characters and together they set off for an even grander and more dangerous journey. I was blown away by the story told by Peter Jackson.

When the second movie was released i begged my father to go see it in theaters. I was anxious to know if Frodo and Sam would be able to complete their journey. Just like the first one i really enjoyed this movie.

By the time the third movie was released i had become a fanboy. I liked the entire story as told by Peter Jackson and wanted to know more about it. I started googling everything about The Lord Of The Rings. As i grew older i started to amass quite a bit of knowledge about it.

I don't know why but it took me a long time to finally start reading the journey as told by Tolkien. While English is not my native language i still wanted to experience it in it's original language. I started reading with high expectations.

I really wanted to like this book. But even while being so biased i still have to be honest and give this book a low rating. Instead of the epic journey as shown by the movies i found a dull and slow travel guide of Middle-Earth. Tolkien described so many rolling hills and sharp cliffs. He filled pages describing every species of tree he could think of. He wrote about the birdless sky and the darkness within the mines of Moria.

I know Middle-Earth better then my own backyard. Give me a map of Middle-Earth and i can show you the way the companions have traveled and every tree they encountered in the process. This is what annoys me. I know nothing interesting about the characters. I know that Sam doesn't like boats and can't swim. I know that Legolas can walk over snow and can see further than anyone else. That's everything Tolkien talks about. I want to now what keeps them up at night! I want to know their story. What do they feel? What do they think about this quest? Peter Jackson portrays Aragorn as a conflicted and interesting man. Tolkien portrays him as a know-it-all travel guide.

I can keep finding reasons why the movies where so much better than the first book i have read. I don't know if i will ever find the strength to read the other two. I still like the lore of The Lord Of The Rings but i think i have to give preference to the cinematic version.

I know the world sees Tolkien's work as the basis for modern fantasy but i honestly struggled to keep interested in the story he told. Maybe it's just me. Maybe it's the difference in years between the creation of this work and my reading of it. I don't know. I only know that i have read books with a lot more zeal and vigor.

Although I enjoyed imagining this world, it was just so incredibly boring and slow. I read this for school (I chose it myself), and for a part of our assessment of it, we had to talk about the climax. I kid you not, I literally had to GOOGLE what the climax was, because I honestly had no idea when it happened. This book is ONLY setting groundwork for the books after it.

After failing to get into the series in my more formative years, I thought I try out the series again in my post-collegiate years. There has always been so much hype surrounding the books and movies that it would have been foolish to miss what all the fuss is about. Unfortunately for me, I just could not get into the story.

By now, we all know the general outline of the plot. There's a great and powerful, but evil, ring that must be destroyed at the footsteps of the enemy. The Fellowship recounts the backstory of the ring and the formation of a diverse group put together to destroy that ring.

The front half of the novel is not paced well. In fact, a majority of the time is spent following the Hobbits as the walk from point A to point B. Along the way they are being chased by the evil Dark Riders, or Ringwraiths, who are deft enough to track down the Hobbit's to a very particular location, but are ultimately unable to find them just feet away. The Hobbit's near-escapes just seemed too convenient, especially with the bumbling nature of the Hobbits themselves.

Of course every novel must have it's exposition and the second half of the novel picks up greatly. Here we meet elves, forge the fellowship, venture into the orc-ridden mines of Moria, and press ever closer to Mt. Doom. Tolkien here also feels the need to describe everything about the journey- the walking, the fatigue- instead of developing his characters. At the end of this novel I couldn't tell you the difference between Merry and Pippin; they are one in the same to me. There is almost no dialogue or banter while traversing the land, only at rest stops and meal and, even then, Tolkien feels the need to subject us to song and verse needlessly.

While I respect the novel for being regarded as one of the quintessential fantasy novels, I just wasn't surprised with anything presented in the novel. There weren't many moments that made me really question anything or say "Aha." Perhaps I'm a victim of the cultural phenomenon that is The Lord of the Rings. I went in knowing the story, having seen the movies, so there were no surprises left-Tom Bombadil being the exception. But even this small character really has no major role in the story. That's the theme in the Fellowship that doesn't quite sit well with me; there is a ton of Middle Earth lore to be explored, but a lot of it has nothing to do with the journey itself. It may be great for some, but it didn't read well for me.

Overall, I would recommend this novel to someone who wants to be immersed in a rich history of Middle Earth stories and anecdotes, but also wants to follow the story of the mighty One Ring. If you just want to be up-to-date on your pop culture, the movies do a great job of honing down the journey to its essentials and capturing the spirit of the novel simultaneously.

reviews.text:
I'm going to assume everybody knows most of the plot by now so there will be a few spoilers.

I know this is a classic but I honestly didn't enjoy reading it that much- I probably would have put it down if it wasn't Lord of the Rings. Tolkien's world building is fantastic, his attention to detail is amazing.... but it's just not very readable. Tolkien describes every painful detail and goes into the history so often it's more like reading a history book rather than a novel in places, with all the references to history and lineage. We get the location described in 360 degrees for hundred of miles in every direction, we get the route described in every turn, we get buildings described floor by floor, ect.

Unfortunately we don't get this sort of detail in the characters- they world they move through is incredibly detailed but the characters themselves have very little distinct personality, the only time I really felt like I new what the characters were feeling was when they grieved Gandalf. The characters are better described than in the hobbit where the dwarfs are fairly interchangeable but not by much. The concept of 'evil' as being absolute- there is nothing redeeming about the orcs is something I'm not a big fan of- the evil seems to have no motivation and we are expected to take for grated that evil is evil.

I found the first 3/4 really slow going (it took me about 2 months to get past the first 3/4), it seems like a lot of the novel is spent waiting- Frodo takes 17 years to set out with the ring (and after being told by Gandalf that he'll need to leave in april he eventually leaves in september) the first part of the trip all the hobbits spend hours at every meal and take naps after lunch,they meet up with strider and eventually get to Rivendell but then they spend 2 months waiting in Rivendell after the council of Elrond (they are waiting for scouts to return but what the scouts say appears to have no impact on what they then do so why did they need to wait at all). We keep being told that the dark powers are amassing but it's difficult to buy that characters are in a hurry and worried about timing when they spend so long not doing anything.

There were also a few things that made me quite uncomfortable when reading it; I found Sam's servantile attitude towards Frodo uncomfortable, it was sweet in places but it's also uncomfortable the way he treats Frodo as his better and all the other characters treat sam as an extension of Frodo.

Also the concept of 'better' races with more pure blood is really uncomfortable to read about.

Very rarely do I enjoy a film better than a book, but for me the film is significantly better- it cuts out everything I disliked and replaces it with characters with personality. Also was I the only one disappointed that Gandalf said "You can't pass" rather than "You shall not pass"?

2.5 stars. This book, while it had its merits, was ultimately disappointing to me.
Firstly, the good:
The basic plot of the book is great - however, that was known to me before I began reading, as I've watched the movie versions of the books many times over. I think Tolkien deserves some credit for his fantastic imagination. In this book, he's managed to dream up a richly described world full of magical and mystical creatures (some of which are known throughout various legends and folklore and others which have been completely invented by him), and intertwine those different beings in to an epic story.
I largely enjoyed the additional aspects of the story line that weren't covered in the movies. It makes for a fuller and more understandable story.
The slow pace of the book, while frustrating early on, actually allows you to take in all of the vast amount of information Tolkien provides about different areas on the map, different groups or peoples and their 'status' as friend or foe. This would probably become very confusing if rushed through.
The final quarter of the book is where the major appeal lies for me (before that it's quite pedestrian). This contains the meetings at Rivendell between all of the races, the forming of the fellowship and the first part of their voyage to Mount Doom, including the episodes in Moria and Lothlorien. Tolkien finally builds some momentum here and it's much more enjoyable to read.
That brings me on to the bad... while the final section is definitely a marked improvement on what came before, it still lacks something for me.
I feel a little like Tolkien is better at creating a story than telling one. On the evidence of this book and the Hobbit (which I read last year), he lacks the ability to really connect you with the characters. Although many of the main protagonists aren't human, I want to feel their humanness, their emotions, in order for me to have empathy with them and I often feel that this is just an account of their actions rather than their feelings. In addition, during much of the dialogue, it's unclear how the characters are saying what they're saying. 'said [character]' is used so much. It's difficult to understand whether it's a passionately made point, a whisper, a shout. Plus, a lot of the iconic and rousing dialogue that featured in the film did not come from the book, which was a little disappointing.
Finally, there is way too much waffle at the beginning about things that really aren't important. The details provided, such as the exact scale and dimensions of the Shire, feels like scene setting on an industrial scale.
Despite the low rating, I'm actually looking forward to picking up the Two Towers as some momentum was definitely built during the final quarter and I'm hopeful that this will carry through to the next book.

Well, let me apologies in advance to those of you I am probably going to offend with my review of this book. I mean no harm, and in the grand picture of everything my review means little in regards to the importance of this book to history... This is just my opinion and my reminder to myself that I never want to submit myself to the slow torture that is reading a Tolkien book. I almost hated this book, what stopped me from giving it one star is that I could see the ghostly bones of a good or great story buried underneath all the crap.

For the past two years I have been trying to mix in a few classics and non-fiction to my reading lists to help keep me from drowning in fluff, paranormal, sci-fi and YA. I though since I enjoy fantasy book I would add The Lord of the Rings to my list for the year since it has a reputation to be this epic fantasy adventure, a true work of literary genius if you will. Now I tend to read fairly quickly and a 458 page book normally takes me just over 2 days, but this monstrosity took me over 5 days... I kept waiting for it to get interesting, sure there were good parts, but they were so few and far between they got lost in the endless over description of everything. The dialog was awkward and where the hell were the females in this world, I swear I could count all the women in this story on one hand. Having multiple names for one character was also annoying. I could deal with the exotic name, books I read often have names like that, but don't keep switching them for the same person it gets confusing especially when you are having a difficult time paying attention as it is. I also do not care for stories that mix in random verse, I'm not sure why but it often bothers me in other stories as well. I think it messes up my reading flow. From what I could tell most of the poem or song, while possibly entertaining, divulged little of the plot so I started skipping them. For most of this story I just felt like nothing was happening, the plot was so slow to move and by the end I decided I really don't care for what happens to Frodo or the ring and I will not be reading the remaining two books. Basically I found the story incredibly boring and the characters either were not developed enough to make me care for them or the endless dragging on of the plot killed any spark of interest I could have developed for them. If I had not made a pledge to read some classics I would not have gotten past page 100 of this book. Reading this book was like taking medicine, I know it is supposed to be good for me but it sure didn't taste good.

The reason the term, "standard fantasy setting", can be said today without a hint of irony, is all because of a man called J.R.R. Tolkien and his most famous so-called trilogy: The Lord of the Rings. I say so-called trilogy because The Lord of the Rings is actually one book, that for economic reasons, was published in three separate printings. Tolkien is credited for giving the fantasy genre reason to be respected and for creating the fantasy tropes commonly used today. Chances are that if you've been alive for the past ten years you've at least heard of the Lord of the Rings, but if you've been living under a rock for the past 10 years, the basic premise is this, a hobbit, which is a small human looking creature with hairy feet, called Bilbo Baggins passes down all of his possessions to his nephew Frodo. Among the possessions is a magical ring with the ability to turn whoever wears it, invisible. It is later revealed by Gandalf the Grey, a powerful human wizard and close friend of Bilbo and Frodo, to be, "The One Ring To Rule Them All": a ring of immense power that turns whoever wields it for long periods of time to the side of evil. Frodo and Gandalf, along with other adventurers, then set out to destroy the Ring in the only place it can be destroyed: Mount Doom. Now the biggest problem I have with the book is that it feels like a giant set-up with no real payoff, which probably stems from the fact that it is only the first part of the book, and is just a setting up a glaring cliffhanger. For example, at the end, nothing is resolved. Now I recognize that naturally the first "book" isn't going to answer or resolve everything, but there should be at least some kind of payoff in the end instead of just an enormous "TO BE CONTINUED". The other big complaint I have is with the main character: Frodo. He's a boring young hero archetype: a wide-eyed innocent with a heart of gold forced out of his comfortable life to go on a dangerous adventure. He's also completely useless, and the only reason he even goes along is that he has the mystical "One Ring" and that no one else wants to risk exposure to the Ring's corruption. I realize that this archetype is used to emphasize Frodo's personal growth, but at the end, Frodo has very little growth, and I find myself laughing whenever Frodo suggests going alone to Mount Doom without his much more interesting and capable companions. So, in conclusion, The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring is fine if you want a history lesson on where current fantasy tropes come from, but just remember, it's all set-up with no payoff.

Tried it in German, tried it in English, tried it as audio book, watched the movie... I can't. I can't be asked to enjoy it.
I find it a tedious and annoying experience.
Having been a geek before there was a word for that, Tolkien and his opus magnum ought to have been in my repertoire, right?
I love fantasy, and immersed myself deeply into role playing games beginning at 10 or 11, book-wise in the novels, the twisted and confusing ones, the long runners, the old ones, the sagas, the cheap paperbacks, the ones from the 60s, the stories from the 30s, the books from the 90s.
I practically like all of it. The highs, the lows, the sad, the solmn, the simple and the funny ones.
But the Lord of the Rings... has always bored me out of my skull.
Has no one ever thought about how cliché the characters are? How flat. I'd say, I hated Sam, but I also hated all the rest of them. Gandalf. The Nazgul. The humans. All of them!
No, the elves I hated the most, we have a winner.
The story seems like it was cut down to a third and then filled up again with piff, puff and pages full of ... those things, until one of the overly flat characters says and does the obvious and the expected. With fairytale creatures in the middle. But not super-charged fairytale-inspired creatures, the mild regular white ones without flavour will be just fine, thank you.
And no one, and that is a promise, has ever had, has now or will ever have any sex or a thought about it. Or grime, or dirt, or grease or booze, or grit or grudge or love or lust, anything.
What is a bucket of wine, a curvy maid or a good flare of rage compared to a bad poem and a second breakfast?
No one is ever taken by lust, bloodlust or otherwise.
Lust as a principle, a driver, is an earthly thing, is not a middle-earthly one.
No one has ever hunger. A distinguished appetite, that's more like it.
Ugh.
And there are no people. No traders, no inns, no hamlets or villages, no peasants. No one ordinary, you know. Everything is clean, white, well-set and sterile for our heros to enter. Like a fairy-tale. Like a bad theater piece, you have the impression that everyone moved only as soon as the spotlight came on them and froze again afterwards.
There is no before. No history. Oh yeah, there is! It is in this other book, Sig-something. But here? Tom Bombadil, the happy swamp creep.
Drama devoid of drama. But with a song!
Tolkien may have had fantastic ideas... like Moria, but this is just a bad story. A boring narration, full of dull and flat characters, tumbling along, numb for a long time, and then something happens. Or sing another song.
And I hated it.

I've tried reading this book multiple times and finally got through a reading from cover to cover.

It just doesn't grab me in the way that other fantasy novels do. I don't know if it's the outpouring of information, the slightly mundane storyline, the fact that I saw the movies first before finishing the books, or what.

No idea what it is! I totally understand the hype of the trilogy but it looks like that Great Eagles have flown past me.

The LOTR groupies will probably send a Ringwraith to destroy me for saying this, but the only reason that I liked this book was that it reminded me of the movie. Actually, it blows me away that Peter Jackson could make such an amazing movie from such a boring book. Jackson, was able to include and improve the best parts of this book while brilliantly removing the unnecessary. It is amazing how Jackson portrayed events and dialog almost identically to how they were executed in the book, but made me enjoy them so much more.



This book would not stand up if it was written in the current era. I understand that when it was written it redefined and even created and standardized the high fantasy genre. However, today’s readers would not be able to palate the terrible quality and consistency of writing along with the lack of detail and pacing for key events and the lack of explanation of characters, locations, and loore. It’s very difficult to enjoy this book without being deeply invested in LOTR. There are many songs, reference, and characters, that don’t make any sense and require considerable more research to understand and enjoy.

The Lord of the Rings is one of the most influential fantasy books ever written and this is the first time I have read it. The tale is divided into three parts, often sold as separate volumes, and I will review them individually. Following on from the high success and popularity of The Hobbit, Professor Tolkien was commissioned to continue his tale of hobbits and wizards, which he expanded upon with more mature themes and an older readership in mind. The story continues some time after Bilbo's adventures and deals with his nephew Frodo's inheritance of the One Ring and all the troubles that come with it. Forged by the evil dark lord Sauron and possessing the ability to consume the wearer and bend them to malevolent designs, Frodo is visited by Gandalf the Grey and convinced to undertake a perilous journey to destroy the ring in the fires of Mount Doom, all the way in darkest Mordor.

After a long reluctance to leave his comfortable home in the Shire, a location probably modelled after the South Downs of England, Frodo finally undertakes his epic journey, accompanied by his hobbit companions Samwise, Merry, and Pippin. It takes over a year for Frodo to begin his journey and it takes half of the book for him to finally reach the borders of the Shire. They dawdle, delay, get lost in the woods, and get kidnapped by wights, and the reader is subjected to lengthy descriptions of the landscape and topography. In addition to his obsession with linguistics, Tolkien was also extremely interested in geography, and his fictitious realm of Middle Earth receives rather more attention to detail than is needed for the story. In fact, his lore and world building seems to be his main priority, and whilst no doubt endlessly fascinating for himself and his many fans, I found a lot of it a real bore. Unlike some other franchises, I am not overly invested in Tolkien's world, so it was a struggle to maintain interest.

The story does pick up a little when the gang are pursued by Ringwraiths, sinister agents of Sauron, but there are numerous other delays and digressions that are frustrating to wade through. Eventually, the fellowship of the first book's title is form, made up of hobbits, men, dwarves and elves, and the adventure begins in earnest. By that time I was too bored to care, and the constant references to the larger world continued to be an unwanted distraction. I also noticed that, although Tolkien can wax lyrical for pages about trees and hills, his descriptions of the characters and creatures that populate Middle Earth are surprisingly flimsy.

I have actually tried to read this twice before: once in high school and again in college. And each time I only made it part of the way through before having to return it to the library. I thought, this being the classic that it is, I ought to read it before seeing the movies. But then a friend of mine related a similar story and recommended watching the movies first, to get a sense of the world and characters. I will say it definitely helped me finish this time, and I loved the movies and the emotional and fantastic story that they tell. And I enjoyed many parts of this book too, but overall it just took months to get through.

It starts out with two of my favorite scenes in Fellowship: Bilbo's birthday and the conversation Frodo has with Gandalf shortly thereafter. Bilbo's party is just tons of fun and introduces the fantasy world and core characters well. And Frodo's dismay at being the one poor soul burdened with the responsibility of the ring is tragic and introduces the core theme (of the Hobbit as well) that the smallest person can make the biggest difference. Frodo's inner strength, despite his size and humble upbringing, is a constant source of energy when parts of Fellowship start to drag.

And drag they do. For many scenes after til they get to the Prancing Pony it is, as many critics of the movies sometimes say, just a lot of "walking around." I am admittedly not as into the maps and paths as other fans of fantasy may be, so these parts lose me. I won't even talk about Tom Bombadil, one of the most contentious characters in all of fiction. But when the Hobbits get to the Prancing Pony and meet Strider the pace picks up again. Then comes a lot more GPS instructions and stories told in the past tense with not so much interesting actions occurring in the present.

There were a lot of scenes in Book II that hooked me a lot more than Book I, but I won't describe them here as there is a greater chance of spoilers (for something that came out almost a century ago, but I digress).

I will definitely keep reading the rest of the series. Return of the King is my favorite of the movie trilogy, and now one of my all-time favorites in general. And I liked it best because I think it gave the most character development to the ensemble cast and spent time getting to know each and every one of them, something I feel Fellowship could have benefitted more from doing. But if you like lengthy descriptions of pathways through forests and mountains, boy do I have a recommendation for you.

Yani şimdi, öncelikle şunu söyleyeyim, ben bu kitabı zevk alarak okuyabilmek için filmin her ayrıntısını unutayım diye senelerdir filmleri tekrar izlemeye şiddetle direniyordum, görüyorum ki çok da gerek yokmuş, boşuna kendimi mahrum etmişim. Neyse...

Sesli kitap olmasına rağmen ancak 10 ayda bitirebildim, sesli kitap olmasa şu an hala %20'lerde olurdum çok büyük ihtimalle. Kitabın ilk %60'lık kısmında gerçekten yer yer çok sıkıldım, devam etmeyi çok istedim fakat hiç içimden gelmedi, bölümleri sırf bitsin diye dinledim ve biter bitmez de devam etmeyerek kapattım. Bu kitaba başladığımdan beri üzerine 9 kitap bitirdim yine de buna devam edesim gelmedi. Yani son %40'lık kısım güzeldi ve birkaç gün içerisinde kitabı bitirdim.

Yaratılan dünyadan, dillerden, ırklardan vs. bahsetmeyeceğim bunları ve Tolkien'in kim olduğunu herkes biliyor, bunlardan yana da olumsuz bir düşüncem yok zaten. Kaldı ki dünyayı ve seriyi zaten çok sevdiğimden dolayı kitaba bu kadar geç başlamış bulunuyorum (kitaplığımda basılmış her versiyonu ve yazarın bütün kitapları mevcut, kısmet sesli kitap olarak dinlemeyeymiş.). Belki Rus edebiyatından zevk alanlar bu kitabın ilk %60'lık kısmından da keyif almıştır fakat benim için bir noktadan sonra çok yorucu ve zorlama bir yolculuk oldu. Seriyi sevmeseydim çok uzun süre yarım bir şekilde kalacak bir kitap olurdu benim için.

Bunların dışında da bir süre sonra şarkı/şiir artık her ne denirse o kısımları sardırarak geçtim, çünkü genellikle ne olaylarla ne de olay akışıyla hiçbir alakaları yoktu ve açıkçası hiç de ilgimi çekmediler. Belki orijinalleri kulağa daha hoş geliyordur falan ama bilemiyorum, neticede bana hitap etmediler.

Son olarak MÜKEMMEL bir seslendirmeydi. Murat Eken gerçekten GERÇEKTEN çok yetenekli bir seslendirmen, işini sonuna kadar hakkını vererek yapmış. Kitabı her şeye rağmen bitirebildiysem ve dinlediğimden zevk alabildiysem tamamen kendisi sayesinde, hakkını yiyemem. Tam kadro film tadında bir kitap seslendirmesiydi, şiddetle sesli kitap versiyonunu tavsiye ediyorum. Hatta Murat Eken'in seslendirdiği her kitaba şans vermenizi tavsiye ediyorum.

Bu arada Gimli ve Legolas'ın daha çok atışmasını görmek isterdim, hemen kanki oluverdiler. :/ O kısım da biraz işlenebilirdi bence, neticede birbirinden haz etmeyen iki farklı ırklar falan blabla her neyse...

Acho as contribuições do Tolkien para a literatura de gênero fantástico muito prejudicias, não auxiliaram em nada na evolução artística desse segmento, pelo contrário, só tornou ela insulada dentro de um setor de leitores e autores "nerds" e de "cultura pop". No século XX tiveram de criar prêmios isolados como o Hugo para contemplar esse tipo de literatura, pois notadamente ela não poderia competir num Man Booker ou National Book Award, junto dos autores "literários" e "sérios".

E eu tenho a perspectiva, com muito descontentamento, de que é porque ela se tornou um gênero pueril e sem ambição estética por conta das influências de gente da estirpe do Tolkien e C.S Lewis.

Deve existir uma centena de takes de senhor dos aneis por aí, um mais genérico que o outro. Todos emulando o espiríto romântico e o heroísmo das obras do Tolkien. Até J.K Rowling, que não trabalha nesse gênero de épico fantasioso, se utiliza da moralidade maniqueísta dos romances da terra média.

Como o Edmund Wilson em seu ensaio demolindo Senhor dos anéis expressou uma vez, é impressionante o quanto é pobre a prosa e a lírica do Tolkien(sim, porque, a rigor,ele se arriscava na poesia naquelas irritantes musiquinhas do Tom Bombadil).

Tolkien tinha uma imaginação muito vasta na edificação de um universo de fantasia de capa e espada que vivia e respirava, assim como na filologia, nas linguagens fictícias que ele construía com muita dedicação, porém era um escritor sem muitas virtudes de estilo.

A trilogia do Anel me suscita uma nostalgia boa, mas fui tentar reler anos atrás, e pude constatar o quanto o autor é limitado como prosador. Pesa muito a mão naquelas descrições afetadas do universo, e os personagens são uma grande bosta, nem dá pra saber quem é quem, todos falam exatamente da mesma forma.
Ele realmente deu uma infantilizada nesse gênero, injetou aquele moralismo cristão de bem x mal sem nenhuma sutileza, que até hoje perdura.

Esta obra tem mais impacto cultural do que méritos pra estar num cânone do ocidente, como o nerd chato quer insistir. Teve poucos defensores, o Auden foi um deles, mas nunca foi consenso.
E o legado do Tolkien foi este. Popularizou o gênero, foi um marco cultural, mas que nunca se sustentou dentro de um cânone. E ainda infantilizou uma tradição de narrativas de mito e fantasia há muito consolidada desde os gregos.

The lord of the rings is regarded as sacred fantasy writ by many people. I unfortunately came to it late in my obsession with fantasy, and had already encountered the barrage of books modelled after Lord of the Rings. It took me a long time to get around to reading it, because it had seemed to me that most of the people who liked Lord Of The Rings, tended to be people who did not love fantasy, in other words muggles; Non-magical people, who didn't understand. There can be no denying that Tokien's writing itself is quite magical. I had already read The Hobbit, my appetite was wetted for his style. The plot itself of the series did not wholly grab me, which is no fault of the series. It was the first of it's kind, but I was growing weary of the model. I had already been numbed to the storyline pattern of an entire realm being threatened by a dark lord, and unlikly heros being called upon to save it, under a deadline. I had already formed the notion that this motif had been created to make fantasy relatable to normal people working in offices, and to manipulate their emotions, and induce them to care, what happened to a group of hobbits in a magical kingdom. Tolkien created such a magical kingdome with middle earth but reading fellowship, and the volumes which followed, I didn't feel he afforded me the occasion to explore it in any detail. From the outset we knew the quest, the time limit involved, and having read a number of fantasy novels in this line, I was fairly sure of the outcome. For me, certainty is the last emotion I want to feel, when reading fantasy, and tends to be a buzzkill. Compared with other more escapist type fantasy, I found this somewhat dull, and it didn't transport me to the realm, in the way in which I wanted. That said, there is a lot in Lord of the Rings which is brilliantly executed, and the characters, each have a subtle allure, which makes them likeable. Fellowship stood out as particularly engageing for me, as compared with the succeeding volumes, which were more like a race against time. Tolkien did succeed in getting me to feel the same weariness, which the hobbits must have felt on their journey. I just wasn't sure if this was the ideal feeling for a fantasy experience.

Just to begin, the novel is not like the movie. Sure, most of the same story happens, but this novel has a completely different feel.

It almost reads like a history book rather than an epic adventure. The novel also lacked any sort of relate-able emotion from all characters. There was tons of world building, but this was all moot as it doesn't seem to really add anything to the story. For every page of action, there were seventy-five pages of Tolkien describing the history of the Hobbits or describing where certain areas are located within the world. On top of that, there was not one strong female character in the book at all except for those mentioned in old lore throughout the book. I realized this to my detriment.

I have to say that I quite enjoyed the part of reading about Tom Bombadil. That was a story within this novel that didn't make it to the movie, and it was a part of the novel that I enjoyed just for its crazy story. The part that I hated the most was, surprisingly enough, the chapter The Council of Elrond. It seemed to drag on and on, and I still don't know what most of the pages within were talking about. Long story short, majority of this novel was like this: it dragged on and on... and on, and by the end of the book, I was almost skipping over those world building pages (which happened up until the very last page).

With all that said, however, this book was one of those books that paved the way for our fantasy and science fiction stories that we have so widely available today. I commend Tolkien for that, and for being a first of its kind, it's a surprisingly good book. I almost wish I could thank the author for that.

Did I enjoy the story? I did... but I think this has to do more with the movie being so incredibly good than this book actually telling a superb story. I will continue with the series anyway, but I have no hope that the writing will get any better. I still loved reading the story from its source.

This is probably the only circumstance in my life when I'll have to say that the movie was better than the book.

This review covers all 3 volumes of LotR.

I'll preface this by saying that I truly appreciate both the scope of Tolkien's creation and the influence it has had on all works fantasy that came after it. That said, good god was his presentation dry, padded, and just plain boring. Even in the most climactic battles, my only motivation to keep reading was the finish the damn thing. His description of the events wasn't gripping in any way, shape, or form. The only time I felt drawn into the book was at the very beginning, when they're running from the wraiths in the Shire, but then he hits me with Tom Bombadil and 80 pages of silly elf song to cool things off a bit. Thank god, too, because I almost felt my pulse quicken slightly.

On top of that, I feel like the character names and the language used both in dialogue and to narrate the story was "fluffed up" to masturbatory levels in order satisfy Tolkein's fascination with ancient Anglo-Saxon English. There were at least a dozen points when I just wanted to scream at the characters, "fucking get on with it!" while they were in the middle of some 8-page monologue about something totally irrelevant to the story. Like when Merry runs down to tell Gandalf that Denethor is about to burn Faramir alive, he takes like 3 paragraphs to convey this. Jesus... crazy mofo is about to burn someone alive, just spit it out already...

What's even more frustrating is that, if you read The Hobbit before diving into LotR, you'll see that Tolkein clearly knew how to write interesting and engaging stories but actually chose not to. Yes, The Hobbit was aimed towards children and young adults, but that does not excuse how uninteresting LotR (which he decided to aim at an older audience) is in comparison.

Again, the only redeeming factors that kept my review score from being 1 star are the scope of Tolkien's creation and the influence it has had on all works fantasy that came after it. My advice: Read The Hobbit, skip the LotR novels, but watch the LotR movies.

One point: I completely respect everything that Tolkien did for the fantasy genre. I really do. I respect that he created a fantasy language, and a rich mythology. I can see the real-world influences he drew on in creating his own mythology.

However, this book is a non-compelling slog of poorly drawn characters and what are (now at least) stereotypes and tropes of the fantasy genre. I will grant you that Tolkien probably originated a lot of the tropes, but when I came this book in high school, I was already well-versed in fantasy, having grown up reading epic fantasy adventures.

I tried. I really did. I slogged through this one to the end. It took me, who could read a book a day if I found it engrossing enough, almost a month just to get through the first book. I picked up the second, saw it was more of the same, and put it down after only a chapter or two.

I've had people tell me I should continue slogging through, because the books got better. But honestly, I didn’t want to read about those characters any more because I didn't find them compelling. I had no emotional connection to Tolkien's characters or world. I had no insight into who they were, other than almost-historical cardboard cut-out figures. And I hated the villain for being a faceless evil that appears to be evil for evil's sake. I found the villains especially boring for their utterly lack of either personality or decent motive. Eventually I watched the movies and got the gist of the whole story, but I still didn't really care for the characters.

"The first part of Tolkien's epic work wherein hobbit Frodo discovers he has a magical ring and starts a quest to destroy it along with a band of men, dwarves, elves, and wizards. I know this is a popular work, but I just couldn't warm up to its grim tone and humorless characters. With the exception of Pip and Merry, Frodo's young friends, I really couldn't identify with any of the characters. I thought Frodo was particularly wooden, with his only emotion being homesicknesses and occasionally, fear.

I was not a fan of the film, so this book had a lot to overcome for me to enjoy it at all. I did enjoy the book more as the journey was more episodic and more detailed, as a good fantasy story should be. But I am still incensed that the novel ends without any real climax. I know what you'll say: "It's part of a three-part story". But couldn't we have a high point within the story here? Boromir's potential betrayal hardly qualifies.

Finally, while I appreciate Tolkien's attempts to fill in history, literature, language, and geography of the Middle-Earth realm, I really found it distracting, going pages beyond what was necessary. How about focusing some care on characterization instead? I much preferred Lloyd Alexander's "Chronicles of Prydain" series which is not dissimilar but with much more heart, humor, and reasonable story telling climax and resolution in a multiple episode series. I don't really recommend this book, but it will appeal to certain audiences. I am hesitant to continue with the series.

You can already see my rating so I'll start by saying that I am a fan of the LOTR movies and I wanted to read the books as well, so I bought the complete box set (including The Hobbit ) because I was sure I was going to like them. Well, that was not the case.


After reading Hobbit I thought I should give Tolkien a second chance but yet again, I was disappointed. The writer focuses mostly on the description of the journey. He goes into every detail of the scenery, the road they followed and some irrelevant events that happened on their way. He doesn't care much about the characters themselves, apart from the two or three main ones. You don't learn anything about Legolas' or Gimli's or Pippins emotional state or character, unless you watch the movies. (E.g. Legolas has only 4 lines throughout the book). I mean, if you're going to name your book with the word "Fellowship" which consist of 7 persons, I expect to learn a little bit about each one.


So, if you're looking for a travel documentary book, this is it. But if you want an adventurous fiction book, look for something else. Of course this book is written many years ago and maybe I'm too taken with the 'new age' fiction books, but this first book is boring. I'm still a fan of the movies so maybe one day I'll pick up the second one.

Merry, Sam, and Pippin accompany Frodo on his journey to destroy the ring of power before the Eye of Sauron finds it. The language is beautiful, and as are the many songs that are sung, and the ending in one you would have never expected.

If I were put in Frodo's position, I honestly think that I wouldn't have been able to do it. He perservered through all of the obstacles, and that was only in the first book! He resisted the powerful temptation of the Ring and I would have given in. For some reason, the ring drew people towards it, and it would especially have drawn me, because I am good at keeping temptation, but something that powerful...I don't even want to think what would happen.

I wouldn't reccomend reading this book because I got incredibly confused with all the descriptiveness. Also, I read it at night and it scared me talking about the Black Riders and such. If you think you might enjoy the old-time language then I do reccomend it, however I found the old-fashioned writing pointless because while it is set in Middle Earth, that doesn't mean it doesn't have to be written like it's the 1700s. I enjoyed this book a bit, with the adventure and everything, but still I wouldn't want to read it again.

I loved The Hobbit and I was so ready to become an avid Tolkien fan. I eagerly bought this book, excited for an awesome journey through Middle Earth, and... meh. It was so sad for me to not like it. I really wanted it to become my number one favorite book, and I looked forward to reading all of Tolkien's highly-respected works, but it just did nothing for me. I was a bit confused, because The Hobbit was one of the best books I ever read, it was so fast-paced, exciting and funny. But then I came to this book, and it was so dreary. It dragged on and on and was both repetitive and slow. It is also strange to me that it is a world-renowned classic, and I always love old classic books. The Fellowship of the Ring had my name written all over it, what with its fantasy world and high stature in the literary world, and because I adored The Hobbit so much. At first, when I had read a little but I didn't like it, I thought that maybe it just took a while to get interesting and I would push through the beginning to get to the awesome part. In the end, I eventually lost hope and abandoned the book after reading almost halfway through it. Maybe I should have read a little longer, or try it again in a few years. I truly wanted to be a Tolkien fanatic and be a L.O.T.R. know-it-all, but reading this book and getting totally bored and underwhelmed just broke my heart. I think I will wait a little bit and read it again, hopefully to love it!

So, I read the Hobbit and enjoyed it, so naturally I decided that I was going to move onto the Lord of the Rings series and this is where it starts. I listened to it on spoken word in my car as I don't have as much free time to read at the moment. I started out with high hopes but soon felt disappointed.

The story seemed very slow and long winded and there were periods of time where I found myself completely tuning out and missing chunks of the story, at first I would go back a couple of tracks and try to pick it up again but to be honest I didn't really care, I found it so slow and boring that I just wanted to get it finished. i persevered all the way through as so many people love it I thought I was missing something, but after finishing it all i can only say that I really didn't care and had no real idea what was happening. I asked my fiance for a summary and gave up and handed the book back.

I don't really know what didn't click for me, but it just seemed so long winded that it never really gets anywhere. I do have to say that there were odd moments that made me perk up and pay attention and that I enjoyed more but overall it just fell flat.

However I have heard that 'The Two Towers' is much better so I am going to persevere once more and give that a go, I just hope it's better than this one.

Sorry Tolkien, but maybe this series is just not for me.

This almost killed my love for reading. The only reason I had this at a 5 before was because my sister loved it, and I was mimicking her when I read this in eighth grade.

Something just puts me at odds with Tolkein bc honestly I'm going to licherally k*ll myself if I get moralized about how utterly perfect the old days were or how flawless and glamorous X person is again... hate that sentimental bullshit! Sorry but I hate Aragorn and couldn't give a crap about Galadriel - my petty degenerate f*g self just wants to see those uppity assholes taken down oh my God!!!! Don't even get me started on Frodo. Sam is only a good person in the meta sense bc he knows his place as a lowly worker and is completely servile to his Righteous Employer Overlord Frodo. I literally can't stand "sir" and "mister" talk unless it's kink play. Frodo DESERVED to be stabbed

And can these bitches please stop SINGING omg like on the way to Lothlorien they kept following the same pattern "here's a landmark, I'm going to name drop a bunch of places and people like an academic and then I'm going to start fukcin singing" AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA

2 stars bc I kind of liked it at first but the second book was actual torture KILL ME. KILL ME NOW. I'm literally going to write a whole entire fan fiction where Sauron wins because I don't know how to properly cope with this TRAUMA

Solo due stelle. Mi è dispiaciuto dare solo due stelle all'epico "Signore degli anelli", conosciuto in tutto il mondo, famosissimo perfino tra i pesci sul fondo dell'oceano, però mi ha delusa.
Sono convinta che se avessi letto prima il libro, piuttosto che vedere prima il film, il mio giudizio sarebbe stato completamente diverso, ma amando io la trasposizione cinematografica, non ho trovato praticamente nulla del film di Peter Jackson nel libro.
"Nulla" non nel senso che il film è stato poco fedele, ma nel senso che il film è molto più veloce (fondamentale, essendo un film, capisco benissimo), mentre nel libro anche solo per salutarsi impiegano tre righe, richiamando padri, nonni, zii, avi, eroi del passato anche solo lontanamente imparentati con colui/colei che si sta salutando.
E' stato un errore vedere prima il film, ma anche qui se non lo avessi visto, non avrei mai scoperto dell'esistenza del libro (dopotutto quando uscì il primo film avevo 7 anni, non potevo conoscere "il grande J.R.R. Tolkien", nonostante leggessi dall'età di 5.
E, dopo averlo ricominciato più o meno cinque volte (quasi al pari delle otto/nove di "Le due torri") e finito dopo più o meno un anno che stazionava sul mio comodino, ho scoperto che i libri di Tolkien non fanno assolutamente per me, nonostante riconosca J.R.R. come una delle pietre miliari del fantasy che tanto amo al giorno d'oggi.
People said I had to read it before I died. Ouff.

I really wanted to like this. You can clearly see that Tolkien spend so much time on thinking out this world and all the details in it. It’s really well thought out. But reading this, it really confirmed to me that what I enjoy most while reading is connecting to the characters, feeling for them, and trying to understand them. This focused a lot on the world itself and all the details in it; the landscape, the history of the world, the languages. I just missed the connection. I just didn’t care about how every tree and bush that they passed looked like..

His style just isn’t for me unfortunately, and it probably also doesn’t help that it was written around 90 years ago. I really wish I liked it more, but at least I finally tried reading it. I would rate it lower than this based only on enjoyment, but extra points for creating this world.

I just got sleepy a lot, especially during the first half. At those moments, I tried out immersive reading. I found the audiobook quite funny. It was funny to hear the rhymes/songs being sung instead of just reading them. Hearing Tom Bombadil’s song in the audiobook had me laughing so hard, and it stayed in my head for quite some time😅 Andy Serkis was funny to listen to doing the different voices, I think he did a great job (both the audiobook and the movies😉).

NOT a fan! I give credit where credit is due. Tolkien was an amazing person. To be able to envision all the differing cultures, histories, languages, arts and political intrigues that cam "before" the series borders on genius. Unfortunately, to me, the books dragged from start to finish. The entire series was written with a sense of impending doom and the need for quick action. To then have the characters sit around and discuss poetry, their motivations and such gave the lie to the entire premise of the books.

The characters were, mostly, 2 dimensional with little or no depth. It was bludgeoned into every scene that each character had a "good side" and a "bad side". We get it! Enough! Move on. Please.

The staging was too descriptive and slowed the flow of the story to such an extent that reading the entire trilogy became work. I don't care to know that there was only one yellow leaf on the tree. It is not germane to the story and was done, in my opinion, to add more sizzle but no meat.

The plot has, of course, become cliche'. As this was one of the first novels of its type I will not point out all the major holes in the plot nor the absence of any real depth.

This is, of course, just my opinion.

Great idea, poorly executed.

If I thought I had mixed feelings about The Hobbit, it was nothing compared to this book, which took me longer to read than any book in recent years. The bad bits first. It is very difficult to read. I appreciate that this is Tolkien's style, and it is an old fashioned one, but this book is significantly harder to read than the Hobbit, with few signs of the imaginative quirks present in its predecessor to keep things interesting in the narrative. In addition to the general style being a struggle to get through, the descriptions (again, in classic Tolkien style) are far too in depth and often interrupt the flow of the dialogue.

That said, the quality of this book is once again undeniable. Just like with the Hobbit, the world that Tolkien paints is incredible, and the story is interesting with prominent characters and locations. So for those who persevere (which, over the years, has been a great many people) there are rewards in this book. But no amount of praise of the storyline and characters can hide the fact that this book, in this day and age, is just a real struggle to get through. I'm glad I have read it, but if not for the sense of duty at 'needing to read it', I'm not sure I would have finished it.

What did I think?
2 out of 5 stars = it was ok

+/- Interesting characters and their descriptions hit their mark. The dark riders gave me the creeps but, and maybe this was Tolkien's aim, I have no real fear of the main bad guy yet.

+/- Setting/scenery overall is interesting. Loved the descriptions of The Shire, the other towns, houses/rooms and the forest (in particular) but when it when it came to their travels (which is most the story, (which is kind of the point of the story)) it became way too bogged down with description and often the same descriptions about rocks, mountains, trees, etc. I found myself many times waking up and realizing that my mind had drifted or my eyes were drooping. At times, the story literally made me sleepy. Guess I am just not a fan of Tolkien's writing style.

- Everything, from people, to places, to things have multiple names to the point where it had become comical, for me.

~ It's kinda weird and awkward when you "kill off" one a main good guy so easily and quickly.

So it's on to the second book in the trilogy. Hopefully the pace picks up. I really want to love these books, but for me and my opinion, Tolkien's writing style really gets in the way of his story.

Lord of the Rings: Fellowship of the Ring is the first part of the story of Frodo Baggins and his adventure with the One Ring of power. Frodo is a peaceful hobbit who spent his whole life in a place known as the Shire. The Shire is a peaceful place secluded from the rest of the world. Suddenly the One Ring is passed onto Frodo, and himself alongside some close hobbit friends must travel great distances to unknown and dangerous lands to destroy the One Ring as this ring is the source of the dark loud Sauron's power, and if he were to obtain it, the whole world would be covered in darkness.

The book is quite a great story, and I personally really enjoyed it. It really envelops you in this well-developed and interesting world filled with fascinating characters. There are points in the book where it is a bit slow, and can get boring and it can be quite difficult to keep track of all the names being constantly thrown at you, but it is a wonderful book that tells the beginning of a powerful and interesting story.

I would recommend this story to a lot of people. It is a bit of a long book, and not the easiest read, but anyone who is a big fan of fantasy, or adventure stories would probably enjoy this book, and the other books in the series.

I really wanted to like this book; I loved The Hobbit and was very much looking forward to taking a crack at Tolkien's epic tale. Unfortunately The Lord of the Rings trilogy did not give me a similar experience of wonder and delight as my first experience with Tolkien. I found these books to be very tedious, it's like Tolkien fell in love with the world that he had created (not necessarily a bad thing!) and then proceeded to write an encylopaedia of Middle Earth under the guise of a novel. While I came to love Bilbo and each of the Dwarves in The Hobbit, I found Frodo and his companions to be shallow and poorly rounded beasts by comparison. Even the Gandalf of this trilogy left less of an impact. Frodo is a persistent whiner, who made me feel very sorry for Sam as his constant companion, and is so much less than his uncle Bilbo. I wish I could have enjoyed these books, even if it was only as a detailed guide to Middle Earth, but the rambling detraction from the "plot" and the shallowness of the characters was too off-putting to bear. I made it almost to the end of Two Towers and gave up, unfortunately I think this is one trilogy that will spend the rest of its days on my un-finished shelf.

Oh my gosh. This may be the first time I preferred the movie to the book - besides Mary Poppins.

I don't get it. I like fantasy. (Or so I thought.) I loved The Hobbit. But The Fellowship of the Ring was so boring. I ended up reading and re-reading the same passages over and over again (and still not getting what was going on). I like poems. (Or so I thought.) But every time a new song or verse came up I groaned inwardly and steeled myself mentally for the challenge of getting through.

The pacing was slow, the nature-related escapades were torturous, and Tom Bombadil? What the hell was up with him? I kept expecting him to morph into an evil being and gobble up the hobbits. I also wanted to slap him in the face and knee him in the groin every time he burst into song. In fact, that imagery was my only moment of pleasure that spurred me through the first half of this volume.

Despite the massive respect I have for Tolkien and the literary world he created, the obvious care and precision he takes with his creations, and the generations of fans he inspired, I think I was just expecting something different. I may prefer fantasy light to deep fantasy! The horror.

Taking a break before I continue on with The Two Towers.

In terms of personal enjoyment this was actually more like a 1.5 or 2. However, I do believe it’s necessary to read this volume at least once to get to TTT and RotK (which are significantly better). So, because this is an integral part of an overall great story, I’m bumping up my rating. I’m also bumping up my rating for the simple fact that this and the other two volumes are the source material for the three most beloved and influential films of my childhood.

Why do I have such issues with this? Sadly (and I’m sure controversially) it’s because I give zero shits whatsoever about Hobbits or the Shire. I know we’re supposed to be charmed by them and their way of life is something to aspire to, etc. But I frankly don’t care or particularly like any of them. If I wanted to hang around a lot of closed-minded, willfully ignorant people suspicious of “outsiders” I could visit with the common clay of the new (American mid)west. I understand that this is neither fair to Tolkien or the story (or my fellow Americans) and I do apologize for any offense, but this was my experience reading this during the unendingly exhausting and nerve-wracking 2020 election season.

I will say, once we finally left the Shire and the cast expanded significantly, this improved a good deal.

Actual rating: 1.5

Disappointing given how revered this series is. I was always confused watching the movie so i never liked it much. Books are usually better than the movie and i assumed this would be the case but i guess this is the exception. I really hoped the book would get me into the Lord of the Rings hype since the movie didn't but that didn't happen.. At least reading this made me appreciate the movie more. My main issue is that between 20% and 60% of the way through the book, it really slowed down. Like a lot. The whole middle of this book was insanely boring and painfully slow. I was skimming pages and flipping through it so I could get to the more interesting parts. It's sad because I can tell this is a good story and I like the plot but the writing completely ruined it for me. It was just way too dull. The last 30% of the book is a testament to how good it could have been. If only the pacing was that good for the rest. One positive about the book is that it did clarify some things that were confusing about the movie for me so I can enjoy it more now. I heard the series picks up at Two Towers so I may read the rest of the books but this was a horrendous introduction.
One of the few books I can say I liked the movie much better.

incredibly dull and boring, i would've never finished this book if it wasn't written by tolkien and considered a masterclass in fantasy literature. i did enjoy the hobbit and expected to like this even more but i simply couldn't. I think the hobbit worked for me because even though the characters were mostly one-dimensional, the pacing was steady and their adventure didn't get sidetracked and kept you involved. however in fotr, the characters not only fall flat but the plot itself strays away from the point more than once. there's too much lore, too many names, places and just endless pages of those annoying songs which are coherent only in their rhyming. i appreciate tolkien's ambition in thinking all this up but a word vomit of myths and creatures doesn't really make a work compelling or fun to read, but likely the very opposite. other than that, i could also see tolkien's colonial, catholic views forged throughout the text and understood why far-right eu countries are so keen on this trilogy. making evil an insular and distinct force from goodness does not work either, there are no moral stakes and dilemmas ultimately making me not care about a single decision the characters made.

I was forced to read this book against my will. My Tolkien-obsessed teacher decided this dreadful fate would befall her English classes. I started this book out kicking and screaming, ready to burn the school-issued book that five other students had already suffered through. The language was difficult. The characters seemed shallow. For a while the only time a female pronoun was used was in the few pages where Goldberry appeared (and you can hardly say she is of major importance to the plot). It all seemed dreadfully irrelevant, especially since we had just finished studying To Kill A Mockingbird, which I loved.
However, by the end I maybe did like it. Just a little. Galadriel was interesting, and the dynamics of the company grew increasingly tense (I do love tension in books. It is possibly my favorite feature in any given novel, when done correctly).
So to each her own. The first 4/5 of the book was painful, hardly worth wading through. At the end it did maybe salvage that whole shallow character thing I was convinced of, but not enough that I'd ever pick up any book in the Trilogy again. Ever. Movies, maybe. Books, never.

I hate giving this book such a low rating.

I really, really hate it. But after forcing myself 60 percent of the way through an incredibly dull, convoluted story, I can't lie to myself anymore. This book isn't for me.

I have the utmost respect for Tolkien. He redefined the fantasy genre and has created an epic novel lots of (other) people adore. Why wasn't I one of them? I can get lost in a good fantasy. I love words even for the sake of words, with or without a strong plot. I'd heard Frodo's journey could be...lengthy...but I KNEW I'd love it anyway.

I choked down the first half like an overcooked steak. I started reading Spark Notes to get me through the second half. Spark Notes? Seriously? I think the last time I opened Spark Notes I was in fifth grade trying to bullshit my way through a book report. Still, I thought it might help to be able to "discuss" the chapters rather than skim my way through them...

I guess what I'm trying to say is that this book just didn't capture me. I love the movies. I love the plot. It just doesn't translate well in writing. And again, I hate to say it, but I was extremely disappointed by Tolkien's writing style.

Where do I start with this one?
I'll start by saying I understand the Tolkien hype. And he is now on my list of 5 people (dead or alive) I would like to have dinner with (not like I know the other 4, but still. Lol). It was wonderful to see how his mind works, and I would love to pick it further over dinner as I try determine how he managed to build this epic, extremely credible, highly detailed world that has influenced the fantasy genre beyond measure. That is nothing short of incredible.
