That being said, the book was slow. I understand he's building the world in the book, but still. Some places were great, others not so much. He could go on and on and on about the trees, lands, rivers ... Yikes. I am a very fast reader but it took me a month to read this. And that says A LOT!!
That being said, the humour is still there in plenty. Gandalf and Frodo are hilarious. As are Merry and Pippin. I can imagine being friends with those 2 hobbits IRL. And the friendship among all 4 hobbits is quite touching, but particularly Frodo and Sam. I would be ever so blessed to have my own Sam Gamgee.
All in all, 2 stars as it was just okay.

I appreciate Tolkien's ingenuity when it comes to the creation of characters, his geographic attention to detail, his care for character genealogy, and his development of new language in the world of his creation, but dammit this book was a slog! I read it with my older son and it took nearly two years to get through. I had no desire to pick it up other than to get to the end. No desire to find out what happened to Frodo and company. And it seemed that very little actually happened in the book. Which is fine. I don't need a lot of plot, but I need some insights on the human condition, prose that moves me, poetry, something, anything to grab on to. But I couldn't find anything here to motivate me to want to read this work. I was surprised by how much JK Rowling seemed to have "borrowed" from Tolkien in the creation of her fantastic world, but that (slim as this interest was) was among the only things that kept my interest in this, maybe with an "aha" moment every fifty pages or so. I would be a severe masochist indeed if I decided to continue with the other books in this series. This was a torturous read.

It really pains me to give this book 2 stars.

I truly love fantasy.
It is my favorite genre, and I wanted so badly to like middle earth.
In general, I like worldbuilding, intricate plot, magic, and epic-scale conflicts.
So why do I not enjoy Tolkien?

It comes down to the characters.
Simply put, this is not even remotely a character-driven narrative.

For every paragraph we get about the inner thoughts of Frodo and the choices he makes, we get 10 times more plant and river descriptions, irrelevant lore dumps from 100+ years ago, song breaks, etc.

I know that Tolkien can write interesting character interactions.

The Bilbo/Gollum chapter from the Hobbit and the Gandalf/Saruman confrontation in the Two Towers are both very strong and interesting scenes. In these chapters, we learn more about the characters and the world, all while advancing the plot in a unique way!

So why doesn't Tolkien do this more often?
These types of scenes are way too few and far between.

I'm sure this is a great trilogy if you like plot or world-driven stories, but with the lack of character, it just seems really boring to me.

Let me first say that I would NEVER EVER be able to deny that J.R.R. Tolkien was horrid. IN fact, he was brilliant. Tolkien made up Middle Earth. He didn’t just give it a fancy name and dump a few interesting magical beings, creatures, and a pretty little castle in it- He made an entire world for us, the readers, to become lost in.

Hmmm…lost…what a wonderful place to start at. (Let the bitching ensue)

I hate these books. No, seriously, I do. And I really, really want to like them, but it’s really hard. Tolkien is a very difficult writer to comprehend. He writes like someone from Elizabethan times and he takes pleasure in describing things until we’ve come to hate the object of discussion because, frankly, we’re tired of hearing about it. It also makes me laugh how many interesting tales are in the gigantic Mount Appendix of Doom. The plot itself, is really interesting. The way it’s told…boring. Perhaps I will come to like his style of writing, but for now I’m content with Peter Jackson’s movies.

If I remember correctly I felt the Hobbit was lacking description and flare, and OH BOY did Tolkien lay it on thick with this book! I know it's impressive that Tolkien created this entire fictional world, one with fictional creatures, mountain ranges, history spanning decades and even in some cases language, but I couldn't help myself but want to tell him ENOUGH already as he waxed on and on about historical wars on mountains, rivers, and generations that were impossible to follow along with. I've read plenty of fantasy books and not all of them need to give you generations of fictional history impossible to follow along with to feel realistic. Each time he went on another history lesson I essentially scanned and moved forward to the next scene with actual action or progress. The entire book could have been slimmed dramatically had he left out 70% of his history no one could follow. Not sure if I'm going to bother reading the other two. This will be one time I'll just stick with the movies.

*growls* This book really annoyed me. Slow, plodding, boring - it meanders along as if the author didn't really know where he was heading with it. The invention, mythology, world building of Middle Earth are all astounding. Detail rich in originality, but I'm afraid the plot is what lets it down.

Let's face it, everyone remembers the films, but of course that is 'actioned' up to make this book more appealing. Lengthy dialogue of redundant history can easily turn readers off, and this first instalment is full of it.

And because the writing is extended, over the top, and slow to get to the point, the book can be immensely confusing, which makes the book a chore to read at times. Add this to the annoying songs, and well, you have a recipe for disaster.

Elves, Hobbits, Dwarfs, an ageing wizard - they all make for fantastic company, and Gandalf the grey has to be my favourite. Unfortunately, everything is over polite and formal, which adds stinted dialogue. It does get better towards the end though, and I'm actually looking forward to more action-based sequel.

Well, I found the book quite ordinary. Probably if I read it a couple of years earlier or if I did not read so many books, my impression of the book would be better.

The story is quite good, but the way the book is written does not allow to fully enjoy it. Tolkien created a very detailed world with rich history and culture. While reading the book I see only hints and fragments of it, but never a full picture. It's like to look at some secret garden through a hole in a fence, I can see it exists, but I cannot enjoy it.

The same goes to the characters in the book. Most of them are not properly written, even the main ones. They do this and that, but those actions do not show who and what they are. I could imagine a couple of versions of the character, that will be in line what the book tells about him. But I would like to know how Tolkien saw them.

I'm also a bit disappointed that some of the events that could be really fun and exciting are quite plain. It makes the whole book rather plain too.
certainly Overrated or just not my type . was boring on certain Points .

I think it was okay. It wasn't as good as The Hobbit, which was filled with whimsy and humor. The Fellowship largely lacked lightheartedness. Worse, I didn't care all that much about the characters. Even Gandalf's fall - which I remember being absolutely shocking in the movie - had almost no effect on me. Tolkien will spend three full paragraphs describing leaves, and then in a parenthetical say "(and then Gandalf suffered defeat and will not be seen for the rest of the book.)" Those things that are least important seem to get the most attention, and vice versa.

The book really made me appreciate the movie all the more though. With a chapter to go in the book, I really didn't care what happened next. But the movie was suspenseful. You cared about the characters. You cared about the quest.

As far as fantasy books go, I'd say the Harry Potters - so far - rank way higher than LOTR, though the LOTR movies are way better than the HP movies.

I had a really hard time actually reading this book. The storyline was good, but it just progressed way too slowly. The entire trilogy spans over 1000 pages, but I think the entire story could have been told in about 350. Tolkien goes into great detail about every surrounding and every person, and everything that happens, that it takes FOREVER for the story to progress. And when he finally gets to an excited part, he just skips over it and gives it the least amount of detail possible.
The book was so boring that I actually caught myself in the middle of a chapter with no recollection of anything that had happened so far. This is a rarity, but I think that the movie was far superior to the book. I can't think of any other book where that is the case, but it is true. The lack of needing to describe the surroundings, and instead spending the entire time progressing the story, makes the movie much more entertaining.

I did not care for this book at all really. It tells of the journey that Frodo, Sam, Merry, and Pippin make to join with Aragorn, Legolas, Boromir, and others. Then, the entire Company sets off with the Ring (carried by Frodo) to either Minas Tirith or to Mordor. Frodo, the bearer of the Ring, would decide to which land they would travel once they reached the point at which they must choose. They reached that point at Frodo chose to go alone to Mordor to spare his friends. The author never goes into any detail, really, about the consequences of choosing to go to either place or reasons to choose one place or the other.

This book tells of many smaller adventures that the Company had while on a much bigger adventure. I believe that this book could be very exciting. However, it isnt, I'm sorry to say. To be honest, I could not wait to finish it, so that I could start another book. At the same time, I didn't enjoy reading it, so it was hard to make myself read it.

Ugh. Okay.

I refer (as do a couple other people) to the review of Doc Opp, who has stated my exact opinion on these books better than I ever could hope to.

I have incredible respect for Tolkien as the father of modern fantasy and an amazing worldbuilder, but I swear, the man couldn't write a novel to save his life. 80% of Fellowship felt like wading through wallpaper paste, and the other 20% was barely competently written dialogue. After the fiftieth page wasted on describing rocks on a mountain, I gave up and switched to skim-reading.

The saving grace is the world that it is set in, but jesus christ does it have some ground to make up. I started Fellowship adamant to get through the trilogy this time (I've tried unsuccessfully a few times, usually flaking out somewhere in the middle of Two Towers), and am now keenly aware of why it was such a struggle in the first place. I will persevere with the other two, but not after a break, and definitely with a general sense of dread.

Being part of the so-called "Generation Y" renders me with a short attention span. This low span of attention and constant fidgeting were truly tested in the first of TLotR trilogy as I suffered to get past the first forty pages of the Shire's history, family tree, and the drawl of prose describing how green the grass was and how it was different in Hobbiton and Bag End (it's been a while, so excuse my misspellings of the names). Sure, it starts off slow, and then picks up the pace before becoming slow again, and then we are introduced to the creepiest and most perverted character in any text, Tom Bombadil.

The last third of the book is amazing however. From the formation of the Fellowship, the battle in Moria, and the cliffhanger as the Fellowship dissolves, it manages to hook you in and you can easily ignore the longwinded descriptions of the mountains and the shape of Legolas' ears.

Having read the Hobbit twice my expectations for this, the first part of Tolkien's great trilogy, were high. When you consider that there is a party, consisting of four Hobbits, a Wizard, an Elf, a Dwarf and two men, setting out on a quest, you expect a great deal of adventure. After all, Tolkien did it in the Hobbit. Unfortunately most of the book was taken up with descriptions of the landscape: trees, streams, etc. There is one sentence in chapter seven of book two (the Mirror of Galadriel) which sums a lot of it up; it goes, "it seemed to them that they did little but eat and drink and rest, and walk among the trees". Alas, this sums the book up quite well. Given the cast of characters assembled, one would have expected more adventure.
I think the problem with 'the Fellowship' is that it is not one story in a great collection of three stories, but one third of a bigger story.
I had already purchased the three books in the one volume, I just hope the others are an improvement.

This goes against every fiber of my being, but I have to give an honest review, although I know my opinion my hurt some die hard fans hearts. I had a really hard time with this book. I found it too be excruciatingly slow and boring. I tried my hardest to like this book. I really did! But, when it comes down to it, I felt it dragged in certain areas and I felt the momentum throughout the story lagged. The characters felt very two-dimensional and I couldn't attach to any of them throughout the entire book. Perhaps the movies have ruined this book for me? Perhaps I need to give it another chance and re-read it? I am planning on reading The Twin Towers as I hear it is much better than The Fellowship of The Ring.

Here's to diving back into the world of Middle-Earth and hopefully it is much more interesting than the first book. BTW...I have read the Hobbit and thoroughly enjoyed that book!! I gave that a 4.5 rating!

2.5 stelle

Putroppo non mi è piaciuto.
Avevo già cercato di leggerlo l'anno scorso ma ho mollato dopo cinquanta pagine perché mi annoiava. Dato che odio lasciare le cose a metà e volevo dare un'altra opportunità a un colosso del genere fantasy ho deciso di riprovarci, e l'ho effettivamente finito, ma obbligandomi a leggere almeno due lunghissimi capitoli al giorno.
La trama potrebbe anche essere avvincente se trattata con un minimo di umorismo, o di vita in generale, ma lo stile di Tolkien la uccide. Queste descrizioni del viaggio e del paesaggio, monotone, dai primi capitoli fino agli ultimi e inframezzate da lunghe canzoni potrebbero scoraggiare anche i lettori più incalliti. I personaggi mi sono sembrati poco caratterizzati, forse l'unico che si salva è Sam per la sua lealtà.
Non so se proseguirò con la serie, o se rinuncerò ai libri e guarderò i film per scoprire come la storia andrà a finire, ma sicuramente adesso mi serve una lettura leggera.

Look I'm pretty sure the Bombadil segue made me throw this book (I think I have the 3-in-1 edition, it's really fat) at my wall. One day I will read the rest of the trilogy, because I respect Tolkein's love of linguistics enough that I will submit myself to detailed, jaw-dropping world-building and the "daddy of modern fantasy", but I 'tis a uni student and right now is not the time.

The rest of the book was pleasant enough and I can see why Tolkein is held on a pedestal when it comes to world-building - just the sheer creativity/also historical basis of the lands and races and languages is *chef's kiss*, but by gods, those chapters served no apparent plot purpose or real character building that could be done elsewhere and need to be burned (or force-fed to Tolkein's poor university students).

2.25 eagles out of 5. Not enough for a full fellowship, but enough to help two hobbits escape with a ring.
Boring for 85% of the book. In the last 15%, the story finally gets moving.

Oof.

I have so many conflicting feelings upon finishing part 1 of LotR. I wanted to love this book. The Trilogy (and the Hobbit) were probably the only books my late dad ever read voluntarily and he loved them. I wish I could talk with him about them now.

My sister assured me that The Two Towers and Return of the King are a vast improvement on Fellowship but all the same, I need a pallet cleanser after this slog.

After enjoying The Hobbit, I was excited to continue this Middle-Earth journey. And there were certainly plenty of aspects of Fellowship that I did enjoy. But man, this book could have easily been half its length. I appreciate the intricate world-building and wordplay that Tolkien OBVIOUSLY lovingly poured over over the decade he wrote the Trilogy. When you haven't fully inhabited that world as he did, though, its introduction often comes across as overwhelmingingly convoluted and needlessly detailed.

And lord almighty, did that man relish in songs. Oy vey, did he. 😑

Olha, fui um guerreiro em terminar esse livro xD

A história em si é muito boa, dá super para entender o motivo do Tolkien ter o título de pai da fantasia, mesmo que ele não seja o pioneiro no estilo. Gostei mesmo, tanto que foi esse o motivo de ainda dar uma nota razoável para este livro.

O problema mesmo é que demora DEMAIS pra história se desenrolar. Metade do livro (sério, não é exagero) se trata de descrições de lugares por onde os personagens estão vagando. Ermos, montanhas, vales, desfiladeiros, florestas... é uma leitura super cansativa.

Eu só continuei lendo mesmo pq a história é instigante, mas tenho dúvidas se vou continuar a série.

Se você planeja se aventurar por aqui, já vai preparado! Para aqueles que gostam de leituras mais descritivas, é um prato cheio. Ainda mais se você é daquele tipo de pessoa que tem facilidade para montar cenários na cabeça.

Enfim, a história é excelente, mas muito lenta.

I DNR'd this at 39%. I did read "The Hobbit" prior to this. However, I felt this book droned on too long. I found it, dare I say, boring. I so badly wanting to love this book as I am a huge fan of the "Harry Potter" series and thought they might be more similar. I may make a second attempt in the future.

this is a terrible book. I understand how Tolkien was a pioneer and we all owe him great thanks, but damn he was not a very good writer! 531 pages long and about 80% of it is pure description of surrounding, so detailed it's borderline OCD and could easily be left out. There is way too many useless and unprenounceble names that is of no consequence to the story and are just fillers to give the places a sense of history, which could be done in other manors. Oh and the dialogue is so terrible and akward, written in the style of circa 1780 that it actually pained me to read. I dread having to read the last to books in the trilogy, because I have a feeling they are just like this one, and if you cut all the crap and very unnecessary stuff out, all three books could be turned in to one book of about 300 pages. Frankly, I'd rather just watch the movies and be done with it.

The Fellowship of the Ring - Lord of the Rings Part One - by J.R.R. Tolkien, was one of the most enchanting pieces of literature I have ever read. Tolkien generates this world that is so vividly described you feel you are a hobbit too. The only challenge I had with this book was the author would introduce a new place or character without explaining it. I found this highly frustrating. I also had a difficult time relating to the book and receiving a deeper insight because of this issue. Despite this difficulty, I felt the story-line and the adventures that took place in this book were very gripping and exciting. I do not think I would read the rest of the series because I fear I would run across the same issues I faced in The Fellowship of the Ring. I recommend this book to those who love fantasy, adventure and action.

I only read this book as part of a course I'm doing at University and it honestly just confirmed why I'm not into the entire LOTR Universe. I loved The Hobbit movies and all the dwarves, but this book (and presumably the next ones) and the films just fail to capture my attention. The backstory and ridiculous amount of names are just too much for me. Although I do get why it's fantastic for the fans of the series to have so much details thrown into their beloved universe. I mean, as a major Harry Potter nerd myself I can completely relate to the savoring of every detail given.
I would, however, never recommend this book for someone who was not a) a major LOTR fan to begin with or b) massively interested in fantasy novels and the world that comes with it. Since I am neither, this book was clearly just something I had to get through for my course.

Just to be explain about my rating of two stars😱😲......i know its Tolkien......how can you give Tolkien a two star rating?.....who do you think you are?

YES its Tolkien.....YES he IS brilliant.....YES he is THE author who helped created a genre, he created a world upon which all fantasy worlds since model themselves.....he wrote the rules and they are good.....I KNOW this is a brilliant, exceptionally well written masterpiece of world building...I KNOW (intellectually) all of that.......BUT........I didn't like it🙁. Sorry.

I base my reviews on whether I liked the book, and I just didn't like this one. I could go into the reasons why I didn't, but they are all subjective...so no point really.

Everyone fantasy fan SHOULD appreciate Tolkien and his enormous contribution to the genre.....but you don't HAVE to like his work.

I know the Lord of the Rings novels were groundbreaking and all that, but I found this to be an incredibly tedious read -- especially in comparison to The Hobbit. It's hard to believe that the same guy wrote in such vastly different styles.

I read this twice when I was in middle school and high school but I still found it a really hard row to hoe. The narrator is super-serious. Although I can appreciate just how difficult it was for Tolkien to make up new languages, I found their presence irritating.

As to the plot -- well, nothing much happens. Think of it as a honkin' long introduction to the final two books in the trilogy.

The 1978 mostly animated John Hurt movie was goddamn embarrassing, so skip it. The 2001 remake was miles better, and also miles better than this book.

Death. Deathly. I was loving it through the first hundred pages, but the following... 3 million? They just about killed reading for me.

I suffer from insomnia and started to use the book as an alternative medication. I enlisted my girlfriend's help, and we started reading it to each other at night. We'd both be passed out snoring before finishing a single page.

It didn't help that every paragraph ends with Frodo and his pals curling up for a cozy sleep.

I couldn't help, however, feeling sympathetic towards Tolkien. The camping out, the endless marches towards a grand, world-defining duty one never signed up for, the feeling of impending doom, the reluctance to confront it, the homesickness, the longing for the creature comforts of the Shire--it was impossible not to hear in this Tolkien hearkening back to his experience in WWI.

2.5 Stars

This full cast dramatization is extremely abridged from the actual book--which unfortunately annoyed me to no end, even though it largely follows the material excised for the movies.

For me, the problem was twofold.
The voice acting wasn't close enough to the movies to satisfy my now ingrained bias, true... but I also found some of the voices deeply irritating. The hardest to listen to were Sam and Merry. There was a shrillness about them that made me want to quit and find a different version.

The other enjoyment-impairing issue was simple a matter of the lost cadence and eloquence of Tolkien style, as it was sacrificed to expediency and summary. You are given the gist of the story, but without much of the original beauty. It was shame enough that I'd have to recommend people forgo the radio-play theatrics and spring for the full audio version.

якщо в певний момент свого життя вам видається, що ви прокрастинуєте, просто згадайте Ґендальфа, який десятки років напружено спостерігав за тим, як у світі все йде по пізді, і зрозумійте, що у вас все ще не настільки критично.

і якщо вас переповнює сором за те, що забули привітати важливу людину зі святом, нагадайте собі про наших героїв, які не оповістили ельфів про втрату одного зі своїх, бо не помітили його відсутності й зовсім забули про "велику втрату і страшне горе", задивившись на краєвиди.

в результаті я розчарована персонажами, які ні на що не здатні, і рятує їх лише доля випадку. розкриття, розвиток персонажів та стосунків між ними відсутні. про логіку і хоч якесь пояснення світобудови в книзі можна не заїкатися. а пафосний та абсурдний виклад призводить до закочування очей. мені дуже хотілось вподобати цю книгу, однак я не повірила нічому, що в ній відбувалось.

I can see why it's a classic and why it's so influential, but unfortunately it's really not for me. I enjoyed the main cast and I enjoyed the few action scenes that are present, however there was too much standing around talking and extra explanations or descriptions for my taste. I think I'd just would rather have more going on in a story as well.

The audible narrator was pretty good though! I could tell the different voices apart fairly easily and the narrator was definitely the reason why I was able to stick through with this (instead of dropping it at the first or second chapter like in my first attempt). It would have been better if there was a second narrator for the women characters though. There aren't a huge number of them, but it did sound a little silly when the narrator voiced a women character.
Strongly disliked this book. Had some good moments but overall boring. Good book to read if you're an insomniac.

Muy lento. Habiendo leído antes el Hobbit, se vuelve increíblemente denso y repetitivo, el libro se basa en el viaje de Frodo y la Compañía, por lo que se hace muy aburrido por momentos y uno está deseando que pase algo y dejen de caminar por prados y caminos interminables. Además, muchas veces es muy confuso, y no se entiende que ocurre a nivel global en el mundo o qué pueblos viven en qué zonas. Entiendo que es un libro de antaño, pero aun así peca de muchos de los problemas del Hobbit y en mayor medida.

Es una pena, porque el final del libro y las partes en las que Gandalf o Aragorn van al grano, metiendose en la historia propiamente de lleno (y no estamos caminando montaña tras montaña) el libro es muy agradable y las páginas vuelan.

Una historia que podía haberse contado en 250 páginas se cuenta en 400 (en mi edición), espero que Las Dos Torres mejore.

I badly wanted to love this book and fully expected to, and I know it is objectively incredible. Tolkien develops a beautiful world with rich and diverse characters, a compelling plot basis for an epic, and so much more. But by god, is it bland!!! The entire plot felt incredibly drawn out, with about 80% of the book either being unnecessary or too slow. It completely lacked pace and engagement, the plot was extremely predictable, the writing style did not keep me engaged well and I felt extremely unattached to the majority of the characters. The entirety of Book I could’ve been done in about half the length that it was, and there just needed to be more intense dramatic peaks. I have never had more difficulty finishing a book that I was so excited to read. Perhaps the rest of the trilogy will leave me feeling differently, if I can ever motivate myself to pick them up.

Okay, a solid two stars. No offense to anyone, okay?
Why? I've got numerous reasons.
So firstly, WAY TOO MANY characters, like WAYYY TOOOO MANY!
Secondly, there was just sooooo much info dump in the climax and the ending, which is why I couldn't keep track of the whole story.
Thirdly and finally, there would be times when I would be reading and suddenly nothing makes sense, I have no actual explanation of why that happens, but it does, okay?
Aside from all this, I actually liked the character development of the main characters, especially Sam. I also loved the way the plot was going till the climax, cuz that's when nothing started making sense.
To the people reading this, I wouldn't really recommend this book, or maybe the whole series. BUT, if you are a classics fan, then I think you can handle this. Sooooo, yeah. That's all Imma say.

It took me three or four tries over more than a decade to finally make it through this book. It starts off half-way interesting and then just drags before finally getting half-way interesting again. I only made it through this time because I was required to as I will be teaching this book to high school students in summer reading classes. I can see some of the contributions Tolkien made to the genre of Fantasy (though I think saying he created the genre is giving him too much credit) and can understand the import there and I can see why others might find these books to be good, but to me the few interesting bits aren't good enough to make up for the exceptionally boring bits and I have no interest in reading the remainder of the series.

I'm not going to say that this book was bad. The storyline that Tolkien uses is genius. The world of "Middle Earth" and the different languages are also super cool. Everything that was in this book has been an extremely interesting read.

Although, I didn't like how it was written. There was so much action going on all the time, but even at the most exciting parts, my mind would be wandering and not focusing on the print in front of me. The language used is hard to follow sometimes, and if I can had to reccommend it to anyone, I would deffinitly say someone who can handle an adult reading level.

While Tolkien's ideas were amazing and make for some GREAT movies, I can't say that I enjoyed reading this book, and I won't read the other ones.

I tried reading the books when I was like 12 years old, didn't work out...so, I waited till I was 20 years old to try again as many LOTR fans adviced me.

didn't get any better.

And the thing is... I keep wishing it does because I find the story REALLY interesting and exciting, and my friends get all hyped talking about it and explaining me its genious details (that the movie apparently skipped), and I get all "YEAH! IM SO FEELING IT!", grab the books, and start reading again, but, it doesn't happen. It never happens.

It feels so hollow and slow and can't stand the GODDAMN SONGS every 2 pages.

I'm surprised I could manage to finish the fellowship of the ring...twice (I'm pretty proud, actually)

The movies are cool though.

As a self-professed nerd I wanted tot love this. I read The Hobbit about 20 years ago and remember really enjoying it. I expected more of the same here as I finally got around to Lord Of The Rings. What I got however was sadly a little boring, very tedious, and wordy to the point of confusion. Tolkien certainly has created one of the most amazingly thorough fantasy world. However, his writing style is so verbose that by the time he explains whose talking to whom you can't remember what's being talked about. The actual novel could've been a quarter of the size and probably more enjoyable. I haven't given up on the entire series but it'll be awhile before I feel the itch to read Two Towers. :(

I wanted to love this but unfortunately and I am sorry to admit it: it is slow and dull! There were passages I had difficulty maintaining interest and focus on, it was a struggle and a relief to get to the end.

It is an accomplished book, the personalities of the characters in particular. I thought Sam's idiosyncratic speech was great, and I laughed at unexpected moments. I know the narratives give us insight into their thoughts but a lot of dialogue is rather long considering they 'don't have time'. I found Legolas refreshing because he is an Elf of few words.

I prefer allegory than popcorn entertainment in the literature I read. I'm not widely read in science fiction and I compared, anticipating the scenes in the film adaptation...tail between legs.

I chose Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring by J.R.R. Tolkien because I had watched the movie and I enjoyed it. In this epic thriller, Frodo, a 4 ft. tall hobbit, must take the one ring to Mordor and destroy it. He is accompanied by many followers such as Gandalf the Gray, Gimli the Dwarf, and Aragorn, the hier of Rohan. My favorite quote is," One ring to rule them all, one ring to find them, one ring to bring them all, and the darkness bind them." I enjoyed this quote because it is one of the most anticipated line in my opinion. I enjoyed the third person fantasy writing style of this book. I would not recommend this book to action seekers, or to most people really, this book is for those who enjoy slow, long books.

I first read this when I was in 9th grade. It was one of my first "big" fantasy novels. I grew up reading The Hobbit countless times, but I wanted to read the books knowing the movies were coming out soon. The only way to describe my first reading was magical. I came away a changed person. I couldn't find anything to read last week and picked this back up, over 20 years after the first reading. Damn, I feel as though it had changed dramatically for the worse. The countless songs that go on forever, the lack of character development from anyone who isn't Frodo, Strider, or Gimli. I couldn't believe how negatively I viewed the book this time around. I don't think I will continue, leaving the classics just as they are, classic.

I find Tolkien really hard to read. I decided to give it a real shot though and I knew it was long so I'd have something to read at jury duty this month. Still, I found it dry and boring and there were times when even though I had nothing else to do during jury duty, I didn't feel like reading it. Sure there was more detail than the films, but it wasn't interesting detail and I find the characters less developed in this first book than in the films. Sam, for example, has some intense loyalty to Frodo, but why? Apparently he just does. We don't really know why he'll risk his life to follow and serve Frodo and with him calling him his master all the time, it feels less like a friendship than a loyal slave. Not sure I'll get through the other 2 books, honestly.

I really wanted to love this book because I love fantasy novels and I loved the Hobbit. So since this book is practically the father of all fantasy I felt that I should give it a go. Unfortunately I found it to be so so boring! I liked the Hobbit way better even though I know that's more of a children's book. But with this I found myself reading this as fast as I could just to get it over with. I'm sad that it wasn't as engaging as I expected - with how famous it is and how many people love it so much, I was expecting to be sucked into a world that I wouldn't be able to get enough of, but rather I found myself bored and unconnected to any of the characters.

Also what's up with all these fantasy novel cliches?! (ha)

I did not enjoy this book, save two or three chapters.

Tolkien directed all his efforts into forming this world that the other elements were neglected.

The major events are too prolonged and lengthened that it suspends all the excitement and suspense. And when the characters are confronted with that feared event....it's just too late?

The characters are one-dimensional and somewhat lame, and flawed (which is not at all a problem unless they were meant to be perfect A.K.A the elves).

So many unnecessary details and stretched descirption that is entirely needless.

P.S: if you are planning on reading this book just skip the first 300 pages, and the songs, oh my god, the songs! The very embodiment of irrelevancy.

I feel like a traitor to all reader-kind, but I had to force myself to finish this. I haven't seen the movies, so I went into it with no prior knowledge. Admittedly, I've never been a fantasy fan. Harry Potter is the major exception, but I think the reason I love HP so much is that it's really hybrid fantasy - incredible world-building, but constrained by and set within our own world. I just don't connect with true fantasy, and the invented worlds, languages, and histories.

I respect that Tolkien essentially founded a greatly loved genre. But, it's not a genre for me. I don't think I'll read the other two. (Although I might watch the movies - epic battles and fantasy worlds do make for good movies, even if I don't want to read about them!)

I had not returned to LOTRs since Peter Jackson's first film. I thought it was good but I had never been fanatical about it. More recently, I decided to try the book. I had expected it to be technical, complex and dark but the opposite seems to be the case. That's an observation rather than an opinion but, despite their differences, at the end of it, I came away with a similar feeling as I had had towards the films. I can see the attraction and understand the appeal but overall I didn't get that effect. It is a difficult book to rate. Two stars seems unfair but I would be more willing to rate the film higher. I don't know if I'll complete the series but I'll probably read Tolkien again. Perhaps a story independant to LOTRs.

It was so difficult, for me, to read this book. I found that I got uninterested, not because the plot was dull but because of the writing. It was so difficult for me to enjoy it because I found it so hard to get used to this writing style and to enjoy the actual process.

This world is so beautiful and well crafted. I love the characters and everything. I liked the magic and the fantasy elements, but I had to put it down, stop reading it, and pick it back up read another few pages and put it down again. It was a long process for me to read it and because of that I couldn't enjoy it at all.
I am going to continue with the trilogy because I do like this world and I wish I got used to the writing style to make it easier for me to continue and enjoy the plot.

i’m sorry but i just couldn’t enjoy this book. it was so BORING and i quite literally had to force myself to read it. i watched the lotr movies for the first time in 2022 and wanted to try reading the books too. i loved the movies, but could not get into the books unfortunately. i appreciate and commend the world that tolkien has built up, but i just don’t enjoy his style of writing. i already knew this book would just be the characters “walking around” but for some reason expected tolkien to present it in a more interesting and digestible way. but, alas, he did not. i don’t have the patience to sit through two more books of more of the same, so i will not be finishing the series. i’m only giving this 2 stars because i think tolkien is talented, but just not the author for me.

I feel like if I was super into LOTR lore and knew all the locations and people and everything, this would’ve been thrilling. But having only read the Hobbit, I struggled with the world-building and couldn’t really put it together in my head very easily. Mostly just focused on super important places and people and tried to latch onto that. So for me, it was really slow for the most part - part of that of course being my fault for taking so long to read it. Gandalf’s fall at the hands of the Balrog and Boromir giving into the desire for the ring were really the only two moments that had me super engaged. Still planning on reading the next two books, and maybe with a bit more background, I’ll have a more concrete idea of some of the lore and things.

I know its a classic. I know its the foundation of most fantasy being written today. That's why it got one more star than I really think it deserves, because this guy loves the sound of his own voice. He is long, he is wordy, and he makes the incredible adventures and amazing battles he is describes boring. I came away from these books with a confused sense of lots of walking crossed with bad emo band lyrics (Frodo.) I would only recommmend it for its status as a classic - after reading it, I realized where so many of the conventions in contemporary fantasy come from. Can we move on and develop something new now, please?

I really like the universe created by Tolkien. As far as fantasy goes, his world is amazing. What I don't like about Tolkien is that he was a man and a scholar, and as such he writes books from that perspective.

This book was very long, and it took me three summers to finish it. I'd pick it up, read some pages, put it down. Pick it up again, the following summer, read some more and then put it down. There are too many names you'll never see again, too many descriptions of places. yes, they help build up the world in your head, but they're pretty boring for a young girl like me at the time.

I think I'm one of the few people who didn't read this as a geek growing up. I read it after I saw the trilogy of movies and while I wasn't disappointed, I was bored with it. There was too much history of the world and strange elvish names I'll never remember, and I couldn't stand the deus ex machina of Tom Bombadil.

Read it if you feel you're somehow incomplete as a fantasy lover without it, but don't feel any special need: you're not "unclean" or an "infidel" if you don't like it.

I'm probably one of the few huge fantasy fans who admittedly doesn't like Lord of the Rings, so much so that I could barely get through the first book in the trilogy and gave up completely on the second about fifty pages in. Maybe it's because of its complete lack of female characters. (yes I know there's Galadriel, but come on, she's only around for one chapter) Or maybe it's because even after all that walking around and fighting and stuff nothing seemed to get done. Yes, Fellowship is horrendously boring in parts, boring and wordy and self-important. Not the sort of book I usually care for. So go ahead and give it a try if you want to. Maybe you'll enjoy it more than I did.

Yes, i know, there are people out there that just put me on a list due to the rating i gave above. But as i always say "you are entitled to your own oppinion, however wrong it may be". I admit, that possibly in this case it is me that is wrong, but this book put me off reading for a few years. I found it so boring that i could not bring myself to reading. But, since i started, i felt i had to finish. In one of the Clerks movies they summed up the 3 lord of the rings movies (it applies to the books even more apply) quite well. Not wanting to introduce spoilers, i will read that to whoever reads this review to dig up for themselves.

I already read this once but when I tried to read it for a second time I just couldn't manage to read it until the end. I stopped when they were at Tom Bombadils house and just couldn't motivate myself to pick it up again.
I loved the movies and I also really liked The Hobbit, and to be honest I'm kind of disappointed about myself for not finishing this book (for the second time, but still) since the plot and the whole story is brilliant. I just couldn't stand the old-fashioned style of writing, I guess...

A lot of this book I found entertaining. It's not fast paced, but more of a slow, enjoyable, and adventurous read. There were times though when I felt bored. I felt as though certain things were over explained and stretched out. I was tossing ratings around in my head while reading this book. I constantly felt the need to rate it 4 like I did The Hobbit. But I don't find this series one that I can read one after the other and still appreciate it as much as the first. I'm constantly comparing this book to The Hobbit (with reason) and in doing so, I feel that it weren't as enjoyable, but I still liked it (3 stars).

A very thorough book. Parts of the book were definitely interesting, but overall it took way to long to get to where the book ended. I understand that the author wanted the readers to understand exactly how long the adventure took, but when the progress is slow with little action it's quite boring to read. I actually had a hard time finishing the book because it progressed so slowly. However, there are some positive things to note about the book. The book shows a lot about character development and how each person progresses individually even though the main focus in on Frodo. The book also does a good job at making visuals easy to conjure.

I listened to The Fellowship of the Rings on audiobook. The narrator was great, but the story was just ok for me. While I can see the influence this story had on other books I love (Harry Potter, Game of Thrones), I found this story to be looooooong and in some parts, boring. Perhaps it relies too much on fantasy or perhaps there was not enough action. Maybe there was just far too much walking. I will undoubtedly listen to the next book, as many have told me the first book is the least interesting in the trilogy. Much like giving birth, I will first have to forget how little I enjoyed this one, before moving on to the next.

Unpopular opinion time.

I really struggled to get through this in my youth. And I was all about the fantasy, the elves, the dragons, the sword fights, the orc battles, etc. It was just so boring. And a total sausage fest. I blame it for setting the tone and structure of most of the fantasy epics to come, major problems that we're still trying to overcome. Epics don't have to be epic in size! And apparently most "mainstream" fantasy absolutely must have a cis male lead, usually young and green and cradled in prophecy.

The Hobbit was so much better.

I so wanted to enjoy this book...unfortunately I found myself painfully bored and annoyed almost the entire time I was reading it. Maybe 'epics' just aren't my cup of catnip, but really the entire book was "we're walking, it's far, woe is me." And Sam, gah, he was subservient enough in the movie but in the book he literally sleeps at Frodo's feet! Most of the characters seem either self-centered and arrogant or all sorts of whiny. In a fit of lunacy I've decided to subject myself to the rest of the series - they have more action, right? - but really, if my dad wasn't such a big fan I don't think I'd have made it through even this one. My apologies for the rant.

Okay, let me start by saying this is a very well-written, brilliantly descriptive epic fantasy narrative that deserves its classic status. However, I never fell in love with it like some of my other "personal classics," which includes the Hobbit. In most situations, I chalk it up to me and give an average score. The "only two stars" is mostly because of the horridly slow pacing. For ages it felt like nothing was actually happening. Up the mountain, down the mountain, up the mountain...and down the mountain. When I stopped to ponder how many mountains were left, I set the book down and never picked it up again.

Por fin acabo con Tolkien. No voy a negar la influencia del libro ni su importancia histórica, pero hoy en día ha perdido mucho. La historia está bien. Los personajes están bien. El problema con Tolkien es su estilo. No para de romper la velocidad de la narración. Se va por las ramas con detalles de su mundo totalmente superfluos, las descripciones a veces son una basura como cuando describe una pelea con la frase literal de "Boromir y Aragorn mataron a muchos". Y los poemas. Los putos poemas. En casi todos los capítulos hay al menos un poema y al menos para mi es un coñazo.

En resumen, es un buen libro, pero el estilo ha envejecido MUY mal y es un coñazo de leer hoy en día.

I didn't like it because it is a book that has to do with the hobbits and I have never read that before. That referred to stuff about the hobbits throughout the book that I did not have a good understanding of because I have never read stuff like that before. Also I have seen the movie before and the movie left out important parts of the book which did make me like the book more than the movie. The parts that I did like about was it was journey that was very interesting and it showed friendship's that were formed throughout the journey. it wasn't my favorite book of all time but it did have some positives to it.

I feel guilty calling one of the "greatest books of all time" terribly boring. I am so grateful to be done with it. He throws so many mythical names and places at you in the beginning that I had to listen to a chapter twice just to understand which characters were actually important/relevant. He knows this is confusing to do, especially in the beginning of a book (he literally judges elves (or dwarves?) in the middle of the book for being bad at telling stories because they give too many names/places/details which is exactly what he does). You can tell he wrote this for his own enjoyment (creating a mythical land with a made up history and crazy names).

2025 review: my second attempt didn't really go better. Stopped page 194 of 527. Halfway through Chapter 8. Really wanted to like it but it's soooo slow.



2024 Review: DNF. Stopped page 122.

I really wanted to like this book, with hobbits who love rest, food, and are kind and supportive to each other, elegant mysterious elves, complex languages, and the backing of its legendary status in literature, I was sure I'd fall in love with LOTR. I'm sad to say I found it too slow for me to take the time to finish it. The writing was quite beautiful, the characters weren't too difficult to care for, but nothing. Was. Happening. It was just too slow for me.

Tellement déçue d'attribuer une note aussi basse à ce premier tome du Seigneur des Anneaux. Il m'a fallu quasiment un mois pour parvenir à bout de ce livre. Je n'y arrivais tout simplement pas. Dans ce livre, vous trouverez 9o % de vide et 10 % d'action vraiment intéressante. Je donne une étoile supplémentaire pour la richesse de l'univers, mais autrement, j'ai dû me forcer à terminer ce livre. Moi qui adore les films, que j'ai vus plusieurs fois, je ne comprends pas ce qui a pu se passer. Je pense que l'écriture de Tolkien n'est tout simplement pas faite pour moi. Je ne lirai pas la suite de cette trilogie.

Man this DRAGGED ONNNNNNNNN

I feel like there was just nothing happening. 90% of the book was about travelling which got boring and repetitive. Not enough going on for me. The pacing was just too damn slow and that’s why it took me so long to finish this

Despite this I do like the IDEA of the plot itself. It just needs to move faster with more action and less descriptions of the landscape

Sam is my favourite little cinnamon roll 🫶🏼

I went into this with really high expectations since people seem to love it so much but I was underwhelmed to say the least

I will try to finish the series but I’m not that excited tbh

2.5 stars

If you are reading this and you loved this book... I AM SO SORRY ! It hurts me, too.



I could have sworn that I read this series when I was younger, but I definitely think I would remember something that was THAT boring. And I am SO sorry that I felt that way.

I have way more to say about this, but I feel like Anne said it all in what might be the greatest and most accurate review that I have ever read.

At the risk of alienating everyone I know, I just didn't like this book. I read The Fellowship of the Ring and half of The Two Towers, and finally had to quit. I'd started the trilogy because I'd enjoyed Harry Potter so much, and everyone assured me that if I liked Harry Potter, I'd love The Lord of the Rings. For me, the characters were too flat, and I just didn't care what happened to them.

I actually bought the whole edition with all the books a few years ago. It just looked really... boring? I mean look at it and open it does that look like an interesting book? AND the print is small so it's a definite that you wouldn't like the book. But it's actually quite interesting because it's like a fantasy land and it's so well written and creative. Reading it was a little confusing at first because you sort of have to imagine A LOT of things but it's a really huge adventure just for a ring because everybody wants to get there hands on it.

i tried i really did ... but i hated this book ... i liked hobbit....Tolkien has alot of ideas i mean the characters the 10 page lineage of each character is laid out really well in his head... however to me it got a little boring its interesting when you start readin it but somewhere in between you just loose track and then you just decide to skip that part and go to where the story left off ..... well his imagination is impressive but then which fantasy novelist`s isn`t ........
ps: i was ridiculed due to my loud in-acceptance of this book

I've had this book for years, and finally decided to buckle down and read it. I was disappointed with it. Although the writing is great and the book is well done (epic, really), the story itself seems to drag quite a bit. Also, I think if I hadn't seen the movie I probably would have been confused in some parts. I tend to skim a bit when I read, and this isn't a book you can skim through and expect to understand. You really need to pay close attention. I did like how it shed light on the movie, and I would read the other ones if only to enjoy the movies more. Is that sad?

More like 2.5 to be honest.

I liked some parts of it like the quirkiness, the humor, Sam's undying love for Frodo (it's real, don't fight me on this).
I'm not a fan of overly-descriptive style, but I can forgive that in fantasy.
But I had real problems with the prose which I found too cumbersome, the constant infodumps, and the characterization of everything fair/white as good and everything dark/black as bad...

Anyway, I struggled through it, enjoyed the second part much more than the first, and I'll read the second book in July.

Oh. My. God. Absolutely stupefying. The 12-year-old that remembered this as a 5-star journey has died...and traveled through the Purgatory of reading this soporific again. (The 12-year-old I just re-read it with still can't believe what a slog it's been; we started 21 months ago.) I don't care what you call a rock in Elven-tongue or what rune one looks for to identify a Dwarf's outhouse. If it takes 45 pages to ford a stream, and only 4 for an epic battle with Orcs to reach its denouement, something is terribly wrong.

I really wanted to like this book, but I was disappointed. The writing is just plain boring, even the battle scenes are blah. The narrator keeps telling us how sinister the Nine Riders are, but it's hard to believe because they never "do" anything but creep around. Besides that, there is no character development. I realize that it is a trilogy but, at this point, I'm not interested enough in the characters to continue.

I have to add that it was interesting to read this from an historical view. I can see why many say it is a template for future fantasy writers.

One of my new year’s resolutions was to read this list:
http://www.flickr.com/photos/fireleaf...

It’s the 50 books to read before you die. This trilogy is first on the list. So I understand that people might roll their eyes when I say this, but I did not care for the book. Don’t get me wrong, the writing was excellent; I just didn’t care for the story. I actually feel bad that I didnt like it because I know there are so many people are in love with it. I am glad that I read it, but it’s just not my thing.

Ok, so that only took about 3 months to read (hear the sarcasm). Not going to bother with the other books. Tolkien is WAY too wordy for my taste. Way too many characters & places for me to keep up with. I hate to not finish something I start, so after gritting my teeth and baring it through a whole book, that is enough of an accomplishment for me. Maybe if I was more into fantasy I could handle the abundance of strange names and places and creatures and lengthy descriptions and songs. I tried. Proud of myself for that. The Hobbit was a much smoother ride, altho I would say the same for it.

I could never finished it. I couldn't keep track of the characters, so no matter how much I liked the plot and subject matter, I really couldn't get into the story. I'm sure that if you have no trouble with the first five chapters, then you will love the entire series.

Merged review:

I could never finished it. I couldn't keep track of the characters, so no matter how much I liked the plot and subject matter, I really couldn't get into the story. I'm sure that if you have no trouble with the first five chapters, then you will love the entire series.

I remember loving this book when I was younger, but I found it tedious at times while reading it to my son. Tolkien spends a great deal of time describing the countryside. Truly, many many paragraphs. And the songs and poems, some of which go on for pages, rarely illuminate the plot or the characters in any meaningful way. Yet there's still much magic here, and when Tolkien finally gets going, the scenes are intense and well-paced and the characters come to life. Maybe those sections work so well because he lulled us to sleep before. Forgive me if I've blasphemed.

My parents have been pestering me for years to watch the Lord of the Rings movies, but I always wanted to read the books first. Here I finally got around to reading the first of the series, and needless to say, I was thoroughly dissapointed by the plot. A 500-page book devoted to nothing but the Company journeying thorough Middle-Earth became tedious, and any climactic moments were only given about three pages each. Given that I read and enjoyed The Hobbit, the Fellowship of the Ring did not live up to the hype.

I started reading it when I was a kid and I never finished it because I thought the writing was dreadfully boring what with the descriptions of every single path they took or glade they had a sit down in. I'm glad others read the books, found them enjoyable enough to love and care about them, and finally made great movies out of them because I never would have. I might try to read the rest just to have done it but it's gonna suck. I'm starting Song of Ice & Fire books and already I'm five times as happy with my life because he doesn't go on and on about every shrub the characters walked by.

This is my second re-read and alas, Tolkein's writing style doesn't improve upon extended acquaintance: it's so unbelievably dull that it masks both the epic nature of the story and the impressively thorough world-building. If you played a drinking game where you had to take a sip for each time that the narrator informed you which way the road turned or mentioned one of the points of the compass you'd be plastered by page 75.
Possibly the only time I've felt that the movie version is better than the book.

Tolkein had a serious problem: he had an amazing imagination, a brilliant plot and fantastic characters. His problem was he really liked describing things. So much so that it takes him four pages to say 'and they walked through the forest'. Description I understand, but Tolkein over kills it to the point where you're bored out of your mind, struggling to finish and a little confused because the fight scene you're reading started 80 pages ago and you're not sure what's happening and who's alive.

Now, before you start trowing sticks and stones.
I'm sure this book is a fine piece of literature and if ever was a time to apply the phrase "It's not you it's me" it is now.
But, there are only so many songs i can read, so many characters i can absorb, so many plot lines i can follow and so many history i can understand...
So, although the movie was A\OK and the plot (of the book) is without a doubt flawless, this book was a pain in the ass for me to finish and i will not keep on reading the next...

This is so slow. And long. Did I mention slow?

I've seen the first 2 films years ago and because so many people insisted I read the book (including Goodreads) I finally gave it a try. Holy mother of god.

It's pretty much the film, I'm just going to say it. Anyone who read the books first I'm sure will disagree but honestly it was like replaying the film in each scene that took place. I guess that means they did a pretty good job of it. So yeah if you've seen the films just stop there, your not missing anything extra that Wiki can't just give out to you if you have any questions.

I have been wanting to read this series for quite a long time, but after reading it I feel disappointed. Besides being hard to remember the several names of places and people, there is really nothing wrong with the book itself. It has a lot of great elements and I understand why it is so well renowned. It's because of this that I feel so disappointed. I thought I would really enjoy this series and although I have been assured that it is an acquired taste, I almost feel as if I have somehow failed by not enjoying it.

Not really sure how to feel about this one. My honest opinion is that it is more of a history book telling the events in sequence, than a story book. Pacing is slow, it's not an action packed book. Of course, this may be because by today's standards with more fast paced books and shocking twist, this one is is more easily disregarded. Anyways the story is original and without this one, fantasy wouldn't really be as great as it is. So at least it started the genre, that's probably the best thing this book did.

People go ga-ga over this trilogy, and I'm not quite sure why. I guess I'm just not into fantasy-fantasy, even though this is probably the genre's crowning achievement. It just doesn't do it for me. I love The Hobbit, and I'm a big fan of its humor and pacing, but The Fellowship of the Ring just felt slow to me, and I hate how every character seems to be related to one another (Faramir, brother to Baramir, uncle to Sharamir, second-cousin to Claramir...).

Overall, I dig the movies much more than the books. Yeah, I said it.

I read about 1/2 of this book and I fell asleep every single time I picked it up. Although it is beautifully written and inspiring and the plot is a good one, there is too much fat to chew through in order to get to the story itself. A friend told me to watch the movie and then try to read the book. I had the same problem with the movie: it was beautiful but boring and I fell asleep around hour 2. I hate that I didn't love this book, but I really do not love this book. I'll try again when I'm retired.

I really regret giving this book such a low rating when its fanbase is as vast as Middle Earth itself. But I have no choice.

I read it for more than month because I feel drowsy after reading 5-10 pages. Maybe it's because of my lack of effort to comprehend the places and people mentioned. There's too many names that I have no idea what they're talking about. I also skipped ALL the songs.

Of course I'll still watch the movies and read the rest of the books. Hope it will get interesting.

Btw, shoutout to my bestfriend who gave this to me :) I love you!

Unless I'm missing something, this book was random, pointless, and disjointed. Nothing tied up, nothing made sense. It was mostly a fairly eventless walk through the woods.

I spent most of my reading time feeling affronted on Frodo's behalf. How on earth was Bilbo not corrupted by the Ring? Bilbo used it for trickery and longevity. And inexplicably having had a load of fun with the evil Ring, he just got to toss the enormous task of destroying it onto his poor nephew Frodo?

I'd rather cut off my fingers with a blunt blade than read the other two books in the trilogy.

I am so sad to see Tolkien got such a low score on his life's work. It's a beautiful creation and remarkably detailed, but it is boring! Nothing happens for pages and it took me a long break to finish it. I'm sorry Tolkien. I did enjoy the Hobbit very much and didn't know these books would be so hard to read. This is also the one time I think the movie was better than the book. Peter Jackson did a wonderful job bringing the books to life and I wondered how it could be the same as the heavy book I had on my shelf.

I finally finished this book!! Mainly due to the help of someone reading it on YouTube. There were parts that I really enjoyed, but the pacing and intense description, as well as the sheer fact that I was tired of still having not finished this book, that has made it a relief to have finished. I do intend on continuing with the trilogy, I just hope that the adventure and the character development is better integrated within the prose and not lost in all the descriptions and history of this world.

2.5

"The twigs of the trees above them began to drip."

I really wanted to like this book. The premise is interesting. Also, for school, I had read the Hobbit and I had liked it so I figured I should try to read this trilogy. While I acknowledge that Tolkien writes beautifully, the story is drowning in details like the quote I inserted above. It sounds beautiful, but (in my opinion) it serves absolutely no purpose to the story. I staggered through this first book, so I don't think I'll be reading the rest of the series just yet.

I'm trying so hard to like Tolkien but he's making it difficult. His writing is just so boring. The names are so difficult to remember and there are just too many different characters, many of which don't even have any relevance or add anything to the story. Watching the movies after reading the books helped me understand the storyline. I'm on to the third book at the moment and will finish the trilogy out of commitment, but I honestly just can't really get into it. I feel like the second book gets better though, if only slightly.

I am in the minority here of thinking TLOTR is an incredibly dull read. I have read this book once and I can’t think of ever reading it again. I love The Hobbit and I love the movies but I’m convinced the only way to truly enjoy these books is to either grow up with them, or to love story and lore told to you with little emotion for several hundred pages. The stand out moments are the section with Tom Bombadil, the battle of Weathertop, and of course the battle with the Balrog. Outside of these moments it feels like reading a history textbook of a made up world and that’s not very fun for me.

Notes
-recommended by Aaliyah, Abbey, and Maryam
-actually not a good book
•way too much lore to enjoy plot

•when plot is juicy, Tolkien ruins it with mass description

-good poems
•even though he takes forever to describe things, poems are occasionally fire

-Tom Bombadil is OP

Memorable Quotes
- “not all who wander are lost”


Thoughts and Impressions
-see above—did not enjoy it, but will complete the Trilogy
